text: One of the better tower defenses of its time.

You and your AI buddy, who surprisingly enough has more personality than a good number of VG characters, are on a quest to save to world from aliens with big guns... that are on towers.
There's a nice little "twist" tho: Instead of generic bad guys come in and you have to stop them getting out, you have to prevent aliens taking power cores from the power station and leaving with them... I said nice, not groundbreaking.
There are also nice variety of enemies which vary from your typical speedy and tanky mobs to some stealth and shielded aliens or aliens who project a shield/ a stealth field on other nearby aliens.
It's a good TD game and I would recommend it to anybody who enjoys TDs.

This is not only an excellent tower defense game, it's just plain fun to play. The base game has plenty of maps and a great selection of different towers to place. The game is very challenging to find all the right combo's of towers and also the placement of the towers.

Best grand strategy game ever made. That being said it has a few flaws concerning accessibility. If you haven't played any paradox games before you probably won't understand how anything is working in the beginning. But once you understand the basics you will have unbelievable amounts of fun conquering the world or building trade and/or colonial empires.

The game has some much depth to it that is rarely seen in other games. I have learned more about the era between 1444 and 1820 than I have in actual school. The single player is easily addictive and offers the player lots of freedoms to set play any country in the world, have their own direction, goals, and play styles. Although there is a very small MP community, the multiplayer games are easily the best part of this game. It is a whole new game where political scheming and diplomacy over take military capability of a player. Smaller underdog countries can easily beat larger countries by banding together the enemies of their enemies to their side. The tension and the balance of power makes for a long and intriguing game that feels like what happened in real life. Multiplayer has a Game of Thrones-esque feel that is not present in any other game. Although this game is very difficult to learn and nearly impossible to fully master, once the full depthness is realized, it will reveal its self to be the greatest grand strategy game ever.
DLCs are annoying but it's well worth it considering the time you spend on the game.

An amazing follow-up to Assassins Creed that fixes most if not all of the flaws and gives you a beautiful new city to play around in.
The story is solid but does feel a little spread out at times. The transitions between story segments in and out of the animus is really top notch in this one. Plot on both sides always felt relevent, something I think lacked from most AC games after this one. I really enjoyed the characters, the main cast is funny and relatable but still manages to feel mostly period accurate.
Graphics are great for their time and really hold up for the most part. Environment feels alive and by the time I got to play it most of the bugs were ironed out. Cities feel big, churches and streets are fun to explore just to see the art work on the inside.
Gameplay is solid, its not the best in AC to date but it is a great improvement over the original and is still fun to play. Missions are fun and varied, for the most part. You will still notice repeats of certain types of missions, go here kill that, go here get that, and the god awefull tailing missions that I still hate. Blending in with crowds feels silly, maybe thats just me, but if an armed dude walked up to me and some friends while we were talking, I dont think we would just continue the conversation. Combat is varied, fun, and satisfying. At a certain point the mission is combat is not to stay alive, its to make a spectacle of slaughtering your enemy. This is where ACII really shines. Planning out an assult and following through is one of the most satisfying parts of this game.
Aside from some annoying tailing mission and some minor glitches ACII is a beautiful, immersive, and fun game that I would reccommend to just about anyone.

This is the best Assassin's Creed game. No doubt about it. I have only played the first two games and the sequel to this (the one set in Rome). But I have also closely followed the franchise, sadly limited by my mediocre PC. AC1 was clearly revolutionary but like any revolutionary step in gaming there are uncertainties and places where mistakes were made. The wise developers realized their mistakes and fixed them in this!
This time you play as arguably the most loved asssassin, Ezio, who runs around a beautifully aesthetic rennaissance Italy, interacting with fictionalized people of that time (Leonardo da Vinci for one). The plot revolves around the revenge Ezio seeks against the Borgia/Templar group.
The gameplay is sleak, seamless and natural, the visuals are beautiful and interesting, the soundtrack is worth downloading and listening to by itself, the game is dotted with amazing levels of detail and actual historical places and people with a good lot of information for the historians who also game.
I said it's the best game. After this game the level of innovation never really justified Ubisoft spamming the world with more and more. In some cases more of the same is fitting and appreciated. But somehow it doesn't work for me.
If you want to start with any of the games choose this.

Tl;dr people, this is not a review for you. This review is up-to-date as of 27/9/2017
RAID: World War II is a first-person strategy game published by Starbreeze Studios who are well known for the Payday series. The game itself is simply about four WW2 spies who bond together to weaken Hitler's power during World War II. This game is ideal only for people who've never played Payday 2, because the game has a lot of obvious similarities to its "modern day counterpart".
[GAMEPLAY]
When I played the 2-week beta of this game, I felt that the game itself was an enjoyable experience for a while (I even preordered the special edition because of the free Payday 2 microtransactions) until the missions became repetitive and boring. The gore in the game did however create some satisfying SS Officer deaths and moments.
It sort of goes the same for the full version where the good side is that Lion Game Lion (LGL) added plenty of more diverse missions in the game which helped eliminate repetitive gameplay temporarily and this is the part when it gets a bit tedious; the levelling system is very long and the unlockables (such as weapons, upgrades, etc) are on levels that are too high and once you've completed all the missions in the game that exist currently, you're stuck with the same objectives and missions and it defeats the fun.
How Payday 2 beats this game when it comes to avoiding repetitive gameplay is that they make you play the same old missions, BUT on random difficulties and better rewards the higher the difficulty PLUS, the difficulty is only based on enemy density and not particularly stats. RAID however does give you a choice based on what makes you comfortable but eventually, you're just going to grow tired of the same mission.
I'm sounding a little bit harsh here but a few good things I've found about the game is that it brings the game style of Payday into the battles of World War II, making it a good combination when it comes to the first person genre. Another thing I did find good in a way is that the skill system is more simple than Payday 2's and fact that the player has to choose wisely on which skills to apply, allows them to play RAID their way. Yet another good side of the game's mechanics is that you're able to pick a class while still being able to pick which character you like to play (Let's say, you want to have the Assault class but you still want to play as the German guy, and there you have it; your wishes are still not broken) which tackled many of the flaws of character customization.
Since this game is currently mediocre, I still need to go back to talking about the main flaws of this game. Although stealth isn't my primary cup of tea, I still like to be able to hide from enemies and complete tasks without a single notice, but in RAID: World War II, the stealth is really vague because the SS Officers have too much health for a knife and simply just "stealth-killing" them will just make them survive and blow your cover, making Payday 2 stealth beat RAID's take. There is even no silencer mods for any of the guns in the game, making it much more tedious to a good stealth game like Metal Gear Solid. Starbreeze, I wish at some point that you guys can implement silencers and increase the damage of melee weapons.
Another thing that defeats the game's purpose is that the developers basically removed a few minor features from Payday 2 and didn't implement them into this game. For example: in PD2, you can throw bags onto bots' backs to save you time but in this game it's removed, creating more repetition and time wastage. These lack of adapted features from PD2 make the game look like an early beta for PD2, since the developers were most likely in a desparate need to distinguish this game from their "modern day" counterpart.
Overall, the gameplay needs a much bigger overhaul in the near future so I'm going to give the gameplay concept:
5/10
[STORY]
RAID: World War II is a game with a generic WWII plot; Hitler is winning, weaken his power. You get a good portrayal of "Control" as portrayed by the legendary John Cleese who is basically the "Bain" of this game. The cutscenes after a game where the actor who plays Hitler either boasts or outbursts whenever the player loses or wins gives the story a good satirical take on the war with its slapstick and humour. Overall, the plot itself is generic and there isn't really any important keys to the plot that you need to know since the game revolves more on gameplay rather than story.
8/10
[CHARACTERS]
RAID: World War II follows four WWII heister; one Russian, one British, one American and one German. They all work for "Control" (as portrayed by John Cleese) to prevent Hitler from winning the war. I personally believe that these characters aren't so likeable unlike PD2 Heisters who do have charismatic personalities and hilarious quotes but in RAID, these characters are just copycats of the original PD heisters.
6/10
[VERDICT]
Overall, the game itself is enjoyable for the first 10-20 hours of gameplay until it gets repetitive and tedious. I don't recommend this game at this point, but hopefully Starbreeze will improve the game with better mechanics and bug fixes.
[PROS]
+ Well executed satire in cutscenes
+ Interesting idea of combining WWII with Payday
+ Good and simple skill system
+ Good performance by John Cleese
+ Good gorey physics
[CONS]
+ Unlikeable characters
+ Poorly concepted stealth
+ Repetitive gameplay
+ Didn't point out in long review, but some bugs
+ Tedious level and XP system
OVERALL SCORE:
6.25 / 10

I think if the enemies were a different color and the pen and paper feel was simply a dual tone between the two it would help the gameplay out completely. The second and third major downfall are tied hand in hand, there was a lack of depth to the game and no difficulty progress. I usually felt myself dying just because I didn't see an enemy because he blended too well into the scenery, more than me dying simply because I made a stupid mistake. I did find one game breaking bug along the way however, which further holds it back as well... The rifle would give me infinite ammo. This really jarred me out of the immersion that I had grown accustomed to. The bug came with a nasty visual sore that I got a
of.

Have you ever bought a game you were unsure about, & quickly found yourself with buyer's remorse?  Yeah, we've all been there before.  Anyway, this game was the exact opposite of that.  Not too long after I purchased ToME on steam, I learned that there's a free version you can get from the website, & that what you see here is a 'premium' version that's also availble to donators.  Meanwhile, I don't regret a single penny I spent here.
I'm somewhat new to roguelikes, & more preferred the fluff of swords & sorcery.  What you've got here is a graphically simple single-player turn-based tactics-style rpg.  Different modes include one life, multiple lives based on level, & infinite lives to learn how to play.    Certain features are unlocked with different achievements, including specific classes, races, &, oddly enough, redheads.  Every class I've tried has been a new experience, promotes a different style of play, &, most importantly, has been fun.
The support is amazing; every issue or bug I've faced has been addressed, worked on, & fixed in less time than it takes for me to get ahold of a real person on most customer support lines.  The player base is helpful with in-game questions.  Oh, & the game's creator has a fun habit of giving out random buffs or extra dungeons to everyone online when he's feeling squirrelly.
Overall, I'd have to say this has been one of the most satisfying game purchases I've made on steam,  or anywhere, for that matter.

I've only had this game for a few days, and it is utterly enthralling and fantastic so far. I've truly been blown away by the quality of the experience ToME offers, as you can see by the crazy amount of time I've spent after only a few days of owning it.
ToME manages to stay incredibly faithful to the roguelike genre, offering the big three parts (turn based gameplay, randomized maps, and permanent death) but providing it in a way much more relevant to today's gamers; there are varying levels of difficulty, allowing you to play with extra lives or turn off permadeath (at the cost of not being able to earn achievements or upload your character to the server to show off) and it comes pre-loaded with a beautiful graphics pack so you needn't play in ASCII if you'd rather not.
The amount of content in the game is fantastic and the randomization handled well to provide excellent replayability and a truly enjoyable experience; it can also be tuned to provide that insanely grueling challenge that Rogue and Dwarf Fortress survivors like to call "Fun."
If you're a fan of the genre at all (or have been interested in the past and have been turned off by some of the more hardcore features), I find myself unable to provide eloquent enough words to praise this game's virtues- get it! One of the best games I've ever played.

I got this game before I had a graphics card that could handle it and back when Steam wasn't refunding games. I have new card and it's running well now. I felt like the game was supposed to be a lot more than this based on the comments of John Carmack regarding the ID engine at the time.

Overall top quality, but with flaws, not fully implemented ideas, and you also need to understand what it is.
There are A LOT of ingredients here and things it's trying to be but at it's heart its a top tier ID shooter. It's not about stealth or planning, it's about amazing linear level design, gorgeous level art. A super tight, dirty, sci-fi shooting experience and an endless stream of enemies. I was particularly impressed with the way they climb, roll and leap through the environments. It's about car combat, and while it's well done it's oddly sort of core and also hidden behind an NPC offering races. I enjoyed them but left with a taste in my mouth that wanted it to be more integrated into thge core game. Maybe more open-worldy.
That said, it's an ID shooter and there are some things you need to accept: linear levels, invisible walls, shooter tropes and lots of blood.
If you liked the new Doom, are into that classic super-tight "balls to the wall" FPS experience and want a taste of something with the same heart, but a different ambition this is what you want.

Well, it is not a bad game. At least better than most of its era, but do not expect too much from it.
It displays to you as a open word free roaming fps with car races, crafting, and a lot of collateral activities, more like mini-games.
The game has indeed all of this features, but no one of them is deepened enought in durability e quality.
They just put a bunch of different stuff together and developed them enought to make them look long and complex enought to persuade the casual player they are good and many, therefore this game is immense and cool!
I bet every Hardcore player noticed that and reacted as I did.
So, don't be surprised if you find reviews that describe this game as conceived to be a demo for their graphic engine more than a game itself, or to be an "introduction" to post-apocaliptic games for newbies.
That was an overall, now let me talk about some details and the reason why i liked or disliked them.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
Again, game for casual players therefore worths to spend half of the budget on it.
It is really cool indeed, expecially textures of the rocks. The game is plenty of rocks and I really liked the way they look.
That is actually the main element of the game. If you speed-run it you will spend 90% time shooting and ony 10% in racing and exploring. There is nothing particular here, you got the canonical set of weapons. Only thing is you can craft and find different kind of ammo for some of them. Three or four of them transforms your weapon in a different one. Well, actually this happens mainly with the shotgun, who can become a granade launcher or a laser rifle. Nice feaure, not deepened enought, like everything else.
The game is linear, but if there is something I liked it was the enemies AI. Most of them just run recklessly to you screaming and swinging their weapon, but they attemps to dodge your shoots, with jumps, flips, preventive dodges, almost of the times successfully! It gives you a reason to sharpen your reflexes and don't waste (too much) ammo.
You have less then twenty recipes in the hole game, including an handful that is an enhanced version of a previous project.
Considering you have cod-like health recover, 2 charges of respawns that recharge in a minute or less, and lot of weapons, what makes you think crafting a wingstick (kind of a boomerang) or a bandage is of any need?
Also some of them are not balanced. Let me tell you of the auto-turret which enemies will knock over istantly! You can place it and literally count up to three to find the turret on the ground, totally useless.
INSTEAD there is the sentry-bot that is definety overpowered! It a spider-like robot with a machinegun that is hard to kill, hard to hit, can even melee attack, follows you like a pet, extremely powerful, efficient, and with perfect aim. You can drop it on the ground an almost make him finish part of levels for you! Oh, it costs as much as the turret.
And lastly, the remote controlled explosive car! This is a fun one because enemies will see it immediately and one-shot kill it, no matter the distance. It is also has a short range explosion. 'Nuff said.
Totally useless. You actually have only a city and the arounds that includes entrances to fps levels, and race tracks. No reason to hang in there. Also, jumping (on feet) is useless: there are barriers everywhere and it is impossibile to try to be in places where you are not supposed to be. I literally counted that only ONE TIME I needed to jump to reach a place.
This is really a great point for this game! Every character is characterized, on its design, voice, way they talk, and they fight (if enemy). I really like of colourful this game is on this point of view, and even be surpriced of how much an npc can be detailed even if you meet only once.

Is this game worth your money?
Certainly, you just have to cease thought that it is reskin of Payday 2. Its just plain wrong... game has way more to offer, its more action packed and more cinematic. It feels also more like Left 4 Dead thanks to character interaction, gameplay is closer to Payday The Heist then Payday 2 (ironically, most people claiming it to be Payday 2 clone never played first Payday).
There are basic differences in comparison to Payday 2:
1-There is no armour, you lose your health instantly.
2-Enemies are more likely to miss, but when they hit they instantly do cause you more harm then in Payday.
3-Forget about running around like idiot, there is no dodge in this game.
4-Flammenwerfer, such equivalent of Dozer from Payday but way more dangerous, do not even try to get close to him to shot right in his head, he will melt you in 2 secounds.
5-Deployables, they are non existant.
6-AI appear more responsive then in Payday 2, might be due to fact Payday 2 is bloated by content at this point.
7-There is no Bain.
8-Weapon customisation is similar to Payday The Heist one, more upgrade based.
9-Skills are more Payday The Heist like as well.
10-Lockpicking is a minigame, no more "HOLD F TO PICK THE LOCK" for half a minute.
11-Game has "Operations" you play few raids in row in campgain fasion, you can do other raids without finishing entire operation!
12-Maps appear way more dynamic then in Payday 2, you blow up entire bridge or entire zeppelin. You use 88 cannon to breach to the bank, et cetera.
13-It makes more sense then to fight endless waves of cops.
14-You can hit with butt of every weapon you have (including grenades), not just melee weapon like in Payday 2.
15-Graphics are not as important as people make them, even if you take it as priority there are some improvements in regards to it in comparison to Payday 2, we have for example gore effects, when you shot BAR you feel like you shot BAR and you see effects of BAR on enemies, you see how their limbs are being teared from the body, how their head is being teared et cetera. Same thing with shotguns and overally all weapons, they do not feel like toy-guns.
16-Randomisation appear way more interesting then one in Payday 2, might be due to fact the overall setting of game makes more sense and allows for more, time will tell how predictable the randomisation is.
17-Characters, you get to play as British ex-officer, American bandit, Soviet psycho and German who got betrayed by his people.
18-RAIDs, I do not mean these "Hero raids" you do because Control/Mrs White tells you to do, I talk about the RAIDs you can do once you unlock them by collecting intel, these are not autorised by anyone, you just go there to steal and everything you steal does end up with you as gold. So far I could play only one such raid, small Galery in Berlin, raiders had to steal paintings, there was also safe in backrooms of the galery, you did need key to open it, so no worries no drilling and senseless waiting like in Payday 2. Map itself was basically Jewelery Store from Payday 2, its neat thing for veteran Payday 2 players imo.
19-War cry, its somewhat special ability of each class, each class has different ability.
20-4 classes.
So what do I think about the game?
+WW2 setting - it does give huge oportunity to add content you otherwise would not be able to.
+Gunplay - it is satysfying, also as I did mention earlier shoting BAR feels like shoting BAR. Every weapon is going to leave a mark, bloody nasty mark.
+Lack of armour/dodge mechanic. Its way better this way.
+More skill based gameplay (Read up)
+It works on imagination, as long as you have one.
+You have to pick health, also you do it by pressing F, it won't magically heal you when you walk over the medkit. there is no skill which will constantly regenerate your health. Minus one of class war-cry, its charged by you killing enemies tho.
+You have to pick ammo, also you do it by pressing F, it won't appear in your pockets magically.
+More tactical gameplay then in Payday games.
+Censourship, or rather lack of it.
-Censourship in Germany. (+ Germans can still play with rest of the world)
-It might be too hard for modern generation of gamers. Too tactical for casual players, it might be also reason why it gets so much hate from people as well. There was once guy on forum blaming minigame (real simple minigame I will add) for inability to finish tutorial.
-People with no interest in WW2 will feel lost.

It's not Metal Slug, so let's get that out of the way first. Mercenary Kings (MK) does borrow a lot from SNK's long running series (like rescuing hostages that say "Thank You!" after or the general look of the game), but it also borrows ideas from other games, like Metroid, Metal Gear Solid, and Contra.

For a $10 game (on sale), I've squeezed 20 hours of gameplay out of it and we're not even half way done with all of the objectives. Possibly the only TD I'll ever play, and for one reason: this one makes you an integral part of the action.
Build your maze, build your turrets, co-ordinate with a buddy (or three), and blow up some alien critters. The upgrade system is intuitive and interesting as both your turrets and weapons can be upgraded, making both you and your maze a force to be reckoned with. Having a gun in your hand and seeing things in a first person perspective is really what sets this apart from the other TDs where you build your turrets and sit back, letting them do all the work. Depending on the enemy wave, you could sit back and watch your turrets annihilate the enemy, or you could build gigantic, winding maze and do all the dirty work yourself, but eventually it'll balance out to where both you and your turrets are splitting the damage fairly evenly and concentrating your upgrades on either weapons or turrets will lead to failure.
As an added bonus, the scenery is absolutely gorgeous in the surreal areas you'll be visiting; there is some astounding artistry put into this.

I've only had this game for a few days, and it is utterly enthralling and fantastic so far. I've truly been blown away by the quality of the experience ToME offers, as you can see by the crazy amount of time I've spent after only a few days of owning it.
ToME manages to stay incredibly faithful to the roguelike genre, offering the big three parts (turn based gameplay, randomized maps, and permanent death) but providing it in a way much more relevant to today's gamers; there are varying levels of difficulty, allowing you to play with extra lives or turn off permadeath (at the cost of not being able to earn achievements or upload your character to the server to show off) and it comes pre-loaded with a beautiful graphics pack so you needn't play in ASCII if you'd rather not.
The amount of content in the game is fantastic and the randomization handled well to provide excellent replayability and a truly enjoyable experience; it can also be tuned to provide that insanely grueling challenge that Rogue and Dwarf Fortress survivors like to call "Fun."
If you're a fan of the genre at all (or have been interested in the past and have been turned off by some of the more hardcore features), I find myself unable to provide eloquent enough words to praise this game's virtues- get it! One of the best games I've ever played.

Before this review, i would like to tell people that are thinking about getting the game that they should not look up ANYTHING and experince the game blind. If anyone wants a general idea of the game, this review involves one huge spoiler, so don't go near the last paragraph. Thank you for listening, the review will start now.
First, my opinion. This game is amazing. I had only the best experience. This game will haunt the rest of my, or anyone's life and you will never forget anything. You get attached to the characters like if they were real people, it's almost sad that you have to say goodbye to them forever when you complete the game. If i was going to compare this to anything, it would be Undertale. In both games, you and the main protaganist get put into this unfamiliar, but quite nice world. You will not only be baffled by the amazing scenery, but be blinded by the out of this world coding and, like me, fall in love with Niko, who's the person you "control". Even if it's highly unlikely, i hope there's a sequel to this or at least more games that had this much effort put into it. The reason why i want a sequel is a huge spoiler, so if anyone reading this doesn't know all of the endings, i highly recommend you buy the game for yourself and find the endings.
Second, the amazing plot, so if you read my warning, skip this right now. You dowload the files and jump straight into the game, not knowing you unwillingly became the god when you first meet Niko. This cat-looking, 9-ish year old boy is also dragged into this unknown situation that will change the both of your lives. Now, you have to guide Niko through this alien land, on a quest to return the sun, which is an abnormally large lightbulb, to save this land.
Finally, my suggestions, which contain gigantic spoilers, so for any new players, AVOID this as much as possible. Come back to this once you "offically" beat the game, that will be all. The reason I feel like there needs to be a sequel is quite obvious... I want Niko back. In the "Solstice" ending, the world is saved and Niko goes home. How he exits is so heart breaking and my fragile heart cannot stand it. If you make the world machine "restart" the game, it's only replaying Niko's memory. So, i want a true sequel with the same feel that allows you to visit Niko or at least a update that allows it. I am fully aware there might never be a sequel and i also accept that... maybe it should be that way.
For anyone still here and didn't get lost into the pilgrimage that is bestowed on them, thank you for reading my review and have a fantastic journey with Niko, who's not a cat.

Just purchased this game today, though I have owned it for X360, as well as PS3 in the Ezio Trilogy. However since I no longer own any consoles, I'm in the process of obtaining all the games again. I was uncertain about this, as I've heard many horror stories of problems ranging from technical issues to just downright not even being able to play the game due to Uplay. That being said, here was my experience with the game.
Upon initial startup, it would not load with an error stating that the Uplay service was unavailable. This was easily fixed by downloading the current Uplay client from the website. Once I did that and installed, I restarted the game. Uplay loaded fine, linked accounts perfectly and the game started right up. When Evolve was released about 1 year ago, it had a very interesting concept but was lacking some content and versatility. But instead of releasing most of it for free, 2k decided to make you pay for every DLC - which was a lot. People got sick of it and left, until only 200-300 players were left and finding public matches became very difficult.
Now they try to turn the tide by rowing back to Beta and make it f2p. Good decision? Can't tell for sure.
First of all, f2p is the only way to make sure players will regain interest in this game. In addition, there's a chance that even new players will join, since they didn't want to pay full price + DLC for the "old" Evolve. But as in each f2p game there's some huge flaws about this:
- the balancing is totally f*cked up.
In the early days of the first beta and during the first few weeks after the release, most matches have been very exciting, fun and long lasting. The monster was trying to hide, hunters were..hunting.. and when they met, sh*t hit the fan. If either one of them got a disadvantage they were trying to flee the fight, regain strenght or even evolve to the next stage, just to get back in the fight a few minutes later. It was like a rollercoaster ride. But now, when monster and hunters meet, they spawn the arena to trap the monster and the battle begins. And in 9 out of 10 matches, the monster wins, since hunters have been nerfed beyond any recognition.
- character rotation in Evolve is absolutely useless
sure, if you wan't to make some money with a f2p game you want players to spend it on something. But why not just skins and other cosmetic items? Why the characters? Monsters and hunters are the most important things about Evolve, you NEED to play the one you're best with in order to make sure that you're going to stand a chance. Bucket and Hyde for instance are (mostly) a terrible combination, but if you may only choose either one, there's nothing you can do about it. So what's the point in a char rotation? This only results in terrible matches due to unbalanced, unfair teams and players having to deal with chars they don't even know (and maybe aren't even willing to know).
This does make sense in a MOBA, but in Evolve it's just utter bullsh*t
- why did they let every player spawn an arena?
now the trapper is 50% more useless than before. His job was to hunt down and trap the monster in order to fight it. This required some skill from the trapper, since he had to drop the arena in the right moment, not too soon or too late. And now everyone is free to do so whenever he likes. Oh some newbie spawned the arena too soon? Well, your problem - you're f*cked now. Now you have to wait for another 5 minutes until a skilled player may get a chance, but don't worry, you'll be dead in 5 minutes anyway due to the balance.
- the match making is awful. just plain awful.
before, there were lobbys. you coldn't choose them yourself, but if you cought a good one with nice buddies and balanced opponents, you were free to stay as long as you liked - unless they kicked you ^^
But now, you join a lobby for 1 single match and afterwards you need to search for a new game again. you don't even get a chance to stick with the people you've played before, you're simply forced to search for a new game, whether you like it or not.
All in all, the change to f2p made the game much worse than ever before. Yeah, you don't need to pay anymore to play it, but that's the only upside about this mess. The balancing is absolutely terrible, the character rotation useless and against everything that's been good about this game, the matchmaking makes you wanna cry and this is just not fun anymore.
I enjoyed Evolve very much before all the players left due to the unfair DLC policy. And I thought f2p might be an idea to keep the game alive. But with all these changes it just got worse than ever. Maybe 2k and Turtle Rock will come to their senses, but I honestyl don't think so. This game is dead.

Dark Souls + Metroidvania done right.
I think it's fair to say that if you like these two genres, you are doing yourself a disservice if you don't play this game.
What an incredible surprise this game was. Really blew me away. I bought this game on recommendation from some guys online who love Dark Souls and I was sort of worried I might not enjoy it... GAME IS SO GOOD!!!!
- Tight controls, great combat - seriously great: Parry, Counters, Dodging, Combos, Magic (!!), good fighting requires learning about your opponent and calculating the right times to act and how to act.
- Great level design (one giant world with lots of loops like Dark Souls 1 - very, very good!)
- Magic is just great, really surprised me with this one. I decided to go mage and had a blast but also still had a good challenge.
- METROIDVANIA!! Dark Souls + Metroidvania... I cannot stop weeping. Two of my favorite genres of game design... my tears are great.
- Bosses... wow. This really got me. There are so many well designed bosses - not pushovers at all. Some are optional, but all of them are excellent.
- The art. At first, I thought it was a little weird, but the art did grow on me. It's weird and creepy and perfect for this setting.
- The lore! This is hidden mostly, kind of like Dark Souls (in the right ways). The strange bits are tied together near the end, though. Very interesting story as it turns out and I actually enjoyed it :)
10/10, highly recommend

First, I'll start by addressing the cons many people mention. This game does revisit the same areas. What it does right about this mechanic is that it will often lock certain areas of that map until you clear specific missions, and the variety of the missions more than make up for this.
The crafting and customization that a person can use to suit their playstyle is varied enough to suit anyone's taste. Homing guns, projectiles that explode with shrapnel on impact, piercing rounds, elemental rounds, and even player buffs that can make a melee build one of the most lethal.
The multiplayer co-op is the most fun feature of this game. Whether local or online, the players are free to explore separate areas of the same map, versus locking you in the same screen (as does Metal Slug, a game that cleraly inspired this one). The only negative part that players may find is that local co-op is split screen, so plan to be close to the screen if it is not a large one. Also, players can leave whenever they feel like it (even the host) without forcing other players to quit, and players can join at any point in between missions.
The most impressive ascpect of this game is the commitment that the developers have to ensuring that it is a great game. Their persistence in ironing out bugs is rare for an indie team. This is reason enough to buy the game, and to buy future titles from this team.
Graphics are one of the last thing I care about so long as the game works, and it does. On that note, the art style in this game is fantastic.
TL;DR: Lots of crafting and player build customization, varied missions, drop in/drop out co-op campaign, great art style/graphics, dedicated developer team.

A fresh new type of game genre, Sanctum allows for new tower defense style while keeping it fresh. The multiplayer option is a great way to enjoy this game as you can upgrade your friends towers as well! It may not seem like much at all but playing this game is a "blast!"

Sanctum is a fun and challenging game. It requires you to balance resources and defense structures. The goal of each map is to defend a core from incoming waves of monsters. Simple right? It's not. Each wave is unique in that the content varies. Some waves may only contain one monster, while another wave can contain many types. Each monster has a specific weak spot that you target to kill them more effectively. You have to destoy these waves by constructing an efficient maze of towers and guns. But you don't have unlimited resources; only what is given to you after each wave. That's when creativity and balancing come into play.
The game is even more fun under mulitplayer mode. With more people, you have more resources to spend to defend your core. However, the monster waves are random and stronger than the single player version. Communication is key to having a sucessful game. A method that can be used have each person focus on a type of tower (one person can focus on anti-air and floors, while another one could focus on ground and laser towers)
This game was worth the purchase. It provides you with a great challenge. Be warned though because each round can take up to an hour or more. If you have plenty of time to kill and want a challenge, then this game is for you. But if you don't have the time or patience to play, skip this game. There will be times where after playing for 45 minutest to an hour, you find out that your core has been attacked and you no longer have that 100%. You quit and then you resume from last save. So have paitence when playing this game.
One last note: Play around with the multiplayer chat. You'll be laughing a lot.

A really solid game. Turnbased roguelike style RPG, random loot, somewhat random monsters and a slew of classes and races to play around with. Also you can get it free here
and carry over any progress to the steam version if you choose to buy it later.
You can choose if you want to play with a single life, multiple lives (getting more as you level) or infinite lives (if you're a chump). It's easy enough to die if you're not sure what you're doing or get in over your head but most deaths feel fair, with the rare RNG reaming thrown in.
There's a fair few classes to choose from (easily 20-25), ranging from your typical sword and board fighter or fireball slinging mage to disease spewing filthmancers or combination time-mage fighters, though many of the more interesting classes need to be unlocked. A bit of exploring will get you most classes, with some being a bit harder to find. There's also 8 or so races, each with their own advantages and disadvantages, and it's easy to bounce back from each death with a new character or a new build in mind.
This game's a great timesink, it's easy to get into and do decently well without knowing half of what anything means or does and the developer's very active, with new updates being fairly frequent.

Fun, challenging and it keeps me coming back for more. I have put more time into this game that I would have ever expected. I actually heard about this game a while ago when it was based in Middle Earth but I never gave it a chance. I missed out. I finally decided to try the free version and I loved it and figured I'd buy it on steam.
For starters, this game is HARD. If you have never played a roguelike before this is at least more inviting with decent graphics, but it packs all of the challenge. In a roguelike, if you die you stay dead. However, there is a more forgiving adventure mode, and even an unlimited lives exploration mode. In my opinion, exploration mode should be ignored. You need to learn to value your character and every move it makes, and being able to die over and over spoils that.
The main campaign is long and hard. It has a level cap of 50 which will just barely be reached by some races, and not hit by others due to experience penalties. Don't worry though, those races bring great bonuses along with the penalties. You can be a Yeek, a little while furry creature, and summon other yeeks or move faster than one turn allows. You can be a more traditional elf, summoning trees to your aid, or a dwarf that gains bonuses from hoarding his cash.
How hard is the campaign? You might die on your first map. You might die to your first enemy, if you're unlucky or unskilled. However, you will get better. Of the starting classes, the berserker has the ability to fight all the way to the end and survive, while learning the ins and outs of the game. The alchemist is much more fragile, but can summon a golem to aid him; it's nice to have a friend along for the tough journey. New classes, races and categories are unlocked by accomplishing various goals, from killing a certain boss to dealing one million fire damage.
There are abundant side quests, and they offer much needed bonus experience and items. The game has a randomized loot system and powerful uniques, like many modern RPGs. The skill system is deep and rewarding. You will think hard about how to distribute each precious point, and when you die you will look back at where you went wrong and how you can correct it for the next run.
My first character was a Higher (noble/special human) alchemist, and I died on the second zone that I entered. The enemies were higher level than I was, and it was just the wrong place to be in. Second I tried a Cornac (common human) berserker, and died in the game's final battle. That was a painful loss, but I went back to the drawing board and came in with a Wyrmic; a dragon-based character with the power of nature on his side. This time I made it, and managed to unlock almost everything along the way as well (except for the aforementioned one million fire damage, which took me a lot longer).
The game is offered for free, with the paid version offering very little additional content. However, I have to strongly recommend purchasing the game here on steam. This game deserves recognition, it's a really great and lovingly crafted roguelike/rpg. The more purchases it gets, the more it will gain prominence and the more work will be done on it. According to his website, the developer has many more campaigns in the works, including one that lets us play from the side of the villainous (or downtrodden and misunderstood?) orcs. I'm looking forward to more and this game has rightfully earned a spot on my favorites list.
This is a Good Game.

Let me get some things out of the way first. No, this isn't a great looking game. If you're looking for smooth animation, amazing visuals, flashy effects, etc., you won't find them here. The music isn't great (I play with it muted and one of the many video game and movie soundtracks I have on itunes playing in the background), and sometimes the ambience is a little annoying (whoever owns the dog that barks nonstop in every city needs to put a muzzle on it or something). Now, for the good things. The gameplay is hard as nails, unforgiving, confusing at times, and all around frustratingly hard, as any good roguelike should be. You have to option to play with more lives, even infinite lives, but I always play on the "roguelike" mode, where you only have one life, unless you find more. Knowing what is happening around you at all times is a must in this game, as losing focus of even one enemy can mean death, as I learned the hard way in my most recent death (opened a door, orc necromancer on the other side, managed to escape at first, but on my way back to see if I could get around him, was flanked by his summoned army of skeletons and ghouls). This is a true roguelike, with everything happening in turns as you wander through forests and dungeons, killing everything in your path, picking up loot, buying weapons and armour, and, when you make a mistake, dying with no continues or reloads (at least on roguelike mode). All in all, a really fun game full of challenges and endless replayability. 7.5 / 10

Rougelike done right.
I love Rougelikes. They're swimming in options and strategies and are playable in either small chunks or long sittings, their random nature makes them highly replayable, and they're just generally nifty keen.
That said, they also tend to be cruelly unforgiving and really frustrating in the early levels, combined with obtuse interfaces and extremely unhelpful in-game information.
Tales of Maj'Eyal takes the good and throws away the bad. It has more starting options than any roguelike I've ever seen, and has a fleshed-out world for you to explore. The interface, while not flawless, gives you all the information you need to make good choices and the early levels get you used to adventuring without killing you because you tried to mount your horse from the east instead of the west, or whatever.
I highly, highly, highly recommend this title to anyone who likes any other titles in the genre, or anyone who is at all curious about them.

If you dislike other roguelikes but like the concept, this game is still worth giving a shot, because it's not as complex, is extremely well-made, and gives you a tutorial that truly teaches you how to play this game effectively. in two weeks. In other words, I've played this almost constantly during my time away from work, save for a few League games.

Tales of Maj'Eyal is an old-school ascii-roguelike game with a tileset as it's skin. This means that the game offers huge amount of content, almost cluttered UI but for a patient gamer opens up as a solid option for those that want to experience the deep roguelike setting with some improvements.
First of all, Tales of Maj'Eyal is a free-to-play game, by buying it you will receive some improvements/add-ons to it but the core gameplay remains same. As a Steam fanboy and a roguelike fan it was enough for me that the game was on Steam but I'm not 100% sure if it's enough for those counting their last dollars since you can enjoy this game legally without paying, though it's always nice to help the developers ;)
In Tales of Maj'Eyal you pick a race (Human, Elf etc.) and a class (warrior, wizard) with some unique options not seen elsewhere. You begin your quest in pre-determined area (dungeon) and after moving through it you get to the world map and are free to go wherever you desire (although you will get killed in most of the places you *can* go). There are several difficulty options to choose from between few extra lives and permadeath.
You can also unlock new races, classes and quests by achieving different things in-game (no spoilers here) but it will take some time to get to that point since the game is rock hard. By the time I'm writing this I've played something like 6,5 hours and haven't scratched the surface yet so there's definitely a huge amount of content and replayability here.
If you have ever played/enjoyed ADOM this is a game for you.
If you want to see what those old roguelikes would be today this is game for you.
If you hate dying this *might* be a game for you.

The game totally defeats its purpose by giving you gadgets and powers that make stealth unnecessary and reduce the difficulty to super easy, even if you play on "very hard". As a result, you never really feel tense, thrilled or threatened at any moment because you can teleport/shoot your way out of any situation. Even if you die, the quick/auto save functions ensure that you never have a lot to lose, which takes all the bite out of the experience. There is zero thrill, even though it's still fun to play (but more in an arcade/action way).
It's a shame because technically the game is very solid, never crashes, has good steampunk graphics and sound, and the story is tolerable (albeit predictable). The characters are monotonous and forgettable, though.
The developers could have done SO MUCH more with the plague scenario, made the game so much more creepy, but again, they failed utterly in this respect. The plague victims are like Fallout's ghouls, just mindless zombies that you blow away in passing. What a joke. The content that could have given the game more depth is relegated to a huge number of text documents scattered across the game world for you to pick up and read. While the world is immersive, there is no danger, no thrill, no horror, nothing stands out, and so you just play through your missions, slightly (and increasingly) bored, as if it was some generic shooter.
All things considered, this is another neat, nice game that doesn't hurt you and is quickly forgotten when it could have been much more than that. Imagine what the real plague (the Black Death) must have been like, the endless horror, tragedy, paranoia, insanity and fear. Read up on it. Then play this joke of a game. It's 10 percent of what it should have been, plus it wants to be stealth but makes the player near-omnipotent, and that's why I'm giving it a thumbs down, even though I don't fully recommend against it.

A little note before the rest of this review. I take my time on Football Manager. The game is not a sprint. I don't try and get through a season in one session and I actually enjoy watching the games and making tweaks, rather than seeing them as something to get through. I believe this is easily the best version yet. It is the biggest leap forward since the disappearance of tactical sliders.
The dynamics system illuminates you to those oft confusion player interactions of previous years. Now you have a better idea how a player might react. Giving you an early warning when a player might become unhappy.
Injuries seem more realistic. Lots of little niggles mirror the struggles that professional athletes face. You may have to adjust what you normally do with training. This is a new game, don't assume what you have done before will work.
Some of UI is a little clunky, but most of that will no doubt get sorted now that the main release is out, and to be honest this oft boils down to things not being in the same place. Something I have quickly gotten used to.
I like the new tactical options. The ability to gameplan for different situations in-game is a glorious addition.
I like the feel of the new scouting, although I must admit that I set-up my scouts as I always used to, but the main scouting screen helps me parse the information quicker and easier.
I've no doubt forgotten a whole bunch of new stuff, but I'd rather get back to playing the game :-)

I very badly want to recommend this game. I really do. But I can't ignore all the problems this game has. It's bad. Don't buy it.
RAID: World War II has been built up as the spiritual successor to PAYDAY 2. On paper, this is a tall order. PAYDAY 2 is one of my favorite games of all time. I've unwittingly sunk hundreds of dollars and thousands of hours into it over the years. PAYDAY 2, as well as PAYDAY: The Heist, are the primary reasons I love co-op focused games to this day. When RAID was announced, I was almost certain it couldn't hold a candle to PAYDAY 2. But I bought it anyway. I strongly believe that co-op focused games as a genre are dying. Many games have co-op as a vestigial part thrown in last-minute. However, if co-op focused games prove to be profitable, we'll see more of them. So I bought RAID.
Simply saying this game is bad doesn't do it justice, but there's so much wrong that it's much quicker to just say you shouldn't buy this. Mechanically speaking, it's solid enough. Granted, it plays very close to PAYDAY: The Heist, but RAID feels different at its core. Shooting, moving, aiming, completing objectives, joining lobbies, or anything else feels simply awkward. PAYDAY feels modern, quick, snappy, and impactful. RAID is none of those things. Practically everything in this game doesn't work and has been done better in other games.
There's really only one thing I can recommend about this game, and that's the FMV clips. RAID proudly flaunts that actor John Cleese stars in it. While Cleese
an absolute gem, he's not used nearly as much as he could have been. He gives you minor briefings before each new mission, and a small motivational speech before the tutorial. Cleese is fun, but short lived. However, the other FMV clips are amazing. I mean it. Even if you look them up online, you need to see them. After you complete a mission, you're treated to a short clip of someone dressed up as Hitler completely overreacting to what you did. I cannot describe how hilarious each of the clips are. There are plenty so that you almost always get a different clip every time. Every single clip make me laugh. They have to be seen to be believed.
Hilarious FMV aside, there's nothing to RAID. Each and every gameplay mechanic has been done so much better in PAYDAY 2. Hell, even PAYDAY: The Heist is better.

Let me preface this by saying that I probably
recommend it at the current price point, though my review is still positive because I got it cheaper and enjoy the game. The ~$33 I paid for preordering wasn't too bad, but $40 is a bit steep considering that you can get Payday 2 + all DLCs (which has more content) for only $5 more. But at a cheaper price, this would be a pretty good coop shooter if you didn't have much money to spare.
The main reason why I say this is because many of the gameplay mechanics have been simplified from PAYDAY 2. There's nothing particularly wrong with simplifying things, but the lack of complexity can reduce replayability (which makes it harder to justify a high price).
You no longer have both armor and health, just health. Skill trees are heavily simplified into a choice between 3 different skills every level. Deployables are gone, so you must pick up ammo and health from boxes and enemies. Classes are more rigid with preset "War Cries" and a limited selection of weapons, as opposed to PAYDAY 2's more fluid system. There's much more you can distinguish gameplay-wise between the games, but those are the main points. If the game was cheaper, the simplicity would probably be more acceptable.
Assuming you care for them, the graphics are another reason why I wouldn't recommend it at the current price point.
I don't care about graphics too much, as long as the game itself is fun and the visuals don't detract from the gameplay.
But others might. The graphics are undeniably lacking, especially for a title released in 2017. While the shaders and model quality are technically better than PAYDAY 2, much of the visuals tend to look dull, lacking color. PAYDAY 2 isn't exactly good in the graphics department either, but it tends to have cleaner (and more colorful) visuals that make the game look more appealing. For lower priced games, however, bad visuals tend to be more acceptable. I've seen awful looking titles get praise for being cheap and fun.
The final reason (and arguably most important according to many of the negative reviews) is the engine and codebase that the game was made on. I understand why Lion Game Lion chose to go with it (since many of its developers have experience with the engine/code), but the game has suffered as a result. Optimization tends to be fairly wonky and largely dependent on the mission, sometimes running smoothly and other times having FPS drops in the 20s range.
Many gameplay mechanics (such as gunplay and AI) are nearly identical to PAYDAY 2, leading to it being negatively compared to as a reskin. (It's akin to a game made on the Source Engine/its codebase feeling too similar to Half-Life 2). Extra polish and adjustments to further differentiate the game from PAYDAY 2 would've made it a better game at the current price. But at a cheaper price, a game that feels like PAYDAY-lite isn't a bad purchase at all.
To end on a more positive note, I do need to note some of the things that the game has done well. The lockpicking mechanic seems to be divisive, but I found it to be a massive improvement over PAYDAY 2's "Hold F" lockpicking.
The character interaction is fairly well done, with characters commenting on objectives and actions as well as talking to each other. It's a nice refresher compared to PAYDAY 2's nearly mute characters and constant Bain chatter.
The missions (that I've played so far, at least) are fun and distinct enough from PAYDAY 2, having less emphasis on stealing and more emphasis on the objectives. As an example, one had a section where you had to gun down enemy bombers using AA Guns, while another mission has you escorting spies to a plane.
The cosmetic system is also fairly neat, though you can only really appreciate upper body customizations due to the first person view.
I would love for this game to succeed, especially after I've read about the hard work the dev team put into it. But the price  point coupled with the similarities to PAYDAY 2 is going to drive people away. More polishing and tweaking in the future (and perhaps a discount) could hopefully address this.
TL;DR - Simplified mechanics and similarities to PD2 make the current price a hard sell for most. The flaws could be overlooked if the game was cheaper.
EDIT: $10 on sale is better than what I was expecting. Can't go wrong with that.

Okay. Now to be honest, I haven't gone through the entire game as yet. But I figure that I've logged in enough game time on it to give some first impressions.
Admittedly, what initially drew me to this game was the design itself. It was like Contra meets Scott Pilgrim-- similarly designed sprites, chiptune music and such... so it was something of a guilty pleasure.
As a run-and-gun game, there's nothing TOO exceptional about it. The levels are fairly linear, even though there are plenty of nooks and crannies to explore. The story line is okay, though the characters are amusing enough that the plot doesn't plod on.
The real challenge lies in trying to master the levels. Not just in the speed-runs, but also with the secret objectives. Things to help you earn the extra scratch and materials to forge new items to not only make the missions more interesting, but to also unlock hidden perks to get through some of the harder missions.
Missions are basic in nature, but can vary in difficulty due to time constraints and game AI. And the game AI is basic enough to make taking enemies out both easy and frustrating at the same time. There's also the reload feature, which can boost damage, but requires you to pay enough attention to be a distraction at times.
All in all, this is still a fun little run-and-gun, and definitely worth the look when it goes on sale.

Tales of Maj'Eyal is an old-school ascii-roguelike game with a tileset as it's skin. This means that the game offers huge amount of content, almost cluttered UI but for a patient gamer opens up as a solid option for those that want to experience the deep roguelike setting with some improvements.
First of all, Tales of Maj'Eyal is a free-to-play game, by buying it you will receive some improvements/add-ons to it but the core gameplay remains same. As a Steam fanboy and a roguelike fan it was enough for me that the game was on Steam but I'm not 100% sure if it's enough for those counting their last dollars since you can enjoy this game legally without paying, though it's always nice to help the developers ;)
In Tales of Maj'Eyal you pick a race (Human, Elf etc.) and a class (warrior, wizard) with some unique options not seen elsewhere. You begin your quest in pre-determined area (dungeon) and after moving through it you get to the world map and are free to go wherever you desire (although you will get killed in most of the places you *can* go). There are several difficulty options to choose from between few extra lives and permadeath.
You can also unlock new races, classes and quests by achieving different things in-game (no spoilers here) but it will take some time to get to that point since the game is rock hard. By the time I'm writing this I've played something like 6,5 hours and haven't scratched the surface yet so there's definitely a huge amount of content and replayability here.
If you have ever played/enjoyed ADOM this is a game for you.
If you want to see what those old roguelikes would be today this is game for you.
If you hate dying this *might* be a game for you.
Pros
-Graphics
-Hardcore difficulty
-The amount of content
-You can use mouse and/or keyboard
Cons
-Graphics (some people concider tilesets ugly)
-Difficulty (it really is)
-The amount of things you will have to read and learn (Steam guides help with this one)
-You can get it for free

The first thing that should be said is Assassins Creed 2 is a major upgrade over the original game, the game actually plays a lot more like a Sandbox game than the original.   A whole bunch of new tricks have been added to help you live our your fantasies of being an assassin.  Some sorely needed tricks missing from the original game was the double execution, and the double jump while climbing.  Also the you can loot fallen enemies for money and an occasional refilling of your consumables.  You can now buy upgrades to your armor, which improve your fighting ability.  Another new addition to the game is new weapons, no longer stuck using predetermined weapons assigned by how far in the game you've gotten.  If you want to use a mace... have at it.. want to use a sword... you're golden pony boy..  Feeling like a two hander..  find your locale guard and slay him..  You can now roll around like the executioner.  Chopping and Slopping all over town..
The story..  You return as Desmond Miles, a man captured by Abstergo Industries and forced to relive the memories of his ancestors.  Easy enough...  except the fact Abstergo plans to use Desmond until he's no longer viable..  (ok that's totally not cool)..  All is not lost as the first mission in the game sees Demond escape the clutches of Abstergo with the help of the sexy and talented Lucy.  He escapes from the comfortable confines of Abstergo industries to the truck of a car...   Meeting with a group of assassins who want Desmond to go back into the Animus so they can stop Abstergo.. (Wait I thought he was rescued so he didn't have to go back into the Animus... umm alrighty then)  This time around you step into the shoes of Enzio Auditore, a playboy, slacker, layabout... Although he's the son of a wealthy banker in the 1500's so what else would you expect from him.   After a major betrayal (I won't spoil it) he goes off to do what anyone would do when they are betrayed, get revenge by killing anyone involved.    The rest of the story is your typical, kill this person, rescue this person, kiss that person, while along the way building up your Uncles home town.  As a side note I personally found the Enzio story to be far more interesting than the one presented in the original game for Altaire.
Gameplay..  The game play moves away from the repetitive nature of the first game.  Where the first game required you to fulfill 3 our of 6 events to unlock an assassination, this game abandoned that in favor of a more or less story driven progression system.  Now you do story missions to push forward the game.  Plenty of stuff aside from story missions exist, such as Assassination contract, races, fighting events.  Aside from those events the game also has collectibles, gone are the flags and  in their place you have Feathers, View Points, Weapons and Armors.  New execution and climbing animations have been added...  No more killing enemies one at a time with the double execution..   You also have an upgrade-able base, and the inclusion of money, which has some effects early on in the game, but about the mid way point you'll have far more money then you could ever spend, so don't fret too much if you're only pushing a few thousand after a few hours...  Once you get your city upgraded a decent bit you'll start pulling in money hand over foot.
Combat..  Numerous changes to combat made AC 2 seem like a totally different game.  Double executions, no more regenerating health bars (you'll need medicine to heal yourself this time around), the AI has improved slightly, no more sitting and waiting to counter attack, this time around you can button mash provided you have decent enough reflexes to counter attack enemies.  A few new tools added to the arsenal as well..   You now find yourself with a (very limited) pistol, and what good assassin would be caught dead without a smoke ball (perfect for killing high ranking officials... or getting caught with your much larger best friends wife).  Old classics like throwing knifes make a return but they are almost as limited as the pistol in terms of usefulness.
I'll recommend Assassin Creed 2, compared to the first game, AC 2 is like night and day, for being one of the earliest entries into a fairly long series I would personally say it's held out quite nicely in almost every category that matters.  So when asking yourself if you should buy AC 2, I'll leave you with a single question..  Do you enjoy fun video games?  If you answered yes!!! Then by all means buy AC 2 and let your inner killer out..  just remember no shame exist in throwing pesky archers off high rooftops..  It can be the most fun you've ever had :-)

The new Dynamics feature has potential and is certainly a step towards making managing a football club more realistic in FM. It puts players into social groups, the highest been "leaders" these are generally club captains. If you annoy one of your leaders they'll try and turn other players at the club against you until you give them what they want and that's exactly what happened to me early on. Throughout playing the beta I found it to become very frustrating very quickly. I had a few good weeks and things got off to a great start both on and off the pitch. The morale of my players was high, along with my job security, after winning 3 of my first 4 matches. Then before I knew it a team leader asked me for an improved contract, I declined it by simply saying he needed to earn it, which I found to be quite reasonable considering this was only a month into the season and he hadn't had any stand out performances and his stats proved that.
The next thing I knew there was a massive revolt in the dressing room, morale hit rock bottom and the players simply didn't want to play for me any more, in the matter of weeks we went from the top half of the table to then find ourselves in the relegation zone. Which lead to the board calling for a meeting to discuss the situations both on and off the pitch. It seemed like I was on the verge of been sacked as they demanded I got 11 points from the next 5 matches.
The whole "no one is bigger than the club" approach, one I firmly stand by, both as a football fan and an FM player, didn't seem to go down too well. I stopped playing in the beta soon after this incident in the hope that they tone it down with a patch on full release and then I may stand a better chance of turning the mess around at the club.

Sanctum is a fun and challenging game. It requires you to balance resources and defense structures. The goal of each map is to defend a core from incoming waves of monsters. Simple right? It's not. Each wave is unique in that the content varies. Some waves may only contain one monster, while another wave can contain many types. Each monster has a specific weak spot that you target to kill them more effectively.  You have to destoy these waves by constructing an efficient maze of towers and guns. But you don't have unlimited resources; only what is given to you after each wave. That's when creativity and balancing come into play.
The game is even more fun under mulitplayer mode. With more people, you have more resources to spend to defend your core. However, the monster waves are random and stronger than the single player  version. Communication is key to having a sucessful game. A method that can be used have each person focus on a type of tower (one person can focus on anti-air and floors, while another one could focus on ground and laser towers)
This game was worth the purchase. It provides you with a great challenge. Be warned though because each round can take up to an hour or more. If you have plenty of time to kill and want a challenge, then this game is for you. But if you don't have the time or patience to play, skip this game. There will be times where after playing for 45 minutest to an hour, you find out that your core has been attacked and you no longer have that 100%. You quit and then you resume from last save. So have paitence when playing this game.
One last note: Play around with the multiplayer chat. You'll be laughing a lot.

Polished, fun. It's familiar while also providing some wonderful new ideas and twists on hoary cliches of the MMO world. The background lore is rather different and provides the first rationale for immortal players that seems to work. The "rifts" for which it is named are a brilliant idea and break up your play time wonderfully as the ad hoc groups form to beat them back. The flexibile character system is a great way to avoid locking yourself into a play style; for the first time I was happy to be a "tank", since I could also be a healer, damage-dealer, or whatever else as each encounter required. (Way more flexible than WoW's multi specs.)
If you've been wanting to dip your toe into something MMO, give Rift a try. If you're tired of the DIKUmud tradition, it may not be the game for you - but it might bring enough new to the table to get you intereste again.

If you enjoy Dark Souls games, you will most likely enjoy this game as well, but don't expect a straight-up DS clone. There are a lot of important differences between the two, the most obvious difference being that S&S is 2D; of course there are differences in control schemes as well. S&S offers a bit more challenge imo and the lore is a lot more obscure to the point where you may not think it even has lore if you're not paying attention. Unlike DS, there is no clear path through S&S and there are significantly less items than DS. All things considered, this is a great game for a DS fan, but is quite a bit different from a traditional DS clone.

Just as much of an homage to Symphony of the Night as it is to the Dark Souls games, this action rpg platformer features solid level design, frustrating bosses that feel great to dominate, and fluid character leveling.  There is a decent variety of weapons, spells, and items to aid your quest, and a good variety of horrific monstrosities and environmental challenges to impede your progress.
My only problems were minor, and included the very strange character designs that somewhat clashed with the more realistically designed environments.  Also, being a 2d game, the bosses can sometimes corner you against a wall, all but assuring the player's defeat.  Co-Op, while fun, feels tacked on and makes many boss fights trivial.  Also it's very easy to become very powerful, and while the power trip feels good it renders parts of the game very easy.
Sometimes there were minor bugs, involving enemies with grappling attacks warping me beneath the map.
All that being said, fans of action RPG's, action platformers, and IGAvania games should definitely look into this game.  It's length is short, but the fun combat, vast character leveling, and NPC questlines give it great replay value.

For new players, the controls might seem almost impossible to use, but as you play, you will find that you will start to aim really well almost on instinct. I also like the feature of "cocking" your gun before each shot, as is makes it harder to just spam one button and be a machinegun. There are also many reasons to use silent weapons such as your knife, bow, pickaxe, spade or axe, as the enemy will hear loud noices and investigate corpses/blood.

With the official launch tomorrow here is my review of the beta: I believe this is a great version of FM. I have had every version of FM since 2010 except for 2017.
First, to acknowledge some of the other reviews and their complaints.
1) True - some people may find is overpriced for the amount of upgrades included
2) True - it does run slower. FM says my machine is excellent for speed for what I ask FM to do. However, this is running much slower than any previous version. I do not know if this is because of beta version
3) ?? - interface is different, but I find this version much more appealing than other versions. Some may not enjoy it, but I think it is a strong improvement.
4) False - not more injuries, actually this version provides a way to minimize injuries
Now for a brief review:
I am very familiar with mechanics and interface from previous versions of FM. It took me less than an hour to become proficient the new version. Found of the new version to be much easier to navigate and accomplish tasks. This is my favorite change to this version of FM. In game task were simplified and can be done quickly on-the-fly.
Experimenting with tactics showed game mechanics to work well. I was able to get my players to preform/react how I wanted as a team – team tactics. This version gives a simple way to adjust each player by default or a simple click to switch to custom settings such as how a deep defensive midfielder should play. Once a custom setting is entered, it is simple to activate or deactivate or choose a different tactic. It is a great simple feature. Again, I could find a way to get my players/team to implement a strategy be it short ball control – open space passing then run down the ball then cross – forwards coming back to get the ball, etc.
Injuries. Though injuries occur it is possible and fairly simple to limit them. You do have to check into the medical center, but an easy-to-read summary of players is available which shows how practice/matches/overuse is increasing or decreasing their risk of injury. In short, this gives a very effective way of minimizing injuries. My team is 23rd of 24 teams in injuries, because I manage them through practice session and game rotation.
Player dynamics: I can see where some people may find this off putting, but I enjoy it and find it adds another level to the game. In life, my experience has been every team as a true core group of leaders and various groups of close-knit players. In FM, if you get the leaders to buy into your strategy and ability it shows up throughout the team in their motivation during a game and practice. Break this trust, and you spend a lot of time dealing with individual player issues.
This becomes fascinating when trading, releasing or signing new players. Breaking those established bonds, will take time to gel a team again. If you are high up on the league table or in the middle of the competition, this becomes a serious factor. If you are in a rebuild, selecting a quality long-term player with leadership helps the rebuild.  This feature adds a lot to the transfer market IMHO instead of simply looking at player skills/numbers/salary.
This brings me to scouting and transfer market. Again, I find this version of scouting to be a great feature. Send the scouts out – they return with simple easy to understand reports which with a few clicks offer a great deal of information if you are interested in the player. It is also easy to click through each report and either assign analytics, more scouting, or add/remove from future reports. To me, the time spent on scouting has been decreased but the information increased and the integration of player/team dynamics puts more thought on transfer listing and/or transfer addition to the club.
There are other slight changes with some parts of the menu that I also find helpful. The social media section is an interesting twist. Almost all the important information for your club will show up in the inbox, but the social media is a quick way to scan what other teams or specific competitors are doing. If you have the time, you may enjoy this but I do not find it intregal to the game.
Summarized I find this a great version of football manager as this is the best interface I have used and spend a lot more time on each game as opposed to working the menu to get to the various parts of the game. Every year people complain about injuries, but this version gives a practical way to address injuries – minimize them by limiting practice and gameplay as well as a particular players susceptibility to injury - or ignore the risk at your own peril and maximize practice and play the same players in multiple games without rest and hope for the best. As a player, you can devise a strategy for injuries and that is a nice addition to the game.
