In a short and simple summary, Return to Castle Wolfenstein/Enemy Territory came home drunk one night and made sweet love with Payday 2, spawning RAID: World War II.
::GAMEPLAY::
The game shares a similar formula as its predecessors while changing a few things here and there to keep things fresh without alienating veteran heisters and made them feel right at home. The major difference to its predecessor is how the missions are laid out, often involving acts of sabotage or mayhem behind enemy lines akin to Wolfenstein and/or the classic Medal of Honor series  instead of daylight terrorism and robbery (although that exists too, along with a little nod to PAYDAY2's jewelery store heist).
::MAPS::
The starter raid maps has around 11 missions with 2 'secret' raids which can be unlocked, along with the more difficult and longer 'operations' which I assume is similar to those 2-3 day heists of its predecessors. Operations is where RAID shines with its execution, putting raiders in a 6-day raid across a select of single-day map which--despite sharing the similarity to the standard--forces raiders with an entirely different method of approach on the map (the door that you're supposed to blow up in 'Odin's Fall' when you failed the stealth, for example, is now barred shut and instead, you'll start from inside the tower's basement and fight your way to the top and escape).  It's a polish from Payday 2's 3-4 day heists and a welcomed change of pace.
::GRAPHICS::
Graphics are dated, more or less similar to Payday 2 in all aspects with small improvements on the lighting  and shading department here and there, thus the requirements for this game is more or less similar to PAYDAY 2--rest assured, your potato can run this.
::LEVEL::
Level design is what this game can champion against Payday 2, with a few of the levels noticably 2x larger than its predecessors (often requiring some mode of transport to move around) and has the unmistakable Enemy Territory-feel in some cases. Furthermore, enemy AI spawns a bit more aggressively than Payday 2 which made even normal a tad bit challenging for those unfamiliar with it.
::CLASSES::
Classes in RAID is made distinct primarily with its warcry ability and the skill tree (called proficiency), all of which are equally powerful when used correctly. Unlike Payday 2 (where you can just ♥♥♥♥all and spec on all classes), RAID places a greater emphasis on class specialization, making each member of a team a part of a small cog within the machine. At the moment, the 'assault' class is a favorite for many solo raiders for its ability to reduce bullet consumption and an instant heal that effects the team, but don't take the ability of other classes lightly. The Insurgent has increased 'dodge' chance (as high as 70%+ possible) for the team and literal wallhack +crit chance increase, the recon has a literal aimbot and weapon damage increase, while demolitions has bundled grenades which are perfect for anti-horde duty--all of these, when used correctly, are powerful enough to keep Hard-mode enemies at bay and your RAID team alive.
::DIFFICULTY::
This is where things may get a bit dicey. The dificulty spike from normal to hard is similar to PAYDAY 2's jump from Overkill to Deathwish. Leveling your character to around 15+, along with a mix of members each with different proficiency can literally be the life-and-death of your team. There is a tendency of having zero breaks from waves so long as enemy officers are left alive--pray that you or your team managed to deal with them first before you start counting and reserving bullets for each horde.
That, and a prayer to RNGesus for a generous spawn. Last thing you want to see are two flamethrowers walking to you while being surrounded by officer teams and hordes. Offer the souls of plebbians if necessary.
::WEAPONS AND UPGRADES::
Weapon selection is to be expanded as stated by the devs through FREE content updates and reserve DLCs as large expansions akin to the golden age of the late 1990s and early 2000s (basically one huge update with b u t tload of maps/weapons/etc.), according to the devs. Take this with a grain of salt, for now. The base game, on the other hand, offers a small pool of weapons. Sadly, the upgrade system can be rather disappointing for most PAYDAY2 veterans (which I inclined to agree) and occassionally made the weapon little...funky, to describe it kindly (the BAR M1918 can be upgraded into the Colt Monitor, a rare FBI-variant of the auto-rifle). Thankfully, the funky look still allow the weapon to perform oddly better than its more familiar stock look--I still don't like the look of the Monitor for the stats upgrade, however that's just preference. Other weapon variants are mainly unlocked by leveling up specific characters capable of using that weapon, which may be a little infuriating if your lvl 1 new character does not have access to your fully-upgaded Tommy gun thanks to your lvl 40 character. This is mainly where I nick 1 points off.
Would I recommend it? Definitely a yes. Now I can finally lay Payday 2 to rest--one that it definitely deserves. 7/10 points from me.

For those who are knowledgable historians and/or proponents of political realism, this game is the manifestation of international relations before liberalism became a thing, although it is, without doubt, extremely simplified. If you are the amateur version of the people mentioned above (such as myself), you may find yourself citing from Machiavelli or Hobbes as you start your conquest of the world while nodding affirmatively to the esoteric references the game makes to your broad understanding of political science as a way to feel smart, but lose interest in reading half-way through the game. In addition, the title alone would surely evoke pride among Western strategists out there; I mean, come on, a quick Google Translate shows that it's Latin for "Universal Europe". But nevermind my stupid attempt to sound cultivated and knowlegable - let's move on to the review.
:
> Glorious music: I can listen to the soundtracks for days on end. Let's take the main theme for example: from a personal perspective, the game captures the beautiful sounds of classical instruments and orchestrates a symphony of grace and might as you take time to choose a ♥♥♥♥ing country.
> Replayability potential and diversity: Take a look at the preview images. It's literally the world with states existing in its respective contemporary timeframes ready to be led by you. Want to start as Sweden during the Great Northern War and not lose a strategic defeat at Poltava? Go for it. You want to conquer the world as some island state off the coast of mainland Japan? Good luck. The game starts from the year 1444 to 1821 and it'll be a long way so the only downside is that whenever you start the game to finish where you left off, you don't really do that and instead start a new game as another country.
> AI: Not bad, to be frank. Most of the time the AI knows what it's doing, making the game a good challenge.
> Graphics: Compared to its ugly predecessor, the graphics are not bad.
> Supportive fanbase: I had no idea how to play this game until I asked on the forum. Game sure attracts awesome people.
> Memes: endless esoteric may-mayz
> Brilliant modding community: I can't help but gaze in awe at how much effort modders put into making mods that makes the game a lot better and balanced.
:
> DLCs: So much and so expensive. While I support their efforts, I feel as though the developers release them every year and it adds only little to the entire game.
> Kebabs: Ottomans, I just want my Basileus achievement
> Losing your social life (if you had one): The more I invest myself into EU4, the more I realize how great locking yourself in your room is.
> Allied AI: Really ♥♥♥♥ing stupid

A very simple explination of this game would be "2D Dark Souls".
But this game is far more than Dark Souls remade in 2D.
Salt & Sanctuary is a fantastic game that has had me coming back for more, and I only just recently finished the game. There are many different ways you can play through the game and how you approach enemies. I've made several characters to test out several different ways of playing the game and to see all the different items and enemies S&S offers.
There are so many things that you can find by exploring the terrain.
"High Risk High Reward" is a pretty fitting saying for S&S, because going way off the beaten path to fight the biggest, toughest foes, and traverse the most unwelcoming of terrains, you can find some rather amazing items, or a new area to call your sanctuary.
There are more than just a few bosses that will stand in your path, preventing passage to new areas, in most cases. There's never just one way to go about taking down these challenging enemies. Each boss has their own unique attack patterns, fighting stages, fighting arenas, buffs, debuffs, weaknesses, strengths, and health. Some bosses take a lot more damage from say, a sword, than a blunt weapon like a great hammer.
The non-boss type enemies you encounter can also prove challenging to face, and usually arent just mindless meatbags you can take out without even thinking about what strategy you're going to use to face said enemy. Certain enemies can drop immensely useful items that you can use to level up certain weapons/shields/armors. There is a wide variety of enemies, who all have differing attack patters and such.
There are so many different weapons, armors, and shields to choose from and use. Not only are the a ton of equipment to choose from, you can also upgrade the equipment you have to make it better. Most every weapon type is viable and good. Some, better than others. Magic, for instance, is immensely strong late game, if you know how to use it.
Melee is still my favorite way of playing the game, but it does make you play the game smarter and carefully.
The skill tree is really really massive and complex, so i'll just say that if you can think of something to spec into, you probably can do it in S&S.
I probably left some things out.
sorry
In short, if you're interesting on a game that's vaguely like Dark Souls, and a game that's punishingly difficult but also immensely fun and enjoyable with a lot of replay value, I HIGHLY recommend Salt & Sanctuary. The 18 Dollar (USD) price tag is way too small for such a well made game that has so much to offer.

First, I want to say I think they should of put more resources into the writing staff.  As you can tell from the other reviews, the end is pretty bad.  But it isn't just this.  There are these choppy transitions, as well as events that totally negate actions that your character just fought over.  It makes no sense.
Secondly, the main reason why I do not particularly like this game, is the enemy AI.  What gets remotely difficult are the bandits that run at you, but you can pistol shoot them two or three times, and then melee them, and they drop.  The wing blade helps, but let me get to that in a second.  Or, just use a shotgun.  I literally had the BFG gun, and I used it once in the last dungeon.  I pretty much used the shotgun in the very last fight.  The shot gun wrecks face, and a lot of these enemies run into your face.
But that's not the only aspect of the AI that's bad.
Enemies with a gun, will hide behind cover, and literally stick their head and upper torso out from covery, to just LOOK.  They don't shoot at you, it isn't quick, they literally position themselves there, and look.  So yeah, I'm going to shoot them.  But it's incredibly dumb.  It turns into this waiting game, because they peak out of cover and you just shoot two to three bullets at a time, and you maximize on the amount of ammo saved, and you don't get hit!  You just have to be patient.
I didn't like how there was such a strong limit on the race track.  They make a huge deal about decking out your vehicles, but there isn't nearly enough racing credits to be able to do that.  You start decking out one car, and then another comes along, and you start decking that car out.  Which means, you don't have a fully decked out car.  That annoys me.  :)
I wish they didn't increase the difficulty of the game by increasing the amount of ammo it takes to kill a guy.  Like, there has to be some other way.  By increasing the amount of ammo you use, it essentially decreases the amount of money that you have because you have to buy ammo for the next "dungeon."  This component, actually makes money worth something in this game.  However, it is there because it takes a stupid amount of bullets to kill someone.
The writing and AI were the two main things that really took away from this game.  It was enjoyable, but I felt dissapointed, especially during the last dungeon.  If you are going to get this game, get it cheap.
Glad this got greenlit!  This has been a go to game for me for a long time.

Crappy graphics, crappy game design, and crappy gameplay.  The guns are not fun to use, the enemies animate nicely but are not at all interesting to fight, and the game has textures from 2002.
The crappy engine limits you to 60 fps, textures pop in as you turn your camera, literally everything is covered in stitched together tiles of ultra low resolution textures that have had a slightly higher resolution noise filter pasted on them.
I heard a lot about the quality animations of the game before it was released, and it does animate nicely.  It ends up not mattering in the slightest because enemies either run directly at you or hide behind cover, slowly peeking out.  They do not seem to work together at all, and the most impressive thing the AI does is retreat further back to different cover.
It feels like there is mouse smoothing, steering is annoyingly controlled via keyboard instead of mouse, when shot your view becomes 'doubled' which looks kind of neat but is complete crap for controlling and aiming.
If you took Borderlands, removed the cartoon outlines on everything, removed the randomly generated weapons, removed talent trees, removed the humor, limited the fps to 60 and forced mouse smoothing... then the result would still be a game that is far better than Rage in every regard.
There is not really any upside to playing this game.  Only purchase this if you really love ID games, you have completed all other FPS titles in your library, and the game is under 5 dollars.

YES!  ToME is finally on steam!  If you have never played this game, you can download a copy to try at
.  If you enjoy tactical RPGs and rogue-likes, forget trying it, just go buy it, now.  I have been playing this game since about halfway through its beta, and its truly an amazing game.  Punishingly hard if you are careless, but rewards those who learn to really use the abilities of their character.  And oh, the abilities.  Pick one of the 24 (!) classes (fewer at first--you have to unlock the advanced classes through gameplay; this is a good thing, as you would get slaughtered playing these classes as a new player!) and pick one of the 9 races (again, some require unlocks).  These combine to determine which ability groups you get to put points into.  And points can be scarce--pretty much all character classes can be played 2 or 3 different ways, and some can be done 4 or more different ways, depending upon how you spread your points around.  Add in a mostly-fixed overland map with mostly-procedurally generated dungeons and some tough boss and miniboss fights and an amazingly varied loot system...and you've got a game with frightening levels of replayability.  And for good measure, add a developer (All hail DarkGod!) who listens to feedback, talks with his players on the forums, and seems to spend more time than is physically posible working on the game.  (Maybe he is a Chronomancer?)  What are you waiting for?

"Neither yes or no"; Steam ratings need a "neutral" recommendation option.
A simple game much in the style of "Hotline Miami" except mostly with gunplay rather than melee+thrown items. The gameplay itself is basic and clean, but poor level design, a lack of progression, and a pointless money mechanic lead to a confusing experience overall.
Overall, its barely an OK game for $3 or less at best.
PROS:
-A few different guns that need to be operated correctly ♥♥♥♥♥♥the bolt, re-load, etc).
--Weapons are: Knife, 6-shooter (pistol), double-barrel shotgun, and rifle.
-Gameplay is fast and clean. AI is tough but not cheap.
NEUTRAL:
-There is a story of some kind but I skipped past it. The story was told entirely through text and ruined the rapid pace of the action gameplay.
CONS:
-Environments are re-used almost verbatim.
-"Random" encounters are pointless and annoying. You will get interrupted between travels to get attacked by 1-3 enemies. (complete with load screen before/after the encounter)
-Money in the game serves no purpose. There are upgrades to buy but they only appear at certain points through the adventure and next to each vendor is a guy that offers you unlimited "mini missions" for bonus money so you can afford the upgrade. A pointless grind....just give the upgrades for free and ditch the money. NOTE: There is NO other purpose for the money (you do not buy bullets etc).
-Gun looting mechanic makes no sense. You can NOT take bullets out of dead enemies guns. This means it usually makes more sense to drop an empty gun and pick up a dead guys gun rather than to reload because if you reload and run out of bullets, you can not take the bullets out of the guns on the ground (??).
-The "12 is better than 6" upgrade which makes you dual wield pistols is BUGGED. You cannot reload the guns normally (your bullets just disappear, they DO get used up but no reload happens). Instead, you need to switch to your knife and switch back to your pistols to get them to auto-reload. This is especially embarassing considering this upgrade is literally named after the game.
-Dead enemies leave their hat behind. Since the game is 2D top-down view, it can be difficult to distinguish living enemies from dead ones in the middle of a fight.
-Similar problem to above, but sometimes its simply hard to SEE the enemies. The art style is a very simple black-and-white line drawing and the hats have almost no variation/distinction to them.

Better Title: Hotline Miami is Better Than 12 is Better Than 6.
It's already getting easy to forget that the original Hotline Miami hit indie gaming like a brick through a window. It was so good, so original, and so rewarding that it's only fair play to expect it to influence a new generation of titles.
The problem is that pretty much every one I've played has failed miserably to live up - including Hotline 2 and certainly including this.
Basically everything that's good about this game is a direct rip of Hotline and everything that's bad about it seems awkwardly shoehorned in just so that the game is different enough from Hotline so they don't get sued.
Take the blindingly white art style that looks good on paper (literally) and in 40-second bits of trailer but in reality it's a pain to play through. Same goes with the move to manually reloading Old West style weapons. It's an awkward system that only detracts (I guess subtracts?) from a winning formula.
Speaking of blinding contrasts - the original Hotline built suspense by limiting dialogue to mysterious but intriguing snippets. They cleverly turned a weak spot into a strength.
12 is Better Than 6 features an embarrassingly bad story chock full of asinine dialogue. Much like whoever wrote it, I'm not going to dwell on it, but rest assured it's awful. I was actually less shocked by the casual racism than the fact that they put in SO MUCH DIALOGUE given how obviously lame it is.
There's even an achievement for skipping dialogue which sounds ridiculous, but trust me you'll have it in no time.
Honestly though, why stop there? Just skip the whole game and cross your fingers that Midnight Animal gets released.

Do you like Metal Slug? Do you like Monster Hunter? Do you like Paul Robertson?
Yes, yes, and yes, get this game. Finally finished after being worked on and tempered for quite a while, this game is the best we can hope for a 2d mash-up of shoot 'em ups and grind 'em ups.
==THE GOOD==
Amazing spritework from Paul Robertson, or at least designs. Whether or not he did the full animating, it's still a very impressive job. The intro is stellar for setting up an actiony arcade game.
Quick fun and good multiplayer capability. Grab some friends and rampage around! Loot is shared, where one person needs to pick it up and the rest of your group gets the rewards, so having someone branch off to look for supplies isn't a bad thing. Plus, with reviving teammates if they get in over their head, and no friendly fire, having a partner helps.
Gun customization. Slap together your weapon with multiple options. There are sets, yes, and some parts don't work so well with others, but for the most part you're free to craft your gun with whatever you grab.
==THE BAD==
The grind. It's not as terrible as some games can be, Monster Hunter or certain other games considered. But to make some weapons, mods, or ornaments, be prepared to run a mission well into the double digit numbers. Completionists would do well to have patience for this game.
Enemy repetition. Not until about the halfway point in the game do enemies become very varied. Not a huge problem though.
Ultimately, great purchase and fun game.

The greatest strength of this game lies in the relationship between the player and the main character Niko that builds up as the game progress. In this game Niko directly speaks to you and asks you questions. In result the fourth wall is broken and it feels like you are having a real conversation with a person. Because of that you get easily attached to Niko. Another big plus in this game are the unusual game mechanics like searching a password in your own computer folder or the fact that the game closes when Niko went to sleep, Furthermore the music fits the world really well  and creates a  dark but sometimes heartfelt atmosphere befitting of a dying world. Moreover the story of the game is great and always urge you on to help Niko to fullfill his mission. Last but not least the ending was amazing but a little sad at the same time. The True ending with the Solistice update is especiallly satisfying. All things considered it creates a unique, immersive and emotional game that leaves a void in your heart after you completed the game.
Therefore i wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who loves story driven games and unique game experiences.

In the game you take on the role of the commander—God—and the alien robots are coming in to ruin all that is beautiful. And you know--in your divine, human heart--that this shouldn’t be. And so you must unite your most powerful species, the merely humans—the Defense Towers—and put them in the places you think best, and “upgrade” some of them, and watch their interdependence destroy the machines of the devil.
Now, other works of religion and philosophy DO speak of the alien robots and the defense towers, but, as far as I know, NOT simultaneously (an essential missing thing in them and not in this).
We being the towers is, admittedly, self-evident, so before this review ends, I'll just make a note on the cyborg aliens (the game does the true job of explaining them, so here I'm giving you a taste):
To understand their importance, consider this by the great moral teacher Jesus Christ:
“But I say unto you which hear, Love your enemies, do good to them which hate you, bless them that curse you, and pray for them which despitefully use you. And unto him that smiteth thee on the one cheek offer also the other; and him that taketh away thy cloak forbid not to take thy coat also" (Luke:6:27-29). Defense Grid is an even greater moral teacher than Jesus because it shows that we must destroy the aliens with our guns, lasers, explosives, and flame throwers.

Sanctum is a completely different take on the "Tower Defense" genre, it mixes up First Person Shooter elements in it and it does it well.
Here's the catch: If you have your mind set on "I'll only upgrade Towers!" or "I'll just shoot everything!", you're in for an embarrassing defeat. You cannot take everything head on here, you need to balance resources to deal with everything coming towards you: enemies that comes in large quantities, tough ones and tricky ones.
Do you want to do the heavy lifting and shoot most of what's coming or use your towers while you kill whatever is left by the end? Or maybe you want to do both of these things? No problem, all three options are possible in this game.
One of Sanctum's most known aspects is the maze building, you've got room and resources to create your personal enemy slaughtering course, it's far from putting one block here and another over there. If you want to survive the toughest levels of Sanctum you'll need to smart up and create mazes that will force enemies to walk as much as they can.
Unlike Sanctum 2, there is absolutely
grinding in Sanctum 1. You start with everything the game gives you and after a short, optional, Tutorial you're free to do whatever you feel like in the first map. Play and learn, no hand holding here aside from the absolutely necessary.
Balancing resources here can be tough, they are rather scarce early on and woe betide the unprepared. Do you upgrade your towers or your guns? A difficult choice that can be the difference between victory or defeat.
Towers and Weapons can be upgraded up to Level 6, and while they seem extremely cheap at first don't go thinking you can leave a bunch of Level 1 towers scattered and expect them to do heavy damage; enemies gets progressively stronger and soon you'll realize even your Level 3 towers are hardly doing any significant damage. And the same will apply to your guns if you ignore them.
Upgrades will considerably power up your towers and guns, however they'll also become incredibly expensive and on shorter Campaign maps (with 20 or less waves), chances are, you won't be having lots of Level 6 towers even by the end of the map unless you focus more on them.
If you are looking for a difficult game, Sanctum may be your cup of tea. The game is ruthless, but hardly unfair. It punishes poor planning and poor shooting accuracy and you'll probably be frustrated once you see that your carefully planned maze and towers did not work, but amazed when you beat that tough wave with your wits.
The greatest challenge at the start is to understand how to balance your resources between weapons and towers, and until you find your own balance point, you'll be hitting that "Load Checkpoint" button quite often.
The game is merciless and will not shy away from dropping tough enemies, although not without warning: the game provides a list for a number of incoming waves and what will be there.
However Sanctum fail in one crucial point: there is no indication on how resilient the enemies will be. In one wave you may face a single, but extremely resistant, enemy and at the other wave the same type of enemy in larger numbers, however with much less HP. This can and will catch you off guard and is one of the very few times the game will play "dirty".
For those wishing an even greater challenge there is the Insane difficulty with VERY resistant enemies and a core as fragile as cracked glass.
Every level can be VERY long. Even the first one can take anywhere between 30 minutes (if you are insanely fast) to 1 hours and a half and can last even longer. But don't worry: the Campaign has checkpoints between waves which you can also use to correct a mistake as long your have enough resources. It may sound cheap, but picking the "Load Checkpoint" will be something you'll do often here unless you feel there is no hope and click on the "Restart Level".
The multiplayer option ramps this up by letting you set the game to 30 waves on any map, which easily means games going past 1 hour.
The multiplayer in Sanctum is a bit different. Instead of a normal game with fixed waves every game on every map will have
enemies waves coming for you and your friends, that's right, no game will be quite the same and sometimes you'll be forced to change your tactics since the game can be downright mean sending airborne enemies and another wave of tricky enemies right away.
You can also change how long the game will last: from 10 to 20 or even 30 waves, or an endless Survival mode, with increasingly stronger enemies, but with MUCH more resources than the normal, single player only, Campaign. This means more towers, faster weapon upgrades and more towers.
Don't have friends that play Sanctum? Friends can't play right now? No problem. You can Host a game like this and play by yourself if you wish to, or leave open to friends (or other people) so they can join during it.
You can also opt to play with people from the world but be warned: the Sanctum multiplayer is fairly dead and even on weekends it may be hard to get a lasting game with someone.
Multiplayer has a few problems, though. Once you finish a map you are forced to create a new game and invite your friends again which doesn't sound bad, but gets annoying if you play with 2 or more people. It may be also a pet peeve mine, but you don't get levels achievements even if you do complete them with 30 waves setting, however you do keep progress from others like
Sanctum also has an amazing soundtrack, much more relaxing and soothing than what you'd expect for a game about killing hordes of enemies while hearing the heroine laughing and screaming in glee.
For some the music will feel strangely out of place and annoying, for others it will be a contribution to immerse the player.
The game came out in 2011, and even on 2014 it remains one of the most pleasant, satisfactory games to play.
Unfortunately Sanctum is often underrated and overlooked by people, sometimes because of its graphics and sometimes because it is a game that takes time to learn and it won't be afraid to slap you in the face quite often while you learn it.
Sanctum is a game created with care and you can notice it as you play. Coffee Stain Studios did a good job with this game and it is worth your money and time. Even if you are not a fan of Tower Defense or First Person Shooter genres, give Sanctum a try at least in the demo, you may be surprised.

I chose to play as Italy, thinking eventually I would make my own faction (which I heard to be some kind of new Roman Empire) and take over europe and maybe eventually the world. So I started the game discovering that I was at war with Ethiopia. I won easily enough. A short while after the defeat of Ethiopia I decided to expand my lands! I set my gaze on Yugoslavia, so I began justifying a war goal. Conquest of course. When the justification finished I declared war on the Yugoslavians, my massed divisions advancing into their lands. The Yugoslavians panicked and joined the allies, in turn making me panic and join the axis to have the Reich on my side. I started World War Two two years early. I started it in 1937. Over the course of the war I took some lands for myself, Greece and Southern France. The Reich took Northern France, Czechoslovakia, Austria, and many others, even pushing into Soviet Russia. The Axis grew, the Allies grew, too many countries to name.
For a time everything was great, I had gotten rather low on equipment for my armies so I decided to hold my lands and build my armies. The Germans had taken much Soviet land, but a problem arose. Denmark had taken advantage of the Reich's army being at the Russian front. They, backed up by Allied troops, pushed into the Reich's original lands and even taking Berlin! The end of the Axis was near! we were pushed back and lost our land. Our eventual defeat.

Trion's first outing into MMORPG land is a good one showing all gamers that they know what they are doing. For the most part there is alot of familliar aspects to the game design and it will seem like you have played most of it before; so for those of you who don't like having to start new characters in a game may find it a bit of a slog getting back upto the end game. I won't go into those designs now other than to say that if you have played WOW et al, then you will have seen them before.
There are a number of new features though that have been implemented well, which personally add enough incentive for me to keep playing. The first is that your 'calling' (Warrior, Mage, Rogue and Cleric) defines which skill trees you can assign skill points to. At any one time you can choose upto 3 skill trees to define the role that you are performing. Each character can then have upto 4 roles (using different skill trees in each if you wish)  which you can more or less switch between on the fly. This means that you can have a setup that is good for soloing, PVP, Support and so on and not getting locked into a situation that your build cannot handle. What draws me to this is that when playing other MMO's I find it frustrating to face identikit Warriors and so on. When facing others in RIFT's PVP, this helps bring an element of uncertainty to what you are about to face, which I find refreshing.
The second is the rifts themselves. These crop up all over the place in different flavours (water, death, life to name a few) but are not as random as the marketing suggests. There does seem to be areas where they tend to form (albeit alot of them) so if you waited around one will likely appear soon enough. However, the rifts do help add a break from the more traditional questing that goes on and in themselves structured into stages that provide a quick and compartmentalised bit of fun. The rewards are ultimatley good for closing the rifts, but are a grind to get to the top kit.
Overall, I have been enjoying Rift and can see myself playing for a little while longer yet. Whether there is a long term prospect in  the game is still unclear as to me, server populations seem low. Trion are still working hard on the game though as less than a month in, they have already released some new content that introduced a 'World Event'. Trion currently plan to release these regularly but only time will tell if they can keep it up.

I have never written a review before but i think this game deserves more exposure and i hope more people will give this game a shot. I only discoverd this game through sale and bought it because of the pixel art style and the interesting premise. And this game certainly did not disappoint. The greatest strength of this game lies in the relationship between the player and the main character Niko that builds up as the game progress. In this game Niko directly speaks to you and asks you questions. In result the fourth wall is broken and it feels like you are having a real conversation with a person. Because of that you get easily attached to Niko. Another big plus in this game are the unusual game mechanics like searching a password in your own computer folder or the fact that the game closes when Niko went to sleep, Furthermore the music fits the world really well  and creates a  dark but sometimes heartfelt atmosphere befitting of a dying world. Moreover the story of the game is great and always urge you on to help Niko to fullfill his mission. Last but not least the ending was amazing but a little sad at the same time. The True ending with the Solistice update is especiallly satisfying. All things considered it creates a unique, immersive and emotional game that leaves a void in your heart after you completed the game.
Therefore i wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who loves story driven games and unique game experiences.

The best tower defence game I've played on PC or mobile.  Fun, quirky, and at times really challenging, but without going overboard into wanting to smash your keyboard.
The challenge here is all about pathing - there's plenty of different towers to try, and each is good and bad against different enemies - but in most cases, the main issue is figuring out where you can steer the enemies with the available map and towers at your disposal.
Couple of things I really like about DG:
1.  You can complete levels without being 'flawless' - the goal is to stop aliens from stealing your 'cores', but you can finish a level without keeping all of them.  As a bit of a completionist, I always wanted to get through them perfectly with all cores intacts, but the point is you're not blocked from getting on with the next level if this isn't for you.
2.  The balance is excellent, in that your basic gun turret tower is useful from start to finish in this game - there's no sense of "once you get tower X just spam that".
It's a great game, hard to go wrong buying it.

Salt and Sanctuary is a fantastic mix of the best elements from games such as Metroid, Castlevania, and the critically acclaimed Dark Souls series. From the very beginning of the game, players are drawn in by the surprisingly deep combat system, as well as traditional RPG elements such as inventory management, gear upgrades and a sprawling skill tree. The magic/prayer system is as intuitive as it is innovative, and rewards players who invest in 'multiclassing' with a variety of buffs and special skills. The co-operative play is, if anything, even more entertaining than single player, especially as summoned friends can progress anywhere in the game without artificial boundaries being set, and can even (if their faith is strong enough) revive their partners. Finally, the NG+ system creates a fresh level of challenge for players who have beaten the regular game, significantly upping enemy health and damage output.

Negative:
- No in-detail army organization like in Hearts of Iron III.
- Other missing features from HoI III such as the partisan system, espionage or the battle scenarios.
- Dull naval and air combat, also due to...

- Terrible (strategic) AI. I've never seen the AI invade Japan, at the same time it attempts too many pointless invasions at irrelevant locations, with either not enough or WAY too many troops involved (Allies invading Axis Peru with 100 divisions)
- No unique focus trees for important nations like Spain, Finland or China (instead they're working on trees for New Zealand and South Africa. Who plays those?)
- Submarine warfare seems pretty much pointless
- Overpriced DLCs are almost guaranteed
Positive:
+ Fantastic production and equipment system
+ Beautiful graphics and decent performance
+ Lots of fun achievements
+ Interesting tech tree (a little oversimplified) and unique national focusses
+ Thanks to the planning feature you don't have to control every little division anymore. Unfortunately the AI keeps making stupid mistakes like sending tank divisions in mountainous areas.
+ Many future updates....hopefully!
+ A large amounts of modifications which are easy to install thanks to Steam Workshop integration.
+ The AI may be bad, but especially for new players it's nevertheless challenging to try to invade the Soviet Union with Germany, win the Pacific war as Japan or go ahead and try to make Mexico great again by declaring war on the United States!
Despite all the problems this game has, I still had a lot of fun playing it so far and I am looking forward to future updates and improvements. If you like strategy games and have an interest in World War II, you should definitely look into buying either this or Hearts of Iron III. Better wait for a sale though, since I don't think that such a close to broken-AI should be rewarded with 40€.

I really want to talk about Uplay, as it made me worried that my $20 was spent in vain
If you're VERY VERY VERY VERY...VERY VERY lucky, than Uplay will work for you. Most likley, it will not. To fix this, run AC 2. You will be prompted to log in to Uplay, but when you do, it will crash. This is fine, as we will fix this later. Now, open Control Panel and click "Uninstall a Program". Scroll down to "Ubisoft Game Launcher", or something like that, and click "Uninstall". After this, you should probably delete any leftover files from Uplay. Go to C:\Program Files (x86)\Ubisoft (On 32-bit Windows this will be in C:\Program Files\Ubisoft) and delete the foler named "Ubisoft Game Launcher". Then, you want to re-install Uplay (or else the game won't run). You can download it from here
After you re-install Uplay, log in. This should work. Now, you have to click "Redeem a game" or something like that. Enter your Steam product key and AC 2 will be added to your Uplay/Ubisoft library.

My main complaint nowadays is, after having shifted to F2P, the expanded content is a bit tougher to invest in. The newer expansions after Storm Legion cost something fierce to get the new souls (and recently calling) in the most economic way. I enjoyed toying with the new calling for a short week after they released Into the WIld. I don't find it was worth my money sadly, and that may have to do with the fact I have more invested into other current titles that compete for my time/money. I was having fun with the new calling, but found myself bored quickly after leveling for a small time. I still love the soul system for giving all callings the capability to play each role, although it still requires having to unlock the extra souls added in by later updates, which will cost a new player. Like most "F2P" games today, it's more accurate to call it "Free-to-Start"/"Free-to-Try", as subscriber perks/spending money in the store expands the game for you, most notably with the added souls/calling. I understand it's a business and they have to make money through the store and   subscriptions, but some pricing just seems a tad steep for what you're gaining. Unless you're a huge fan and heavily invested in the game, or brand new to the world of MMOs, it's not the worst choice. If you've played WoW or a game mechanically similar to it: It'll be an easy shift mechanically, but expect not as much polish and to have to pay more out of pocket to unlock the full potential of your calling.

Bierzerkers is an over-the-top pvp Viking-rugby game – with sheeps – by Shield Break Studios. If you haven’t figured out by now, the whole thing is a really silly take on the Vikings with probably all possible stereotypes. The whole craziness was why I installed it in the first place but soon realised that things aren't as great as they may look after watching the trailer: The game unfortunately is standing with one foot in the grave.
For me that was a tragic thing to find out cause the game itself can be a lot of fun. In “Bierball” you transport a sheep through the arena into the opponent’s goal. You can score by either running into the goal carrying the sheep or by throwing it in there – though the latter gives less points (3 instead of 7). Domination is all about controlling points on the map to gather points and Team Battle Royale is a simple TDM mode.
To your disposal stand 5 different Viking-style classes: In an attacking role the Raider, a close-combat guy with shield and sword and some AOE damage skills as well as the Scoundrel, a sneaky assassin-type character relying on hit-and-run tactics. For defensive tasks there’re the Valkyrie focussing on blocking enemies or shielding your own and the Huntress, a ranged class with frost skills to slow down or entirely freeze the opposition. Finally, as support and tank there’s the Drunkard, with some damage skills as well as the ability to heal his team mates.
By playing and leveling up each class you unlock additional customization items for each character which don’t have any further effect on the game itself besides making you stand out from the rest of players. The options (weapon, helmet and mug plus clothes colours) are fairly limited though.
Also fairly limited is the game itself, offering only the above mentioned “Bierball” game mode in 5 vs 5 matches limited to 5 minutes on 3 different maps for the quite a long time. More game modes apparently had been in the game before though were removed by the devs for some reason; the two modes mentioned above were now added with the last update (29.04.2016) and especially Domination is a lot of fun.
For training purposes you can play versus bots, though their AI is…limited and when playing in Odin’s arena they aren’t even able to pick up the bouncing sheep-ball in the middle of the arena due to the spikes below it. There also aren’t any difficulty settings.
On the technical side the game is, as you can see in the gameplay trailer, designed fitting to the overall theme in a comic artstyle with a slightly overweight Valkyrie and a slightly crazy Raider, each character having funny poses and voice-overs (the Drunkard can set down a beer barrel for healing purposes, all characters from his team around it start drinking beer from their mugs while regenerating). Some textures could use some improvements, especially on the character models themselves but overall it really isn’t a bad-looking game.
The shop is surprisingly empty as you probably already noticed: You have access to one class (the Raider) for free, the remaining 4 have to be bought for 6€ each or 20€ in a bundle. One of those 4 classes always seems to be in a free rotation resulting in a pretty fair system with reasonable prices. There're no other things to buy, no ingame shop with anything. The lack of other options make the whole thing look weird though, resulting in the question: How do the devs finance themselves?
A question which brings me to the summary that is: Apparently, the financing does indeed not work very well. Currently it’s very hard to even find players to play a proper PvP match, most of the time you’re playing against bots. The recent update brought back some players and finally added some other game modes again in addition to Bierball, though it’s unsure for how long that will last and if this’ll turn things around – the player numbers still are very low. The slow updates and lack of content for example in regards to customization, together with the pretty much non-existing communication from the side of the devs in the forums etc, make the future of the game look rather dark. While Bierzerkers certainly is fun for some quick matches in a silly environment it’s currently hard to recommend the game or even ask people to spend money on.

{Disclaimer for anyone who has not played the game: This review contains some tiny spoilers of the game at the beginning, sorry for this but it was necessary to get my point across}
I really have a lot I can say here but I will only say a little bit of it.
One Shot is an absolutley beautiful game, the first time I booted the game was when I saw the trailed and had finally gotten the game (Without any spoilers mind you.) From the beginning this game entranced me with its nice artstyle, wonderful music and overall smooth quality. From watching the trailer and viewing the Steam page I missed a key detail in the game... "The world knows you exist" This really caught me off guard and truthfully I sat there for a few seconds dumbfounded at the fact it went to that boundary very few games go.
When I learned that there was some force that knew about me, I was intrigued, and I carried on, thinking nothing of it as some games had parts where there was some fourth wall breaking and it could make for cool things. So I played through and was again amazed at its visuals, the game had already been made to me as a title I was going to enjoy, odd story or not, so I ventured out into the Barrens... This is when I met Prophetbot, once again I shrugged it off until it mentioned, "Their god" which happened to be my name as thats what my computer is set to.
I told Niko the name I prefered to go by over my one I had on my computer, the one that my closest friends and family called me, just for fun, I had fallen into absolute love for Niko already, this game made me care for the main protaganist quicker than any game in the past has done, in my head I started putting this as what would be an Undertale sort of feeling, where I would feel acomplished as I went along through the game, and my choices would sway my emotions a little, boy was I right, except I was not fully right, I underestimated this game and how it made you feel, rather quickly I was reading Niko's lines out loud, imagining him in my head saying those words, once again an Undertale esc. feel, but it was a lot different, I felt more raw emotion from this because, I had given Niko the name I preferred to go by, and it felt like he was treating me as a friend, to the best he could and that made me weak in emotions, which was a very very good and bad thing, because there weren't only good feelings but also beautiful or sad ones that made me cry.
This game puts you originally in the spot of any other RPG, as the person behind the screen, but in One Shot, you quickly start getting a different feel, as if you're important to the story; which you just so happen to be. I truthfully felt as if I had to answer those questions asked honestly, and if I didn't I'd feel bad, this game is again beautiful in the emotion that you feel, they made it exactly how they wanted it to be and feel, which is no small task for a game in general.
The puzzles were rather immersive and honestly felt refreshing to the normal puzzling and such of Indie games and even mainstream games too, it was a breath of fresh, relieving air. The puzzles in this game are not insanely hard either, unline some games that have ridcilous levels of difficulty for no reason. I never felt genuinly lost on a puzzle because, I always had Niko or someone to talk to and look at and describe things with, which helped me come up with the solutions to some of those puzzles.
To wrap things up quickly. This game, had feeling, thought and effort put into it that very, VERY few games can match, it lets you bond with the main character and feel like you know them, giving an extra sense of immersion to their rather immersion breaking game, except, whenever that immersion is broken, it feels a lot better when you can actually solve it. Throughout the entire game, "The Entitiy" (As I shall call it for non spoiler reasons) guides you very loosely, whenever you're stuck or lost, you walk around and notice that screen on and you go over to it, only for it to tell you what to do. Around halfway through the game, you can finally start to realize what could be happening at the end, and honestly the thought itself of that idea tore me apart, all because this game immersed me, it made me feel like the characters were real, it made me feel like I was an actual part of that world, it made me feel... like I was actually Niko's friend, and I can't applaud OneShot enough for this, because here I sit, the game open after finishing the ending to the game, and I feel like I've lost a small part of me, but that the small part of me will always be there. This game has sparked emotions inside me I haven't cared to use in such a long time, and its so heartwarming (And heartbreaking) to see the ending finally occur, so good job to OneShot for being able to accomplish such a hard task; making people feel emotions for a character.
So as I sit here and reflect on the whole journey while looking at a small lit up room, I encourage anyone who hasn't tried it to try it, and anyone who has to reflect on it as well, you'll only realize then how much you actually cared, every time I open up the game now and look at the screen, I can't help but tear just a little.

It is still in beta but I thought a quick review would be in good standing to give the game some of it's support.
I have been following Evolve for a really long time. Not with the community, but on my own as an excited consumer who thought 4v1 was the coolest sound genre for online multiplayer. It was and still is to me. I have spent a lot on Evolve over the past 2 years, money and time. I was an Xbox One player and now with the new PC I have gotten access to this beta. All I can say is, good friggen job Turtle Rock Studios.
There is a MASSIVE overhaul to what I once thought I knew, and not just ebcause it is free to play.  The biggest changes lie in it's gameplay, characters, mechanics, and level design for the assymetrical playstyle they have been giving us . TYhey have made ALL the right decisions and the game is WAY more balanced than it ever has been and plays a lot more logically with how classes should and should not work. These are all the changes that it needed to have the fresh start it needed, The first two days was rough since I was still feeling less compensated for what I dedicated, founders pack for PC only (soon to be for the platform you own), but this new formula makes Evolve breathe properly. The currency system is also very easy to obtain and compared to most free to play, the content will be easily unlockable as it stands.
I could not reccommend playing this game more espically now that it is free, you have nothing to lose. Love it or hate it. If this review was worth the read and you are feeling persuaded, join the hunt and make this game even better than what it has become. The hunt still lives on and the biggest thing I can say walking away is that there was always a little flame that made me love this game. It is ignited once more.

The Hearts of Iron series has historically been extraordinarily complex and seemingly insurmountable to the typical gamer.  The game has been greatly streamlined with this latest installation but much of the complexities still remain.  To those that wish to take charge of a nation during the tumultuous 1930s era and guide it to victory, this may just be the best thing out there to sate that desire.
Just keep in mind that the UI itself is not very friendly for people with color vision problems, however, there are many mods available out there to help those of us with the color saturation.  This is the case with most any game from Paradox Dev Studios.  The game is infitely moddable and a blast to play.  I give it a 9/10, if only for its reputation for complexity and lack of built in color vision settings.
DISCLAIMER:  I am an unashamed Paradox fan boy and will be until they have done me wrong.  They consistently take a strong look at their games and provide support for many years after release.  Ever since Crusader Kings 2 (CK2), the polish of the games has increased immensely and has made me fall in love with them even more.
UPDATES:  With the number of expansion packs that have been released recently, the game has been expanded upon immensely with the usual slew of Paradox game events.  The best part is that you do not need to buy them to get many of the events.  Although it is definitely a benefit to get them, they aren't very pricy any how.

Now here is a brain game I can wholeheartedly recommend. If you enjoy brain-twisting mechanical puzzles, Cogs will keep you entertained for a good while.
The challenges in this game generally involve sliding around components on multi-sided contraptions to activate the mechanism for the solution. The puzzles are varied and clever, and pleasing to solve, involving differential gears, steam pipes and other parts to create functioning clockworks, musicboxes, helicopters and more.
Additional points are awarded for efficiency and speed which can be used to unlock more levels, so if you get stuck on one, you can still skip ahead and choose from others.
There are a few levels my son and I enjoy revisiting almost endlessly because the interface is simple and clean, and the solutions are satisfying to perform. The graphics are pleasant and well-designed, with some slick menus, and expandable content in the form of periodic bonus levels.

Mercenary Kings is a nice co-op action platformer which has a lot to offer as far as challenges and customization goes.
First off, there are 112 levels with more than 12 unique bosses which should keep you busy for a decent amount of time. Admittedly, the maps could use a little bit more variety. That's somewhat remedied by way most missions are structured. Each unique map is inherently large so each mission will cover only certain portions of the map (with the rest of it being totally optional).
The game also makes you consider resource management. While you don't need to do every single mission to 'beat' the game, you do however need to plan which resources to bring and decide when to best use them. For example, infiltration or capture missions will require you to make the best use of your C4 charges and shock bombs. Wasting one or more of each item can usually lead to failing the mission. This becomes even more important when speed runs come into play.
Another selling point of the game is the massive amount of gun parts and gun combinations available to you through progression. It opens up a lot of possibilities and it's amusing to see different combinations suggested on various videos and forum posts.
With all these things going for it, Mercenary Kings is not perfect. I'd reckon that the average Metal Slug player will be able to finish majority of the game without even fully scratching the surface as far as crafting goes. I feel that there's a lot of room for improvement when it comes to content. Personally, I feel that the game was too short seeing as I reached the final level long before I even got to halfway on all the crafting achievements.
My suggestion? Steam Workshop integration. This is another one of those games that will benefit a lot from workshop integration to add newly designed maps. BattleBlock Theater serves as a great example by giving the players access to the various blocks that make up the levels. A move like this will go a long way especially to reduce the boredom from having finished the game and moving onto crafting everything else.
My initial impression of this game would be at around 9/10. It was definitely fun but it needs something to fill the gap at the end of the game. For now I'd rate this game as a 7/10 since it is severely in need of user-generated content. Nevertheless, it's still an absolutely fun co-op experience. I do recommend getting the 4-pack.

The thing about this game, apart from the fact that it's awesome, is that it can appeal to any skill level and ease you into its depth, unlike many other rogue-likes out there.  Perhaps it's just me, but I barely had to look anything up.  Everything is well laid out and there are plenty of tool tips to explain everything.  The UI is fantastic and the game even runs on my netbook.  There are also difficulty settings to grant either permadeath or a more forgiving "lives" system that you gain extra lives as you level up, or even no death at all (but no achievements either).  Overall, I'm blown away so far and can easily see myself spending dozens if not hundreds of hours playing every single class... And the fact that you slowly unlock classes as you play is brilliant.  Now I know why this won rogue-like of the year a few times in a row.  Buy it because these games need the support!

Mercenary Kings is a 2D co-op pixel shooter, reminiscent of Contra or, more accurately, Metal Slug. An elite mercenary group conveniently named "The Kings" (and suspiciously led by The King, a generically light-skinned and dark-haired Übermensch) is called into action by a vaguely American-looking military to take down a self-styled dictator who has taken over an island paradise -- not the most original setup, but a solid gameplay loop, intuitive mechanics, and a deep crafting system keeps the player engaged, and art by the inimitable Paul Robertson makes every new enemy and locale a beautiful thing to discover (and subsequently destroy).

He complained to me that he feared I was forcing him out of the club (not true - I just wanted added competition). I tried telling him they competition is healthy and he should be professional (he has a proffesional personality). He threw his toys out of the pram and then turned the squad against me. After enjoying a healthy start in the league, I now have 1 win in 9 games due to poor morale / abysmall managerial support.
My second complaint is the match engine. While I feel it's always been an underlying problem in the Football Manager series, the obsession with long shots is at a new level. Building a steady attack with options either side of the player? Low tempo? Work the ball into the box? NOPE. Shoot from 40 yards. Extremely frustrating.
It's the small features this season which have pursuaded me to buy it. The data anaylst camera, the enhanced graphics, and the additional tactical options. Making decisions and watching the action remains Football Manager's strong point.
As a final point. The game seems to be obsessed with trying to match Footbal like for like in real life. Just a pointer. It's a game. "Don't sacrifice entertainment for realism".
I do not recommend Football Manager 2018 in it's current state.

I was trying to finish this game, at least once for the single player mode, but too bad, it just had randomly frozen several times.
The game uses Cryengine 3 to build the whole world, yet it is apparently not what you may think about, which is totally a waste of the physics engine.

Heyyo, it's a pretty decent game tbh. It's not a AAA Game like Sniper Elite series (The WWII sniper game by Rebellion) but it definitely holds its own. :)
The sniping? Well, since this is a sniper game? I guess that should be discussed first heh. The game takes into account bullet drop, wind direction, stance, elevation and stamina (how many beats per minute your heart is doing) so the mechanics are all there ok. The bullet cam is very much like Sniper Elite, but no model damage on the enemies. They just flop over. There's also the hold shift to slow down time and make it feel more movie-like and make it easier to hit moving targets. If you sit in sniper/scope mode long enough? The game gives you a little red circle to show where the bullet will hit and highlight when ontop of an enemy... so as a sniper game? It's good... but Sniper Elite feels more rewarding when you land a shot since you see what kind of damage you're doing.
It has a decent enough storyline... Quite generic tbh but it was good enough for me to want to finish the game.
The voice acting is also nothing flattering but works good enough to make me want to finish the game.
The Gameplay? Eh, after playing Sniper Elite and Sniper Elite V2? Gameplay isn't as good as those games. There's no disguises and trying to sneak around... the campaign is extremely scripted where you spend most of it doing exactly what your spotter tells you to do or you die.. speaking of which? Once enemies start hunting for you? The AI will definitely 360 no-scope you at close range. Super annoying when I try to ambush them and as soon as they rush through a doorway? Bullets hit me before their character turns around and I'm dead... so that's seriously annoying lol.
The graphics? They're pretty darn good, definitely not the best on Cryengine but I'd say a step above State of Decay (another good game built on Cryengine).
The music? Eh, I think there's only three or four songs for the complete game as most maps feature the same songs... They're ok I guess.
Sound effects? Well? Since most of the game you're only using about three different guns (silenced pistol, silenced sniper rifle and a long range silenced sniper rifle) for the whole game? There isn't that much variety in sound effects. The sounds that are there are pretty good though.
My Steam account says I beat the campaign in 5.2 hours and the asking price is $21.99 CAD... so that equates to $4.22 per hour. I don't plan on playing multiplayer since I'm not much of a multiplayer FPS guy these days I guess. So do I feel like it was worth $4.22 an hour? Kinda I guess. It was fun enough... but there's some older games with a longer campaign for the same asking price that'll give you more entertainment. I'd say get the first Sniper Elite game and see what you think of that game before buying this one tbh. Maybe the same with the first Sniper: Ghost Warrior game.. but of course I don't own that so I can't directly give my opinon on that game, but this one is ok so I'm guessing the first Sniper: Ghost Warrior is also ok.

Honestly this is one of the best survival role playing games on Steam. Yup, community is toxic, isn't most of Steam? Yup, it's brutal, you'll be KoS everywhere you go, like in just about every other survival game on the market. Yup, it's buggy, most are - especially survival games. Yet this game gets mad amounts of hate for it.
All that's outta the way. This game has the most in depth crafting i've ever seen, the different gear you can make and materials you can use is crazy with different appearances for every single piece that you change. You can build a castle, keep, town, fort, or just a simple house almost anywhere in the world. There are siege weapons and many different mounts to ride. Beyond mounts just about every creature in the game can be a pet. Beyond that you can summon demons and various undead with necromancy.
Become a fighter, trader, escort, mercenary, screaming peasant, whatever it is you want to be. The skill system works similarly to The Elder Scrolls in that you learn by doing. Some skills are learned from a book which your character will passively read while playing or offline. Literally any combination you can think of is possible.
Loads of dungeons and hidden areas, many hand crafted npc cities and minor camps. Tons of monsters both real and fantasy and everything has something to drop. 2 whole continents to fight over, bigger than any maps available in other survival games.
Over all it's hard to describe what all you can do with this game, since there are so many options and not everything is common knowledge, you may stumble upon a precious secret not many know of and that just doesn't happen in datamined games with overflowing wikis of information.

Negative:
- No in-detail army organization like in Hearts of Iron III.
- Other missing features from HoI III such as the partisan system, espionage or the battle scenarios.
- Dull naval and air combat, also due to...
- ...no stacking penalties for navies and airwings.
- Terrible (strategic) AI. I've never seen the AI invade Japan, at the same time it attempts too many pointless invasions at irrelevant locations, with either not enough or WAY too many troops involved (Allies invading Axis Peru with 100 divisions)
- No unique focus trees for important nations like Spain, Finland or China (instead they're working on trees for New Zealand and South Africa. Who plays those?)
- Submarine warfare seems pretty much pointless
- Overpriced DLCs are almost guaranteed
Positive:
+ Fantastic production and equipment system
+ Beautiful graphics and decent performance
+ Lots of fun achievements
+ Interesting tech tree (a little oversimplified) and unique national focusses
+ Thanks to the planning feature you don't have to control every little division anymore. Unfortunately the AI keeps making stupid mistakes like sending tank divisions in mountainous areas.
+ Many future updates....hopefully!
+ A large amounts of modifications which are easy to install thanks to Steam Workshop integration.
+ The AI may be bad, but especially for new players it's nevertheless challenging to try to invade the Soviet Union with Germany, win the Pacific war as Japan or go ahead and try to make Mexico great again by declaring war on the United States!
Despite all the problems this game has, I still had a lot of fun playing it so far and I am looking forward to future updates and improvements. If you like strategy games and have an interest in World War II, you should definitely look into buying either this or Hearts of Iron III. Better wait for a sale though, since I don't think that such a close to broken-AI should be rewarded with 40€.

This game is hard to love, it's one of those games that has the promise of combining all the best parts of old skool games. I'm sure at some level this was what the developers are going for, a nostalgic game they would've liked to see, indisriminately taking the things we all loved about platformers etc.
Sadly, it's more like the best and the absolute worst aspects of games from the 8bit and 16bit era. It's as if the developers have learned absolutely nothing from modern game design. This game is extremely frustrating, and most of it comes down to horrible design and core mechanics.
The biggest issue I have apart from the bad overall design, is that while the developers have tried to combine many different elements from successful games, the overall experience is worse off than any of those individual games it tries to imitate.Some gameplay choices don't play well with each other and their attempt at syncretizing these becomes detrimental to the overall experience,
I tried playing this game with multiple friends, and it's hard for me to insist on it when it's obvious no one is enjoying a single second of it.

It's got the run-and-gun action of Metal Slug and the exploration and crafting of Monster Hunter, but somehow none of the fun of either. Cumbersome controls, tedious grind, unsatisfying upgrade system, and needlessly obnoxious enemies make for a pretty lousy experience all around.

Some times you have to capture a boss, but there is no explanation beforehand as to how you do this. I'd battled through the stage only to mistakenly kill the boss because I'd ran out of the item needed to capture him. Both yours and the enemies projectiles are painfully slow. There are only two directions you can shoot in whilst not jumping. Up and left / right. This makes fighting certain flying enemies a major pain in the balls. Especially when they knock you off of a ladder or a zipline when you're just trying to get from A to B. The boss fights are rubbish too. You do so much damage to the boss and then he walks through into the background and appears at a random location on your map. And unless you pay for one of your people to spot the boss, you're left running through the stage blind. Battling the respawning enemies. The worst are easily the slow moving flying drones. So, first off - the game is beautiful, the animation is fluid and funny, the game has a ton of character, it's a Scott Pilgrim nod to Metal Slug.  All those things are great... but the gameplay.  EVERY mission is a timed variation on a fetch quest, and most of the environments look the exact same.  Timed missions ALONE would dissuade me from continuing, but I kept at it because I really wanted to like it.  I figured weapon customization would save the game, but alas, unless you make very specific weapons, they tend to be pretty worthless.  I was hoping for a Loadout-esque customization system, but the game really just wants you to buy parts to make a shotgun.  Or a sniper rifle.  If you get creative in any way, the negatives are so huge that it's not worth the effort - I went from a standard magazine weapon with 6 shots to a larger magazine, and my damage dropped about 80% - so though I had more bullets to a clip, I was doing far LESS damage with each shot.
If you can handle mazey fetch quests, give it a shot.  It's a solid backbone, it has a lot of things going for it, but it just felt too clunky and grindey to me.  Such a shame, I'd been looking forward to playing it for a while now.

Let me start by saying that I have owned every single version of Championship Manager/Football Manager ever made. I have sunk thousands of hours into these games and have loved them. I don't feel the game is developing enough every year to warrant a full price release every year, and the new 'features' that they have implemented (team dynamics I am looking at you) are borederline gamebreaking.
I know this is still a beta but I seriously doubt that these features will be changed for the full release. To give an example, I was managing Spurs. 5 League games into the season Wanyama asked me for more first team football. He had stared 2 games and came on as sub in another 2, so had participated in 4 out of 5 games. I told him that the season was long and he would get his chance. It escalated and I lost the dressing room. 10 games into the season and the game is over for me. The issue is the limited responses that you are able to make inevitably lead to issue's with the players.
You can't register a squad for the Champions League, it won't let you select players at the moment, so forget any hope of playing in that competition. The UI is a complete mess, so hard to navigate around, with multiple clicks needed to get to where you want to be, last year it would have taken one click.
Like I said I really hope they fix these, and many more issues, but I don't think that they will.

The thing about this game, apart from the fact that it's awesome, is that it can appeal to any skill level and ease you into its depth, unlike many other rogue-likes out there.  Perhaps it's just me, but I barely had to look anything up.  Everything is well laid out and there are plenty of tool tips to explain everything.  The UI is fantastic and the game even runs on my netbook.  There are also difficulty settings to grant either permadeath or a more forgiving "lives" system that you gain extra lives as you level up, or even no death at all (but no achievements either).  Overall, I'm blown away so far and can easily see myself spending dozens if not hundreds of hours playing every single class... And the fact that you slowly unlock classes as you play is brilliant.  Now I know why this won rogue-like of the year a few times in a row.  Buy it because these games need the support!

I'm a big fan of Roguelkes, but I was always put off by some of the obscure concepts of the core gameplay. This game takes all the good of the roguelike, the difficulty, the random levels, the classes and all that- And combines it with a solid interface, good music, and an astoundingly fleshed out world.
If you like roguelikes, if you're curious about them, or if you just want a good strategy game/RPG, you'd be a fool not to get this.

If you're a fan of old-school, roguelike RPG's then you can't go wrong with this. Maddeningly addictive, brutally difficult and with a whole host of unlockable and interesting 'DnD' style classes, each greatly varying in playstyle.
By the looks of it, there's potentially a lot of gameplay here too outside of the typical “die, replay new game” flow common with roguelikes. So far I’ve not managed to get a character past level 14 without having them killed and then auto-deleted, and that’s after sinking a good 19 hours into the game. Each time a character has died however, I’ve usually found myself instantly firing up a new game, stubbornly adamant that I’ll get further this time or with a different class (I say “instantly”, there’s always that brief period of time spent just staring at the screen after a death thinking “Shiiiit! I knew I should have been more careful….Shiiiiiiiit!”).
Classes, game modes and special perks can be earned and unlocked for current and future playthroughs by completing quests or accessing certain areas, helping keep your interest in the game after a heavy loss.
All in all, totally worth £6 I’d say, provided you’re prepared from some serious jimmy rustling somewhere down the line (to the likes Dark Souls has never seen)!

Salt and sanctuary is a  combination of dark souls, bloodborne and the metroidvania style. A best description would be "Metroidvania with Souls elements". There are lots of reasons why you should try out this game. I am gonna keep it short, but here are the pros and cons.

PROS:
+ Atmospheric space, really gets you in.
+ Combat is a combination of souls dodge/stagger and metroidvania hit/run.
+ Lots of character customization. Lots of different builds.
+ Rad parkour moments where it isn't clunky but actually fun.
+ Pumpkin head
+ Small details such as the following:
;Hitting a ledge while falling of high ground makes your character flip hilariously fast while falling to their doom.
;Special unicorn enemies, can only be found on one spot, impale you on their horn and throw you around.
CONS
- Clunky ledge grabbing and parkour that requires maximum concentration
-/+ This one's not an actual con, but people put it as one. Character faces DO look weird, but you are wearing  a helmet/mask nearly the whole game, so it mostly doesn't matter.
- The game never explains to newcomers that you have to roll THROUGH the enemies because you have no invincibillity frames while rolling, keep that in mind.
CONCLUSION
So, uh, yeah. Pretty fun game. Get it, I guess. Or don't. Tho you would be pretty dumb if you don't get it on sale.
