WARNING: WALL OF TEXT INBOUND! tl;dr 8/10.
Let me preface this by saying why I'm getting about reviewing this game only now having owned it for a while (actually, being gifted it by my friend Ly, thanks fagt <3). I always figured that nobody's going to see my review, and the game's recommended as it is, so I figured I'd let others speak instead of me. Well, now that Steam actually displays the few reviews posted in the last 30 days, I figured, why the hell not.
Also, I have to say, going in, I'm a HUGE Soulsborne and Metroidvania fan, so this game REALLY hits the sweet spot for me. I may or may not be a tad biased since I was EXTREMELY hyped for the game, but I'll try to keep this as objective as possible.
GRAPHICS:
This one's a mixed bag. While the hand drawn artstyle is really pretty to look at, and in my opinion it's really cool, something that may put others off to the point of not playing the game is the character design. The human characters are, well... to put it lightly, weird. Imagine trying to describe to someone what 'anime' looks like and then them subsequently completely missing the point. The characters have round heads, no noses, wide mouths and REALLY bulgy, insectoid eyes. Honestly, this didn't really bother me, but I know some people will despise it, so take it as you will. For me personally, it wasn't a big deal.
The rest of the game is really well done. The details are crisp and everything runs smoothly. One other noteworthy thing is the animations. They are exceptionally well done, and wielding some weapons, namely daggers, will make you feel like nothing short of an absolute badass. Overall a solid 7/10.
SOUND:
Also a strange section. The ambient sounds, enemy shrieks, weapon swings and the like are all amazing. Very well done and extremely polished. What's not really AS good, however, is the music. Not that the music itself is bad. It's that there's only 3 or so tracks in the entire game. EVERY boss, except for the last one, has the same exact theme. Absolutely every single one. Now that might not be a bad thing if you like the track itself, but it WILL get repetitive after a while. Again, it didn't bother me all that much, but some of you might be put off by that fact. I'll give it an 8/10.
GAMEPLAY:
Aaaah, the meat and potatoes of this review. I'll try to structure this section as well, but bare with me if I go on tangents. I'll try to keep this as concise and to-the-point as possible.
Since this game doesn't try to hide the fact that it was heavily inspired by the Soulsborne franchise, some of the things it NEEDED to get right were the combat and the exploration. And it nailed those.
The combat is VERY satisfying, largely owing to the extremely tight and responsive controls. I do recommend playing with a controller if you can. Anywho, the combat feels meaty, impactful, and most of all, satisfying. Swords swoosh and whirr through the air and you can hear meat being sliced. Hammers thunk with a great amount of force, crushing bone and armor alike. The screen shakes a bit and there's blood absolutely EVERYWHERE. Really good stuff. And, since you'll be doing combat for like 90% of the game, that's a good thing too.
The level design is amazing. The world is HUGE, and while it might not take you over 50 hours to explore everything (it'll probably take you around 20 hours or so), the exploration never gets boring. Almost every bit of every level is crammed with stuff to find, explore (and kill), and there are secrets galore. I can assure you that if you just rush through the game, you'll have missed at LEAST 40% of the game, if not more. One other thing S&S takes from Souls is the shortcuts. The levels are very interwoven, to the point that very late game areas can link all the way back to the first couple of areas of the game. That's pretty insane.
However, not everything is fine and dandy. Some of the gripes I had with this part is the following:
a) You can clearly see a degradation in detail attention in the later portion of the game. Probably due to the fact that the producers tried to wrap the entire thing out and push it to the market. The later areas in the game just don't feel as polished or filled with details as the first few do. Some feel outright void of life and feel more like corridors placed there to keep you from going in a straight line rather than being fun to explore.
b) This game needs a God damn map, period. Unlike Dark Souls, which is a 3D game and it's much easier to gather your bearings in it, this one's 2D. It's flat. The entire game feels like an ant hill with the amount of secret pathways and shortcuts leading to and fro. And there's absolutely nothing to help you figure out where you are or what leads where. Kinda infuriating, but then again, that might just be me sucking at finding the right path or remembering where I was.
There are a couple of key differences in this game as opposed to the Souls games. First off, there's this huge thing called the Skill Tree. If you've played Path of Exile, you'll be right at home. If not, imagine a huge web of nodes all connected some way or another with lines. As you play and kill stuff, you'll be gathering Salt. Salt is used to level up at Sanctuaries (hueh). Every level you gain, you get an item called a Black Pearl. You spend these pearls to unlock nodes in the tree. The nodes either boost one of your stats, or they unlock higher tiers of weapons or armor for you to wear. While it may sound daunting at first, I actually prefer this to the way Souls handles levelups. It allows for much more flexible character development.
Similarly to Dark Souls, instead of bonfires you have Sanctuaries. At the beginning of the game you get to pick a Creed (Covenant) to join. You gain said creed's special item with which you claim empty sanctuaries. Once claimed, you can rest at a sanctuary. You can also 'place offerings' of small statuettes of various NPCs, such as merchants, mages, clerics, blacksmiths, etc. You'll find these statuettes as you play, too. Very cool stuff. There's also one more form of sanctuaries called Shrines. You can light them and rest at them, but you can't level up or offer statues to it. They're more like convenience checkpoints than true sanctuaries.
Next up is the armors and weapons. Like in Souls, there's a boatload of both, but unlike in Souls, the armor here is strictly categorized into two categories; heavy and light. This is supposedly to prevent people from switching from 2 ton armor to dresses willy-nilly. I actually really like this but someone else might not, so take it as you will.
Weapons are divided more diversely, and I'm not going to list all of the types here. What's important is that there's a large variety of both weapons and armor, and no matter the build you want to try, you'll find something that suits your playstyle.
Speaking of playstyle, one other flaw I've noticed is that slower, tank builds are at a slight disadvantage over light builds that prefer dodging instead of blocking. This is because a LOT of the bosses in the game tend to have attacks that'll knock you flat on your back. It doesn't help that some of these are unblockable, so if you want to play a heavy build, it might just be a test of patience for you.
When it comes to bosses there's also a huge variety that you'll come across. What I didn't really find fun, however, is that at least 3 of the bosses are nearly direct copies of bosses from Dark Souls. There's Artorias, Nito and Seath. You'll know them when you see them. Impossible to miss. I get drawing inspiration from a source, that's cool. But outright copying some of the stuff is stretching it a bit. Not a deal breaker for me, though. At least I knew how to deal with the bosses.
Overall, I love this game to bits. It gets a rock solid 8/10. Get it if you're a Souls/Metroidvania fan, or if you have money to spare. You really don't have anything to lose.

In short: A good game but do not buy full priced.
Pro's
-Nice gameplay if you like sneaking and sniping. Defenitely better real 'sniping' experience than for example Sniper Elite. It tries to be somewhat of a sniper simulator but can't really deliver there like ARMA does. However in the context of this game it is enough to make gameplay very interesting and even challenging.
-Pretty decent graphics and nice environments.
-Story not very good but interesting enough.
Con's
-Badly optimised. Although my computer is absolutely fine (can run all games i know at high/very high) this game did not feel fluid. Especially when running it felt weird, a kind of stuttering or something.
-Bugs. This game has its share of bugs. Usually nothing game-breaking but i once could not pick up my gun and the keys to change stance seem to randomly make you crouch, stand or go prone which is very annoying.
-VERY VERY Linear. you don't have any choice to do anything. You can complete the objective in one way and no other.
-Voice acting is a little dull sometimes
-That red dot. The only thing making this game a challenge is aiming. With the red dot enabled (when looking through your scope it gives the exact place you are going to hit) there is absolutely no challenge. There really should be a way of disabling it without having to play on the hardest difficulty. The same goes for the hints and everything.
-Companion AI is bad. When following a companion they always run. I could barely catch up with them and usually i just played my own style and they would just stand and wait out in the open until i catched up.
Conclusion
It is a decent game for a few hours of fun. It gives a pretty good sniping experience where your skill will matter (if you play on hard so disable aim assist). It defenitely immerses you in the role of a sniper. Get it when it is in the sale and you will not regret your purchase

This is the biggest leap forward for several years in the FM series, with the new dynamics system adding an extra layer of complexity, whilst also getting closer to the real life challenge of managing real people. You can't join a new club and instantly sell half the players, especially the aging group, without disrupting the squad harmony. Your reputation and relationship with your players now affects how much they listen to you, want to play for you and also push back against your wishes - taking the time to nurture these relationships reaps rewards.
Scouting system is evolved to be closer to real life (no more scouting thousands of players constantly - it chews through your budget) - you have to know what you want and send your scouts to get it, on top of their regular assignments.
Tactics are proving frustratingly difficult in the saves I've started, but it always takes some getting used to - I'm yet to find several different systems I can get to work with different clubs.
All in all, it's a definite improvement with SI creating another masterpiece. Definitely worth the money - well done Miles and co.

For fans of the classic SNK arcade series Metal Slug be fore-warned, this is nothing like it.
The game pretends to be like Metal Slug with it's visual aesthetic mainly by its featured artist, Paul Robertson, yet does not accurately capture the cartoony animations of the series in any way. This is not to say it looks bad, but for all of us that hope to see a giant crab with a cannon mounted to its back, your better off looking elsewhere. Where Paul Robertson's style worked wonders in the Scott Pilgrim VS the World game, in Mercenary Kings the visual just look boring and Robertson's bad habit of copying and pasting the same face on many of the women really shows here.
The gameplay is even less like Metal Slug and is more akin to being like Monster Hunter with it's weapon crafting system as well as the hunting and gathering aspects of the game. This wouldn't be something negative if it weren't for the fact that Mercenary Kings itself is  just boring to play. Now most games are repetetive in some way but most games also find a way to mix up the repetition in at least a small way. In theory, Mercenary Kings should be able to keep the gameplay fresh with its different types of missions, but as soon a mission begins the player will end up shooting the same enemies, collecting the same loot, meet the requirements, rinse and repeat. Sometimes there will be a boss type enemy to give the player something new to shoot but nothing honestly changes the overall gameplay and it really starts to become a chore throughout. It's a shame because Mercenary Kings showed promise with the team behind the Scott Pilgrim game as the developers, alas not all that glitters is gold and for that you can easily spend your $20 elsewhere. If you really want to give Mercenary Kings a shot though then wait for it to go on sale for at least $10 or lower.
TL/DR Ver.: If you want a Metal Slug type game to get your fix just play Metal Slug or Alien Hominid.

Salt & Sanctuary is compared to Dark Souls a lot. There definitely are similarities, but if you'd play S&S to get "more" Dark Souls, you will get disappointed. S&S is more obscure both lore-wise and gameplay-wise, has less items to mess around with, and the loss of a dimension makes movement, perception and spacing less important in favor of twitch reactions and stamina management. However, S&S has "proper" couch co-op, the gameplay feels satisfying, and despite the game overall being worse than the 'real' Souls games, it's still well above average and a pleasure to play.
The main disadvantage of S&S is the systemic obscurity; you will need to have a plan to play properly, and a lot of important decisions you make early on (such as which creed to pick or how to level up skills optimally) are not explained in-game, meaning you can screw yourself over because you could not make an informed decision. While Dark Souls is about "making the best of what you have", Salt & Sanctuary is about "work towards an intended goal". If you're okay with that, or just want an easier game to see if the Dark Souls hype is something you want to get into, S&S is a solid metroidvania well worth the price of admission. Just make sure you bookmark a wiki or two before you embark.

In a nutshell, RAGE looks and plays like the lovechild of Fallout 3 and Borderlands.  I would say RAGE has a good balance between the feel of a run-of-the-mill shooter and a good story-driven game, even though it gets a bit repetitive eventually. It can have a bit of a horror element what with the soundtrack, dark small spaces, suspense and jumpscares. Overall I'm pleased to say it actually exceeds the expectations one might have.
Pros:
+ A decent story
+ A lot to explore in the open world
+ Plenty of side missions, detailed content
+ Good enemy AI
+ Great graphics for the game of its year, nice overall design, though reminiscent of Fallout 3.
Cons:
- All (not just nearby) enemies are alerted by the supposed "stealth weapons", rendering any such weapons useless. I feel like the developers couldn't decide between going in guns blazing or stealth, and settled for...really  neither. As a person who always opts for long range stealth kills when given the chance, it greatly annoys me that you can basically take one shot with a sniper rifle and then have to switch to something with more crowd control, because suddenly EVERYONE is offended. You might as well just use the AR, sniper weapons literally make no difference.
- Repetitive combat and occasionally tedious missions - you know the mission that drags on and on from one room to the next, clearing wave after wave until you've forgotten why you were there in the first place? Yeah, that.
Eh's:
+/- Voice acting and character work is pretty much average. It's not hate-worthy, but it's not anything special either. I just feel like some NPC backstories and character development would really help the situation.
+/- I personally am a bit annoyed at the lack of maps in interior-ish spaces, since even those areas can be quite large, thus making it slightly difficult to find your way. However, I know many people would enjoy such exploration, completely on their own. Get lost to your hearts' content.
Overall grade:

On sale: 8/10  (score scales up with the discount percentage)
Full price: 6/10

Ignore the hours I have on this game, I have over 4000 logged in the last few years. Football Manager is the only serious football management sim out there. And in this installment, it truly shows that the developers know it.
Should we attempt to market the game in any way? Nah.
Should we help new players to the game, we have made it much more complicated? Nah.
Should we ensure default tactics and set-pieces in the game work? Nah.
Does making injury management into (virtually) a mini-game should fun? HELL YES!
Knowing that they are own the vast majority of football licenses (which you need to make a game like this successful) has made everyone involved in this game complacent, the UI is counter-intuitive and time-consuming, sometimes leading you to question if the developers actually want you to enjoy the game?
Some people may enjoy needing to constantly analyse your formation, your opponents, your tactics, your players, your squad dynamics etc etc and if you are one of those people, great! However, if you admit you don't want to do that and accept being a bit less successful because of it, this game is no longer for you. Only through micromanagement can you win in this game. I spend £30 on a game to get away from the pressures of life but I think they have forgotten that that is what this is, A GAME!  I'm hoping true competition comes along soon to wake this developer up. Until then, I'm out.

The truth is, I always enjoy the new release of Football Manager, so, if your a fan and interested in new features then go for it.
However, I feel it one serious area needs addressing: the UI (interface graphics)
Previous editions of FM were clearly backed by serious interaction designers; so the UI was clear, efficient, easy to use and pretty to look at for hours at a time.
This is not the case with Football Manager 2018.
In FM2018 I feel like their interaction designers left the team; either that, or non-designers had far too much influence on changes in this version. Or both. A big big thumbs up for this tower defense game.

This game wins on so many levels:
1.) It is insanely and maddeningly challenging. You will want to replay every mission in the campaign and try not to have any cores taken.
2.) The game rewards you for strategizing and tactics. Incorrectly placed towers will lead you to scream in frustration. Correctly placed towers will give you a huge sense of satisfaction as you correctly and accurately reroute aliens.
3.) You can level up each tower with resources gained from fallen aliens.
4.) An insanely high replayability factor. You can replay different missions and see what towers and where works.
5.) The voice acting is pretty good, I have to admit. You are kept company on each mission by some British dude talking about his family, his son Zeke, etc. Hammy but a nice touch as you fight off the alien columns.
If this is on sale, grab it. One of the better tower defense games. Very, very well done.

like most paradox games, HOI IV has a pretty steep learning curve if you haven't ever played a previous iteration of the game, or played any other paradox grand strategy games in general. there is a lot of less than intuitve "behind the scenes" calculations and factors that can have a pretty dramatic effect on say the effectiveness of your armies in the field. i played HOI 3, but did not put in enough hours or effort to really learn the nuances of the game, and just ended up frustrated that i couldnt understand why my armies wouldnt move because they had no supply, and couldnt figure out how to fix that, essentially grinding my armies and thus my game to a halt.
I can't really tell if HOI IV is a little more intuitive, or if i have just stuck with it long enough to figure out what i am doing. Once you learn the foundation basics of the game, you find yoursef saying less and less "what the **** are my guys doing", and  can start enjoying the game for what it has to offer. Once you get over the initial learning curve, the game is quite immersive and fun as you try to either recreate history, or rewrite your own version of history of ww2- depending on your gamestyle and country of choice.
Which brings me to the first point, and probably one of the most important for me personally in buying games.... replayability. HOI IV has a TON of replayability with litlerally hundreds of different countries to choose from. Will you play as germany as try to succeed where hitler failed and conquer the known world? or break with history and turn germany democratic and try to maintain world peace? or take a dark horse underdog and try your hand at world domination playing as a small minor country like greece?
the actual visuals and layout of the interface is fairly well designed, it might take a little clicking around to find the information you're looking for, but it's all there to found if you choose to utilize it. there is a crap load of information available, which can be a good thing and bad thing... just depends on your individual preference and your tolerance for looking through and comparing soft attack/hard attack, piercing, defence, etc... numbers for any number of varities and combinations of armies you can create.
Fairly in depth research trees and national focuses allow you to concentrate on whatever items and goals that'll guide you toward the goal you have set for yourself and your country. going to play defensive and just turtle? choose defensive national focuses, beef up your coastal and land forts, and pick diplomatic options to play nice with neighbors or join a faction with others to provide some level of protection. going to go all in and try for world domination? choose aggressive diplomatic options and techs that aid your conquest. the game is deep and allows you to play however you like.
there are a couple small things that could be addressedin subsequent patches or dlc's,,, though these may be minor or nit-picky, but this is a review right? The diplomatic options could be expanded. For instance, once you puppet a nation... that's it, they are you're puppet until the end of time, whether something down the road changes and you want/need to release them... tuff, you cant. the peace conferences seem a little wonky at times, but perhaps that is just the mechanics and decisions of the AI are not shown well or explained. Lastly, the aspect of the factions can probably be expanded, or recalibrated. It can be prette frustrating spending a year or more planning an invasion on a neighbor, building up your production, supply, armies... moving everyone into place... checking and double checking to make sure no entangling alliances are going to bring any other unwanted nations into the fray... you finally get everything right, at just as you declare war, they jump into a faction and now instead of a nice tidy little border war looking to take a province from a neighbor, you're at war with half the world... i know i know, small things. but when you play a game over and over, small things become amplified.
i have seen alot of people complain about the AI. and yes at times, you see them do some head scratching things, or see your own armies leave the front line to travel from once side of your country to the other, only to turn back around and head back... which can be problematic in war time... but i dont find this to be a game breaker. you learn some little work arounds, a learn to try to keep a close eye on your front lines so that things completely crumble before you can jump in a and reroute your folks. but This is a paradox game, and like most others there will be patches and dlc's, further increasing the replayability and improving the game play and rebalancing things and fixing bugs as they go.
i really did not think i would end up enjoying the game as much as i have. this is the only game that i have found myself putting Crusader Kings 2 on the back burner for... which to me is definitely an endorsement of it's quality and playability.
really enjoyed the game, and look forward to the forthcoming dlc's!

First of all, let me say the game is really pretty. It has a great retro aesthetic that moves and feels like an SNK classic. The most obvious comparison being Metal Slug of course. The music is good as well and captures that same era perfectly and is generally catchy and unobtrusive.

My unfortunate first negative review on steam.  Bought this game with the intentions of playing with a friend, but even from the get-go (And all the way up till the end boss) I had nagging issues that continued to hamper my experience with the game.
The foremost offender is the incredibly awkward controlling.  Characters react based on how heavy their weapons are, but even with light equipment, jumps can be incredibly pixel percise with a slow reaction to pressing the jump button.   This becomes incredibly annoying on bosses that rush from side to side on the screen, and you think you press the button early enough only to have the wind up time keep you from clearing your foe.  Aiming can also be an issue when trying to shoot smaller enemies that move through the air (Not to mention chase you after the camera changes and moves them off screen), theres no way to shoot diagonally which means you'll have to constantly run under vertical enemies to hit them or lead them into your shots.
As you get further in, you notice that the mission strcutres all fall into the same few catagories:  Find stuff or kill/capture stuff.  It becomes more tedious in the latter half of the game as the levels expand, leaving you and your friend(s) to traverse large boring structures with occasionally respawning enemies that even with high health and defense items, can still tear away large portions of your health.  And with limited carrying space for items, trying to heal in our outside the hospital zones can be incredibly tedious as there's no ingame way to speed up the hospital healing process.  I suppose thats why most missions have extra long times (Anywhere between 15-30 minutes usually), but it just bogs down the experience.  The bosses are far to repetitive too, having to face the same lot multiple times across the games ranked missions and an occaisonal unique boss at the end of most ranks.
The weapon crafting is an excercise in patience, having to always constantly change out one gun trait for another, taking time in order to get anywhere close to a satisfying weapon.  More so, since the crafting system relies on the materials you find in the stage, you may be forced to run back into earlier levels and hope that enemies respawn AND drop the items you're looking for.
If I'm pressed to say anything positive about it, the presentation has a nice psuedo-Metal Slug/SNK feel thats still unique enough to be a full rip off, and the music often catchy.  But thats not enough to get a recommendation here, its just not fleshed out enough to be fun either by yourself or with friends.

It's very well designed and thought out. Obviously inspired by dark souls and bloodborne. The enemies are incredibly interesting and....dark, if you actually look at them before stabbing. A tree made of men is a little intimidating. The one thing I don't like to well is the platforming, and it's only really bad at one part. Most of the time it's irritating to have to navigate your way through an entire maze just to attempt a jump, and in some cases it can lead to insta-death making you have to walk ALL the way back from a church. The devs seem to know this though, so it's not terrible. The places you go through are very unique, and they reuse enemies very sparingly, so each area feels like another (dark) adventure. The bosses aren't like most bosses in other games where they are just another challenge. Each boss has a new way to entirely destroy you. One boss I fought decided to jump around and throw potions at me, setting the battlefield ablaze. Another decided to straight up shoot me. Basically, bosses vary. The weapons you use feel amazing and great, especially when you land a good hit. The loud *crunch* or *slice* through an enemy is incredibly satisfying. Plus, if you're like me and attack with a huge blade, you usually hit the enemy with a overkill. This causes the immediantly satisfying beheading of an enemy, as their head flys off and soars through the room. Plus, it's two player, couch play. You get a buddy and cut through enemies.
In short, good game.

Dark and Souls. This game takes so much influence from Dark Souls franchise that it's sometimes hard to remember I'm actually playing a hard 2D metroidvania. Here's why.
First of all the game world has distinctive areas. You begin from a shore (after a short playable opening) and enter a grey building. Inside you'll find a shrine, similar to a bonfire from Dark Souls that lets you heal, level up and grants access to a merchant, blacksmith etc. Shrines also let you quick travel between them which saves you from many headaches since the map has so many secret rooms, areas, clifs and nooks that it takes some time to get used to the travelling. Using the shrine respawns every slain opponent (excluding bosses of course) as does bonfire in DS.
Enemies. Most of them are your typical slow crawling zombies that takes couple of hits and pose little threat. Then there are the faster and smaller ones that are hard to catch and deal nasty damage. Big armored knights, huge hulking golems, wizards, skeletons, dragons, demons, abominations and hanged men + many, many more. Enemies, encounters and compositions varied in such ways that I feel the game encourages to experiment with gear and how to approach the fights.
Gear/items. So. Many. Light/heavy armors, swords, axes, whips, ranged weapons, hammers, one and two-handed weapons, staffs, magic, prayers and shields. Usable items for temporary buffs, throwable weapons, different kinds of arrows etc. I played through the game as a cleric in light armors, wielding a one-handed mace with both hands for extra damage, using healing spells to stay alive longer struggles.
Plot. I seriously don't know. I'm bad at concentrating in a story when I can be whacking enemies and killing huge bosses. There are NPC's aroung the world that chat with you and sell you stuff but the further I went to less I read. That's a pity but I feel that Salt and Sanctuary's strength lies elsewhere. It's in the medieval landscapes and in the combat that packs a serious punch. It's in the feeling of wonder and excitement, in failing and overcoming.
Difficulty. Hard. I used a walkthrough at times to mitigate useless running around and to check couple of bosses weaknesses. I love hard games and play for the challenge and this was the best way for me to enjoy this adventure. Some bosses take many tries to beat and few might even force you to do some extra leveling before getting past them. Bosses are nicely varied also and look similar to DS's crooked mythos.
It took me 20 hours to complete the game. I didn't get all the achievements but I did kill all the optional bosses and grinded quickly for a better gear at one point. I believe that it might take closer to 50 hours to do everything "on your own" but 20 hours was more that fine with me. Definitely worth the price. Holy Sh*t, this game... You try it for the first few minutes and you instantly fall in love with it.
Salt and Sanctuary is basicly a game inspired by darksouls, But in 2D. The gameplay works the same: Be reckless, you get ♥♥♥♥ed over, Instead of souls, you have Salt and you spend those to level up and upgrade your gear.
But compared to darksouls, this game stands out on it's own very easyly; Gameplay wise, it's rather different since it's a 2D game, the atmosphere feels claustrophobic once you enter in rooms, sometime in total darkness wich forces you to use up torches to see in the dark or to equip something that will give you a few hits of what's happening around you. Another huge feature of the game is the skill tree. In this skill tree, you start somewhere different depending of wich class you choose at the begining. the left side of the tree is mostely Oriented toward spells, sightly over it, Daggers, then swords, Hammers and so forth. Each point spent in the tree gives you stats that will help you toward  choosing your playstyle.
For exeple; if you want to do a knight, you'll probably go to the top left where the tree have alot of STR upgrades, It's also where you'll find the skill required to weild better swords (Weapons range from level 0 to 4.) And along the way, you could also reach in the Heavy armor mastery skill along with shields, and some upgrades to your stamina and carry weight to be more efficient in close combat.
Another similar thing to the darksouls is the fact that the world is one huge map, only difference is than instead of bonfires, you have Altars, where you can praise an entity. (Little tip; depending of your awnser at the begining of the game with the first NPC, you can actuly get different entity.) And in this altar, you can donate idols wich will spawn an NPC that will aid you in your journey (Merchant, Blacksmith, traveler...)
Another thing is that if you get in an aleready claimed altar, you can level up like normal but cant donate  anything unless you join them.
Another thing that's different from darksouls is the curency. Yes it has salt. but it also have Gold. Gold is used to buy things from NPCs. Meaning that you don't have to worry about farming up as much souls to get the gears  and items that you want. Though, if you die, you loose a good 10% (I think it's 10%, from what I experienced.) of what you acumulated so far.
So yeah. This is a basic summary of what the game is like.
Pros:
+Challenging
+Looks realy smooth, The animations on the characters and enemy are realy satisfying to watch
+The game ambiance is very well detailed and imersive.
+Alots of variety in the class you'd like to play
+Controls very well with a keyboard (No clue about controler.)
+Enemys and bosses are fun to fight against...
Cons:
-...But some bosses are ridiculously easy if you have a good shield. Only exception are the ones that deals elemental damage.
-I got lost. Alot. The game isnt holding your hand at all to show you where to go, wich is a bad but also a good thing since it encourages you to explore.
-The platformings sections with certain enemys shooting you at a distance can be pretty anoying.
Final note: 8.5/10 . The game is realy great, specialy if you love the souls series. Most players that liked those will get familiar with the game very quickly, and it's friendly enough to let new players play it without worrying too much.

Dishonored is one of the most well designed video games in decades.
Every aspect of this game is made to improve your experience, removing almost any layer of tedium other stealth games might include.
You are able to teleport and look through walls to see notable objects and people, as well as a handful of other possibly useful powers (mind you, Blink and Dark Vision (respectively) were the only two powers I'd use frequently).
It gives you the ability to automatically disintegrate people you've just killed, making it easier to remain undetected and not have to deal with bodies. However, the game also encourages you to non-lethally deal with guards and targets, leaving unconcious bodies around, creating a difficulty setting without actually making a difficulty setting. It gives you the power to make the game harder for yourself, which I wouldn't think is very easy to do when designing a game.
There are multiple paths you can take to get to your destination, and I'm thankful many of the best are from rooftop to rooftop. It not only makes you feel like the spooky scary assassin everyone makes you out to be, but it's generally the most scenic route.
It has a scavenging element where you collect maccabre pieces of bone to improve your powers, which the game gives you a tool (a mechanical, talking heart) to find them. Even when unequipped, the heart beats in your pocket when you're very close to items. They could've simply just placed them around levels and mentioned that these items exist in this level, but they didn't.
Probably the epitome of good game design for a stealth game is infinite saves at any point,
to the autosaves it makes. It makes the 'trial and error' approach the best approach, which can encourage risky and generally fun ways to deal with your target(s).
Many of these aspects mentioned above does add up to this game not being very realistic, but it's a joy to see a game that chooses when it needs to be realistic and when it needs to be a game correctly (at least in my biased mind).
For example, you can't contract the deadly disease plaguing your city, even though you're frequently touching and getting spit on by contracted victims. However, what would that add to the game if that were the case? Your health slowly going down during each mission? Weakened powers? A possible, 'infected' ending? I can't think of a good reason to include it, and again, am thankful the developers did not include an element of it (at least in the base game).
Overall, Dishonored is an amazing game that plays great, looks great, and generally feels great. If you're a fan of stealth games, this game is amazing. If you're not, consider giving this a try anyway, because it's very forgiving.

We as a community asked for free to play, because the game's playerbase was so low, that would hardly get a single match in a whole day. The devs actually answered to our feedback and gave us the free to play.
Now, where did they ruined their game?
1st- The developers took away their team deathmatch mode from their servers (the main attraction to the game) and only have 1 game mode and only 1 map. This issue happened before the free to play release, and even after the community gave the developers feedback on how having only bierball available is boring, they didn't care.
2nd- The developers released a "fake" free to play game, where you're forced to pay to be able to unlock more characters from the game (you don't have any type of in game currency). You're forced to stay with only 2 characters. In a heavy teambased game like this, being able to have a way to unlock the other characters is necessary to counter other team compositions. Given that freemium users have this big disadvantage over paying users, this game is considered pay2win (paying users will have the character advantage that will help your team and counter the enemy team).
This was also the reason why you see so many negative ratings, because even after all the feedback, the developers don't care. Which leads to the third, and I will explain why.
3rd- The developers are lazy , aren't able to handle constructive criticism and delete your criticism threads. Me, along with other players that actually cared about the game, posted feedback over the months, that is after the free to play release, constantly ignored. I will give you an example, where I posted a thread saying the reason why the developers ruined the game and where they could fix it. I was once one of the people who defended the game after the free to play release, because I thought that the developers just made a mistake on their free to play model and that they cared about the game. I was wrong, very wrong.
Seeing how the developers ruined their game and them not caring about fixing it. Seeing how they obviously can't handle criticism and make their forums like we're in Germany during the times of Hitler (nothing against Germans ofc).

I liked this game. It gets a lot of flak for not being a "landmark" title like people seem to expect from id, but that doesn't automatically mean it's terrible. But it's not fantastic. [Note: I did not play the co-op or multiplayer modes]
The world is one of the more interesting post-apocalyptic settings I've seen in a video game, with obvious inspiration from Mad Max but with its own twist on the setting. The characters aren't really anything special, just basic NPCs that tell you where to go and what to do, then inexplicably disappear. Despite the cardboard characters, the world itself feels very lived in and real. The various throw-away NPCs scattered throughout towns comment on the events of the game as they unfold, they walk and move around so they don't just stand in one place for weeks on end like many other games, and some even move to new locations entirely.
The plot and story start out simple and strong. It's nothing amazing, but it's done well enough that it works. The entire first half of the game is spent doing odd jobs for the various citizens of the wastelands (mostly killing♥♥♥♥♥♥. Turns out, that's just a way of gaining notoriety so they can explain the terrible second half of the game. Roughly half of the way through the game, the game thrusts you into an anti-authoritarian resistance movement that has literally zero connection to the previous arc, with very little buildup to this sudden switch. You go from a wasteland survivor to ragtag rebel toppling a technologically superpower (that's never been done before!). What really blasts the story's coffin into the dirt is the ending: there basically isn't one. You go to a building, press some buttons, and there's a cutscene.
Mechanically speaking, the gameplay is solid. The combat in general is really fun and just feels nice. I did feel as if certain weapons (the assault rifle, pistol with normal ammunition, the DLC nailgun's default mode) were totally useless once you get alternate ammunition or different guns, but they still served a purpose in the long run. What really surprised me is the variation in enemies. There's really only "two" enemies in the game: mutants and humans. But each faction of the humans has its own unique look and sound and combat style, which makes combat with different factions feel very refreshing despite the enemies more or less having the same set-up. I personally wasn't a huge fan of the vehicle combat, personally. Late in the game, the opposing vehicular forces mostly just spam missiles and shields and it's just exhausting to fight them. That being said, the vehicles themselves felt very nice and responsive - even with mouse and keyboard.

Defense Grid: The Awakening is, at its core, a puzzle game. It's a good one, but the various levels are not nearly as free-form as you might initially believe. Many levels can be beaten in multiple ways, but many levels favor a particular layout of towers. After playing through a dozen levels or so, you realize certain consistent strategies to victory: make the path the aliens travel as long as you can, and build a lot of cannon towers. Yes, there are nuances beyond that, but the strategy isn't really all that deep.
But that's okay. It's an easy game to play in 30-minute chunks; the lack of save game slots (as opposed to the acceptable-but-not-ideal checkpoint system) is annoying, but mildly so. (Although, to be fair, that might be just my own over-saving nature speaking.) It's rewarding, pretty, nicely paced, and has a decent enough plot.
I bought it for something like $2.49. At that price, a great bargain.

I've been trying to uncover the words to quite describe the experience that this game truly is, but it is something that explaining can do no justice.  To me, this is one of the greatest, deepest, most enjoyable, exciting, unique, adventurous and thrilling game I have ever played.  Seriously, the rushes and adventures that come out of a good MO day are like no other.  That being said, to enjoy the game I suggest these things:
1:  Commit at least 20 hours to really getting your toes wet with it.
I remember almost quiting a few times in the first hours of play because I was so overwhelmed by the complexities and was also not at first impressed by the combat.  However, given a bit more time to become fully immersed and to start to realize the mechanics behind the once daunting leveling systems, things really started to take a unique and exciting light.  After having my first major tragedy and first success, and started to truly see just how far the rabbit hole goes.
2:  Bring your Creativity and Imagination into this one.
Seriously, go back into "pretend" time when you play this.  Just use your mind!  You are given pretty much zero direction or instruction in anything, however when you think creatively, you'll find that the mechanics and answers to every question are all thoughtful, logical, and makes sound sense.  This is the part I am having the hardest time describing.... everything is just intelligently and deeply and richly designed that the your imagination really is the limit.  I read the cliché "Open Sandbox!  Do what you want!" so many times now and am still regularly let down by the said "Freedoms" in those games, but MO has really impressed me with it's opportunities.
Leveling is something akin to Oblivion, where you can level skills even like Jumping, and do so simply by doing it.  To improve your Axe skill, just use an Axe.  Everything breaks down into ridiculous subcategories in a good way, expecially the knowledge trees, like "Zoology" breaking down into all of the proper subspecies and geni categories of the actual science.
You can fill all Secondary Skills all the way up, but only have 1100 Primary Skill Points to spend.  This is the same for P2P and F2P players, the difference being that a P2P player can assign up to  100 points on a single Primary Skill, while F2P players max out at 60 points per Primary.  You can shift these stats around even after all spent with an interesting +, -, Lock system of allocating the points.  There are just SO many Primary Skills, to be truly great at something, you will need to specialize.  I realized this most as I went into Taming, which is far more than just "Taming" = 100.
You'll want knowledge of the species to increase your ability, Taming, (Advanced) Creature Control, Domestication, Beast Mastery, etc etc.  To craft, you'll need far more than "Armoring."
You'll need an understanding of the ores and minerals you are infusing into your armors and weapons, how to use the Forge, the Kiln, the Armor Crafting Station, and all other stations you'll want to use, like Bow/Shield/Weapon.
Some skills cannot be learned by engaging in it alone, but must be learned by reading a book on the subject.  Getting your first dabble into the magic schools is done in this way.  Even your Book Reading skill goes up as you read and even that has subcategories like "Skim Reading."  Books are read in a way similar to how Elder Scrolls Online did their crafting trait learning.  Some books can take a real week or  more to get through if you're not a good reader or the subject is something dense.  Even your Running skill is broken down into things like Running Technique, Breathing Technique, and Sprinting, and Swimming has subskilled like Diving, Crawl Stroke, and more.
Full Open World PvP creates for unique rushes, stresses, planning and cooperation with others. There is also Full Open World Building Construction, both personal and for Guilds.  The Guilds actually control territory across the realm, can build entires cities, install NPCs.  Theoretically and practically done already, you can build entire functioning cities that are more active, thriving, bigger, grander, even than the built in cities of the game.
At first I thought Combat was super sluggish, clunky, outdated, and lame. Given some time and experience though and finally getting a grasp on the Parry System, it is really addictive, rewarding, and fullfilling.  There is a ton of skill in the combat.  Attack and blocking can be done from 4 sides, depending on which way you first move your mouse as you are attacking/blocking.  All attacks can be charged for extra damage and a properly timed block will be a "Parry" which allows for a quick  and powerful counterattack.
Early on I was terrifed, and rightly so, of even the lowliest of creatures and dangers about, feeling every bit of the fragile nature of my own Mortality.  I love though how, not just as my stats increase, but as my actually skill as a player increases, you  really start to feel a sense of pride, power, and accomplishment as you look upon the things which once caused you such fear and woe.
The world is quite large and fully open and explorable.  At first impression, it was TOO big and overwhelming.  It seemed unmanageable, untraversable, and though "open" to be explored, it felt inaccessible.  Now, having done a good bit of traversing across the realm I think that the size is just right.   Your first terrifying hike on foot to a new city could take hours lost and wandering helplessly, searching for any sign of the vague landmarks given to you by strangers in the previous town.  Later, you'll find yourself well mounted and soaring across the plains, confident in your direction and ability to reach your destination by dawn's first light.
The world is full of dungeons, adventures, riches, and plunder for the bold to possess, but serious danger lurks too in every shadow.  There is zero fogiveness and a mistake or surprise encounter with a squad of maurading PKers could lead to the loss of every last one of your precious possession.
I'll never forget my gf and I's first real rush.  We had just planned and successfully executed our first venture from our start town MorinKhur to the primary start town of Tindrem, which was awesome in and of itself.  Upon arriving, we were quickly met with a request from a passing player and hired on as mercenaries to gather some precious horn, which could only be found from Minotaurs in the high hilllands a good journey away.  I'll never forget the three of us venturing far into the wilderness, delving into the heart of the mountain, and battling those bullmen in the dark depths of the earth.  We successfully returned with the loot after a narrow escape from several members of a Guild of killers (PYRE) and banked more gold than we had otherwise made in the last 3 weeks of play lol.  It was so epic.... but that's what this game offers.  There is no quest giver who says "get me some horn from the minotaur."  It forces you to create your own objectives, form your own parties, make your own goal, and choose who you are in the world.
Crafting is ♥♥♥♥ing insane.  The resources are numerous and an understanding of them (Skill Points spent in the Knowledge of the material) is necessary for their well use in creation.  Weapons alone have the handles, hilts, blades, etc all of which can be uniquely forged and crafted with a variety of materials, each with their own merit.
Graphics obviously are not the best and were originally the turn off for me and my excuse not to try it out for the longest time.  Now I regret not having dove in long ago!  I really recommend this one and encourage you to give it a shot~!

I got the full loot collectors edition way back when. Stopped playing for half a decade or so. Recently came back. Thoroughly addicted to the full loot seamless open world PvP madness! Basically do whatever you want in game.

I played this game for over 2 years when it first released (i.e. around 2010-2012) and it is a great game if you like PvP and full loot. If you do not like these things you are going to have a hard time enjoying it. I left at the time because the game was being driven in a direction of making it a medieval quake arena instead of a sandbox but I have returned recently (August 2017) to check the game out and a lot of improvements have been made that are making me fall in love with Mortal Online again
Now obviously the game is not perfect but here are some bullet points for you to digest:
- Freedom to make your build, you can make it a straight fighter, refiner, crafter or whatever but the system shines when you can find a mixed build that works
- Full loot PvP - if you hate full loot games there is not much of a point of going with MO. This said there are areas of the game where these things don't happen as often (example, the continent of Sarducaa is usually more peaceful than Myrland)
- The game is not F2P. Consider it instead an unlimited trial which is great for anyone wanting to try out the game but if you want to be competitive you will have subscribe at some stage.
- Free placement of structures allowing you to build your own town (guild recommended if you don't want to be driven insane)
- Dungeons. Simply the best dungeons you will ever experience in any game - mostly because they feel like real dungeons. The echo sounds in the caves, the lighting conditions (or the pitch dark if you don't bring a torch) the real sense of discovery. The game is worth it for this alone.
- There are bugs. It is a small team and the bugs can sometimes be annoying, especially in a full loot game but the devs seem to be actively working in the game so hopefully this will be less of an issue.
So in conclusion, I fully recommend the game if you are tolerant to:
1 - PvP
2 - Full loot
3 - Some bugs
If you can get past that, get ready for an experience you won't find in any other MMORPG
The best open-world, full-loot pvp game you will ever try,

From the screenshots, I was expecting 2D Dark Souls - as the comparison is obvious. Surprisingly, what I played was a deepy involving experience, filled with adventure, constant danger, and fast paced, viceral combat.
Salt and Sanctuary takes inspiration from the Souls series and flips it, incorporating Metroidvania elements across many beautiful environments. The design of the level builds the tension of exploration brilliantly, and the dramatic bosses and deadly monsters only increase it more - though, occasionally I found myself longing for more enemy variety. Often, you will fight smaller monsters, many of whom act and attack similarly; though this is minor complaint, as the variation of the larger monsters breaks this up immensely.
The weapons feel fantastic to use, and the armour looks amazing. That said, for most of the game, what looked the best is what I used; armour values didn't seem to matter greatly. My only real major complaint is that many of the bosses relyed heavily on fire based attacks, meaning that to pass them, I would be required to stack fire resistance items, and that is all. This happened many times, certainly more than the other elements, and I saw little variation in other bosses elemental attacks.
Still, Salt and Sanctuary is a finely crafted game - one that I will certainly play again. These minor issues don't compare to the sense of wonder and curiosity that this game gave me, and I am glad to have purchased it.

So I'm a big fan of the Souls series so when I saw this game, I had to have it. Salt and Sanctuary follows a simple premise, you're a warrior out on a quest to save a princess, like I said it's simple. When players start they'll notice a lot of similarities between this game and Dark Souls. For instance the UI has a similar makeup. It's simple and to the point. The character creation screen is also similar to Dark Souls in that you can create your class, origin, starting gift.
The artwork of this game is really nice in my opinion, it has a very dark feel to it though the character's faces leave much to be desired. There is actually music that plays throughout the game, something that we haven't seen in Dark Souls which for this game is a welcomed aspect. There is a slight learning curve if you're familiar with the Souls games, the switch from 3D to 2D makes it apparent. However, if you're familiar with metroidvania games like this then it won't be too difficult to transition, just come in with an empty cup.
This game isn't necessarily easy but it's also not necessarily hard. It's a little difficult getting started but once you do it eases up. You will probably have to grind in some sections just so you can level up and apply black pearls (skill points). Speaking of the skill system, it's pretty open. It reminds me of the Sphere Grid in Final Fantasy X, actually it's almost exactly like that. For those of you who don't know, you level up and for each level you get a black pearl or skill point which you can apply to things like Dexterity, Strength, Magic, or even a mastery like Heavy Armor.
Multiplayer is a lot of fun in this game but unfortunately it's only available in shared screen so you'll have to be in the same room with each other and have an extra controller. You can access multiplayer by having a "Stone Sellsword Statue", once you do you need to place it in YOUR sanctuary, think of sanctuaries like bonfires. Once the statue is placed you can choose another character in your game for your buddy to play as.
I've seen it mentioned before but there is no mini-map, your best bet is to make note, try to remember, or see if you can find a map online to follow. You will get lost, you will come to the same place over and over again. I've caught myself doing it a few times already. Combat is simple like Dark Souls and you'll recognize that as well. The bosses are interesting, some of them are tough, some are frustrating, and some are a complete waste of space.
Overall, if you enjoy Dark Souls or metroidvania games then you will enjoy Salt and Sanctuary, period.

Right off the bat i have to say the obvious thing, I loved this game because it's so similar to dark souls 1; but just beacause is so similar doesn't mean is a clone; S&S takes all the right things from the dark souls formula (no map, punishing difficulty, several classes) and adds it's own ideas to it.
Some of the differences are that:
- Salt (souls) is different than money, you only lose some money when you die, but all of your salt is stolen from the enemy that killed you, to retrieve the salt you have to slay the enemy (who is stronger because of the salt).
- Sanctuaries (Bonefires) come in two kinds, those who only heal you and reset enemies and those which let you level up and summon merchants, for the second type of sanctuary you have to choose a covenant which affects different things like how your "estus" work.
- The level up system come in two parts, when you level up you spend your salt and that increases some stats, but when you level up you also get a "skill" item which you can spend immediately or whenever you want which increases specifically one stat; this is great if you want to not risk your salt but do not want to actually level up yet.
The gameplay mechanics and atmosphere feels and play like dark souls 1, the "soul" of the franchise is without a doubt there.
Leaving aside the fact that this is a separate game from the soul series I literally think this is a way bettr sequel to dark souls 1 than dark souls 2 (which i disliked immensely), 10 out of 10.

Ska Studios originally made their mark on the video game scene with their Xbox 360 Live Arcade series, The Dishwasher which became a nigh-instant cult classic side-scrolling beat-em-up/hack-and-slash a la goldenaxe, double dragon, etc.
a friend of mine was very hyped about those games and got one of them at least, on his xbox 360 and i got to watch him play the brutal carnage-filled work of art. it was interesting, to say the least.
however, Steam's indie release friendliness has proven far more fruitful for newer developers and quite honestly i'm glad that the company has decided to bring what will probably be their biggest title for a long time, to steam, as well as many other platforms (including the vita apparently).
Salt and Sanctuary is a strange metroid-vania beat-em-up/platform/hack-and-slash side-scroller hybrid that takes the best of Ska's original Dishwasher series in terms of stylization and function, and mixes it with features from the most popular of brutal, unforgiving hack-and-slashers to-date: the Dark Souls franchise. this is no mere 'souls clone', and although it may not be for everyone, it is a gem of a game that i don't see getting one-upped for awhile.
you play as a shipwrecked survivor (whom you design a bit, yourself) who was originally enlisted to protect someone and after a bad night on the seas... have lost track of that person... and you have also been shipwrecked in a strange land, seemingly overburdened with undead and bandits... and giant bearwolf things... yeah...
so here's the breakdown: if you like metroidvanias, especially dark, grotesque, atmospheric artsy-ish games, you may want to give this one a look. if you like darksouls and don't mind side-scroll platforming, you should probably check this out. if you grew up with some of the craziest nes, snes and sega genesis games out there like double dragon, golden axe, battletoads, and so many more beat-em-up platformers, you may enjoy this title as well. so here's the scores
1) GRAPHICS- 9/10
the graphics are the most artistic thing about this title, and what sets it apart from other games. it has similarities to ska's other hit series the dishwasher, but it is not a clone of that in terms of style or details. it's kind of its own thing. and it does what it does quite well. my only gripe is that sometimes i don't see an enemy until i'm walking into it and then... i'm getting clawed at ._. but these visuals are stunning to say the least.
2) SOUND EFFECTS/MUSIC- 10/10
I havent let the music set in too much yet or had it up very loud but it really does paint the atmosphere nicely when it's there. it feels retro at times but has a modern-tech sound as well so that it doesn't just chiptune you to death while you're trying to emmerse yourself. it fits the game well. a more pixelated game may have benefitted from a more cartoonish or chiptunish soundtrack but this game has what it needs for sounds and you'll not have much of a gripe here yourself, i am sure.
3) STORYLINE- ??/10
i like what i've found so far on the story but i'm REALLY not that far in and can't say much about it so i'm just going to leave it at... it's interesting, but in the same vein as the souls series, it's not extremely story-based so you don't learn a whole lot at first... possibly ever... but it's enough to be intriguing.
4) GAMEPLAY- 9/10
it's solid. i'm struggling to learn some of the weapons i've found and many seem a bit harder to wield than they should be, like the hitboxes are very specific and the area of your weapon closer to the hilt on a longer weapon won't hurt enemies it seems, but if you learn the hitbox area and timing you can typically do pretty well here. if you have a one handed weapon and a shield, or a two handed weapon, it seems blocking is a viable option, and a necessity. timing is everything here as well... it's also a bit too easy to get overwhelmed with enemies that 'spawn' behind you and in front, and some of which are hard to see until you're getting pounded by five to ten guys, some of which can do some harsh damage... ugh. but, as per the souls series, you drop your experience if you die once and have to go back for it- the twist is, the enemy who killed you takes it and you have to seek revenge to get it back. if you die while an enemy still has your experience, you lose what he had forever... ouch. this can be a bit unforgiving, and with the few clunky things this game has going against it, may turn some away, but if you are a souls fan at all you are used to this sort of grind. thankfully there doesnt seem to be a durability factor in this but i could be wrong. i hope i'm not, because although that worked in the souls games, i don't want it in this one.
OVERALL- 9.5/10
seriously, this game is pretty epic so far. i've heard you can get up to like 30 hours from one playthrough, which isn't bad for the price (and if you get it on sale that's a damn good amount of hours for one playthrough, and the game has definite replayability). if you like souls games, metroidanias, beat-em-ups, hack-and-slashers, horror-ish games, grindfests, gorefests, brutal, unforgiving (yet mostly fair) experiences, and/or indie games, you should check this out, for sure. maybe wait until a sale if you feel the price is too high for you or you're still unsure after reading reviews... but definitely look into it. i warn you though, sales don't seem to come often for this one... but it's new-ish, so that's to be expected.

My only recommendation is this: if you get this game,
. Seriously, do NOT spoil anything for yourself! Don't look up videos, don't look up walkthroughs or plot summaries - that will take every last ounce of fun out of the game.
Overall, 10/10 game, and it easily makes it as one of my top favorite games of all time.

When I discovered how good charge was on a video, I got closer to my HDTV to read all these little texts, and it made the last few missions easy as well.

Farabel is a charming and addictive little turn-based strategy game. The central premise of "turning back time", while interesting to the plot, does not really change the feeling of working through progressively difficult levels. Everything is balanced to provide a good upward hardness curve. However, unlike something like Memento - where gradually seeing the past makes earlier story make sense - I couldn't shake the feeling that Farabel was simply a series of interesting scenarios, without any cohesive plot. Although, lowering the main unit's abilities each turn provides an interesting twist, while working out which specific abilites you can least live without.
Turn-based strategy itself is nuanced and rewarding. It's similar in feel to something like Crowntakers or Banner Saga. Mastery of unit abilities make you feel like you're controlling the battlefield with skill. The optional challenges for each level provide replay value and the battle sandbox with two variations (win a series of battles or survive on a single battlefield for as long as possible against spawning foes) provide plenty of value. Worth every penny even at full price, I would say.
In terms of difficulty, the AI is not afraid to pick on weak units or focus attention on game-losing objective, so it feels like a fair fight, rather than massaging your ego.
Pros:
- Bright, clean style
- Addictive and engaging turn-based combat with interesting unit balances
- AI tries to win
- Varied scenarios
- Story dialogue kept pleasantly tight and short
Cons:
- Animations feel a bit basic
- Enemy units hard to distinguish in some areas (goblin soldiers versus snipers, mounted cavalry)
- Can't rotate the battlefield
- A strange absence of multiplayer skirmish. I don't really play a lot of multiplayer, but I know this will deter some players.
- Line of sight not always clear around scenery

You can play in classic mode with randomized battle ground, various army sizes and different levels of AI difficulty. You can also play in endless defense mode and trust me, it's a real challenge. The army composition with a defined budget is a strategy game by itself.
Last but not least, with the addition of these game modes, you can now play both races, humans and orcs! And they have very different units and play style.
From a strategy point of view, at the time I write this review, some minor details may be improved, like the horsemen who not always choose the best path to charge an enemy, or the lack of zone Of Control. But regarding the last free update and how the developer seems to improve its creation, I'm not worry about the future of this game.

I highly recommend this game to anyone who was, or is, a fan of metal slug. This game uses similar mechanics, but also does away with intsa-death, for you and your enemies.
It also adds further depth with customization options, such as knife-type, gun-types, ammo-types, and bionic mods (akin to passive boosts).
Although the campaign does run a acceptable length of time, some people may find the levels repetitive - you are required to do several missions (about 7) per area, and you will revisit the same areas. There are 108 enemies, so enemies repeat.
The music is great though, I certainly didn't mind listening to the same track often.
Overall, I'd say that even though the game has some repetitive elements, I found it very enjoyable, completed the game, and did not regret a single hour of my time. If you're a fan of 2D platform-shooters, this is definitely for you!

A reboot of those old-school action packed platformers. But with RPG elements, like crafting your own prefered equipment. Sounds good right? Well this game is not very good. It is boring.
The problem is threefold:
- you now need to "grind" materials for upgrades. And then you need to build a bunch of random stuff to unlock proficiencies. I got bored with this system and the available options about 10 missions in. Surely late game stuff might be nice and all, it is an unattractive system early on. Especially because you have no idea where you should be farming in the first place.
- the maps are the same, over and over again. Same enemies, but that is not all, they are applied in a very repetetive way as well. Sniper on a ledge where you need to get close, rifleman jumping down on you, spearmen attacking from above, drill in a hole, metal drone when you zipline down. Repeat 20 times every stage. There, spoiled the first 3 maps, on which you do at least 3-5 missions each. Boring and annoying.
- the "quests" you get to do are boring. Gather 10 of this. (random drops or in boxes, so walk around the entire map. Again) Go to this NPC. And even the Boss, which could have been interesting, is annoying and boring. He moves from the scene at random. So you have to go through the level you got to know by heart by now, AGAIN to find he moves away after just one attack, so you have to track him down AGAIN.
Oh and it gets worse: Then you get to do that boss AGAIN. Same map, same fight, but now you have to finish with a shock grenade. Which is the first time you get to use these, they are hard to use, you get only three, so then if you fail to get it right 3 times, you can just as well go and restart the map. After two runs so facing and beating this boss 3 times I had enough.
No more waiting in an infirmary for 50 seconds (!?!) to heal up, no more cleaning up / skipping the same enemies 20 times over and finding that you have 50/9 for one craftin component and 1/2 out of some random rare drop you never can seem to find.

This is a great game that unfortunately falls into the curse of "gets good a couple hours in". It takes a while for the mission structure and crafting to click, and not all the missions are super well designed; map checking is often required (but easy), and the map is useless for a couple of off-beat missions.
The real meat of the game is building and customizing gun parts, but unfortunately since this requires materials, you can't jump right into making a gun, you have to play the first few levels, which are basically tutorials. And even once you can make a few gun parts, the guns don't get really fun until you start adding elements and special bullet types (freezing bullets, shotguns, bouncing bullets, homing missiles that pierce walls!) I feel the game would have been much better received if this were explained better and you got some materials to play with out of the starting gate instead of having to use the starter pistol for a few levels.
This is, however, a great chill-out game, and if you enjoy grinding materials and crafting there's plenty of that to do. People call it Monster Hunter crossed with Metal Slug, but the gameplay is a bit more like Mega Man (with a single, customized gun rather than switchable energy-based weapons). Bosses roam certain maps sort of like Monster Hunter, though the crafting and mission structure are really where the Monster Hunter influence shows. Unlike Metal Slug you have health so you don't die in one hit, but health is still a fairly precious resource.
The gameplay is surprisingly deep; gun weight affects how high you jump and how fast you move, you have consider how all of your gun's parts sum up into a good (or awful) weapon, and there's a bit of inventory management as you can only carry a couple healing/progression enabling items (but you can call for a couple more items mid-level).
Co op gameplay is great--all players get all resources collected, so there's no fighting over drops. This also means playing online with randoms isn't quite as annoying as say Borderlands 2, because no one can swipe your rare drops.

Rage plays out like the brain-damaged lovechild of Fallout and Doom, but is ultimately a fun and exciting experience.
In this game, your guns are practically secondary weapons to the gadgets you'll acquire. From homing steel-edge boomerangs to robot spiders with chainguns, your arsenal fights alongside you. Not to say that your guns are useless, as your weapon upgrades come in the form of specialized ammo, some of which will cause hilarious executions. Every enemy encounter is an opportunity to kill them hilariously and grab their stuff.
Personally, I feel that this game is one of the rare few that may have needed a linear approach, as the open world seems more like a tacked on experience due to the general lack of random events in the overworld that connects various levels. But hey, you can play however you want, and it's still fun to ride and kill in the wastelands, so that's cool. There's even some mission packs (called Wasteland Stories) that you can play with a friend like a regular FPS campaign. Just don't expect it to be easy, you get an auto-revive but you don't get to prepare stockpiles of gadgets like in the main game.
This game is worthy of a sequel, even with all the DOOM4 hype. Probably even more viable because of DOOM4's success, because some of the gameplay can be transplanted here while still retaining the fun little kill-toys.

Developer: InkStains Games
Year: 2015
Genre: Action, Indie
Franchise: N/A
Engine: IDK
TL;DR
Imagine that Hotline Miami is a racehorse. It's fast and slick and stylish, and it gets you across the line with an elegant simplicity. The sequel is like a recently retired racehorse, still fast and slick and stylish, but it gets you across the line with a lot of excess wheezing. This game is like a camel. Sure you can ride it just fine, but it has several excess humps and it limps a bit. For under 5 New Zealand dollars it's a fun little distraction on the way to the grave.
REVIEW
Story:
Woof. The game purposes to be about an escaped Mexican slave trying to regain his memory but it's hard to pick up through the layers on layers of edge. Profanity laden and clumsy, the dialogue and exposition feel like a deviantart port of Hotline Miami's genuinely disturbing and hard-edge story. With that said, you are allowed and encouraged to skip dialogue, so no big deal. 4/10
Graphics:
The sketchbook aesthetic is all well and good until it comes to combat. Looking at small black and white enemies on a black and white background can be disorienting, especially when you are dealing with long ranged foes. The only colour is blood, giving an interesting contrast, but differentiating the enemies from the background would go a long way. 6/10
Gameplay
Now on to the aforementoned humps. A big part of what makes these sorts of games so special is the fast paced action, killing without having to take breaks. This game makes the bizarre decision to have every weapon be manually loaded, which at best adds a level of authentic tension and at worst ruins the pacing. Enemies are far too accurate and can track you endlessly, but it seldom feels overly unfair. The gore leaves a lot to be desired, with no discernable difference between killing an enemy with a shotgun and killing them with a revolver. Ammo is frustratingly rare and the melee combat is far less fun and useful than it needs to be. Everything feels muted, like you're in a Wild West themed LARP rather than a true firefight. Cogs is a fine little puzzle game. The puzzles are of the sort where you slide interlocking tiles around on a board. You probably played with a puzzle like this when you were a child, one with tiles numbered 1 through 15, and you worked to get the numbers in order. Cogs uses similar mechanics, except you're sliding tiles with pipes and gears on them, creating a huge crazy machine.
There are a few dozen puzzles in here, of increasing difficulty. I had to do some diagramming for the last 8 puzzles.
The presentation, however, is the best part of this game. The sound is fantastic - you can hear the steam hissing, the gears grinding, the balloons filling. It's just wonderful to sit with headphones and enjoy the sound as you play.
If you stick through to the end, make sure you score enough to do the "Final Credits" puzzle. It's difficult, and so worth it!
