Everyone mentions the fact that this game is like 'Hotline Miami', but most fail to mention the more memorable moment when you meet 'Johnny Depp' in the game for the first time. Seriously! There is a hand drawn character that could easily pass as 'Johnny Depp' (hence female gamer interests are satisfied), but there is no mention of his stardom being used in credits. I see a lawsuit brewing...
'12 is better than 6' is also mistaken by many to be referring to the fact that 12 bullets are better than 6. It isn't referring to that at all. It's actually an old saying that means to have 12 in a jury is better than having 6 people carry your coffin. In other words it's a world where it is better to kill than be killed. This is the mentality of the character you control Juan who seems to be quick to pew pew his gun in this hand drawn world. Where ultimately the goal is that your hat has to kill all the other hats, to be the dominating hat in town.
Your adventure starts with you (Juan) who has a loss of memory as to who he really is, gunning down a bar patron who recognises his mug from a WANTED poster. As you continue on trying to evade attention, you eventually make your way to a church where a pastor requires your help as it seems that the church has become surrounded by bandits. You try desperately not to get yourself involved, as you don't need the extra attention, but the bandits won't have any ear to your case. Your guilty by association, and you will be gunned down whether you like it or not. Defending yourself against this group of bandits, which strangely includes one Indian (explained later), your then greeted by the knowledge that the men you just defended yourself against was actually the sheriff’s men, and now you’re REALLY in trouble.
With the corrupted law now against you, every bounty hunter is hot on your tail and soon the enlisted help of military, Indians and Chinese workers are also trying to kill you. It seems that every hat in this Western world is a 'bad' hat and even some hats that you thought were good to you, at the conclusion of the game will be hinted to have you outwitted. As all the npc's are playing with that same '12 is better than 6' mentality as you are.
The hand drawn art style is simply gorgeous and is what benchmarks this game as something completely different, it also was made with the game maker studio prog which really dropped my jaw to the floor. The musical score is very fitting for a spaghetti western game and will have you bopping along like your some type of invincible Clint Eastwood.
The mechanics of the shooting can be infuriating at times especially in the 2 bonus levels. Often i found that the knife stabs in the game would not always register, regardless to the fact that I was standing on top of my opponent. Likewise even some of the long range pistol fire would not always be accurate, even though my cross hair was directly on top of my enemies sleeping head.
The weapons have their pros and cons...
The knife is silent, but miss and you'll find that your alerted enemy will kill you in a heartbeat. The pistol is good for long range kills without alerting huge amounts of enemies, but come across an army and you could be in some serious trouble. The Shotgun mows down any enemy with its fragment spray, but alerts practically everyone on map. The rifle is more accurate than most and has more bullets, but again is very loud and will have a huge amount of attention directed your way. The bow and arrow is a silent deadly weapon, but the ammo is sparse in some areas. Shovels and pickaxes are longer and quicker striking melee weapons, but again they seem to have the same troubles as the knife. The turrets will mow down anything you point at, but alerts everyone when used and if they make their way to your turret from several different angles you could find yourself quickly overcome.
There are also two bonus levels available...
Arena - This requires you to make a stand against various waves. After 3 or 4 of them you then get greeted to a different landscape, and if you die you can continue from that particular landscape. This allows you to build up on your total wave tally, but if you ever completely exit out of the 'Arena' then you have to start from wave 1 again, as the game does not register your progress. This means because of the level of difficulty, the Arena will be seriously fun for a very limited few people who either cheat or are crack shots.
Purgatory - Your dead and the only way to come out of the state of being dead is to kill people and collect their souls and return them to an altar as they were all sinners. This really doesn't make any sense whatsoever and seems to be an attempt by the developer to say "sorry I made a game with such a terrible ending". There are 13 locations in this bonus mode and if there is an end to this you will unlikely ever see it as there is no saved progress. Since the games detection of aiming can be dicky and one mistake can be very costly, plus the fact that the ai in the game are always super triggy happy and you will at times be spawned into a 'bad' position again makes this particular bonus level fun for a VERY, VERY FEW people. You again either have to be a cheat, or a master crack shot to progress anywhere.
There is also DLC which involves an art book and the soundtrack, but in all honesty I thought this should have been bonus material for the game itself more than extra costly dlc.
In final a unique shooter made by ink game studios which will grab your attention for quite a few hours. The below video will show you the two bonus levels quickly and then I try to see how far I can get in the story mode of the game without killing anyone. It’s not far and the developer seems to have made it that way on purpose as the whole story is based on the fact that you kill those sherrif men. Still it was further than what I originally thought i would get and is enough of a sample of the game for you to work out if this is the game for you. Thanks for reading...

I bought this game because it seemed like a budget spaghetti-western knockoff of Hotline Miami and I'll be damned if that's not what I got.  While they gameplay was decently emulated the quality suffered in writing and controls.  Identical to Hotline Miami you can hit shift to extend your view away from your character and this is something that is effectively required in many parts of the game to hit distant targets trying to hit you, unfortunately in this game if you look sufficiently far away from your character they cease moving leaving you a sitting duck.  The writing is short and relies alot on it's offensiveness and "tough guy" edginess that goes beyond what you might see in a western, frankly it is bad.  The reoloading and hammer cocking is nice touch, but ammo pickups and hammer cocking sometimes seems unresponsive and unintuitive.  While the visuals are stylistic, the lack of color sometimes feels as though it wasn't so much a style decision as it was that they ran out of money or something, which is to say that the lack of coloring or shading holds the visuals back, even within a niche style.  Last but not least, with the problems in controls and visuals, it's just not that fun to play.  Whereas the AI in Hotline Miami feels intelligent and aggressive this AI just feels aggressive, albeit with better aim.  All in all the game felt like tedium when trying to progress and so I doubt I will play it through to completion.

I enjoyed this one quite a bit.  Many if not most games I've played that try to mix tower defense with a controllable character fall flat because the balance doesn't work.  In this one, though, you can't only focus on one aspect.  If you just level up your weapons a ton, you'll run up against cooldowns and ammo restrictions and never be able to gun down all the enemies yourself.  If you only build towers and try to take a smoke break during the level, you'll be overrun during waves that have skill-dependent enemies.
The inclusion of enemies with a weak point that the player can aim for, but the towers won't, is an inspired choice.  It forces you to build and act in concert with your defenses.  Tough enemies can be slowed down, things that are only vulnerable in a single spot can be sniped, and swarms can be intelligently targeted with AOE attacks.  The sole drawback is that you can only hold 3 guns, and the sniper rifle and cold gun seem, to me, indispensable.
The other complaint I can make is that the 3-D nature of the game isn't fully supported/exploited.  So, unlike most TD games, a tower can't just shoot anything in its 'range'.  It has to have line-of-sight (in most cases).  This is good, as it forces you to think about where to put your blocks, which ones to make shot-transparent, and what obstacles in the level will affect your fields of fire. It's bad, though, because the game will show you a circle on the overhead view that denotes the tower's max range, but nothing else.  If you want to learn what it can actually see, the only solutions are to put your character's perspective as close as you can to the tower's (usually impossible, since you can't stand inside it, and the towers are mostly a lot taller than your PC) or observe what it shoots at during the levels (which requires you to look carefully at the overview while the action's going on, and
participate in the defense).  A feature that gave you the POV of the tower would make this
much easier.
Of note, this recommendation includes the free add-ons unlocking new towers and weapons, as well as the paid-for DLC granting new maps.  This adds much-needed variety, and I would probably be less enthusiastic if I'd played it at release.

Each scenario is well balanced with enough variety in towers and placement, as well as game modes per level, to keep things interesting. Each of the 10 or so towers you can build are unique enough that even late game, you are using a wide variety; there's no "best" tower. Every tower can also be upgraded for more damage/faster fire rate/increased range.
Leaderboards are done extremely well in this game. Your score is ranked worldwide, but then you also see your friends and their scores. This gives it a much more competative feel since you can see how you measure up to your friends per scenario.
The story isn't anything fantastic, but compared to other tower defense games (which usually have no story), it's good.
There is no multi-player and no map editor. Check Defense Grid 2 if interested in these.

Rating 8/10
Overview: Tower Defense
The Good
+ The premise is a bit different than most tower defense games. Rather than the enemies reaching the end of the map, this game has the enemies collecting 'cores' from a specific point on the map and then moving towards the exit. Because of this , your strategy has to be a bit different when placing your towers. In addition the more resources you collect the more interest you earn, thus spending your resources to build/upgrade your towers may not always be the best strategy especially in the beginning of a level.
+20 Main missions and 28 DLC missions. Every map is completely different from the last, some maps have multiple entry and exit points, core locations, pathways. Every map almost feels like a new puzzle, trying to figure out how to make the optimal path to win.
+ The DLC missions are unique and fun. The best DLC levels is mixing the portal universe with this one. Each level is unique and provides an interesting twist to each level altering your strategy.
+ Every mission features a variety of different modes. The modes that cause you to rethink your strategy are probably the best ones. For example, one mode has the entry and exit points reversed, another you can only build level 1 towers, etc.
+ The game features a variety of different towers each one with a unique purpose. The type of tower and the placement plays a big role in the game.
+ Great graphics and effects for this type of game
+controller support
The Bad:
- Other than a variety of different modes per level, this game offers little new.
-Some modes can be very repetitive. Once you figure out what works in a level, you can play different modes with the exact same layout. However these modes are optional.
- The game feels like it was designed with the controller only in mind. Why can't I map every control function on the mouse?

I played this game back when it was in Open Beta in Stage 1, and I really liked it. The only reason I never purchased it was because I didn't have the funds. Now that it's Free to Play, I highly recommend everyone at least try. They're basically remaking the entire game, so it's sort of in beta again, so be prepared for bugs and stuff like that as of July 9th, 2016.
About the game:
The entire game is focused on the theme of 1 vs 4. The player who's all alone controls a monster, which has massive health, armor and damage, making it on par with the hunters, who are the team of four. It requires a lot of coordination as the hunters to win, but the monster has it's own challenges too. Certain things on the map can reveal it's location, and the Tracker (one of the hunter classes) can do the same. The monster goes through three stages of Evolution, evolving from level 1, to 2, to 3. At level 1, it's rather weak, and the hunters can (if coordinating well) easily kill the monster. At level 2, things are more of an even playing field, and at level 3 the monster is stronger than the hunters. The objective is to kill the monster before it kills you or the power relay (a special objective that only shows up at level 3).
Pros:
+Fun
+Lots of different characters
+Low skill floor, high skill ceiling
+Can organize your role preference, and the game tries very hard to give you your #1 preference
+Everything can be unlocked with in-game currency
+Most things can be found by listening well
+In-game voice chat for Hunters
Neutral:
±Games are relatively short, on a 12 minute timer (paused during Combat)
±Have to unlock everything on your own timer, allowing you to get confused by what everyone else does, or save up and buy someone and main them
±No penalty for leaving, so people often do if they don't get their preferred role (usually Monster)
Cons:
-Things aren't very well explained at first, so you need a bit of initiative and intuitiveness
-The monster has a higher chance of winning, and on average I'd say games are about 70% won by Monster
-Still in beta, so bugs pop up that result in CTD
Overall ☆★★★★
Graphics ★★★★★
Sound ☆★★★★
Gameplay ☆☆★★★

OneShot is an adventure game, where you guide the cute little (not-a-cat) child through a dying world, and make some friends and some tough choices.  The fourth wall is very flimsy, which makes for a very different tale than similar adventure games.
Both keyboard and Steam controller worked well for controlling the game.
In-game gameplay uses typical item combination puzzles, fetch quests, and a few logic puzzles.  Where it gets interesting is in sections where the fourth wall breaks down.  It's definitely good to know how to navigate through Windows explorer.
Graphics fit well, each area looks unique.  It looks dark, especially early in the game, but that fits well with the story and adds a bit of spookiness to the environment.
It's strongly recommended by both the game itself and me that it is played in Windowed mode.  This may be a little hard for people with very large resolutions, but it was fine at 1920x1080.
Music and sound is excellent.  The music has a bit of a haunted feel, also very fitting for the environment.
The recent update, Solstice, adds a new ending which can be played on "new game plus", but only once.  It gives a very satisfying ending to the story.  You are still able to get the other two endings, and all the achievements, after doing Solstice, but not get the Solstice ending again.  The only way to get around the single play limitation of the Solstice update currently is to turn off Steam Cloud saving, and manually deleting the saves and settings files in your Roaming AppData.
Overall, I strongly recommend purchasing and playing through OneShot.

Contract is a newly released side-scrolling shooter, think Gunpoint meets Hotline Miami. Your brother has been taken and the only way you can get him back is by completing a number of assassination contracts for the only person who knows where he is. As an ex-cop you know your way around a gun but you’re out of your depth as a new assassin, do you have what it takes to get your brother back?
Full Disclosure: A review copy provided by the developer.
Contract has a nice pixel art type appearance going on and it looks great. Its appearance is clearly inspired by the likes of Gunpoint but the dull colours throughout and the contrasting blood red make the visuals stand out. Contract’s crosshair makes up one of only two UI elements in the game and it’s done very well. The crosshair’s size increases the further you move your mouse away, giving you a rough idea of where your bullet will hit and making it obvious that your gun has better accuracy at close range, it sounds simple but without it, aiming in Contract would probably be a lot harder. The other UI element is a simple counter in the top right of the screen telling you how much ammo you’ve got, not much to say about this one.
At the beginning of each mission you’re given a short briefing on what you need to do, often including some information on the building you’re going into or the business that operates there. Once you’ve been briefed you just have to make it to your target, kill him and then find an exit. Some missions have an alternate route to your target and you can pick between the two, deciding which one you want to take. It’s also worth mentioning that your target is the only person who has to be killed for you to complete the mission, killing other enemies will award you with a small cash bonus but there is, of course, a risk that you could get killed.
The game has five different kinds of enemies:
So on to the character you’re actually playing as. With the default gear you can take a couple of shots before you’re down for good but if you manage to survive after taking a bullet or two you’ll gradually return to full health, I have no way of knowing how fast that occurs though as there’s no health indicator. You’re given a bog standard pistol to begin with but you can purchase a silenced pistol, assault rifle and submachine gun once you have enough cash and you’re at the safe house. As well as guns you also have a melee attack which can be used to kill all of the enemies apart from the dog, unless you somehow manage to punch it before it kills you. When you’re at the safe house you can also buy new clothes, most of which have an effect on your stats. For example, you can buy medium armour which increases your health, meaning you can take more shots without dying.
Some of the missions also contain things for you to interact with, such as computers to unlock security doors or switches to turn off the lights. These don’t play a huge role in the missions like they do in games like Gunpoint but since the switches and computers are often in isolated rooms with only one way in, trying to find them adds a nice challenge sometimes.
The game’s combat is pretty simple, it’s just shooting back and forth, yet it’s a lot of fun. However, the game does have a cover system, crouching by an object will give you cover and make you harder to hit as well as increase your accuracy. Crouching away from cover also makes you slightly harder to hit and, as with cover, increases your accuracy slightly.
What Contract lacks in soundtrack variety (there are only two or three tracks) it makes up for in how good said tracks are. They fit nicely with the game’s style and while they do of course get repeated a lot I didn’t find myself growing tired of hearing them. The sound effects for the guns are also very good, they make the guns seem like they have a real punch to them, something you would of course expect from guns.
Contract is a great side-scrolling shooter that’s easy on the eye, has simple yet satisfying combat and a good amount of content for the price. If there’s one thing I’d like to see it’s a mission generator but if you’re a fan of the genre or just fancy taking a side-scroller for a spin then I’d suggest you give this one a go.

To be honest, when I played this game for the first time, I simply loved it. To its hand-drawn aesthetic, to its gameplay that  is greatly inspired by a popular game known as Hotline Miami. But as I continued to progress through the storyline, the game started to slowly get boring and bland as the time went on. Before we get on to the negatives on the game, let's first start off with its pros.
+ Its Art Style
Unlike other games, 12 is Better Than 6 values its hand-drawn environment the most. It's unusual art style really adds to the uniqueness of the game which makes it stand out from the crowd from games that rival Hotline Miami.
+ The Reload System
On several occasions I have frantically panicked to reload my gun to pop off another shot, only to then get killed by a mob of enemies. The reload system is basically the saving grace of this game. Compared to Hotline Miami where it's one mag and yoathis game is different. You actually have to load your gun manually, bullet by bullet. This can lead the player to create many memorable moments where the player may have fought off 10 enemies with a six-shot revolver in an open area. Because of this system, it adds to the experience of being in the Wild West.
Now, the wretched cons
- Enemy encounters and repetitive levels
Throughout the middle of the game, you'll be traveling to different destinations. Now you can't choose where to go, the game does, so this limits the player's freedom in the way. However, as you travel, you can get random enemy encounters, and your job is to somehow escape from these 'vile beasts.' At first, this could be seen as a wise decision from the developers of the game, to keep you focused on the action, rather than just waiting to arrive at your next area, but as you travel more and more, it just gets repetitive and the game starts to lose its touch. After getting encountered by enemies countless times, the levels start to repeat itself over and over again, until you start getting annoyed when you get yet again, another enemy encounter. The repetitive levels aren't just for random encounters though, because they happen every other time you do a mission for one of the townsfolk in your area. It's gotten to the point where I've almost memorized every level layout the game throws at me every time I do a job for more money, just to get a single perk. Speaking of the perks...
- The Perks
Most of the perks
are what I call barely an upgrade once you buy them off of the shelves. I've never ran into any moment while playing this game, where I thanked one of my perks for saving me in a vicious gun fight. For example, (minor Spoilers)
(end of spoilers). Therefore, the gameplay just remains bland and dull with its boring stages.
- Its disappointing ending
The ending to this game was beyond disappointing. I won't spoil anything about it, but the ending was just confusing and so sudden that just made me think, "Is that it?" I can't really say anything else; just unsatisfying.
- Its short playtime
As shown from my playtime, I finished this game in about 3 hours, all in one sitting. For a 11$ you would expect something longer; and to that I would say... NOPE. All there is at the end is an endless survival mode, and because of its ending, you wouldn't even want to continue the game. Due to my cons listed, my total experience wasen't very pleasent indeed.
In the end, I can't recommened this game, to its repetitive levels to its terrible perks, I would suggest to get this game on sale rather than to buy it at its full price. However, if you're begging for a Hotline esque game and don't care about these cons, this game would be for you.

Hearts of Iron IV is a game i liked. Sure, most people bash it for being incomplete and for its AI. Are they right? Yeah, mostly, but that does not stop me from liking this game. This revew covers my basic opinions in this game, and basic info on the game.
HOI IV is a game in which you play as a leader of any country that existed in 1936. You could either start in 1936 or 1939, you can change how history progressed. You can convert Great Britan to a facist country, and invade all europe with it, or succesfuly invade europe as Germany. You can play with Mexico and invade all of the americas, if you want. The game focuses on alternate history in WWII.
HOI IV has much better graphics than its predocesor. It looks great, you can also cusomize some of the graphics settings, ex. removing cities, forests, ambiental effects, etc. It is also A LOT easier to understand than its predocesors, insted of using NATO simbols, you can have the alternative of images showing you which unit you are controlling. If you want Infanty, it will show you a helmet. Tanks, a tank. Mountaneers, a mountain simbol. If you liked the old nato symbols, you can change them. This is also a much simpler predocesor, something most people complain about, but being simpler does not mean being worse. Hearts of Iron III was extremely complicated, with tutorials that really didn´t teach you much about the game, HOI IV however, is a lot more simple and understandable. It is also intriguing to see how you win your battles, and how you expand by either pupeteering various countries or outright invading them. The thing that most imporved this game, is that the game is finally understandable. HOI III was extremely complicated, with unclear tutorials, unclear rules, a bad and uninformative hud, you would have NEVER understood the game if you had not seen a guide online. However, Hearts of Iron IV is a lot simpler. It has a more expleinable hud, more user friendly diplomacy, easier trade, laws, regulation, control, etc. HOI IV really imroved on this aspect. The workshop is also a HUGE addon. You could add new focus trees, new countries, new scenareos, weapons, units, etc. The workshop adds a LOT more to this game.
Something i have to complain about, is that the AI is outright stupid. They leave unprotected areas by enemies that you could have easely invaded, they dont push weak forces, they dont defend against a strong army in a front compared to your small 2 division defense, they usually dont push smart, they spread like idiots... The problem is huge, because this game focuses on the planning of invading a country, and if your planning is broken, you know you are doing something terribly wrong. Plus, the developers are already realeasing DLC, even if the game has that major flaw!?
TLTR/Opinion: I really enjoyed this game. I liked it more than HOI IV, not only because its simpler, but it looks better, it runs better, it is easier to understand what you are doing, and I did not find it as tedious as HOI III. But it does have its flaws, the big one being stupid AI.
7/10: Great game, big flaws.

TLDR: Worth it at almost any price, if you like any sort of TD games.
DG:TA is a the perfect execution of a standard tower defense game. As usual, the first few missions unlock new towers as you go, but you have all tower options available for the vast majority of the game (rather than only the last couple levels like many TD games). There's no experience points or carry over from level to level. All towers can be upgraded twice, increasing their range/speed/power. Tower variety is really good.
Story (8/10) - For a tower defense game, this is probably the best storyline you'll ever find. It's touching, believable, and satisfying. The voice acting is superb, which really helps with the immersion. While I've not played more than a few hours of Portal, even I can appreciate the ties to the game in a hidden bonus console, as well as an entire DLC devoted to it. The game is worth playing through on the easiest difficulty simply for the storyline.
Gameplay (10/10) - Levels are very well balanced. Zoom features are great. There's a "rewind back to a checkpoint" button that autosaves every few waves (and you can rewind back through multiple checkpoints). Different levels force different tactics, so you'll use almost every tower at least a bit. Artillery can miss. Rewinding can alter the rest of the mission simply because it resets where all the bullets are, and some may/may not miss. Fast forward feature works flawlessly. There's both fairly set path levels, as well as completely wide open levels that you can maze up to 'til your heart's content.
Replayability (11+/10) - Every level has a whole mess of "challenge" options, such as "out of bullets" (no towers that use bullets), "reverse" (level is reversed), "hard", "no upgrades", "poison" (the objects you're defending kill the enemies if they're dropped), and on and on and on. There's a leaderboard, and multiple medals for each different option on each different map. This is literally hundreds of hours of content. The DLCs are equally as impressive, with a stronger showing of "open concept" levels, they are much harder and present countless different ways to win, and it's rewarding to replay them to find those ways.
Sound (7/10) - The effects are good, cannons and explosions are satisfying, ambient noise/music is fitting although you'll probably turn it off if after the first 30 hours (which is pretty darn good anyway). I put the voice acting under the story, but there's fairly consistent comments from your sidekick during the missions that somehow never got annoying even after the millionth time I heard them.
Graphics/UI (7/10) - Solidly above average for a TD game of its age. You can zoom in quite close, or zoom out for a view range that's more than far enough. Things look like they're supposed to, enemies are all easily distinguishable. Faster enemies will sometime "outrun" where something hits them, so the bullet hitting animation can be slightly behind an enemy (fairly minor problem). The levels show a really good variety without ruining the believability. Menus are very well laid out, as is the ability to see at a glance how you did on each mission (great if you're trying to get all the medals). Nothing here will blow you away, but nothing will annoy you, which is awesome for a TD game.
Achievements/Steam Cards (10/10) - They are there, and work flawlessly!
Overall (9/10) - For what it is, it might very well be 10/10. I, personally, enjoy continuity between levels, which is the only thing I would have changed to make it perfect in my eyes. Questions like "Is clicking on specific towers easy, or is mis-clicking common?" are questions that just won't come up in this game. There is nothing that will detract from the fun of this game, nothing clunky, nothing annoying. You will like it, or not, based on the game concept itself, because the execution is simply done right.

I played this game back when it was in Open Beta in Stage 1, and I really liked it. The only reason I never purchased it was because I didn't have the funds. Now that it's Free to Play, I highly recommend everyone at least try. They're basically remaking the entire game, so it's sort of in beta again, so be prepared for bugs and stuff like that as of July 9th, 2016.
About the game:
The entire game is focused on the theme of 1 vs 4. The player who's all alone controls a monster, which has massive health, armor and damage, making it on par with the hunters, who are the team of four. It requires a lot of coordination as the hunters to win, but the monster has it's own challenges too. Certain things on the map can reveal it's location, and the Tracker (one of the hunter classes) can do the same. The monster goes through three stages of Evolution, evolving from level 1, to 2, to 3. At level 1, it's rather weak, and the hunters can (if coordinating well) easily kill the monster. At level 2, things are more of an even playing field, and at level 3 the monster is stronger than the hunters. The objective is to kill the monster before it kills you or the power relay (a special objective that only shows up at level 3).
Pros:
+Fun
+Lots of different characters
+Low skill floor, high skill ceiling
+Can organize your role preference, and the game tries very hard to give you your #1 preference
+Everything can be unlocked with in-game currency
+Most things can be found by listening well
+In-game voice chat for Hunters
Neutral:
±Games are relatively short, on a 12 minute timer (paused during Combat)
±Have to unlock everything on your own timer, allowing you to get confused by what everyone else does, or save up and buy someone and main them
±No penalty for leaving, so people often do if they don't get their preferred role (usually Monster)
Cons:
-Things aren't very well explained at first, so you need a bit of initiative and intuitiveness
-The monster has a higher chance of winning, and on average I'd say games are about 70% won by Monster
-Still in beta, so bugs pop up that result in CTD
Overall ☆★★★★
Graphics ★★★★★
Sound ☆★★★★
Gameplay ☆☆★★★

I picked up Salt and Sanctuary because I'am a big fan of Dark Souls series. I think it will be more honest if I start with the things I liked about this game.
And  to tell you the truth, it is almost everything.
Fights, bosses, enemies, atmosphere.
Everything is really captivating. On a level significantly higher than what you would expect from a non triple A game.
Fighting system is a bit repetitve,and bosses begin to seem all the same after a few of them, but in which Souls-like game they are not?
On the other hand, figthting is varied, offers you a lot of styles and meaningfull choices. Right my alley, I would say.
Soundtrack is great. Also a bit repetitve, but still really enjoyable.
Atmosphere - let's just say whis game would be a great succsessor to the Demon Souls atmosphere, although a bit more grim.
Now, for a few negative sides of the game...
There are generally two big issues that I feel ruined this game for me, and made ne unable to enjoy everything else.
1) Many enemies are created without even a bit of thought about counterplay in them (namely, Horsemen, Angsty bones, Invisible guys  and many. many others)
They are made to be annoying, not to be interesting or challenging.
Their abilities are just not fun to play against. It's not that they are too hard quite contrary - they are just don't serve as learning experience or require special techniques to overcome. Wouldn't it be better to design enemies, whose abilities would be fun although challenging to counter?
2) Platforming. Just...
When I play this game, I always remember Prince of Persia, both Sands of time-warriors withtin, and 2D ones - 1 and 2.
I think about those because many of the things that are bogging down this game are already fixed there.
How many times did I fall to my death in Salt and Sanctuary because I just bounced off from platform, instead of grappling on it? How many times I fell through the elevator without any apparent reason? How many times I had to not even try going for the pitfall, hust because that ment that I would have to run back here from Sanctuary? Many.
Too much for my liking. Why couldn't I just try this jump, and then turn back time (PoP or Braid style)? Why do I have problems with grabbing onto platform edges so much?
Especial in Haggers cavern. A couple of times, I just had to stay on one place and jump there for a minute, trying and trying again to reach the edge of the platform just couble of inches from my head...
Ultimately, for the main question of a platformer is how you deal with punishing players errors. Braid, Prince of Persia, Super Meat Boy - all these games were trying to minimise the impact, which single failed jump may have on your game overall, while also teaching you to play better. Is maximizing the punishment fro failed jump a good idea? Is running back from the sanctuary because of failed jump worth it? I don't know. Not for me, it seems.
Dark souls souls-lost-on-death system is in my opinion doesn't play well with platforming.
If you remember Iaito jump in DS1 or jump for Ostravas shield and sword in tower of Latria - take this, multiply it by ten hundred, and throw it, distibuted evenely, in the game. This is Salt and sanctuary in the nut shell.
Also this is magnified by somewhat glitchy and unresponsive platforming, especially in the Hard Light brand parts.
tl;dr Great game, buried under endless boring and infuriating platforming.

I've been playing FM since 2005 and I have to say this year's game is the only game where I felt like the UI has gone significantly worse. It is true that some of the changes could make the game maybe a little more realistic, yet it is crafted in a very poor way. Just like how Apple's phones are made to make our lives easier, changes in football manager should allow the gaming to be smooth with new applications.
I do love the dynamics addition of the game but as of yet the game needs serious improvements on UI.

I have no idea what I am doing... the learning curve is so steep and I can't seem to find much out.
I am thinking about starting a real football team. Probably would be easier.
Edit: The downvote is for not providing a way to teach the player without having to seek outside help. They have small tips but nothing that really sets a player up for success. I am going to be looking outside of the game to get help because I want to enjoy it but a failure to help players understand is a big problem.

To be honest, it's hard to make a review after five hours of play, because it's safe to say that I've barely scratched the surface of the game, but my initial impressions are that it's going to be a good one. I felt like there was a decline going into FM16 after 15, and FM17, despite some dull features like social feed, was the start of a turn into something friendlier to play and easier to work with. FM18 certainly continues that trend.
With a newly introduced "Dynamics" system to help visualize the team's social hierarchy and friendships that's always been under the hood but not graphically represented, and with an expanded medial center and scouting network bringing real use to jobs like the data analyst and club doctor, I feel more in the know on the inner workings of my team, and it's helped me for the better. Also, as a rather poor tactician who is used to using other people's tactics, I'm finding success so far in creating my own, because the tactics screen now shows what my weak spots are, how suited a player and his selected role is to being effective in a particular zone of the pitch, and I even like little things like the drawn lines to show untested partnerships, which could potentially affect performance.
That said, there are things I dislike. The stadiums look a bit nicer and so far designs seem less stupid, like when you can see an Old Trafford sized stadium on one side, but then see a small 10 row section on the other end like I've seen before. The graphics look a little sharper as a whole, but as usual it doesn't feel like there's that much more of an upgrade than was previously there.
I also so far find the matchday experience to be a bit lackluster. The popup with the player lineup was cool the first couple of times, but after a handful of games I grew tired of looking at it. After being basically the same interface for years and years, it's jarring to look at and maneuver through the in-match interface because the buttons are so small and moved into a corner out of the way. I'm also disappointed in the panels on the highlights. The center three are customizable, but the two outer ones that show the team's players, rating, and body language leave something to be desired because they can't be changed. At the very least I wouldn't have minded if they put up the percent of fitness they had left there, because alongside average rating, I use their remaining energy as an important gauge for when I am ready for a substitution. It's a case that, like in other games of recent years, I think an interface change was made for the sake of saying it's a feature and a change, but not necessarily one that's beneficial in the long run to the player.
Overall, while there are gamechanging updates that I do appreciate after a couple of years of lackluster features, there are a lot of additions and changes that are unneeded and don't necessarily supplement my gameplay. So far, I'm enjoying the game, and as a whole it's got enough new things going for it to be worth the upgrade.

Post release bit added at the bottom.
Beta Review:  Si have just 2 weeks or so to release a polished and finished product, so I can only assume that the in-house build is massively different to this mess.  From graphic glitches to input lag, the most unintuitive UI that the game has ever had & some good ideas so badly implemented that they could be the faultering steps of first year game design students, FM 2018 is quite simply not ready for public consumption.
I am at a loss as to why Si, year on year insist on breaking what wasn't broken and completely change everything for changes sake.  If they had kept the UI and functionality of last years offering while adding the new and good ideas like dynamics, the medical centre etc.  there would be a lot less complaints but no.  FM2017 was clean and crisp with everything at the players fingertips.  FM2018 has thrown this out and now what used to take one click takes at least three and most of the information that is actually useful is once again part of the FM mini game of hunt the info.  As an example, during a match if you want to change your tactics or something in the tactic there is a tactics button.  So far so good right?  well no, as that tactics button takes you to a totally unnecessary screen that gives you none of the information that you actually need.  What's more is that there is no hint at all as to how to get to the screen that you actually want.  For those that haven't found it yet there is a small 'tactics' heading on that screen to the top right that looks like a heading and not a button, which in fact it is and pressing that gets you to the screen you want.  So click on tactics, spend a few baffled minutes wondering how to get the stats you want, stumble across the hidden button and finally get to the screen that took a single click to get to in FM2017, and that's one of the easy ones to find.  Good luck with setting scouts to do what you want.  Here's a hint, the chief scout is set by default to allocate all scouting assignments and you need to change this before the game allows you to do it.
The new dynamics system is an excellent idea so badly implemented that it truly is a painful fun killer rather than the useful tool that it is meant to be, why?  Because if you♥♥♥♥♥♥one player off, regardless of who it is you will lose the dressing room, at which point you may as well let your great aunt Mavis and her friends take to the field as they would have about the same chance of winning the match and not cost anywhere near as much as the tutu wearing prima-donnas in the dressing room.  I imagine that this is something that Si will tune down by a large amount in time for release, at least I hope so.
The medical centre is a good addition and fills in the information gaps that existed in previous versions.  It is functional and well laid out and it is refreshing to be able to say that.
In 2013 Si completely changed the match engine and it took until 2016 for them to iron out 90% of the bugs.  They have completely changed it again this year and predictably it's a mess.  Eye killing bright green grass, a tiny white ball that gets lost amongst the glaring & awful textures ( even on very high graphics settings ).  Totally black players on some systems, terrible sound that persists even after the match has finished, bad decision making ( a feature of most FM titles ), 90% of goals come from crosses ( a problem that existed last year as well ), a bug where the team defending a free kick just line up along the edge of the area and don't bother moving when the free kick is taken leading to some stupid looking goals ( definately a bug so expect this one to be fixed for release ).  Players that don't give a damn what you have to say ( you could be messi managing a non-league side and the players would still be disinterested in what you have to say ).
I do hope that the release version will address most of these problems but at the moment the game isn't worth the money and I suspect, as in previous years that it will not be worth it until the end of march next year after the final patch has landed.  If you absolutely must buy this game then do yourself a favour and wait until April when you should be able to pick it up in a steam sale.  If you are not desperate for the game then wait for FM 2020 when the match engine should be in a reasonable state.
The game is now out and..... It's pretty much the beta with a different version number.  Hardly anything has been fixed but there have been some code changes.  Some people are reporting that the game now runs smoothly for them but for each of those reports there is another saying the game now runs worse.  There are now multiple crashes for some and there are still people that have not even managed to start the game.  For myself I have checked out the release demo and found it wanting in so many areas that it isn't even funny.  Miles should hang his head in shame and then resign, or at least take a step back to allow someone with a fresh outlook to take over.  FM 2018 is the worst FM game by far and I urge everyone to stay away from it.  Of course there will always be those that buy it anyway and I salute their dedication but stop to think for a moment.  If the sales tank then just maybe that will send a clear message that they must do a great deal better.  It will certainly cause Sega to start asking questions.  So if you want a decent and fun FM for god's sake don't settle for this crap.  3 / 10 for potential.

So, I've been playing Football Manager since it was called Championship Manager back in 96/97.
I buy the new version EVERY SINGLE year, so needless to say I've been a huge fan of the game, until now that is.
Football Manager 2018 doesn't feel like it's a newer version, it feels like an older, much worse version.
1. Improvements in live match were claimed to exist but are non existing, the players, managers and fans still look like muppets and it's horrible to watch. But this is a simulation game where we are managers, so this is not the worst of it.
2. A player who isn't getting in the first team expresses his concerns, you tell him that another player is in better form and that's why he hasn't been playing, he disagrees, his moral goes abysmal, the rest of the team expresses their concerns about "the way the player was treated", you say that you made the decision to leave him out because it's what's best for the team, the rest of the team disagrees, all the team's morale goes abysmal. This is just wrong, and it doesn't happen once in a while, 3 or 4 players already complained about not  playing in just 10 matches, and every time the team disagrees, really bad game mechanisms, this is all about making the team happy now rather than having a good team.
3. Injuries happen all the time, too often, it's not realistic, I get 2-3 players injured every week.
4. Team talks do nothing, it always shows that "the players don't seem at all interested in what you have to say", we, as managers, should have more influence and power over players and team talks, it didn't make a difference, once, in 10 games, in fact, there was one where I was winning 2-0 at half time, I told the players not to get complacent, they all showed green as in they reacted well, and the game ended 2-2 in the end.
5. I am a Porto fan, I don't know about other teams, but the Porto team is not realistic at all. Porto is by far the best team in Portugal, it's top of the league and compared to Sporting Lisbon and Benfica, in this game Porto is worst than them. In addition, we play with 2 strikers who have 8 goals in the league so far and are really good players, while having a 3rd striker on the bench who hasn't played a single match this season. The 2 strikers who are playing and are the best goal scorers have 3 stars each, and the one that sits on the bench has 3 and a half stars, same goes to other players but this is the most obvious one. Also, and to finalize this point, the budget is not real. A team such as Porto has several millions to spend each year, and in the game I only have 300k to spend in the transfer budget, when in reality, Porto has spent several millions this season already, by purchasing Aboubakar's pass and renewing until 2021. In the game, I can't renew his contract or Casillas for example.
All in all, the game went from being the most relisting football manager that ever existed, to the most pathetic one, it's far from realistic, and all in all it's about keeping the players happy, football isn't about keeping players happy, it's about being professional, doing what's right for the team, and the players know that and they respect and follow their manager.

rue. This is the most emotionally-invested game I've had the pleasure to experience. Even after the end, it haunts me till today... and my emotions are so messed up just thinking about my experience that it's difficult to even review it. Even so... I'll try.
Oneshot is
story-driven puzzle-adventure game. You play as a cat-like persona named Niko in a
ission to restore a world's lost sun, a large lightbulb. You only have one chance to save the world. It seems very straightforward.
...
xcept you're not playing as Niko. You are considered a separate entity.... yourself. By opening the game, you unwillingly become "god", in charge of a world that operates, exists and disappears at the click of your mouse. Niko, meanwhile, is just dragged in as the "protagonist", waking up in a different, crumbling world... a child trying to get back home, to the waiting arms of mommy. You are essentially Niko's guiding voice, in a world both of you have no understanding of, and are in charge of leading Niko to bring light back to the lands... and at the same time, bringing Niko back home.
Of course, its not that simple.
he game is sentient, aware of how it's a program running on your computer, and will attempt throughout your journey to keep you from returning the sun. But in the end, it is unable to control your final decision... and yet, it still gives a last stand by denying you a perfect ending. It's in control of the story and is hiding things, and without you thinking outside of the box to beat the game's coded "story"... Niko, the world, and the
itself... will never find peace. The writing and story in and of itself is one of this game's strong points, as the amount of fourth-wall breaking and events that reveal the true nature of the world is extremely compelling, especially since its all addressed to who the ingame people think is "god"... you.
The biggest draw to this game, however, is simply
ow personal it makes the relationship between you and Niko. Leading Niko feels like leading a younger sibling, in which Niko doesn't really understand what's going on, but will deal with events in their own childlike, innocent way. During your advanture, Niko also comments on
very action you take and even questions you about our world all in your own name... which further got me attached to Niko. Standard game mechanics are also used to strengthen this bond, as when Niko is tired, you have to find a bed to let Niko rest in; this is the only way to save and close the game "naturally", and also initiates dream sequences along with more dialogue between you and Niko. If you decide to close the window instead, Niko will be afraid and in a state of shock when you open the game again, as you brought darkness to the
orld Niko is in. This happens often, to the point where you'll likely be afraid to hurt Niko by closing the game.
Yet, despite your cluelessness and inability to explain how you can access things out-of-game... Niko trusts you. It's a sort of child-like trust towards an adult that's so innocent that you can't help but love Niko back. When the game denied me the
pportunity to respond to Niko, who was frantically calling my name... I
ealised that I could do nothing but stare at the screen. That feeling is horrid, accompanying a person almost all the time... and then being denied the chance to say "I am here for you". Eventually, I wasn't playing for the sake of the world... I was playing for Niko. For Niko's happiness, and to hear Niko speak to me again.
Niko felt real. I wasn't ready to let my little cat-like child go, even though that's what I was fighting for this entire time.
And that made the full game's ending all the more painful. You wouldn't expect a person's happiness... to hurt you so much.
OneShot is initially a story of trust and moral decisions, but its true lesson is of attachment... before
etting go. The initial ending will make you think of your consequences. The true ending will make you cry, reluctant to pass the credits. You only have one shot, as once you complete the story... you'll want it to stay completed. And yet... I
on't want it to end.
I'll never forget you, Niko.

This is an amazing game. In many aspects it is better then the first Assassin's Creed.
Pros:
- Captivating story. Although you can sense a little bit of what might be coming, I was still amazed that they went full blast on that concept.
- Not as repetitive as AC 1.
- Great graphics, and environment in general. History lives and breaths in this game. From music, through architecture, details and famous and fabulous painting. Even weaponry of the era.
- Eagle vision is useful!
- Interesting characters.
- Decent length of game play.
Cons (not many):
- Combat is very similar to one from the original game. Can feel clumsy a bit sometimes.
- Although you have a wide variety of weapons to chose from, I hardly ever used throwing knives (unlike AC 1) or felt necessity to use short blade (unlike AC 1 again).
- From time to time you might get irritated when camera's twists and turns mess up your jumping or other acrobatics.
- Although far less bugs happened, I've captivated pretty hilarious one. In Venice you may encounter legions of guards on one tiny bit of rooftop. Out of the sudden. They just HAPPENED there. The more you killed trying to clear out the area, the more would pop up in their sted. Creepy.
Apart from that, the game is one of the rarer kinds when you have a blast playing and can learn some history. This is of great value as well, and AC series so far has been also educative. I know I'll be fishing for other titles of AC now. Yeah, I've heard the rumours about meh protagonist in AC III but... I must yet get disappointed by any game of the series. So far so good.
Recommended!

It was a decent game. To start things off we'll talk about the setting. Rage is set in a post apocalyptic wasteland, the scenery is mostly vallies of stone and sand with remnants off dead trees and various other small flora like dune grasses here and there. Not a whole lot,though it is a desert like setting where water is scarce so it makes sense. The general vibe is very steam punkish with a lot of rust and metals with weapons ranging from modified crossbows to machines to plasma cannons etc.. Indoor settings are mostly tech like and/or mutatant infested sewers or a combination of the two.
The graphics were well enough. I played through on medium settings and it looked good and ran rather smooth on my laptop. No blocky square head or hands, the animations weren't clunky and looked proper enough for the actions.
The controls were easy enough to get accustomed too ( you can change them anyhow if you don't like them in the settings) and were accurate. They were a bit sensitive though.... Straffing was very fast as well, peaking around corners for stealth turned into full blown assaults very quickly lol. The jump button was pretty pointless as well, I couldn't jump over anything at all in the game and I tried just about everything >.< .
Sound was alright along with voice acting. Never had to shove my head into my screen to here characters speak or had stuttered speech. Few well known actors voiced.
Haven't played alot of multiplayer yet but from what it seems it is  Racing, V.S, and Team version campaign missions from the game.
All in all I loved the game and reccomend it to others. My biggest dislike was the fact that after the main quest line there is no free roam.   SPOILER:
After Lassard has go you collect the I.D decryptions  just before Marshall has you activate the Ark Capsules  be sure to get all of your exploring and side quests in. After you leave wellsprings for the resistance you can go back to the other settlements at any time, prior to the last mission. As stated I advise you do for the full experience.

Sanctum is a first person shooter mixed with a "Bloons Tower Defense" game. You start off with a giant grid of blue squares that signal where you can build you blocks. You must strategize your blocks so that you can make the longest possible path for the enemies. The reason you must do this? You're protecting your core. The enemies are trying to kamikazi their way into your core, which damages it, until the point it reaches 0% life left, where it explodes and you lose.
Anyways, these blocks you place are used to equip various towers on top of them, which shoot the monsters as they go by, helping you stop their relentless attack. Being that there are many different towers, each with their strengths and weaknesses against the many different monsters, it makes the game a very strategic problem. Each tower can be upgraded to become more damaging and quicker. Being that there are so many towers, you must choose your favorite ones before starting, as you can't have them all. Often, I was always pounded with the inability to decide if I want one tower or the other tower more.
The monsters come in many different shapes, sizes, strengths, and weaknesses. One wave, you may have 100 really small and fast crawling bugs, while in the other wave, you may have 5 extremely strong but slow "tank" monsters. Each monster has a weakness against a certain tower/weapon, but it's up to you to figure it out. For instance, the tank monsters are undamaged by most assault gun shots, but are weak against rocket launcher attacks. Each monster also has a major weakspot on its body, where it is most damaged if you hit it there. Each monster's weakspot is in a different place, some are on the back of their heads, while others (known as bobbleheads) have it on the top of their heads and move their heads around, making it hard to hit. Oh, did I mention that some of the monsters fly? Yep, that's right, they fly right over your maze and into your core! Luckily, the game has a tower to take on each monster.
Finally, the game lets you fight WHILE the wave is happening. So you set up your maze and press enter, the wave starts. Now you, the player, get to shoot the monsters, helping your towers in the attempt to stop their advance. You also have many weapons to choose from, but can only have 3.
The game itself is great. The music is just amazing. If the game was more popular, that music would be getting awards. The graphics...just wow. Each map is in a giant world, full of color and hidden easter eggs. Between waves, I would constantly go out and just look around at all the amazing designs. If you press escape, it enables you to see what is coming in the next few waves, informs you about the monsters, and helps you figure out what the towers and guns do. Not to mention, the typing in game does that whole google translate voice, so whatever you type is actually said out loud. Oh yeah, you can also rocket jump.
Finally, the lagging...or lack of it. At times, you have 60 enemies flooding through your maze as you shoot off rocket launcher rounds into them, while your 30 towers are firing shot after shot into them and as monster part fly everywhere, AND YOU'RE STILL NOT LAGGING. I've only experienced lag once in this game, and it wasn't even major lag in the slightest. For instance, one of my favorite towers in the game is called the "Scatter Laser" tower. It shoots low damage bolts of electricity at the enemies extremely fast. Now, I'll spam these on a bunch of my blocks and have 40 of them helping me defend. So I'll just stop firing and look at them shooting, all 40 of them shooting about 6 shots a second and how smooth it is. If you're worried about lagging, this game won't supply lag.
Sanctum is an amazing game and deserves way more attention that it gets. I really hope my review influences you to buy the game.

12 is Better Than 6 is a very creative, top-down, hand drawn western themed shooter.

At times the game can be highly frustrating, the bad guys don’t ever miss.
Which means you die a lot and planning two, three and four moves ahead quickly becomes essential.
Finishing any level feels like a reward but at the same time levels are designed with such care and precision that it shouldn’t take more than a couple of retries to complete any of them.
It is way too dangerous to run in and shoot at everybody you see, The bad guys are extremely good at hunting you down.
The only way to make it through some areas is by using stealth mixed with shooting or even using explosives.
I definitely recommend this game.
Hopefully, the developers are going to add more content to the game such as a co-op option.

Wait for a sale and get EU4, Art of War, and Common Sense. Necessary DLC is the only strike against this intricate machine of a game.
In EU4, you are the *spirit* of a nation; you guide your state through the chaotic ~400 years between the fall of Constantinople, all the way through to the French Revolution. You can play whichever nation you wish, either a European superpower, or a total underdog nation. EU4 gives you the freedom to approach the game however you want- this game is best enjoyed with a sprinkle of roleplaying. You can try to conquer the whole continent if you're ambitious, or just 'play tall' and try to moderate the angry kings around, and the angry nobles within, your nation.
It took me the tutorial and 2 miserable campaigns until I fully understood the basics. But it is SO worth it. Just push through the confusion. Once you get over that first hill, the game really comes to life.

Europa Universalis 4 (EU4) is a Renaissance era nation building simulation. It starts out at the end of the Medieval period and picks up with the political beginnings of the Wars of the Roses and the 30 Years War. England still has chunks of France, and the Hapsburgs dominate European dynasties. This game differs quite a lot from its predecessor, Crusader Kings 2 (CK2). Where CK2 focusses on dynastic survival and the intricacies of relationships, EU4 looks at nation building.
In EU4 there are no victory conditions, and you only lose when your nation no longer holds any territory.  This game emphasises national identity and nation to nation relationships. If you try to expand too fast or too much, other nations will quickly ally against you. If you fail to establish strong alliances and appease your stronger neighbors, you may not survive more than a few years. In addition to this paradigm, you contend with the historical events that shaped history. Fail to come to terms with the Catholic Church when playing as a Protestant nation, and you may not survive the intricacies of the 30 Years War. It is a truly fascinating and educational game, well worth the money and time spent playing it, especially if you are a history afficionado.

Hearts of Iron IV is a game i liked. Sure, most people bash it for being incomplete and for its AI. Are they right? Yeah, mostly, but that does not stop me from liking this game. This revew covers my basic opinions in this game, and basic info on the game.
HOI IV is a game in which you play as a leader of any country that existed in 1936. You could either start in 1936 or 1939, you can change how history progressed. You can convert Great Britan to a facist country, and invade all europe with it, or succesfuly invade europe as Germany. You can play with Mexico and invade all of the americas, if you want. The game focuses on alternate history in WWII.
HOI IV has much better graphics than its predocesor. It looks great, you can also cusomize some of the graphics settings, ex. removing cities, forests, ambiental effects, etc. It is also A LOT easier to understand than its predocesors, insted of using NATO simbols, you can have the alternative of images showing you which unit you are controlling. If you want Infanty, it will show you a helmet. Tanks, a tank. Mountaneers, a mountain simbol. If you liked the old nato symbols, you can change them. This is also a much simpler predocesor, something most people complain about, but being simpler does not mean being worse. Hearts of Iron III was extremely complicated, with tutorials that really didn´t teach you much about the game, HOI IV however, is a lot more simple and understandable. It is also intriguing to see how you win your battles, and how you expand by either pupeteering various countries or outright invading them. The thing that most imporved this game, is that the game is finally understandable. HOI III was extremely complicated, with unclear tutorials, unclear rules, a bad and uninformative hud, you would have NEVER understood the game if you had not seen a guide online. However, Hearts of Iron IV is a lot simpler. It has a more expleinable hud, more user friendly diplomacy, easier trade, laws, regulation, control, etc. HOI IV really imroved on this aspect. The workshop is also a HUGE addon. You could add new focus trees, new countries, new scenareos, weapons, units, etc. The workshop adds a LOT more to this game.
Something i have to complain about, is that the AI is outright stupid. They leave unprotected areas by enemies that you could have easely invaded, they dont push weak forces, they dont defend against a strong army in a front compared to your small 2 division defense, they usually dont push smart, they spread like idiots... The problem is huge, because this game focuses on the planning of invading a country, and if your planning is broken, you know you are doing something terribly wrong. Plus, the developers are already realeasing DLC, even if the game has that major flaw!?
TLTR/Opinion: I really enjoyed this game. I liked it more than HOI IV, not only because its simpler, but it looks better, it runs better, it is easier to understand what you are doing, and I did not find it as tedious as HOI III. But it does have its flaws, the big one being stupid AI.
7/10: Great game, big flaws.

Paradox did a good job with the look and game mechanics, but when it comes to the substance they dropped the ball. Its shallow.
The leader choices are lacking. The map is lazy. Provinces are just random blotches. States are arbitrary. Obvious and extremely necessary releaseable countries are missing. The AI just does not know how to deal with HOI4.
This game might be good one day - when a mod team actually fills in the giant holes left by Paradox. But at the moment the game is boring and no mod really fixes it. I regret my purchase, don't buy this game.

Don't buy this game - or any paradox game for that matter, if you want to play Multiplayer. They are good singleplayer games, but multiplayer on paradox games isn't what it used to be. I should know - I have many, many hours on EU4 and HOI4.
Back in the day, everyone could enjoy a decent game without a mic - without discord or teamspeak - and, most importantly, without rules. These days, every MP game you join requires you to join some discord or teamspeak (some even require that you have a mic.) In addition, just about every multiplayer game you will join will have 2 or more pages of rules that you have to read. According to the people who make these rules, they 'prevent trolls' or 'make the game balanced.' All they really do is ruin the fun of the game, and make the game something different than what it was originally meant to be. I have uninstalled all my paradox games - stellaris, EU4, HOI4, and CK2, despite the fact that I spent thousands of hours on these games back in the days when MP was actually good.
In a nutshell, game is good if you are only interested in Singleplayer, but if you want to actually play with other people, get a different game.

Evolve Stage 2 is a heavily modified version of the original Evolve focused on a f2p model instead of p2p+DLC model. It features a redesigned UI, trimmed download size, and largest of all, the new Evolve is 100% free of any payments. There is no paywall OR cash shop of any kind. Instead of unlocking content via challenges, characters, skins, and monsters are unlocked by means of currency earned from playing the game. This currency cannot be bought, and as far as I can tell, you cannot purchase the currency. For a new player, the game will be quite enjoyable and has a fair character unlock system that isn't a grind, but you won't unlock everthing in a few hours of play. The current con to the game is that "founders", or people who purchased the game prior to the Stage 2 patch, got essentially penalized from the update, having all progress on their character ranks reset and the only compensation being 3000 silver keys and some animated badges. This is fairly low compensation for what could be hundreds of hours of work to level characters. It can br argued that the ability to play the game comfortably with a sizable player base is worth it, but that's up to the individual. In order to save space on the game, they also cut a considerable portion of content, between some maps and many gamemodes, but the core gamemode, Hunt, and a permanent arena fight mode, Arena, are still in the game. Considrring that it's still a beta, it's very likely that the cut modes will return, but at the moment, they are excluded. Overall, Evolve Stage 2 was the best decision for the game's longevity, and is quite enjoyable to play if you like either coop games or feeling like an unstoppable murder machine. Bringing friends is recommended but definitely not required.

"Borderlands, Contra, and Gears of War had a baby - they called it Mercenary Kings and it's pretty. Now go away, I wanna keep playing it."
Mercenary Kings is hand drawn pixel art at its finest, brought to you by the same folks who rendered the Scott Pilgrim game. The art alone is enough to gawk at, making expert use of animations, sprites, silhouettes and the like. What's important about it, and why it deserves such attention, is because that EVERY pixel was lovingly and knowingly placed to give Mercenary Kings a very distinct look and feel.
The plus side is that when you start putting that much effort into every pixel, you start to care about where they're all going - the controls in this game are tight and responsive, especially if you play with a game controller. Layered on top of this are several fun and exhaustive features, including but not limited to active reloading, collectibles, and a unique brand of rocket jumping that involves a minigun.
Where Mercenary Kings falls short, however, is in its pacing and length. The game has a lot to offer, A LOT, and one might even argue it has a bit too much. Grinding drops for better gear isn't always a bad thing, but it can get tedious mission after mission during the long campaign of the game. What's more, the formula doesn't change much over its course, so in time the game itself can feel like a grind.
However, all in all, this is action gaming done correctly. While the metroidvania genre only recognizes two games, it's important to know that Contra, Megaman, and more added a worthy third style of game to the mix that involves a few more guns - Mercenary Kings is the pinnacle of that.

Another year and another year of beta testing FM. My first impression after 90 hours is that there are fewer bugs this season than previously, so that bodes well. By this time last year, I had at least a dozen fatal crashes, this season I have had 4 so far. Not a lot seems different yet but the new features are what everyone wants to know more about, so I digress. The game is slower overall.
Let me start by saying that since I joined the SI Forums back in 2003 I have always been a fan of the wish lists. In 2009 I started making a list compiled from the most commonly requested features, at the time I was curious how many would be implemented. I have kept this list going and still have it with each subsequent year Wishlist thread added to it. I can safely say that from 2009 until this 2018 version SI have added exactly 5 things from the 25 most requested features people want to see. This is not a good ratio. How many people asked for a manager on the sideline last year? It wasn’t even in the top 100.
This season has two “major” additions, first the Dynamics, which adds an even further element of making this managerial game into a babysitting simulator. It is not enough you have to argue with limited AI players constantly just to keep your job but now they gang up on top of it! Where did dynamics rate on the top 100 most requested features? Again, not even in the top 100.
The next big addition is the way scouting it done. Now instead of scouting and getting lists of players in your inbox you get one screen with a list of players you must go through one by one. Instead of having to scroll to the top to have read them all, you can just click one button to have them all go away. Or, you could go through them one by one, but once those lists get large it gets tedious to do. It is slightly more streamlined, or at the very least, appears that way.
There are numerous other smaller additions that really do not register as having a large affect on the game itself and things most complained about such as the repetition of interviews has not changed at all. It is still the best football management game available but that says very little since the competition is thin at best. Will I play it? Yes, probably for thousands of hours again, because there is no real alternative to FM and that alone makes it the best but would I recommend it? No, this is another season with few changes and even fewer that anyone asked for. It makes me wonder why the Wishlist thread existed at all, since it is rarely used. My list compiles the 100 or so most recommended features for FM, and I am not going to post it here but most people know some of the bigger ones, whether they support them or not. In no particular order here are a few (disclaimer, these are not MY suggestions, I do not even support them all, these are compiled from the official SI forum Wishlist thread since 2009, which is now its own forum since the thread was closed);
1.	Something you can actually use your managers money on. Right now, it is supposed to be used to determine part of your job stability but we all know once you are at a huge club it makes no difference. Also, has anyone ever noticed that you can’t ever become the highest paid manager? I have overtaken Sir Alex atop the Hall of Fame every season and have never been the top paid manager in the game. Pus you can’t actually negotiate a contract, it will let you take less money for more years but very little is actually negotiable with your contract, it is more or less take it or leave it. The most common suggestion is to use your money to invest in a team or buy a team later in your career.
2.	More modes than just a manager mode. Now this one does seem a little silly since it is called Football MANAGER and that is usually the line given to those who suggest this, but in this same vein a major requested feature is the ability to manage teams other than the big club, like work your way up from U18 or U23, I count this as the same suggestion when tallying for my list.
3.	This one has been worded in many different ways but the gist is a training mode, something you can use to see your tactics out of a game and tinker with it so you can actually see what your instructions do.
4.	A very subjective one and this one is taken from a lot of different suggestions and kind of mashed into one but people really seem to want to see less “unrealistic” results, which are actually quite realistic but they seem to want to win every game in which they “play better”, match this with the vast and overwhelming number of people who want to see less injuries and what do we get? Really this boils down to one large suggestion, setting sliders. Yep, customization is a huge thing people ask for year after year and these are just two things they wish to adjust to their desires. Most sports simulation games aim to have a good level of customization, FM is one of the few that really gives you little option in what happens in your game universe, realistic or not.
5.	It is amazing how many people post every year about how they want more options in their interviews, we have had literally the same set of questions and answers for an eternity it seems. People want to be able to say what they want to say, not choose from 5 bland answers that they would probably never say in real life. How is that realism?
6.	Fix the transfer system. This one is also suggested en masse with different ways to suggest it. The most common being something akin to; “why did I not get player X for ten million and the team Y got him for eight million?” or even, “How is player X ‘worth’ 10 million but he actually costs 80 million? Isn’t he worth 80 million then?”. Now I don’t pretend to have all the answers, much, but this one gets posted a lot and I have no real idea how they would do it better.
7.	A wider and vaster academy system, not just some random youth players who come in every season. Simple request.
8.	Customization. I know I said it before, that one was related to the two most posted, game results with skewed statistics and injuries but this request is vast and includes things such as; turning off star ratings, sliders on small things like PPM difficulty (who likes having their staff constantly tell them they don’t think player X can do the thing you want him to learn?), optional social media and interviews, optional Brexit and more. This list could go on forever but I think many people say things like “just look at OOTP”.
Now if you got this far, you are probably wondering how this is a review for FM 18 and it has to be said, most reviews are about what is in the game, I am using my data to show you what is still not in the game after all this time. These suggestions are the top few on the Wishlist thread since 2009! This tells you how much your voices mean and what kind of game to expect. I am by no means saying to stay away and don’t buy it, because we all need our FM fix and this game is still the best in the market but I am saying I do not recommend it this season for the fact it just doesn’t add enough to make it worth buying in my opinion.
