Alright, 12 Is Better Than 6 is done and dusted. It’s hard to know for sure because of IM, but I’d say my total play time was around 6 or 7 hours. Initially, I died a lot, but as you go on, get upgrades, and especially as you get dual wield pistols (the 12 in the title), you pretty much become an unstoppable force.
The story was pretty silly overall, and yet you still want to see it through to the end. Basically, you are a Mexican ex gang leader seeking revenge and trying to find your lost memories. In fact, you are known simply as “The Mexican.” You have no love for the white man, Indians, or even other Mexicans! Basically, you are just angry at the world. However, you do have a sense of humor still (and that comes out nicely in the dialogue), and despite basically having no good intent, you still manage to do some good as you wander around Texas.
I feel the story merits an 8 out of 10 overall. Although a bit sparse and heavy handed, it is also compelling and effective.
The art style was awesome: nice black and white world with red highlights (basically, any blood spilled). It was very cool looking, especially for a top down game. I will mention this a few times, but 12 Is Better Than 6 pulls from the obvious blend of Hotline Miami and The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly influences to craft a stunning world
The graphics get a solid 10 out of 10.They could not be more perfect for this one.
So, it is similar to Hotline Miami in a lot of ways, but far more forgiving. You can hide from aggro’d enemies with more certainty of success and, as long as you keep moving, enemies will miss with their weapons more often. It’s still twin stick shooter goodness though. You can use the environment to your advantage in both the applications of stealth and of violence.
The gameplay itself was seamless. I encountered zero issues throughout; no clipping, no weird physics, no stuttering or freezes or crashes. In every way, it performed immaculately.
I give the gameplay 9 out of 10. It is fluid and nearly perfect.
The music was awesome. So much so that I bought the OST today. Really was perfect for the game, and generally awesome anyway. You could jam to this with no regrets while driving or running or whatever you choose to do. Not to keep bringing up Hotline Miami, but the soundtrack for this game is to Westerns what HM’s soundtrack was to…well…Miami (Vice era).
The soundtrack is an easy 10 out of 10. Some good stuff there.
I think overall, I would give this game 9.3 bullets whizzing by your head as you drink tequila and plot your revenge out of 10 possible.
By the way, there is an endless mode after you finish 12 Is Better Than 6 (you can probably play this before, but I didn’t) called Purgatorium Mode, where you have been condemned to a hellish undead existence and must kill all the other sinners. Check it out if you can.

Despite being a game I can recommend, this is a really interesting, nuanced title. A retro offering in more ways than one, it is crucially retro in the way that it is simply not a perfect, uber-polished shooter, and that this becomes a virtue as it delivers a title that stands out from the crowd, has a point of difference and, if one is prepared to compromise somewhat, a real charm.
So what do I mean by RAGE being a retro, unpolished title? Well, let's look back to the first half of the 00s. This was a time when, before a relateively select span of companies (EA, Bethesda, etc) begun to dominate the industry, there existed a teir of titles that is somewhat less evident these days. A sort of B-teir, these games were identifyable by their newbie or unknown developers, somewhat strange production objectives, relatively unoptimised or scratchy graphics, etc.
Take a look at Operation Flashpoint. Produced by Eastern europeans, the game was by no means a beautiful, watertight package. Don't get me wrong, as I said in my OpFlash 2 review the original Flashpoint was the best title in the whole of the ARMA and Flashpoint series combined, but this game was not perfectly made! Cutscenes and set pieces were all built within the simplistic mission editor engine, the English language script was iffy, models were boxy and only vaguely humanoid, textures were cloudy and the foliage was all just a collection of two-dimensional sprites arrayed rotationally around a Z-axis. Everything looked vaguely amateur, especially when held up against a game like Halo: Comabt Evolved, but as I've been hinting at thus far this was by no means an indictment of the gameplay experience: Operation Flashpoint was an era-defining, industry-leading title in it's own, specialised ways.
And while RAGE does take on the
of a AAA title, at least in screenshots, it is in actually a half-baked, simplistic, technologically incomplete offering. It is an experiment for the IDTech 5 engine which, while a success in certain targetted areas, is by no means a holistic gaming experience.
So why am I recommending it? Because it is a really fun, lightweight, occasionally stunning and even thrilling title.
First of all a word on the graphics. This engine is obviously an intellectual triumph. Famous ID mastermind John Carmack came up with some magic method that allowed game artists to basically do whatever they wanted with a setting at no cost to performance, and the result of these innovations in RAGE is that it is a bloody georgeous game - at least when viewed in stills. Landscapes simply cannot be faulted, nor can the really intelligent way that lighting has been handled: this game can be really breathtaking.
The environments, the lighting, even the movements of the characters are all really well done - but it isn't perfect. Character models move in a really expressive way, but the way they distort to accomodate this movement is somehow unrealistic and spoils immersion. Likewise the pace with which you move through environments, and the relatively low attention you are asked to pay to them (it plays like a rail shooter more often than not), prevents you from truly appreciating them and feeling as if you are part of an environment. In sum, and this is a point that highlights the quirkiness of this title: The game looks great, until you're playing it, then the visuals become forgettable until you stumble upon the occasional well-made set view.
The gameplay is also pretty simplistic. Intended clearly to be a vehicle-heavy game, there are races and Mad Max-style road battles featuring limited vehicle physics and auto-aim guns. The shooting play is solid - greatly boosted by the elusive movements of your impish enemies which make aiming a really active experience - but repetetive. Missions are short and not too difficult (though occasionally you come up against big bad enemies who can be a real exclamation point) and in general there is a really light touch on the gameplay on the part of the creators (you would have expected more from Bethesda), something which isn't called for, since the gameplay is so clearly lacking something.
So, I'll have to meld this hodge-podge review into a coherent final statement: This is a great,
game. Get it when it's on sale. Get it for your weaker laptop to play on international flights. Get it for the fun gameplay, get it for the occasionally stupendous visuals, get it for the very low drain the game will exert on your mental resources. Don't get it if your machine can play Witcher 3, or somesuch, and can afford those games too.

From the perspective of a storyteller and lore junkie, RAGE is cause enough to RAGE. It seems to get the recipe right: Post-apocalyptic setting, competent voice acting, guns that are fun to fire, enemies that are fun to dispatch, huge cars with huge guns, and good graphics and sound work. So where it goes wrong?
The world is dull. It's about as derivative as post-apocalyptic settings can get and simply boring. None of the characters are particularly memorable (except for Dan Hagar and that's only because he's voiced by John Goodman, whom I adore) and the setting is... To say it's barebones is to be generous. There's very little world building and it offers no cohesion, nothing beneath the wallpaper of pretty graphics and animations. You'd think Apophis' impact would create an unique setting with special mechanics, but as it stands, RAGE could very well stand in for a particularly sunny day in Fallout or a mysterious new Zone of Exclusion in a game based on Roadside Picnic (yes, I could stay STALKER, but that's not a direct adaptation, now is it?).
Perhaps the worst offender is the Authority. You are constantly being told how the Authority is bad and evil, but the game never actually shows it beyond a handful of comments about hunting Ark survivors (who usually join them) and their leader doing a Bad Thing by messing with the Ark timers. Oh, and they wear red, black, faux-runes, and their flag is a barely modified Reichskriegsflagge. So, Nazis AFTER APOCALYPSE, fought by a Generic White Military Dude.
As derivative and boring as the story is, the gameplay is pretty solid. Scrounging up supplies and crafting stuff to fight enemies more effectively is fun, the alternative ammunition adds variety (well, when it isn't a simple damage multiplier), and the foes you fight offer for a varied experience (with the caveat that they tend to be bullet sponges by the end game).
Still, there are far better alternatives on the market. Far Cry comes to mind, which does everything RAGE purports to do, except better.

But even that, it is possible to play very differently than "the real world". You can make Ottomans a Catholic country or colonize Americas with them. The playing style varies somewhat between countries you select as the Catholic ones politic with Papal state and HRE ones politic around Holy Roman Empire. With Ottomans for example, I have tried to attack anyone on sight and tried to convert my people to Sunni faith, at the same time trying to evade the coalitions formed because of my aggressive expansion.
Although the game has techs and armys and like, it is not CIV or war game. It is difficult to play at first, if you have not played e.g. Crusader kings or this kind of games before. You will make mistakes and you will learn of them. You need to learn when to backstab, when to ally with your enemy or when not to go to war, even if you are allied with someone. Europa Universalis IV is a beautiful game to experiment with and to learn new aspects of history. Much of what I learned of world history came from this game (a huge thanks to Paradox for investing the time and resources spent collecting the information). You take command of a nation's fate, and how you guide it is ultimately up to you. You could even reduce yourself in size, enable a coup to remove a monarch/household from power, grow into an extensive empire, or develop into the economic power of the globe. Become a mediator between nations serving as an Elector in the HRE, a fledgling Italian city state looking to unite Italy, a wrathful Byzantine seeking to restore the glory of ancient Rome, prevent the fall of the Qing Dynasty, or even recreate the Mongol Empire! I have countless hours poured into this game and I am still learning new details about the game mechanics and the information it has in store for the player.

Very interesting and unique experience of a space management game with a casual-esque feel. Very peaceful and relaxing with an OST to support this.
Problems:
-Even in SANDBOX MODE, you need to do contracts and research the new modules and upgrades. I mean... what? This is what sandbox is for- to have all the upgrades to test or play around with.
-As people said, it gets grindy fast and pretty repetitive. You can't time warp unless all your satellites are sleeping, so you have to sit and wait for contracts to be finished- even/especially when there's only one in range.
-MASSIVE spook every time a new tech. is researched or contract completed.
PLEASE give us a way to turn that notification off.
-The earth survey missions,where you need to scan locations on the earth's surface, are very fustrating as you either need to alter a satellite's orbit and make it super distorted, or launch a new one. And they orbit at realistic speeds, one orbit every ~90 minutes.
-Hardcore is the most fustrating and least engaging, ironically, in that everything is harder and you need more contracts done before you can use any upgrades. The starting satellite has the battery of an iPad and dies even when fully charging. Unlike other hardcore/serious game modes in other games, I don't feel much accomplishment for doing this mode.
-The game would probably take about 6-7 hours of play to beat all the contracts to 100%.
Overall, was worth the price I paid, I'd reccomend for very casual gaming or for an intro to Kerbal Space Program astrophysics, as it doesn't let you do much outside of orbital mechanics.

Many of you are probably leery (as I was) about dropping 20 bucks on this game. I hope that this review will help you make your decision. The game is certainly not for everyone, but I will go into it's pros and cons shortly.
First, I would like to adress many of the complaints I have seen in other reviews.
Many seem to think that the controls are clunky. This is true- at first. after 30 minutes or so of gameplay, the controls seemed natural to me. If they really bother you, you can always remap them quite easily. I also read many reviews which stated that the jumping seemed unresponsive. The only time I have noticed this is when I have attempted to jumo when in a prone position (laying down). Otherwise, the jumping mechanic seems just fine to me.
Some also complain about the reusing of maps. I can certainly see why some people may become irritated by this, but it doesn't bother me. Since you're always completing a different mission, the maps do not seem too repetitive.
Let me just say that Mercenary Kings is a fantastic game that deserves a lot more attention than it is currently getting. The retro-style gameplay combined with the endless weapon customization makes for one of the most enjoyable gameplay experiences I've had. The character animations are worthy of an award, and the maps and backgrounds look fantastic. I'm not too far into the campaign, but so far it has been fantastic. At first, it may seem overly difficult, but if you just do some part swapping with your gun, you should be fine. I will update this review with some of my favorite beginner weapon setups soon.
The only thing I have found irritating about this game is the lack of a chat menu in multiplayer games. This is extremely minor, however, and will most likely be fixed in a later update.
Overall, I would highly reccomend this game to anyone looking for a great retro-style gaming experience. It's well worth the $20. I hope this review was helpful to all of you ladies and mentlegen.

I am genuinely rather happy with the game. Right now, there are a few obvious beta bugs that need to be ironed out but, that aside, this is a rather big change for the FM series.
The game has never run faster than before. Load screens are quick, looking for jobs and scouting screens are significantly faster, matches are longer and more in depth, and the new systems in place in FM18 are both interesting and fun. The Match Engine is improved, as a whole, and the game has significantly more nuance than before.
FM18 does suffer in some areas, namely User Interface. It's difficult to find a lot of the old features, as they have been moved or hidden under a "sleek" exterior. I found it particularly frustrating for scouting as it required some digging to figure out how to search for a specific attribute.
While I don't agree with the UI changes, I do believe this is a very solid addition to the series and worth picking up for FM fans. I recommend it with one caveat, be patient with the UI. It can be clunky and difficult to navigate at times and is, for me, the worst part of FM18.

After 300 hours of playing, a relativly small amount of play time for a game such as Hearts of iron 4 I decided to give my opinion on the game. I'll split this up into different sections, if you just want a ya or nah then go to the bottom for a TL:DR.
Gameplay:
Gameplay is massivly different from other stratergy games and even other paradox games, such as EU4, and is much more different than other games such as the older Command and Conquer games or the Total War Franchise. It offers a much different type of stratergy game, less of the single battle type gameplay of Command and Conqeur nor the Individualised battle format of the Total War games. It offers much more of a mass warfare type of experience, where the game focuses on allowing the player to have the experience of a true battle field commander. HOI4 gives you the option to build any army composition that you really want, the true German Armor focused blitzkrieg, the small but elite British Expeditionary Forces, the utter failure of the French Army, the large and elite forces of the United States or the pure hoards of armor and infantry of the Soviet Union, it offers it all. This doesn't mean the game is without fault, as much as many of the games fans may not want to admit.
A.I:
Honestly, if you play and sort of Hearts of Iron 4 multiplayer or discord you will hear the ever infamous "A.I improvments" joke (rightfully so.) Most all Paradox games have god awful A.I, and this game is the worst of the bunch and sadly so (this nearly ruins the game for me.) Seeing the Germans declare war on the Soviets at 1936, seeing the Soviets refuse to defend their Japanese border, The UK refusing to garison their towns of their home country making them easy pray for the German Fallschirmjager and or Marine divisions, honestly I could go on and on and on about the failures of Paradox on behalf of their A.I. Mods can fix this failure on behalf of Paradox, but honestly at best they make the game slightly below what the game should have been on launch. At best the A.I fixes on behalf of Paradox and the dedicated Hearts of Iron modding community is less stiches and clean bandages and more a ripped up pillow case in terms of the fixing the problem (crude, and honestly doesn't do much.) For this you cant blame the modders for trying to fix the a.i, the prvious HOI3 A.I wasn't perfect by any means but it was leaps and bounds ahead of HOI4's A.I . HOI3's A.I was a old, stone bridge, it didn't look nice but it got the job done, HOI4's A.I is a thin piece of gold wrapping papper nailed to each side of the river, looks nice but can't handle nearly as much weight as the previous system.
How fun is the game? :
If you hope for non stop action and slaughtering millions of Krauts a second, sorry wrong game, go back to Command and Conquer for your genoside fix. Honestly, for most nations, the first 2 hours of most countries are boring in terms of action but give you the ability to pre-plan a up coming war as they did in our timeline (or even better.) New players will likely get slaughtered by the easiesty of A.I, as what you may think is the 'correct' way to play gets decimated by the German Blitzkreig. Focusing to much on one kind of power will leave you up♥♥♥♥♥♥creek without a padel, with the Luftwaffe bombing your♥♥♥♥♥♥sky high. Focus to much on Civilian Industry, enjoy having no guns and getting steam rolled by your Fascist Next door. Invest to much in Military Factorys, have fun waiting 2 years to build 1 factory because most of your civilian industry will either be undeveloped or stuck in consumer goods. Invest fully in Infantry, the Blitzkreig will have fun grinding you for Army Exp. Invest fully in tanks, have fun in mountains, reivers, forests or pretty much everything besides flat grounds to which there is very little. Invest fully in your navy, have fun sailing around after your country is taken over because you haven't invested in your land army (ignore if you are the UK, Australia, New Zealand or the USA.) Your level of fun is dependent on how good you are at the game, how much you like slow gameplay and who did there homework both on the game and their enemy before declaring war.
Warfare:
The best part of the game, not saying much, is warfare. Like seeing millions of Soviet troops starve and be slaughtered, but your not the leader of a great nation in real life? HOI4 is for you, the infamous encirclement in HOI4 allows a much smaller nation to royally ♥♥♥♥ a larger nation (that's really the main way for Germany to ♥♥♥♥ over the Soviets.) The satisfaction of breaking through the enemy line with a pure core of armored divisons, seeing the USA doing 'join the allies' as the UK can never be matched, playing miltiplayer is the best way to play (just make sure you play with good/non memer players.) Honestly, if the warfare wasn't good then this game wouldn't be worth but thank the gods the game is saved by the pure satisfaction. However, alas, the game has been massivly dumbed down from Hearts of Iron 3 as most wars end up with drawing an offensive line and pressing the 'go' button againts most nations. If you want a more rewarding war, I advise Micro Managing your units, it makes you feel like much more of a battlefield commander and less of a arm chair general.
TL:DR:
Despite the flaws with the A.I and lazy implemented features for the warfare aspect, but honestly the game is really fun and I would recomend it to those who need a strategy fix. It's quite hard to do a numerical rating, but I'd give it a strong 6/10 due to Paradox now royally taking the♥♥♥♥♥♥with their DLC model (doing what modders do except charging for it, a scummy buisness model and one I hope will stop one day.)

If you like GSGs, it's worth owning. People ♥♥♥♥♥ about the AI, but people always ♥♥♥♥♥ about AI in games if it has to perform anything beyond the most basic of tasks. Have you ever heard people compliment AI in a more complicated game? I haven't. To say HOI3 is somehow "the thinking man's game," with a more robust and realistic AI is utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. When I played Axis USA in HOI3 (latest version), the UK threw a huge chunk of their army with some of their best units into invading Newfoundland, lost it all because I surrounded them by default, and replaced practically none of it by the time I invaded the British Isles. I was expecting a tough landing, but their remaining forces folded at slightest sign of trouble. All that to say the AI in strategy games nearly always make stupid moves eventually. In my experience with HOI4, the AI performs about the same level in this version as I'd expect it to, sometimes much improved from HOI3, sometimes dunderheaded and occasionally worse. Keep in mind, some people have put 1000s of hours into both HOI3 and its more difficult mod, "Black Ice." It'd be no wonder they wouldn't find an incredibley harsh challenge.
Truth be told, if a game deviates from the previous entries in enough of a degree, people♥♥♥♥♥♥on it and call the older ones better, Then another comes out, the cycle continues ad nauseum. This is my experience with any dedicated fanbase that isn't a total pretentious circle-jerk like the Witcher fanbase.
Where HOI4 improves much I find is in the planning phase. For HOI3, this was one of the more dry parts. At times it's an inverse from HOI3, with some people enjoying the planning phase (the early game) and feeling disinterested in the latter parts of the war. When you play it, it feels more involved and exiting, and less like dull micromanagement. If you say somehow HOI3 is "more realistic in its simulation," you're ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ yourself. None of the components of the simulation are absolutely true to life in any of the games. They all use abstractions at the end of the day, and HOI4's are not inherently worse nor prevent it from being worth owning, though it has flaws.

This is an early impressions review.
So...2D Dark Souls. And in a lot of ways that describes to extreme detail what you're going to be seeing. If you've played Dark Souls, a lot of the mechanics will become instantly familiar. You have melee combat with sword and board, dual wield, or two handers, block and parry mechanics, health restoring items that restock at checkpoints, a currency to level up that you gain from each kill, lose at the point of death and must recover, often unforgiving difficulty, replays of other players deaths, messages from other players, and so on. The basic framework is that of taking dark souls and porting the mechanics pretty much directly to a 2D game.
That's not a bad thing, at all, as a framework to build on.
You've still got a grimdark setting, still a lot of zombies early on, and the overall aesthetic is ALMOST fantastic. And this is where we start to hit our first snag. The vast majority of things in the game are an intensely monochrome palette. I wouldn't mind this so much if they'd found ways to make enemies stand out more. A lot of the enemies just blend right in to a lot of the background, leaving me halting for some unknown reason for a moment until I get smacked and realize what's going on. This is by far my biggest complaint, and while it doesn't ruin the game entirely it does make some sections frustrating for entirely the wrong reasons. I can chuckle it off when I die to a boss mechanic that is avoidable but I just didn't execute properly, but getting destroyed because I literally couldn't see what was hitting me as an unintended side effect of the art design is a whole other level of frustrating.
Souls veterans might also find occasional missteps in where it almost copies the formula but doesn't quite. Smacking against your shield seems to impose no penalty on enemy melee recovery for example, and I found myself working a lot to improve my parrying skills because blocking often, although not always, had problems. The dodge roll works about how you'd expect after some practice, and melee combat felt good.
The level up system, I'm not a fan of. It is daunting, honestly in some ways it's more opaque than Dark Souls. You have an absolutely massive, sprawling skill tree to travel along, and making a plan early on can be very difficult, especially when you haven't had as much of a stab at the mechanics yet. Respecing is extremely limited, which comes in the form of grey pearls that can only refund a single skill point each and are only good for an occasional total oops...complete respecs are entirely out of the question. The very complex skill tree and the lack of solid respecs might be fine individually, but put together I'm not a fan of the system.
Overall here, there's a lot to like. The combat is solid, and for anyone that's waiting on their next genuine Souls/Born fix this should be pretty good. It could absolutely stand for some improvement, but so far I'm enjoying what's here and I don't see why that should stop.

Anyway, I love the game and would recommend it to anyone because even if you don't think you would like a tower defense game, this is the one game to play before you are sure, if it doesn't turn you, you cannot be turned.

Mortal online is a special game, not everyone will like it, but if you look at the people who stopped playing they mostly have less than half an hour in game... thats not even enough to be out of the tutorial. You need to be able to deal with death, this game is not for the weak. If you wish to give this game a trial I personally recomend you consider weather you are able to handle death even as a new player. Changes to the game come and go but one thing that remains is player interaction, this is the best part of the game even if you are just traveling the rush of passing someone you can feel the tension between eachother, out in the wilderness of nave it is a constant standoff. This game is one of my all time favorite, its not the best designed hell its not even the best looking, but if you give up on the game before you can see its full potential and give it a real try you are missing out on a world of adventure and excitement every turn you make is a rush every decision must be carefully made. Hey there!
Quick disclaimer; This'll be quite the review! Head on down to the "Bottom Line" if you've not got the patience or time to read through this wall of text!
As a newbie with a little over 60 hours in the game, this'll cover my first impressions along with what I think the game does wonderfully, and what could be improved.
I highly reccomend giving this game a try for yourself if you can muster the courage to work things out on your own, or have enough of a thick skin to interact with the community and it's wonderful and not-so-wonderful members to ask for help when needed!
As a newbie, you're dropped into Mortal Online and greeted by a familiar quest arrow pointing you to the nearest NPC, who will teach you the ropes and get you up to speed.
However, don't think that 'up to speed' means sprinting the 100m like Usain Bolt! 'Up to speed' in this case means gently strolling accross town with a basic understanding of a part of the game's mechanics. :)
Basic swordfighting, interacting with NPCs, crafting armor and taming wild beasts -- bunnies in this case :) -- are on the menu during Mortal Online (MO)'s first few minutes. Once you have ran a few errands for NPCs to get to grips with the game, you meet the captain of the guard who opens the world of MO up to you, and you are free to go!
By free to go, I mean litterally free to go. Once the first few steps in the game are taken, you are left to your devices with a handful of good information -- accessed through the (H)elpful Information menu -- and basic gear -- rags for armor and a good ole' basic sword!
The rest is up for you to decide! Want to make the best armor possible? Want to become a renowned mage, feared by many? Want to run around naked and sing songs to the people of the land on top of your lungs? It's all possible!
Yes. I've seen a naked dude run around singing songs -- well, it was more like screaming... Don't ask.
As a side note worth mentioning, this game does include nudity in the form of a tick box in your options, so that when someone unequips all armor, they are genuinely naked, as opposed to the usual MMORPG 'I've got no armor or anything else equipped but I still have clothes'.
I found this nudity somewhat age-gates the community to a certain level of maturity, or atleast mostly. So I'm not against it whatsoever! Plus, to some of us -- me included -- this just means a more immersive experience! :)
Visually, the game shows it's age. From what the community has told me, it is over 10 years old, released in 2005-2006, and that is appearant in the graphics. Very reminiscent of Oblivion without the soft blur and fantasy elements to it. Very gritty, the game's color palette is quite down-to-earth -- litterally, most things are earth-colored. I quite like it, as it makes me realise that I'm not in an overly fantastic setting!
Gameplay-wise, it is very hardcore and deep. Everything you can think of besides your granny has a 'skill' related to it, which gains experience the more it is used, making your character a neverending growing and changing work of art.
The game is also what is reffered to as a "full loot" game. Meaning that if you are slain, you drop your entire inventory; hotbars, equipped items and all. This makes the risk factor of the game skyrocket when you learn that PvP is non-restricted, making nearly the entirety of the gameworld undoubtedly dangerous, adding a kick of suspense to your expeditions and general going about your business in the Nave -- the name of the gameworld/realm you are thrust in.
As a newbie in MO, I learned as much as possible from the tutorial, and read nearly every single article within the (H)elpful Information window and skimmed the ones that were obvious.
However, after a solid 45 minutes of doing the turotial, getting to grips with the controls and UI and reading the aptly named helpful information, I was left with one question:
"What now?"
The game does a decent job at introducing it's basic mechanics, but not it's core concepts. I was warned quite thoroughly that "it's dangerous out there, store your stuff in banks or you run the chance of losing it all", but I wasn't told much else after the tutorial, which felt quite.. unsubstantial?
A good tutorial makes sure that whomever comes into your game gets hooked. It facilitates player retention and makes it so that newbie players are all at a certain level, it evens out the playing field by having everyone know the same basics.
However, MO's tutorial puts every newcomer at the mercy of what the community will tell them, as most of the information is found either on the official MO Forums, or shared through the in-game "/help" chat.
As far as I'm concerned, the game has very very deep skill and crafting systems which I have, do and will enjoy for the forseeable future. It's neck-deep implementation of PvP mechanics along with satisfying character growth and promising player interactions make it very unique!
However, it does still require additional polishing for it to become a *fantastic* game!
Here's a quick TL;DR of the two small additions I'd put in the game to make it into a must-play!
At the moment, I'd definitely consider MO to be a must-try-for-a-decent-amount-of-time, as it needs a bit to 'grow on you', but rewards you with a very satisfying experience overall, and the potential for meeting great people to form bonds with!
There you go! Those are the thoughts of a newbie that thoroughly enjoys the game, and wishes nothing but the best for it's future!
Feel free to discuss further in the comments of this review, I'd love to hear the opinion of other newbies and vets alike! :)

This is an interesting sattelite mission game.  It is obvious that this is a ported game to PC, but the graphics are quite nice. The gameplay is mission based: you will be given missions regularly that you must complete within a specific amount of time or suffer a reputation penalty; too may failed missions and you will fail the game!  Completed missions reward you with funds, reputation, and progression.  You can also research technologies to make your sattelites more efficient space tools.
To note: this is NOT an open world, sandbox game like Kerbal Space Program.  You are limited to controlling sattelites that are placed into Earth orbit for you.
That being said, anyone with a decent grasp of orbital mechanics will be able to play through the game without great difficulty.
If you are looking for a nice filler satellite management game and can get this on sale (I paid less than $10 for it on sale) then Satellite Command will scratch a nice itch for you.

I wish I could recommend this game, but I really, really can't.  The controls are sluggish, jumping is floaty and aggravatingly unresponsive, weapons either take too long to kill something or spend too much time reloading, and the entire experience is a slow-moving slog.
The underlying issue with this game is that EVERYTHING is designed to take far too long or is intentionally tedious.  There are many missions with mission timers 25 minutes longer or more, with the goal of just scouring each and every room to find weapon parts.  If this sounds like MMO fetch quests, you're right, and these missions are just as grindy, made even worse by the fact that you will do them on maps where you have ALREADY been through the map 4-5 times already.
Movement speed?  Way too slow, even with light weapons.  Even the firing mode is lousy, giving you a pathetic 4 firing directions instead of the bog-standard 360-degree joystick- or mouse-based method that has been around for decades now.  The view frame is much too zoomed-in, meaning you frequently can't see where you're going, causing you to blunder into enemies or traps, as well as triggering incredibly excessive amounts of off-screen enemy respawns.  Map layouts range from mediocre to aggravating, with a great many paths hanging just over your head that you can't access unless you walk halfway across the map to a ladder or something.
The customizable weapons system SEEMED interesting at first, but it's both poorly balanced and based on grinding out items to get the items to make decent parts.  Machine guns have low damage and high magazines, making dealing with many standard enemies, and especially several bosses that have only limited vulnerability, very tedious.  Shotguns deal huge damage and have low magazines, with their "balance" mechanism being semi-auto firing; this means you spend HUGE amounts of time mashing the fire button, which is just plain ridiculous when they could have easily just left the shotguns as full-auto weapons for the simple sake of ENJOYMENT.  On top of that, many of the parts look different, but have minimal performance differences.  And even the bullet types are blocked off by forcing you to have the right level of compatibility with your current weapon parts, so custom weapon diversity is severely curtailed if you ever want to use different ammo types.
There are also dozens of missions, but without much actual variety.  Go fetch these crafting items, kill X soldiers in area Y, destroy this thing, and hostage rescue is about it, with maps recycled CONSTANTLY.  There is a severe mission bloat, with you doing the exact same things over and over and over again on the same levels to make the game seem longer/bigger than it is.
The perk system is also pretty poor.  Unless you enjoy scouring recycled maps for boss/target locations, you'll just end up slapping up on the perk that puts targets on your map, which, in other games, would be part of the standard game design anyway and you wouldn't need any sort of silly perk to see them.  The roll maneuver is almost entirely useless until you can get a perk to give it invincibility which, again, should've been a completely standard thing anyway.
I could honestly go on, but it would just be redundant.  The artwork looks solid, but the game itself is mediocre and entirely third-rate, suffering from a whole raft of fun-robbing design choices.  Basically, unless you legitimately enjoy grinding out item collection for MMO-esque "make this weapon that is sliiiightly better than your current one", skip this game and just get the Metal Slug games.
Too complicated controls and annoying jumping method degrade this game to the C-class indie.

I picked this little gem up when it went on sale. I figured "Hey, it looks like fun, it's multiplayer, and it looks similar to Metal Slug" In some regards it is, but in others, it's a whole other beast. First, I'll draw the similarities.
When you first start up Mercenary Kings, you'll notice, "Hey, this plays a lot like Metal Slug" (if you're familiar with the series). Controls are a little strange at first, though I'd recommend changing them, but once you get down to the nitty-gritty stabby-shooty, you don't seem to notice as much. There's the familiar, arcade-style run-and-gun type gameplay that you'd expect from the screenshots, but what really makes this game unique is the differences from which the game breaks the stereotype.
The crafting system is extensive that sometimes it can be overwhelming, but if you're the type that loves to tinker around and figure out what works best (which varies, depending on the mission), or if you fancy yourself a virtual gunsmith, then you will love this crafting system. A few RPG elements are added in that there are a few stats to keep in balance as you prepare for each mission, but other than that, there's not too much else to the game. I do, however, really like the way multiplayer (both local, on one machine, or over the Internet) is handled. From the in-game base camp, players can join their friends or find other players online and team up to accomplish missions seamlessly (think drop-in/drop-out style, but only for this one area).
In short:
PROS:
Excellent and fun selection of weapons
Familiar gameplay style feels fresh
Seamless multiplayer matchmaking - You can find a team rather quickly, and if they leave you, there's no penalties to you. (A big bonus!)
Lots of pew pew pew
CONS:
Controls can be a bit awkward at first. I felt like a noob who never played arcade games before
Crafting system can be a mite overwhelming for players who just want to jump into the game
Missions can be repetitive if you're grinding for crafting materials
Overall, I highly recommend this game, it was worth every penny.

This is truly an amazing game, I have played it from start to finish more times than I can recall.
The game isn't terribly long (9 Missions in total) and can probably be completed in a few hours, depending on your playstyle.
To me, the draw of this game is not the story or finding all the collectibles, but rather setting my own challenges.
The game features an assortiment of supernatural powers and enhancements which can be bought and upgraded with runes you find in the world.
I personally like to limit myself to 2 different powers and a certain playstyle and complete the game that way.
For example: Right now I'm playing a stealth playthrough where I can use only the Double jump and Possesion to get around.
Graphically this game is an odd one.
It isn't crammed with insane resolution textures or small details in the world. It uses an art style that I can only compare to that you might expect in a painting, but the rather blurry textures keep it from looking truely beautiful.
I'd say the enemy AI is pretty solid, when the see you they rally each other and try to surround you, which can really cause some tense situations and really helps making them appear capable in their jobs as guards.

A game's stealth mechanic loses its point when the enemies are too weak to be a challenge, you can warp around and disappear with impunity, and there are no great consequences for being discovered.
Dishonored is to Thief as Bioshock is to System Shock 2. It's an enjoyable game, but an unfulfilling one compared to its spiritual predecessor.
The immersion is ruined when you realize the solution to being discovered is to kill an enemy, pick up his body, warp up to a place no one can see, and leave it. The AI is too dim to understand what is going on, and, without story spoilers, there is a high central wall on the last mission you can teleport up to. Guard in your way? Knock him out and leave him on top of the wall.
And the last enemy was a joke. I don't know if there's supposed to be some grand fight or anything, but he doesn't even see you coming, not even on the highest difficulty. Warp down, insta-stab. Such fail. It's just sad. All this build up, all this planning, and... that's it? Fail. Total fail. It makes me so sad to be so disappointed.
If you like blowing things up and killing people for no reason like a psychopath with no attached challenge for doing so (the game is easier this way, and with the power you wield, you always ask yourself why you're sneaking around to begin with, which undermines the stealth mechanic completely), this game is for you. If you like stealth games, this game is pretty watered down and disappointing. Thief 1 and 2 still stand tall today and are well worth playing. They're both old and exploitable in their own ways, but despite this, no one can say they're not challenging and well-thought-out. They will give you a run for your money each time you play.
Dishonored has pedigree, from Thief to Deus Ex, and it fails to catch even part of the spark of what made both games such classics. Sorry. I wanted to love it, instead I only liked it.

12 is better than 6 is a interesting take on the well established “twin stick shooter” genre.
Take Hotline Miami, stick it in a western and give it some stylized art direction. What makes 12 is better than 6 unique aside from its visuals is the mechanics of each weapon. There are 5 in total and each handle rather differently. The revolver requires you to fan the hammer. The rife requires re-cocking after each shot. You must also reload each bullet for all weapons types including the shotgun and the bow as well as the weapons mentioned before. There is also dynamite for when things get too hectic.
The visuals create a stark contrast between the environment drawn with purple lines on a paper aesthetic from the vibrant red blood strewn down from your bloodlust.
The campaign is roughly 4-ish hours long and has a decent story and seems mostly satirical. There is also an arena mode that is quite enjoyable. The campaign features some buyable upgrades should you acquire enough money to buy them such as attaching dynamite to rats and having them seek out enemies. There are also some side missions that personally I found quite challenging to earn some extra bucks.
Another thing that makes the game mechanically more interesting is the light stealth mechanics. You can knife people silently or use the bow. Obviously having someone see you or have the dead body be found sets off an alert, not an actual alert but a search is started near your last seen location or near the body.
The game is very fast paced, death and comes in one hit or a couple of grazes, respawns are fast, sometimes so fast I ended up firing and alerting everyone to my location. But the respawns are so fast it was no matter at all.

Defense Grid is one of the best tower defense games ever made. It doesn't deviate much outside the norms for the genre - you accumulate funds over time by killing enemies and gaining interest, and then use these funds to purchase and upgrade towers around the path(s) which enemies take while trying to steal your cores. Successive waves are more difficult, and in some levels you actually build the path yourself by blocking their ability to progress with your towers.
Later levels are quite challenging, there's a wide variety of towers, and there's also multiple modes which can add different twists to the gameplay. It's extremely well balanced, allowing for multiple play styles to come up with valid combinations which can be effective.
Any fan of the genre should own this game, and it also makes for an excellent introduction to what tower defense games can offer.

Evolve Stage 2 is a heavily modified version of the original Evolve focused on a f2p model instead of p2p+DLC model. It features a redesigned UI, trimmed download size, and largest of all, the new Evolve is 100% free of any payments. There is no paywall OR cash shop of any kind. Instead of unlocking content via challenges, characters, skins, and monsters are unlocked by means of currency earned from playing the game. This currency cannot be bought, and as far as I can tell, you cannot purchase the currency. For a new player, the game will be quite enjoyable and has a fair character unlock system that isn't a grind, but you won't unlock everthing in a few hours of play. The current con to the game is that "founders", or people who purchased the game prior to the Stage 2 patch, got essentially penalized from the update, having all progress on their character ranks reset and the only compensation being 3000 silver keys and some animated badges. This is fairly low compensation for what could be hundreds of hours of work to level characters. It can br argued that the ability to play the game comfortably with a sizable player base is worth it, but that's up to the individual. In order to save space on the game, they also cut a considerable portion of content, between some maps and many gamemodes, but the core gamemode, Hunt, and a permanent arena fight mode, Arena, are still in the game. Considrring that it's still a beta, it's very likely that the cut modes will return, but at the moment, they are excluded. Overall, Evolve Stage 2 was the best decision for the game's longevity, and is quite enjoyable to play if you like either coop games or feeling like an unstoppable murder machine. Bringing friends is recommended but definitely not required.

No news is good news....seems currently to be alot of negative reviews here, its a BETA! Seems very harsh to me. But from the SI forums it appears to be a few things getting peoples goats:
1. A very minor change to a 2D Match Engine
2. Change in UI design
3. Polish (minor gripes and mainly usual BETA led issues)
So my feedback:
Match Engine
So far so good for me, haven't seen anything strange and loving the immersion, wish there could be more tbh!! But its a start. And anything I may have seen "wrong" will be because "its my tactics!" rather than anything game breaking. Its a BETA, so I am reserving judgement for implementation of tactics as ones that work will soon be redundant after the countless posts here are reacted to and the engine is adjusted accordingly. Found it harder with lower league teams at the mo than top flight, but most likely as I always have the top flight mindset ingrained after succeeding in previous versions. Animations are still a little wooden, but after sinking into FIFA and PES for the past month again my brain has probably become conditioned to them there! lol! But its certainly the best beta release I can remember!!
2d lovers and those unable to run it leaving on mass? Probably...but maybe not eventually, many a steak and kidney pie is being spat out at the mo!!! I can sympathise with this view to a certain extent and yes there is going to be many players that will be phased out this year and going forward as it becomes more tech heavy. But there are also some of the "hardcore" fans that also love the new graphics engine and the immersion that comes with it, myself fully included. Been playing and been hooked since the first Champ Man and the game is slowly becoming what my 14 year old self back in 1993 could have only dreamed of!! I remember the same outcry as CM4 was released and I had to upgrade my PC for that version (and I did!!). Its a tough choice and road to take, BUT there is a 2D version, much like the text stayed in CM4...that was too a watered down version of the previous in CM01/02. Again just progress and this 2D Classic is hardly a killer and I can see from the outcry on the forums here that it will take a while for change and progress to be accepted. Normal to be honest.
UI
Interesting one. I neither love it or hate it. I don't like how I cannot see the height and weight of a player on their profile. But skins will be my friend soon. Capitals? Its a non issue, but a choice of taste. Also there are not enough options to fill the boxes with different info on the player screen, hopefully to be resolved as having the same info there twice is odd. Overall though its familiar and consistent and still the most intuitive UI for a sports management game out there...full stop. I agree with the posts about scouting needing to be in the inbox, yes I get that I can set weekly reminders, but it would be easier to get emailed a scouting update when completed. Oh and pleeeease can the tactics UI on the match day be changed? Its a killer that the same screen from the tactics menu cannot be entered, its on its side with no analysis and just not user friendly, have to say its the one thing that has had me close to the word "hate" so far!!! But overall its certainly a step up from previous versions and I havent found it mind boggling to get my head round it as have some. Just took some looking and a very small amount of patience.
Scouting
Love it! Best ever in my opinion. I will openly say that I have resorted to Genie Scout in previous versions in the end, but this year its already different, it feels extensive and accurate according to the stats of your scouts, I actually love finding players now in the game again. I like how in my shortlist I can view their scouted ratings, like the data analysts, its now close to being the real thing! Yes!
Transfers
I haven't again seen anything out of the ordinary here. AI appears to behave normally and also give me two fingers as do players if my offers are low etc. Top tier teams seem a little more conservative in their purchases, but also to fill the gaps they need. I purchased a DM from Lazio and almost immediately I could see them desperately trying to plug the gap with a new player. Feels like FM17 and just with better options, so a non issue for me to be honest. And its feedback that its GOOD, positive feedback. :)
Tactics
Its FM17 with additions, simple. But one addition is amazing, analysis. Love it! And the feedback given is far more extensive, bordering on sometimes way too much information everywhere, but this is a simulation right? So its loved and wanted! Just cannot get Blackburn to play football in my lower league game, but maybe its true to life right now!!!! Arsenal I was a wrecking machine and Wengers rightful replacement!! Worried to experiment as I said earlier as no doubt everything will be changed...which is annoying as tactics should be ala football and not changed to counter people complaining which then turns it into tactics to beat the AI only and not football, so please babysteps in this area, no knee jerking, remember those who complain will always have the loudest voices. :) Tactics are easily the best they have ever been, easily!!!!!
Performance
No issues. At all. Occasional lag on screens, but nothing where I need to run out of the house screaming in the street. Sure there is more optimization coming, but like "its your tactics," "its your pc." Or very simply put its a BETA people, they will optimise the game going forward for release.
Graphics card requirements have gone up this year from what I can see. Guessing that will be the cause for most peoples gripes and issues (aside from it being a BETA!!), could be first version of now many that wont work with without one at all, to be expected though in this day and age now, soon will probably be far more important than a processor and most likely make them redundant as hardware.
If I run a game in minimum specs (any game) I expect to play it, but all be it very barely. Perhaps recommended specs should be on the Steam store page as well, or game publishers provide a 3 tiered level of spec requirements getting rid of minimum altogether as often minimum now doesn't mean this game will run fine. Combine that with numerous other PC issues that contribute to whether a game runs smoothly or not, its a nightmare to develop for I'm sure as users have so many variables on their systems as to why a game may or may not be running!!!
Runs at a good speed here. FM17 is faster, as its like lightening now in terms of processing and match engine (after all patches) and with FM18 being the newer version was expecting it to be slightly more intensive on my hardware, but runs well so far to be honest. But given the amount of frustration being shared on Steam they will need get some work done before release, think though given the backlash and the frustration voting on Steam (IN A BETA!!!??!!!) I can almost see an early release BETA becoming a thing of the past which would be a shame as its meant to be so we can give constructive feedback to improve a game we clearly all love. Not to bash SI to death during a beta, give feedback like yours here (kind of) as it would help though with such feedback to provide specs and anything else useful.

Overall enjoying it so far and can actually see myself getting back into this years more. Last version I sunk over 1000 hours into was FM15, (FM16 and FM17 just over 500 each). So hoping for some solid gaming and some immersive, simulated management football this year and next!! Is it worth full price? Probably not as its a face lift with more options (albeit a probable new engine), but nothing new (Madden, FIFA, PES, NHL and any other sports game on the planet.....I swallow them and will this as Im sure the development team hasn't just been sitting around for a year chilling!!) Its a beta as well, so will await the updates and full release. But well done! :)

"Go to this person and get something.
"OH, that person's something has been stolen.
"Go to a Raider's camp and retrieve it."
There is no actual Open world, everything is oddly convenient. Also, you can't pick up enemy weapons and gear. The game is very, very, basic. Which is unfortunate, it had potential. Rage has a Mad Max feel to it, you can race with your buggy and combat enemies with mounted weapons, but sadly the world just isn't open enough to justify it.
This game is simply nothing exciting, but truth is I'm enjoying the game for what it costs. I would say give the game a try if it's on discount. I wouldn't recommend paying $10 as for this game honestly doesn't feel like a $10 game.

Updated 12/21/2016:
Two days after the post launch review and an update has been pushed out for this game, which addressed many of the points they mentioned brought up and that I wanted to see in the game. Playing it again was definitely worth it, it feels better and now acts more like I was looking for in the game. While it's a bit harder to mess things up/more casual, you are still punished when you forget to do something, like leaving the battery charging while trying to build a new satellite, forgetting to start charging once the satellite is in the sun, or when you have a tool running. Started a new game to see all the changes and I played for much longer this second time around.
Would still love to see hard numbers for the satellite resources, both when creating satellites and once it's been launched. Tutorials still need work, I don't think there was a popup window when first entering the engine menu/options for inclination/altitude changes, which while not needed right off the bat, should probably come up when you first enter the menu, or when you first get a mission to H-CAM something on Earth's surface.
Final thing I'd like to see changed, or an option added for, is at present is when switching between satellites while in the planet view, the camera zooms in on the newly selected satellite and you have to return to the planet view. It would be awesome if the camera could just center on the newly selected satellite, without zooming all the way in on it, or having some option to change what happens when selecting a different satellite. Not game breaking or anything, simply annoying at times when trying to get multiple satellites woken up, or pointing to a mission object and having to re-orient the camera with each satellite switch.
Can't wait for further updates and am no longer considering trying to refund this. I would say this update brought it to a place for those new to these types of games to give it a try and see if it's for them or not. Tutorials may still need some work, but they are clearly better than before the update, and Stormtide seems to be very fast on updates and responding to user feedback.
Hard science and KSP fans/players, wait for a hard mode and further improvements, which, if Stormtide keeps updating the game this quickly, could be sooner rather than later.
Initial review 12/19/2016:
I purchased and played this over the weekend, intrigued after seeing Scott Manley's review of it. While I did enjoy it, I felt there were a number of things that could be greatly improved on and was considering returning it for now as it felt like it was in a Beta state, rather than a full release state.

However, I saw this morning that they had a post-launch review and that they would be addressing a number of concerns I had with it, specifically a rebalance of the overheat mechanics and the targeting system. I look forward to the easy and hard game mode types, as I  would love this as something more casual.
I feel the time for a satellite to wake-up was fine as it was, though perhaps if the satellite is manually/properly shut down, rather than auto shutting down due to overheating/power loss, then the wakeup time should be reduced. In-game reason could be that's it's skipping a diagnostic step or five.
Something I would like to see that wasn't mentioned in the post-launch review, is more information on the resource displays, even just a percentage. It would be helpful and more immersive to me, though since in the system window it gives absolute values of resource gain/depletion, knowing the hard numbers would be even better.
All in all, for hard science types and KSP players, this is, or will be, a good buy. For those wanting to get into these types of games, I would wait for the tutorial updates and an easy mode to be made. Overall a good game with potential.
I will try to update this review as I play more and see the game updated further.

I really want to love this game.  I'm a fan of Paul Robertson, action rpgs, and weapon customization.
But the game makes it so hard.  The very core design of the missions is just dull.  Over and over you are given a timer to search a giant maze like map for a randomly placed item or enemy.  Because the maps are large, even if you luck out by heading in the right direction it's still going to take you 5 minutes. If you get unlucky it'll take 15 minutes easily, and if you run out of time or die you have to start over.  It's like they greatly overestimated how much people enjoyed this, because constant navigation is built into things that don't make sense at all.  You spend 10 minutes searching the random boss spawn points to find which one is active, only for the boss to move to another part of the map mid way through the fight.  Now you spend another 2-5 minutes finding the new location, rinse and repeat, and hope you don't run out of time. The game actually expects you to wander through each map a hundred times at 10-20 minutes apiece.
The weapons you construct have no creativity to them and are just not fun to use.  Sure they are creative art-wise, where you can create a toilet gun, but the moment you try to create a shotgun with more than 2 ammo the game cripples the damage so much as to make it useless.  The real potentials for creativity (piercing shotgun?) are completely unavailable, because you are forced to create a 100% sniper rifle to select piercing ammo.  So you are stuck with a few preset weapon paths, creating incrementally damage increasing versions of the same weapon.  The balance of it works against the mission design, because when you are searching aimlessly through a map of endlessly spawning enemies, making it take 3 seconds to dispatch each enemy (from either low damage ouputs or excessive reload times), it just makes the thing a chore.
It's highly unlikely that this will be patched either, the devs seem hung up on this idea of a grinding time sink somehow being fun, as similar things were in scott pilgrim too.

Mercenary Kings is an incredibly faithful exploration of retro gameplay, modernizing out many of the shortcomings of the games of yesteryear. It features gorgeous pixel art reminescent of the 16 bit era, heavily inspired by the arcade classic Metal Slug, and a glorious chip-tune soundtrack.
One might expect Mecenary Kings to fully lift the run-and-gun stylings of Metal Slug given it's style and theme, but instead it actually picks and chooses a wide selection of mechanics from the Mega Man franchise. It notably draws on the Mega Man Zero and ZX series, with a wide selection of collected gems from across the earlier titles.
The game features missions with a variety of optional challenges that are a delight to revist with different armaments; the same level feels different when approached for speed or when explored thoroughly for resources, and players are well rewarded for become familiar with enemy patterns, level layouts, weapons and items.
I was actually very surprised when I started joining in on multiplayer efforts with how wonderfully multiple players integrate, and just how diverse the weapon selection is among players. While it seems natural for players to gravitate to a single weapon layout to me, it turns out that there is little consensus between players on what equipment works best; clearly the weapon crafting system does an excellent job of addressing individual play styles. There is something for everone.
There are some short comings. It is difficult to construct weapons that utilize the unusual ammo types, generally forcing one basic gun type; stocks and sights don't really contribute much to weapons overall except to craft weapons for very specific ammo types. Biomods and Proficiencies are good overall, but there are a wide range of abilities that just aren't present. It's not that the options available aren't significant, it's just that there is a great deal of options that could be added, like modifications to rolling, or jumping (like double jumping). It feels a lot like the more unusual options aren't present for the certainty of avoiding game-breaking bugs or opporunities; it's not bad but it feels overly "safe".
Also, while materials within the game are broken down in to common, uncommon and rare drops, it isn't clear that this doesn't actually reflect the value of any individual drop. While boss drops are only obtainable in a few, or single locations, it's easy for a player to grind for one or two of those individual drops, where some "common" materials, like Rubber, Chromium and Regular Pins, are found only rarely but are required for a substancial amount of crafting. Players can burn an enormous amount of time digging for some less interesting items like Scarlet Pelts just to craft a few basic items.
Mercenary Kings is a game I fully believe exemplfies the ideals of the Indie Game development community; deserving high recognition. And the end credits drop hints for a sequel, which cannot come soon enough; my hope is that it will carry the existing bar of excellent, and push further by promoting more dramatic, more experimental gameplay options. That said; even just an expansion of new maps and enemies would be well worth my time.

Mercenary Kings is a strange beast. It’s like the unusual lovechild of the aging, but still strangely attractive Metal Slug and its sleek, modern boytoy Borderlands, but being raised by the GGG Contra after Borderlands refuses to take custody of the child.
Let me explain: You play as the Kings, a batch of mercenaries that were sent to Mandragora Island to defeat CLAW, a strangely Nazi-esque group conducting strange experiments in advanced technology and some-such. In the process, you die, but are revived with the help of a special Mandragora serum, developed by CLAW to make super soldiers. And that’s about where any semblance of plot lies. You have a cast of kooky characters that are little more than hyperbolized caricatures (Cute female weapons specialist? Check. Caffeine-addicted, one-eyed general? Check. Australian blade expert and all-around outdoorsman? Check. You get the idea), with a lot of gaming and pop-culture references that are entertaining, if not particularly fulfilling.

Extremely good side-scroller Metroidvania game. Works fine with Keyboard+Mouse but Gamepad is still the best choice. Your first run from beginning to end will take about 20-30 hours. Each subsequent playthrough will take considerably less time as you'll know all the shortcuts. If you like 2D games there's no reason to skip this game.
Pros:
Strong skill choice system, let's you get a diverse build.
Depending on your weapons/shields you can have fast paced combat or slower more methodical combat.
Plenty of secret areas with interesting items and gear. There are even some secret zones with their own bosses.
Plenty of rings with different effects to choose from. Functions similarly to Terraria's accessories.
Plenty of different weapon types (16 total weapon types) and armor types.
Generous Invincibility frames when rolling. Possible to kill bosses without being hit if you're good enough.
Mostly non-linear gameplay. Once you make it a few hours in you have multiple zones to visit as you wish.
Cons:
No ingame map. You have to remember how each zone connects to each other or use an external map.
Some of the bosses (19 total) are lackluster and not very memorable.
Some of the enemies rely on grapple attacks that can bug out and make you fall into the void.
A few of the NPC quests (not required) are basically impossible to finish without a guide.
Some of the weapons are simply better than others, like the Greatsword/Greathammer.
The faction system (Creeds) is fairly confusing at first.
No mod support at the moment. Hinted at by devs as possible in the future.
Doesn't hold your hand at all tutorial-wise. Some may see this as a good thing though.
I'm not a big fan of the art style, especially the human faces. The backgrounds are fine though, if a bit samey in some zones.

Give the game a shot and form your own opinion of it, i'm glad i did.

Another year, another version of football manager that will take up 100’s of hours of my time.
This year feels different though, last years entry was probably the best since 2012 but it was largely just refining areas like the previous years have been. Some people were annoyed at the lack of innovation but it felt very polished - minus a few things like Social media - however whenever anyone points out the lack of innovation the obvious counterpoint is ‘well what can you really add to a football Managment sim that the game doesn’t already have?’. Well this years version does have innovation, the medical centre, dynamics and new scouting system all make visible and noticeable changes to the game experience. However as with every new innovation the game has had, some of these features will need to be refined in future releases. I’m fine with that, after all you’ve got to start somewhere. I’m sure not everyone will see it that way, people that often cry out for innovation will no doubt now complain that certain areas aren’t as polished as others, I suppose SI can’t really win in that sense.
The medical centre puts info that was already in the game or behind the scenes into a much more visual format, I imagine this is both aimed at being a realistic tool but also a functional one, aimed at those users who do not do so well when it comes to player management. A nice addition.
The Dynamics feature feels like the best addition, and despite what others have said this definitely isn’t a UI thing only. Players actually have to integrate with your squad now, and you have to be aware of aggravating certain players. No longer can you walk into a club and sell your best player because he doesn’t fit your system without there being any ramifications, especially if that player if a leader in the team. It’s a brilliant system that seems quite far reaching and I’m sure I’ll notice more impacts from it in the future.
Scouting is an odd one - I like bits of it and dislike others. The UI needs some improvement here as certain items are harder to find than they used to be. I like the attempt at realism though, after all it’s not realistic for a manager to be sat in front of a database searching for specific players (although you still have that choice), now your scouting team bring targets to your attention in a better way than before - it’s going to take some getting used to, I’ve been playing these games a certain way for a long time now, I feel areas like this I need to go into with an open mind in order to enjoy them fully.
There are of course a host of other improvements, the new contract clauses look very fun, however I miss some of the camera views in matches, there’s also some odd UI choice but then again I do feel that’s something I say every few versions only to then get used to them after a few weeks.
Overall a solid 8.5/10 - there are bugs at present but based on previous beta experiences 90% if these will be gone by launch day. Some innovation to the series that gives SI a really good starting point to then polish in FM19 - this is better than FM17, just as FM19 will be an improvement on this, but if you love Football Manager you will love this game.

As a seasoned player and a long time fan of Football Management games, each year I looked forward to the release of the new ones. And while each year it felt more and more like an major update with some minor additions, this edition is the first one where I feel the need to write a review. And it's not because I'm so positive about it.
Yes, I am aware we're playing the beta, and on the discussion forum I wrote I wouldn't judge yet, but a few hours later, I cannot see SI fixing this product.
And I don't even know where to start.
Lets start with the GUI.
It is both counter intuitive and build without thought. Some buttons are in a really misplaced; so badly that you probably will miss them half the time. Other options that are absolutely mandatory seem to be missing from certain screens, unless I'm blind. For example, during the match, you can change players on the field from more than 1 screen. But only on 1 screen it will show the option to have a chat with them. Another example of bad GUI is that you can't mouse over on all players and see their match fitness and match sharpness. Some show those percentages when hovering over the circles, others don't. The bars that show the proficiency with tactics appear to be flying all over the place, and the GUI in general feels extremely sluggish and slow.
But ok, that's only what you -see-. Now lets look at how it plays.
I was looking forward to several new features. One of those is Dynamics. This sounds interesting but is horribly implemented. During the teammeeting before a match, and during the match itself, the whole team is completely indifferent to me, or too busy doing other stuff, or not interested in anything I'm saying. This has been going on since the very first day I joined.
The morale is great, everybody is happy. But nobody is listening. It might be me, but if you suddenly have a new boss; you -listen-. You wont be, and I quote: "preoccupied with something else". LIKE WHAT?!?! PLAYING ON THEIR PHONES?!?!? No. This addition had potential; social clusters within the team, a hierarchy, being the top dog. But they implemented it half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Instead of making it in a way that the social clusters are merged within the team and club, it's just an added artificial difficulty. It's not merged into it as a part of an entity, but as a seperate unit. It's not easy to explain, but a few hours into it, you'll immediately get what I mean.
The scouting apparently also had an overhaul. And it got worse. Now every so many weeks, you get to seive through two dozen scoutingreports, half of which are useless. The star-rating, as far as I know, denotes the usefulness of a player for the club. Why do I get 7 suggestions for 2 star players then? Don't I have a head of scouting that can already discard all these useless fodderplayers and only give me the players that he thinks are actually useful?! You'd think that, right? Well, after adjusting the scouting settings, none of that changed.
So no, 2 of their major additions they praised so much, are already irritating and badly implemented. It feels like a rush job, and the setup of the GUI definitely doesn't change that feeling. It feels they ran out of ideas 10 months ago, 6 months ago they thought 'maybe this and that', and when they finished those ideas, half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ 3 weeks ago, they realised they didn't have a GUI suitable for it.
But, all of that, it's not important, right? Through all the♥♥♥♥♥♥ you can still manually find your pearls for purchase, and implement them in your team, nice and smooth. For me, the game is only important for 2 bits; finding and purchasing the best young players for the lowest price, and winning matches.

This is literally how the transfer went:
> 20.5 mil + additional clauses for that player
>> 36 mil + addition clauses you offered, we want!!

>> OK DONE DEAL HERE!
Is this the 'improvement for realistic transfers' SI talked about? Ok, if by improvement they meant 'same as FM2017', then sure. Fine. Lets do the match itself. Maybe that can redeem all of the negativity now.
Spoiler: It can't.
I'll give several examples here.
Long recap:
> My players with high passingstats (yes, primary/secondary included) are unable to pass over a distance of 5 meter without screwing up. If this happens under pressure, sure, I understand. But these guys have 3 different, clear, options to pass to, yet they pass into the opponents feet.
> Decisionmaking sometimes doesn't exist. I see this happen a lot so far: one of my players has the ball, and one or several teammates close by. No pressure from opponent. The player just waits with the ball when an opposite player comes running in, and loses the ball. I'm not talking about split second actions here; I've seen Ricardo Rodriguez hold the ball for a full 4, 5 seconds to lose it, whilst both Romagnoli and Biglia were within 5-10 meters, in the clear. And not once, but several times, with several players.
> Opposite player instructions seem to be odd. I expect world class players with high def/markstats (again, yes, primary/secondary included) to know how to mark. But more often than not, an opposing player (AMLRC, FC) seem to be allowed to walk freely around.
