I tried playing with 3 in the back, but no matter how wide I set the width setting; the 2 outer CB's are always close to the sideline, or at least halfway between the box and sideline. If I play Narrow, I want those 3 NARROW. Not spread in the complete width. And yes, tactical familiarity is high to very high. They just don't seem to listen.
To give you an idea, I was cursing here at it. My girlfriend came over to ask whats wrong; she knows NOTHING ABOUT FOOTBALL AT ALL. I explain what my problems where, she looks at the screen and asks "so whats that guy doing there?"
Yeah exactly. Nothing that I've told him to do.
Anyhoo, it's 00:42 here, you get the idea. I can absolutely not reccomend it as it is now. The above examples are just a few, but there's much more that is irritating. So irritating, I'm seriously considering a refund.
Think of it like this: if someone completely inept at the game (=other half) can see why it's not working; wonder if you, as a fan, should bother with the purchase. Unless you want to pull the hair out of your head. Then knock yourself out.
Update: Requested and received refund. Couldn't continue playing this, the illogical behavior of my players, the crap GUI and the halfarsed implementation of the new features were too much to swallow for me; and I stand with my original observation on the discussionboards; this doesn't feel solvable within now and release, nor any time soon after. SI really needs to start scratching their heads and look how to streamline their game. Maybe skip a year, and rewrite the whole entity from bottom up again. Involve the community more and look at their suggestions. But FM18 will definitely not appear in my library any more, and from now on I will only purchase an FM if it looks like SI is actually trying to make it better, not just a patch.

I can't remember how far back my FM gameplay goes... 97/98 I think... and it's had plenty of ups and downs over the years.  For a beta, this version is better than some and poorer than others.  It's an improvement in some respects from FM16 and FM17, both of which were absolutely dire in my opinion.  Some improvement isn't enough.  The franchise has been running long enough that it should be far better than it is.
The "revolutions" in game development that have been claimed in previous years give the appearance of being woefully misrepresented and served little purpose other than to break something that worked.  Yes, the intention might have been a more realistic experience, or a prettier gameplay engine, but at what cost?
The new 3D match engine claimed for this is "new" but is hardly a vast improvement, and certainly not grounds for the fanfare it seems to have been given.  Animations don't look significantly different from the last 2 versions, but there are some subtle changes.  The stadia, lighting effects are improved... but that is icing on a mouldy cake.
The match engine is still poor.  The AI is poor.  Based on previous years, it'll take 4-5 months to patch it up to anything approaching an acceptable standard, but then come the next version it reverts to ridiculous again.
Every year, it's new features that are frosting while the core of the game remains broken and far too random.  And while the developers insist scripting isn't part of the game, I remain unconvinced of that.  There are just some teams and some results that are too ingrained regardless of whether I'm controlling the team or "go on holiday" and let the computer play itself.
I keep buying this every single year, jumping into beta and every single time I wish I hadn't bothered.  This is the last time I'll buy it early, if I buy it at all in future.  No more early access, no more beta, probably no more buying it until at least after the final patches are done.  Then I'll consider reviews and consider whether I'll touch FM19.
Based on the evolution over the last 3 years... I won't be back until well into the 20s.  The only saving grace this version has, is that it's better than the last 2, neither of which I played more than a few seasons (and lost those in a reformat).  I'll stick with this until I get frustrated enough to quit, but that's more because I have nothing else to do than because I truly enjoy it.

Missions in the game are the following, rescue hostage,kill a boss,kill a certain # of a type of mob, kill all the mobs in a certain area, meet with and individual,find and destroy an item/s, or collect a certain amount of a item. Now this might not sound like many mission types but the game throws enough at you to not make the missions boring,at least for me.There are secondary objectives for each mission including secret ones not listed.The reward for the other objectives is typically more money and/or parts. You might say meh to that,but when you want to buy/craft that once piece those harder to find items you might get from  them might be worth your time. Thanks to a scrollable in game map the game makes finding your way to your objective pain free though not all objective types will be marked.
Level time can be  a fun time or one that will make you wish for tons more maps.The game has a set number of maps that as you play through the game you will revisit area and unlock larger portions of the areas. This is not a bad thing because you will be more focused on the combat and your objective.Early on in the game it can become a bit tiring to constantly play on the same map,but as you get further along you get a nice variety.The maps themselves are not small and can take you a bit of time to travel around.

BugZy's Review: 12 is Better Than 6 - The fast-paced Wild West
The following is my opinion.
Greetings from the excellent hand-drawn and very inky Wild West of 12 is Better Than 6, a top-down shooter like Hotline Miami but where everyone calls everyone ‘amigo’ instead of blowing each other’s brains out. That’s not to say there isn’t an incredibly satisfying amount of shooting people on sight, but your intent isn’t to massacre every living thing in the area. Or is it?
In this dangerous world you will find yourself coming across friends, foes, blue and red ink and guns, which will fail to help you if you don’t have fast reflexes. Your best friend in the Wild West is your reflexes. If you turn a corner you will need to have your gun cocked and be ready to pull the trigger or lunge your knife into your opponent, because wait half a second and your enemies will chop your limbs off and make a nice stew out of them.
The game has unique shooting mechanics, where you press a button to♥♥♥♥♥♥your gun and press another to pull the trigger. Sometimes it can be tedious, like when you are trying to take out a large group of enemies but makes you feel better about managing to kill them all in the end.
Something I believe is great is the ability to choose whether to go in guns blazing or be stealthy, which this game executes in a perfect style. The first option can be dangerous but is very possible, and the second option is all about timing and waiting for your opponents to walk in a certain direction, allowing you to sneak up and take them out from behind or sneak past them altogether.
The basic story is that you are a Mexican prisoner in the late 19th century fighting for freedom, ultimately making your way through the dangers of that time to get from Mexico to Texas. If you choose to pay close attention the story can be quite interesting, but if you aren’t patient or decide not to delve deep into it you can just skip most of it.
The visual side of the game is a stunning hand drawn masterpiece and, through killing lots of enemies, quickly becomes very bloody. The game is based around this graphics style created by talented artists almost entirely and, without it, would probably be ‘just another shooter.’
It has a great soundtrack too that can go from calm piano tunes to ‘LET’S KILL SOME PEOPLE’ in the space of three seconds. It makes the adrenaline rush through you as you hide behind the cover of a table, popping your head out while your enemies aren’t shooting and shooting them back.
Overall the game is lots of fun and I recommend you buy it if you enjoyed Hotline Miami and other top-down shooters. You’ll have a blast!

12 is better than 6 is a top down hardcore gorgeous looking shooter with a western theme. The gameplay is very similar to Hotline Miami series but this one has a stealth element as well. Setting takes place in the late 1800’s. Your main character is a slave who has escaped and is trying to reach Texas.
The game looks absolutely gorgeous, it’s art style is amazing. The game is hand drawn which gives it a very unique and interesting art style. The backgrounds are white in the whole game with the objects and characters drawn just like pen and paper. When you kill someone you get the blood which is in red color sort of like Hatred. In between the acts you get these visualization pictures of the current scenes. One such as seen below. I have to say the graphics and art style are very impressive
.
When you start the game from Steam you get a couple of options. You can start game in low resolution or high resolution. Both of these work fine but the high resolution is the one I used and I didn’t encounter any problems. The game ran very smooth as is required for such fast action shooters.
Every single western themed game I've played has the most amazing sound track. This game has one of the best sound tracks I have ever heard. I can listen to the music all day long. The shooting and stabbing sounds are nice too. The shooting sound especially packs a good punch.
This game is much more tactical compared to Hotline Miami where you have so little time to shoot and the gameplay is much faster and unforgiving. This game however is still fast paced but you can get away with missing a shot. There are two ways you can approach your target, you can go all bang bang and shoot everyone in sight or you can stealth kill or even get past enemies to reach your goal. I think this makes the game very unique and tactical. You can view past your vision by holding shift so you have a better idea of where the enemies are.
This game features a unique shooting and reloading feature. To shoot you have to♥♥♥♥♥♥y our revolver or rifle, you do that with the right click of the mouse and every time you have to shoot you have to♥♥♥♥♥♥your weapon again. This can be tricky as every single shooter whether top-down, FPS, third person I have ever played you just press the mouse button to shoot. So I took a few failed tries for me to get used to that mechanic. The reloading mechanic is also different as you load every bullet individually. You have to keep pressing the reload key (in this case ‘R’ key) to reload all the bullets. Other than your regular weapons you have the knife which you can select with the ‘Q’ key and you can stealth kill enemies with it. I found that knife Is your best weapon in this game, it’s much better to go with a stealth approach as you won’t have 5 enemies running towards you and shooting you. You die if you get hit one times (though I could’ve sworn there were a few times I got shot and lived, just the screen would have that blood filter like those FPS shooters. Maybe you don’t die immediately when you’re not shot right at the center of your hit box). Game also has TNT bombs which you can shoot by pressing ‘F’ key. These will land where ever your cursor is. Later in the game you also get a bow and arrow.
Most of the missions have you going to a certain place in the map which is marked by an skeleton arrow marker on your screen. You don’t have to kill everyone, you just have to get there so you can basically do most missions with just stealth. The enemy AI Is pretty clever, sleeping enemies will come to the aid of their friends. When someone finds a dead body they will look for you and they will try to bum-rush you with guns and knives if they spot you. Sometimes that can be a good thing though if they run at you in a line as you can get more than one kill in a shot. Especially the rifle you can get multiple kills with one shot. The dialog can be hilarious and racist (it was the 1800’s what do you expect). The game’s story was not the greatest but it was funny. Some gameplay footage can be found below:
The game is hilarious and very fun to play. On top it looks and sounds absolutely awesome. I would highly recommend this game. The story is not the greatest but dialog is hilarious.

Fun 2D Dark Souls-esque game with a tech tree to customize your character in a myriad of ways. It was a bit of a slow start for my chosen playstyle due to lack of weapons but once I got a giant axe and hammer I loved crushing things into the dust.
The combat can be tough but fair though once properly equipped it may be on the easy side. There are blocks, parries and rolls (and fat rolls when you wear too much heavy equipment) to keep you alive though the enemies can also react quickly to make up for only being in two dimensions. The bosses were suitably epic and could be quite challenging if you were not prepared--only one I really call BS on due to a number of OHK at its disposal. The scraps of lore and story are intriguing and a nice motivator though hardly necessary to follow. The settings are interesting and varied and the art style can be a bit ugly but it's still very charming. The music is nice and gritty to get you in the mood for exploring this wretched land. The areas rarely outstay their welcome and you can make a good bit of progress in short bursts.
My only complaint is the platforming controls could be a little tighter--that or I'm just bad at platforming, which is true. Trying to grab on ledges to climb up could be an exercise in frustration at times.
The game could be a bit obtuse about some mechanics. I do recommend just opening up the wiki pages when in doubt.
It clocked in at ~17 hours and I had not completed all the optional dungeons. If you're looking for something to scratch that Dark Souls itch I'd definitely check it out.

Here we are then with a post-apocalyptic futuristic dystopian pseudo-western shoot ‘em up. Sound familiar? It should do if you’ve played Borderlands or any of its sequels and it’s easy to draw comparisons between the two games because they both have the same aforementioned premise. However, the similarity ends here because RAGE lacks Borderlands’ sense of humour, and, more importantly, its driving storyline and wonderful characters. As such, RAGE gives a series of cookie-cutter missions that seem to have no real coherent storyline to motivate you or give you purpose and the NPCs you meet are one-dimensional at best, plain boring at worst. All this adds up to a game with no real personality or flair and I have to admit that I didn’t enjoy it nearly as much as Borderlands and its sequels.
As far as game interface is concerned, it is overly complex and one wonders how many gamers have lost patience trying to find out how to throw a grenade or use any other equipment other than guns. A PDF user manual would be useful here, rather than wasting valuable time surfing the Internet for solutions to simple problems (such as how to monitor health) from other gamers. This left me feeling frustrated and disenfranchised from the whole affair. At one point early on in the game I was told to assign attributes to my vehicle. “How do I do that?” I asked myself. The silence was deafening.
Speaking of vehicles, mention must be made that this game is biased towards driving and vehicle combat in particular. This means that if you use a game controller, as opposed to a keyboard, you will experience far less angst and you will certainly spend far less wasted time trying to beat lap times set by the game in order to progress. In short, if you like vehicle combat and racing using just your PC keyboard, then this game is for you. If, however, like me, you prefer combat with feet on the ground using keyboard and mouse, you are probably not going to like RAGE much. If, however, RAGE had adopted Borderlands’ keyboard and mouse system of driving (allowing steering with the mouse), rather than just the ASDW keys, the game would have been much more fun for us PC users.
On the plus side, the graphics and sound are very good and whilst vistas of derelict bombed-out cities couldn’t really be described as “eye candy”, they are presented very well, but they are mere window-dressing in what is essentially a soul-less and not very entertaining game. I found myself gratefully saving and exiting to get on with some work in the real world, rather than the other way around. On a marks out of ten basis, I would give this game a grudging four out of ten.

If you are reading this review right now, and consider buying the game, do it. It's that simple, the game is totally worth the money. First of all, it's a First Person Shooter Tower Defense game. It's rules are simple:
- Choose your personal Towers and Weapons.
- Build blocks to create a maze as big as possible.
- Build towers using resources that you gain for completing waves.
- Upgrade your gear and towers.
- Defend the core at all cost.
Sanctum has this good feeling of progression. Each new wave provides another, a more difficult challenge. And the player must keep up. By upgrading the towers and weapons. Which by the way, come in a surprisingly pleasant number. There are a lot of different towers to choose from. Some are used to deal damage to the creatures on the ground, and some to those airborn. So it's a good idea to buy them both, and experiment with their placement. Another very nice addition, are the "Support Towers". They can manipulate your enemies in various ways. The "Slow Field" for example, slows every creature that steps on the ground where it's placed. There also towers that amplify both yours and your tower's attacks, make your enemies more susceptible to damage, and so on. Speaking of enemies, each type of creature has it's own good looking alien body. That comes with a certain, sometimes hidden, area called the "Weakspot". Each alien has it's own unique abilities, like "Charging", "Soaking", "Dodging", well, you get the point. They not only behave differently, but also look so. Very cool and fantastic-looking models.
Your towers are the main source of firepower in Sanctum. But the player is as important. You get to choose from 6 unique weapons like the "Sniper", "Freeze",and "Tesla" guns. Which come in very handy when dealing with certain enemies. Especially those that somehow survived your defenses. You can create some really awesome guns and towers combinations if you think about it. You could, for example, use your "Freeze" gun to temporarily stun all the enemies in a certain radius. And then blow them all away with a charged "REX". It's really awesome come to think about it.
Another thing worth mentioning is the variety of maps (16 if have the DLCs) and game mods (like Bounty, Stamina, Pre-Build, and Standart). Which add a certain feeling of freedom. And the maps are pretty awesome. They look vibrant and alive, full of fauna and flora. Which is so strange looking that it makes you love it. Giant spores, glowing trees, multiple Suns, huge flowers, and mineral-rich caves. But the best thing about the maps, are the Easter Eggs. There are so many secret spots to find. So well-hidden and camouflaged, that you'll spend some time looking for them, and when you'll finally find them, they'll put a smile on that face.
And now, my favorite subject, the Music. I never thought I'd enjoy Sanctum's music so much as I do. Every map has 2 pieces of music attached to it. The first one plays in the "Building" phase. Usually a rather slow and tuneful loop, which I always like. And the second piece plays while the "Action" phase is in progress. A very pulsing, rhythmic and dynamic song, that I just love. Just listen to
or
. Please do, they might seem simple and plain, but they feel so complex and sparkling. 16 different maps, 2 songs for each... You do the math. All the credit goes to Coffee Stain Studios, and more specificaly to the genius Gustaf Tivander.
The last but not least, the best feature of this game is the Cooperative play. You and up to three of your friends get to build, upgrade and defend together. It's fun and effective, it grants even more creativity and firepower. Letting you get the most of this game. Which I strongly recommend if you're looking for either a good Co-op, or Tower Defense.

An “ok” non-AAA game that provides a mainstream stealth and sniping experience.
Presentation and writing are mediocre and clichéd, but I was already expecting this. Otherwise, the story is not bad, and slightly more down-to-earth than most Call of Duty games of late. Levels are very linear and heavily scripted. You are guided by your spotter who stays at your side most of the time. This provides good immersion and manages to convey the sense of working as a team, but his AI is a bit unreliable when in open combat.
The scripting is fairly basic and lacks some polish. There were various issues, like dialogue getting cut off, or checkpoints not reloading correctly. A few times my character would confirm over radio that I had the target in my crosshair, but the target was no where to be seen on my screen. The checkpoint save system has the usual irritations associated with such a system. It is also a pity the difficulty settings offer no more options beyond “easy, medium, hard” - I wanted to play “medium”, but without the “red dot” aim assist that ruins the sniping challenge. Also, once you have started, there is no option to change the difficulty later. I had a few crashes to desktop. All these issues were very annoying, but did not ruin the experience.
The graphics are decent (as you would expect from the CryEngine) but do not quite have the same visual quality as the Crysis games. Some areas look really nice, but others less so. The standard quality setting are poorly optimised. I achieved much better fps after careful tweaking (tip: put “object detail” on low for massive fps boost and next to no quality loss).
Controls are ok, but feel a bit clunky and are unresponsive in some contexts. Fortunately there is no mouse lag or acceleration. Weapon handling and ballistics are ok, but not simulator grade. The game lacks a detailed tutorial and you cannot “zero” the sights to various ranges like you can in ARMA and Red Orchestra 2. The simulation of wind on bullets feels artificial because the wind speed is not effectively reflected in the environment - vegetation does not respond accordingly and there are no other indicators like the sound of wind or moving dust etc. The displayed distances seem to be fake - an ingame distance of 400m is actually closer to 200m (a sin many mainstream games commit one way or another to be more accessible to console peasants). Compared to Far Cry 3, this game was clearly made on a smaller budget, with less content, freedom and polish, but in the end I still liked the single player campaign more here. It is more cohesive and serious, while Far Cry 3 was a theme park of absurd sensationalist violence.
Overall this is a decent second-rate game I mildly enjoyed. I had very modest expectations, and it satisfied them. Get it when on sale.

There is a really great game with powerful crafting abilities hiding underneath an extremely unfriendly introduction.
Here's some of the problems with the game's first rank:
1) Your starting weapon is weak, short ranged, and has a small clip to boot.
2) They chose one of the worst maps ever for the starting missions. Confusing layout, lots of little unconnected rooms, and tons of elevation changes; apparently just to screw with you.
3) Very poor mission choices to start with, including a gathering mission and a rescue 8 hostages mission which, combined with the annoying map layout and the fact that the stuff you're looking for isn't marked on the map (most missions are kind enough to give you an 'x' to head towards,) seemed to have been chosen specifically to weed out new players.
4) Your extremely limited choices to upgrade, once you finally manage to pick up some crafting supplies, really don't give you the tools to significantly modify your weapon.
All told, it'll take you somewhere around an hour and a half to get out of that horrible slog.
So why am I recommending this game?
Because as soon as you start to move up the ranks, all kinds of new stuff is unlocked which greatly improves the experience. You start getting all kinds of real choices for your weapon: bullet hose machine gun or single-shot sniper rifle? Shotgun or pistol? Submachine gun or magnum? Your choice! Mix and match pieces from each to completely customize your experience and unlock the ability to use special ammo types with a variety of effects.
You'll also start seeing some interesting choices for hand-to-hand weapons: Do you take the tiny knife that won't weigh you down, or a massive sword or spear that can inflict massive damage at range (and never runs out of ammo!)
The ability to choose two perks that can really help customize your character. Need to throw more bullets at things? Double your magazine size or pick up faster shooting. Looking for crafting materials? Make it so that enemies always drop items and/or make them drop rare items more often.
Better maps!  Now, not going to say it's all roses (I really didn't like the temple, which is another extremely vertical level), but it's all a step up from the starting jungle map.
Mission choices! Past the first rank, you generally don't need to complete every mission to get to the next rank. Have a mission that's kicking your♥♥♥♥♥ Skip it, then come back in a rank or two with a bigger, better gun.
Pros/Cons:
+ Great pixel graphics.
+ Great music.
+ Great customization.
+ Epic boss fights.
- Horrible starting levels.
- Control scheme that sometimes feels like it's fighting you.
- Why can't I shoot diagonally? (Most of) the enemies can!
Overall:
+Worth the starting slog.

Don't get me wrong, this is a great game.
It's a really epic grand strategy, with plenty of history for you to discover and change. The mechanics are very well crafted and the paradox grand strategy games are really unique - you probably won't find this type of gameplay anywhere else. If you want to hear more of the reasons why this is a great game read the positive reviews.
With all that said I don't recommed you buy this game. It has a terrible DLC policy. I bought this game quite a while ago and I've been punished for buying it earlier than now. The developers continually evolve the game, adding in new mechanics and features, yet they charge so much for what are essentially very big updates. This, in addition to the fact that there are so many expansions, means that to get the full game you have to fork out a ton of money. Too much - and remember this is coming from someone who's spent a decent amount of time with the game.
To add insult to injury, if you're playing singleplayer then not having some of this DLC almost breaks the game. For instance, the AI can develop their provinces - but I can't as I don't have the "Common Sense" DLC. This puts me at a significant disadvantage.
The only saving grace is that if you are playing with someone else, in multiplayer, who has all the DLC then you get it too (although this is to be expected - otherwise you would literally be put at an advantage against  real players).
Sadly Paradox has an essential monopoly on the grand strategy genre, meaning if I want to play a grand strategy game I have to buy a Paradox one. As of late they all have this horrible DLC policy. Seriously, take a look at how much it costs to buy either EU4 or CK2 with all the DLC. It's disgusting that they would charge this much. Furthermore it's disgraceful I see people defending this practice with how enjoyable the game is. The quality of the game doesn't take away from the Dysentery that is it's DLC policy.
So don't buy this game and don't support this type of anticonsumerism. If you give them an inch, they'll take a mile.

Then let's ignore the fact that the very first place where noobs are sent to train and level is a cess pool of random ganking by high level characters and neither the players nor the devs seem to give a♥♥♥♥♥♥that it only serves to chase potential players away.  The game promotes high level characters running around naked with nothing but a weapon, smashing random noobs or their pets and suffering only the loss of a cheap weapon.  If they do kill you and manage to get away from the guards, in TWO MINUTES their flag goes away and they can walk past the guards like nothing happened, with all your gear in their pocket.  Thieves are broken to the point it encourages them to run around totally naked.  You can become a criminal and be killed just for looking at another player's inventory. Mages cost an absolute fortune to get started and to be any good, you need to spend hours using autohotkey to spam damage spells on yourself in order to skill up.
But ignore all of that.
Here's the real fun.  If you own an AMD processor, you're screwed.  You'll have to reduce your audio settings to CD quality or you'll lag out immensely when you die.  Next, you'll have to turn the game's graphics down to the absolutely lowest settings, otherwise the memory leaks after an hour become so intense that you're running at 5 fps.  And then there's the random crashes with render errors.  They always take place at the most opportune moments, like when you're in a pvp fight, or you're running from something trying to eat you.  The help channel will tell you precisely why these crashes happen.  The game has not been optimized.  I think it's been out for what, 7, maybe 8 years and they still haven't optimized the graphics code?  Compared to fps games like Rust, the graphics look ancient. And when you turn the settings down in order to keep from lagging out, they look even more horrid.  Bugs abound.  Creatures falling out of the sky, rising up through the ground.  Crossing the bridge to the 'new' continent with pets and you most likely won't have any pet afterward or you'll find yourself hundreds of feet above the ground.  And that new continent came out in an expansion 2 years ago and they still haven't fixed half it's bugs.
The game really had potential once upon a time.  I really wish I COULD like this game.  But the fact that noobs are given ZERO opportunity to learn the game (there isn't even a wiki to document things) before they get swords shoved up their asses by griefers who've played for years makes this game a closed loop. Rage is a first-person shooter set in a post-apocalyptic world that offers plenty of enemies to shoot, and a variety of other mini games to play.
As far as the world is concerned, there will definitely be a lot of comparisons to Borderlands. It is certainly a darker, and grittier version of that world, but it is less expansive and even less characterful than Borderlands. Also, the game tries to progress the story through a series of quest-givers to make it feel even more like Borderlands, however without any of the RPG elements such as character progression, talent trees, or loot, it seems out of place. In fact, because there are no RPG elements, the story could have been presented in a much more immersive way.
The game tries to add in other diversions to make the world feel more immersive. Crafting allows you to create various gadgets and weapons, but you can easily get through the game without crafting anything. Often, it is simply easier to just buy whatever you want instead of crafting it. There are a variety of mini-games, including a card game where you can collect cards found throughout the world. However, not everyone in this world plays it. In fact, only a very few NPCs play this game, and they can be beat without finding all the "best" cards, so it takes the incentive away from trying to hunt down the cards. The game also tries to shoehorn in a driving aspect and even lets you upgrade all the parts of the vehicle: and you can only get these upgrades through a currency you get from racing. But in the end, the racing is not really challenging nor particularly fun.
So finally, that leaves the shooting element of the game. There are certainly many enemies to shoot in this game. But none of your guns seem to pack a visceral punch. They don't sound or feel strong enough, and even when at point blank range with a shotgun, most average-grunt enemies still require 2 to 3 shots to down.
All-in-all, Rage is a game that has many dimensions, but none of them are fleshed out particularly well. If you are a fan of first person shooters, you may find some interest in playing through this title, but it's certainly not going to be a title you will have a great experience playing, nor will it be particularly memorable. It's pretty much the definition of "middle of the road."

Ok, so I decided I would redo my Sanctum 1 review since I did terrible Sanctum 2, so I'll just explain why I prefer THIS one over the 2nd one.
PROS:
The game itself: I want to point this out to EVERYONE who apparently likes Sanctum 2 better, Sanctum 1 is a tower based game with FPS elements, so you can help your towers out as well as have something to do than just sit there.  The 2nd one is FPS based with towers involved and I HATE that, the best part about the first one was the huge maps, level up weapons, level up towers and killingfloors to high levels to do a s%#ton of damage with, teleport around the place getting in enemies faces, get infront of them to block them off so they couldn't get closer, etc. and that's why I loved it, the FPS part was just there for some entertainment and to help out friends/towers so you would have something to do
Large maps: A good chunk of the maps in this game are actually really big, seriously, some of the maps are ginormous and you have to be careful about where you put your towers, as well as where you should stand to help them out.
Weapons/Pick your own weapons: There are multiple weapons to pick from, i'm not going to list them all but i'll say my favorties are R.E.X., the Tesla Gun, and the Sniper, and leveling them up means more damage and more ammo, as well as quicker reload times.  And to top it all off you can pick your weapons instead of being forced 1 weapon, AND you also get 3 weapons instead of 2, making it more fun.
Level up weapons: This is another thing I adored about the first one, the level up system for weapons.  How this works is that you switch to your weapon inbetween rounds with SHIFT, and hold LMB (if you have enough money) And it upgrades it to the next level, the higher the level the more damage you do with it, there is a limit but it does a lot of damage.
NO. F%$KING. TOWER LIMIT: I hated this SO MUCH about the 2nd, there isn't a tower/block limit, there isn't, if you have the money and it isn't blocking the enemies path then you can put it there, and that's why I liked it, I hate how the 2nd one you have a limit, why a limit? That was one of the great things about the first one.
No stupid boss fights: There are no boss fights in this game, and that's another thing I like and don't like, I wish there was a big enemy to fight but in the 2nd one he's just a a$$hole.  Me and my friends spent 20 minutes in Sanctum 2 on the last wave and putting towers in places and making a longer maze for the boss, well apparently the boss gave us a middle finger and plowed through it all, making all of our time and money utterly useless, after we saw that we quit and played the first game again.
Towers:  Like I said in the first statement that this is a Tower based game with FPS elements, which means the towers do a good chunk of work and you are the support instead of it being vice versa.  There are multiple types of towers, my personal favorties are the killing floor which sits on the ground, and any enemy that runs over it takes damage, AND slows him down for a few seconds, and theres also this one with a long a$$ neck that pretty snipe enemies from across the map in a few hits.  There are others of course, try em out!
Teleport system: If you fall off the map or are wanting to go up to the front/back of the complex to get at enemies or just for the fun of it you can teleport around if you put down some teleport pads, makes it easy to swap around the map and help out friends or to get to enemies quickly instead of running there.
You can't die:  Yup, you aren't able to die at all and I like that a lot, it doesn't put a whole lot of tension or anything, if you fall off the map you just pick a place to teleport at with no worries.
Core: The Core is what you are trying to protect the aliens from, if too many get in it explodes and you lose, the bigger the enemy the more health it takes off, and you can't get any back, so keep those b@$#ards away from it at all costs.
No timer: I hated this about the 2nd as well, in the first inbetween rounds you get no timer, as much time as you need to set up your maze for enemies or put towers in places, get to certain high points for sniping, anything.  In the 2nd inbetween rounds half the time you get like 30 seconds to do whatever it is you have to before it starts and I hated that.
Enemy hits: If a enemy hits you you don't lose health or anything, he just knocks you back and shakes your camera around, making it a little woozy, then when your senses come back you can go after the guy that hit you.
CONS:
Teleport pads: At times when I was playing I would hug against a wall so I wouldn't get knocked back, but I ran back somehow cause a telepad came down to pick me up and I went back too far and into the hoard on the other side and I kind of got stuck.  I don't know if this is a nitpick or something that people hate cause my friends do it constantly as well and they get annoyed with it.
Towers: Some towers feel utterly useless, for instance there is a slow-pad for the floor like a Killing Floor is used, it slows the enemies down alot but doesn't do damage, when the Killing Floor does damage and slows them down abit.  And some are useful for only certain types, for instance gattling guns are for ground units only, and missile launchers for air targets only, some of them are mixed though, so they hit both air and ground units.
Longer waves mean harder enemies: When you upgrade all of your towers and weapons you would imagine you would be set, sadly that isn't true, as waves go on enemies get harder and harder with each wave, one time I had all of my towers (except 2-3) and all of my weapons upgraded and I was expecting to wipe the floor with everyone, but halfway through the wave the enemies were getting past my maze pretty quickly, and still had chunks of health left so I had to go back to the core and pick them off one by one, I lost sadly.  I would recommend you play with friends that way you can all gang up on the aliens.
WHAT I THINK:  I think this was the actual good game of the 2, even half of my friends who played the 1st and 2nd prefer the 1st one instead, I still play this game on occassion because it's still entertaining to me, and I love it for that, it has quite high replayability, and the text-to-voice chat system is just downright hilarious, I give this game a 8/10, it needs some fixing with some things but it's still very fun all around.  Worth it on a sale or as it sits!

Bierzerkers has great potential. While the gameplay is quite different I get a pretty strong "Loadout" vibe from the game. If any of you are familiar with that game then you will understand why I am taking more of a wait and see stance with Bierzerkers. As it stands you have to pay to unlock other playable classes, for cosmetics I would understand but for classes that can turn the tide of a game if used rightly? To me that is pretty pay to win, and I would very much hope that that system goes the way of the dodo in favor of having all classes unlockable through in game means leaving cosmetics to cash only if need be.
The gameplay itself takes place in an arena where your goal is to get the most points for your viking team by scoring goals with the sheep. Each playable class has a variety of abilities at there disposal to help the team, from shield throws to sword spins each class has its own way of fighting, That I myself have not experienced much first hand do to the class pay wall.
I cant say much for player population for now, but I can say I enjoyed what I played Bierzerkers and hope it gets more populated than it currently is. While I am content waiting and watching to see how it turns out it has the potential to be a good game, and I hope the devs make the changes to ensure its success.

This game is mediocre at best. The strong point of the game is the customization of the guns and a very workable multiplayer online experience (from when I played through it with my friend) but that is about it.
The game relies on getting materials to make weapons as the driving force for replayability. The missions take place in stages with very slightly different objectives, like fetch X amount of material, rescue X hostages, or kill X enemies in one specific area. The platforming feelings awkward and clumsy, but later levels shoehorn it in or damage must be taken by stage hazards. The combat feels slow as enemies feel like they have tons of HP for the sake of it (might have been from playing 2 man multi and always splitting up). Many of the bosses are elemental re-skins and any interesting ones come too late in the game and too infrequently for one to care. I feel this game is in an odd spot where it has the look and feel of attempting to be a game like metal slug or contra, but lacks the level design and style to do it. the gimmicky ammo is cool the first time or two, but doesn't really do much that is exciting after the small "ooo ahhh" factor is gone. 2/5

Dishonored is one of the most fantastic stealth games to date and if you haven't even heard of, let alone seen someone else play it, you are seriously missing out on this absolute gem.
Dishonored is an action-stealth game developed by Arkane Studios, and marketed by Bethseda Softworks. It puts you in the shoes of Corvo Attano, a man on a mission to clear his name and get revenge on the man who framed him. At your disposal are all kinds of weapons and gadgets you can use to beat up (or kill) the bad guys, along with some supernatural powers you can use to outplay and outwit your foes. But they have some tricks up their sleeves, and I can tell you, you'd best be ready when the pull out the music player.
Dishonored can be played in all kinds of playstyles. With all the gadgets and powers the game gives you, you could turn it into a first person shooter! Or, you could flip those gadgets on their heads and use them sneakily but deadly, taking out every foe around the corner without even a peep. And the game rewards you for whatever playstyle! Like go FPS?  Here, have more coins and loot on guards! Like to go sneaky and merciful? Here, have fewer rats, hagfish, and enemies to deal with! This may sound like a godsend, but be warned, on any difficulty higher than normal, these make not a slight difference, as your enemies are keen and watchful like a hawk, and will strike down with full force on anything they beleive to be a threat.
This brings me to my next point, the difficulties. There are 4 difficulties (If I recall correctly) Easy, Normal, Hard, and Expert. Each one of these has slight changes to the game that will make a large difference. You see, I'm a completionist. I like to get everything, kill everyone, spare everyone, etc. This game is a wonderful example of a completionist mindset put into effect while developing the game. There are all kinds of items to collect, achievements to get, and playstyles to play, you can strech this game's mere 8 hours into hundreds, trying to collect all kinds of things!
The enviroments in Dishonored feel real and living, and the story is amazing. You get sucked into a steampunk universe, in a time of turmoil and betrayal, and you feel like truly you are the only one who end these people's suffering. You explore beautiflly crafted maps with each bit of loot, each person, body, or note put there by the developers themselves. Each place along with it's people and notes and loot feel like they have a story and each one, their own part of suffering. One of my favorite examples is in the level "The Royal Physician", where in one of the houses in the second part of level you can find a table and two chairs, one knocked over. There is a rotting corpse on one chair, and on the ground next to the chair on the ground there is another rotting corpse, with a knife in it's head. On the table is peice of paper, a coin of 5 and a coin of 10, along with other coins strewn around the room. The paper reads "Card Scores", with one side getting large numbers and the other just zeroes across the board. I'll let you figure the story out on your own.
Now onto the loot. As said previously, the loot feels real, like somone meant to put it there. It's absolutely stunning the amount of time it must have taken the developers to put the loot there one by one. And there is plenty of loot to collect, with some of it giving you special powers and abilities. Another thing I love about it is that any item that isn't useful will be automatically sold for coins so if you picked up for instance, tyvian ore, it would give you "35 coins" instead of the ore it's self. This is great for inventory management and saves lots of hassle that is associated with loot In most other games.

I looked at the game quite a bit before playing, it looked super interesting and I still think it has some awesome ideas. That being said, this should be an early access title. Its riddles with bugs, crashes regurarly during gameplay, looks dated, feels rather dull, gives me motion sickness after longer periods of play etc. The ideas here are awesome, but this one needs a lot of refinement, especially for a game that expects you to pay a subscription fee for late game play.
Some of the things that need to be changed before I could recomend it (based on 2 hours of playtime):
-Graphics, they need an upgrade. The game tried to go for a somewhat realistic artstyle and just falls flat on its face as it does not have enough put into it to look so, making it look cheap
-Combat feels unresponsive, kinda like Skyrim's combat with even less feedback
-Moving around is slow and abnoxious. The movement speed is way too slow for the spread of the world and the huge amount of bobbing causes the process to be abnoxious and nauseating
-The UI is clunky and needs more customisation options
-The game lacks direction, you get a basic rundown of the obvious mechanics such as combat, movement and crafting with some long walls of text around the place. After the tutorial you get to choose a starting class and you're off with no further direction. I understand its meant to be a sort of game where you do whatever you want, but its hard to do so when the game does not direct you into any of the possible routes. At first I choose to be a mage, but I couldn't work out how to case spells, after some trial and error, I found that my skill level was not high enough to cast the spells I was given, with no real tips or direction on how it could be increased.

Mortal Online (MO) Is a great game, with a great concept. Think of what ESO was supposed to be and that's roughly where you're at imo.
There is a deep crafting system that takes time and attention to detail to "master". A full loot pvp system that lets you claim the spoils of war from the corpse of your enemies after battle. A rather large open world map full of caves/dungeons to explore, materials to gather, things to build/craft, enemies to battle, NPC AND Player built cities. That's right, you can build anything from your own personal shack to an entire guild empire that controls half of a continent (that happened).
There is everything to do from fighting 50 ft bugs  and treasure hunting to just sitting around on the edge of a pond and spend the day fishing ( even fishing has it's own system to catch various fish with different baits, depths etc).
With over 1k hours on steam and an easy 3k+ before and after steam I can say the game has held my attention for a very long time. It has been a favorite that I check back in on every now and then even when I thought I have moved on and probably will continue to do so for a while to come as the devs have been on a roll with updates as of late.
I'm not going to lie... there has been a list of bugs that trailed on for a while there (silly AI and other minor bugs), but like I mentioned the devs of the game have been pretty on top of things and most of if not everything is far better than earlier days. Not to mention all sorts of new stuff being added pretty frequently. New mobs, magic types, armors, new housing and more have all been added fairly recently and in a short span of each other and that isn't even half of their planned content.
The biggest problem I see is that it can be overwhelming for new players with everything to take in and get accustomed to (especially the full loot/open pvp aspect). If you are willing to stick around long enough to get the hang of the game you won't be dissappointed. Try bringing a friend or two, or look for a guild/friends in game as it can be 10x more fun with a buddy having your back :P.
P.s- While many players are actually pretty helpful and friendly, some are just a nuisance.Leave the city you start in immediately and head anywhere else, all the griefers and trolls live there to pick on new guys giving us all a bad rep .

As someone who loves history, geography and simulation, this game is almost perfect. Playing this game has taught me a lot about the 1400s-1600s, which is a time period that isn't delved into all that much in school, especially events outside Europe.
This is one of the best grand strategy games I've played and my first game from Paradox. The game has huge replay value, because you have a huge assortment of countries, each with their own quirks, difficulty and strategy. You can try to mimic history, do a reserved campaign with some role-playing, or blob hard and try a world conquest. The games achievements also give you interesting goals for your game and the satisfaction of getting a hard achievement is immense. However the game has a BIG learning curve and you'll spend the first couple of hours just learing what all the buttons do and how to use them.
While the base game gives you a complex and rich game, EU4 has TONS of DLCs that for the most part are way over priced for their usefullness (aside from Art of War, Common Sense and Rights of Man, which have some core mechanics that honestly should have been included in the base game). If you want new mechanics and ways to make the game more interesting, some of the DLCs could be worth it, but only if you get them on sale.
Even with over 1000 hours into the game, EU4 manages to be engaging, exiting and sometimes rage inducing. If you love strategy games, I highly recommend it, but the DLC policy keeps me from giving it a perfect score. 9/10

Some short observations for those who are on the fence:
The game is beautifully animated, as can be seen by any screenshots/videos.
The game is predominently boss stages. There are a few platforming stages, but the game definitely focuses more on the boss battles. If you're looking for more of a platforming game with stage exploration, then this game might not be for you.
Mastery at the boss stages (and platforming stages) takes both skill, memorization, and a wise choice of abilities (you can choose two weapons, one special, and one passive when going into a stage).
You will die a lot. Sometimes it will be fair, sometimes it will be due to something you haven't seen before and will need to memorize. However...
Most stages take two minutes, or less, once perfected. Because of this, it may not be as rage-inducing for some since there is not a lot of "lost ground" to recover.
All this said, I thoroughly enjoy the game.

This is the first AC I've played since it's the first one in the series that was ported to the Mac. I tried playing the first one (and I would still like to finish it), but it's horrible to look at on Parallels and I unfortunately do not have a PC.
My favorite parts of this game are the soundtrack and the parkour aspects. It has the best soundtrack in any of the games up to "Black Flag" (since I haven't seen anything past that). Even when I had to do a mission multiple times and got frustrated when the same music signaling I was in the chase sequence or whatever kept playing and I would mute the music to stop bothering me, I could still come back to it and I enjoy it a lot. The parkour aspect - after I figured it out - was REALLY cool. It's just fun to jump up and around obstacles and not feel limited by where I could go. It's how I imagine Spider-man would work without the web-shooters, which is great cause Spidey is one of my favorite supers.
They took it out for this game, so I didn't experience it until I loaded up "Brotherhood", but I am really, really grateful this didn't have the "meet the scene requirements" aspect. I get why that matters, and it makes a lot of sense, lore-wise (e.g., Ezio killed this guy by dropping a ladder on him, if you're reliving a memory, why would you kill him by stabbing him?), but it is SO frustrating, particularly when you're still figuring out the controls. Personally I liked not having to redo a ridiculously long walking sequence so I could try, again, to get ONE requirement done.
The graphics are good and the story is okay. Probably the hardest moments were when you unlocked mini scenes with Ezio collecting the feathers for his mother. At 50, your uncle walks in and tells you it's hopeless and Ezio lowers his head sadly. He doesn't say anything, but that scene said a LOT.
The puzzles were tough and I had to look up how to get through at least one assassination - the stupid boat one - and the guards could be irritating. But otherwise it was a pleasant game.

An open letter to SI
Like many here, I have been a fan of this series for many years, there is a special place in my heart reserved for this game, and even though it has single handedly caused me to lose girlfriends and jobs, I forgive it and you, because when the game is good playing it is an incredibly rewarding and immersive experience.
So in a sense I view this game as a bit of an old friend, and as a friend I feel duty bound to point out when you take a wrong turn or begin to make choices that hurt not just yourself but us too, now is one of those times.
Twenty five years, this game has been around for more than a quarter of a century, it predates the internet, it's older than many of your customers and let's be frank, it has netted you over the decades many many millions of £'s, and of course now you are making money off the back of the database, thanks to various partnerships with businesses in the real world, so it's fair to say that the old cash flow situation has never been better.
So why is the game getting worse while simultaneously getting more expensive? If the database is effectively a standalone business with it's own revenue stream what exactly is it that we are paying for here? I mean we all know it costs next to nothing to clone packets of code, there's no manuals to be ordered from the printing press, no haulage firms freighting units from warehouses to retail outlets, if anything you could easily afford to charge less the last couple of years and still be making more.
Let's talk about Public relations, you don't like criticism do you? Let's be honest about it, you pretty much ban anyone who voices reasonable criticisms on your official website and indeed on Steam, even when no rules have been broken, if you can't answer the post with reasoned debate it's 'delete and ban', now over the years how many good customers do you think you've alienated? a few hundred? a few thousand? and that's just by being over sensitive and employing trigger happy moderators, SI that is very bad for business.
And then there's the chinese, the most populous nation on the planet, and one of the fastest growing economies to boot, where football is gaining ever increasing traction, look how you lied to them, look how you refuse to properly cater to them, alienating one fifth of the worlds population lol, I mean seriously, whose bright idea was that? It's not like you can't afford to hire a couple of translators ffs.
I don't know if it's arrogance, poor leadership, naked greed or just that you don't care anymore, but what goes up must come down, nothing lasts forever and once the competition smells blood in the water it's only a matter of time before a successor appears on the market, a rival who will absolutely value every single customer and shall strive to deliver real value for money, don't make the fatal mistake of thinking your position is permanent, I personally know many of your customers who pray daily for a competitor to step up and teach you a painful lesson.
I think you need to take a step back and have a serious rethink, about your relationship with your customers, about the business model, you can't keep charging AAA prices for a reskin and a database that has already been paid for, you might want to stop pretending to release sequels and actually start work on an actual proper sequel, while that's in development you could sell database updates as DLC, in fact you could sell all kinds of things as DLC, stadium packs for example, anything cosmetic that doesn't directly affect the players ability to manage a team.
Think about what kind of game you might have had with an approach like that, after 25 years and countless millions to invest, it's never too late to change direction and admit where you've gone wrong, it's time to listen to your friends before it is too late. I think years without any real competition, and customer willingness to shell out AAA cash every year for a patch has made you dangerously complacent, and if you don't snap out of it soon and get serious again you're time at the top will end.
The state of this game right now is frankly a disgrace, why aren't you embarrassed? where's your pride? you really need to get a grip and fix your♥♥♥♥♥♥ it's time to climb out of your bubble and start working to win back the trust and respect of your customers, and most importantly of all for Gods sake make FM great again.
How to salvage something from the wreckage
step 1
Apologize for years of charging AAA prices for a patch and a database update (that's already been financed by 3rd party business partnerships)
step 2
Roll back to FM 2017, update the database and offer a partial refund, at least 50%
step 3
Announce a new approach and business model, tell your customers the era of fake sequels is now over, explain that from now on you are going to charge customers a fair price for the database update while working on the first ever actual real sequel
step 4
Begin work on the sequel, start with the foundations and completely rebuild the entire game, new AI, new engine, new UI etc
step 5
Stop deleting uncomfortable truths and perma banning anyone who presents you with criticisms you can't argue with. Regain the trust of your customers and begin cultivating a more positive relationship built upon mutual respect. Employ a team of Chinese translators.

First of all, of all the Bethesda titles I've played, from Morrowind to Skyrim, and Fallout 3 and New Vegas, This has to be THE best title to have Bethesda's name on it.
First off, that for it's generation, it's a graphically beautiful game. The artwork, level design, and animations to me are all just things of beauty.
The soundtrack is absolutely on point! The music always seems to match the level and the events going on, something, so few games seem to actually nail down. And yes, I'm counting even games from my childhood, from the Original Famicom(NES) until now, which is 27 years of gaming. I also want to give huge props to Jon and Daniel Litcht, for the ending song "Honor for All."
The story is amazing. I absolutely loved playing through this game's plotline, and even more so, I loved watching the NPC, guards included, interacting with each other. Salt and Sanctuary is a great 2D action platformer/metroidvania in the veins of Souls games. The dark enviroment along with the great soundtrack gives the perfect feeling of being in a strange land with a ominous atmosphere.
The game plays as a platformer, with precise jumping and clibing. On the Souls-like side, you have stamina bar which drains when you attack/use magic/evade/block. The parry/inv dodge frame mechanic are present as well, requiring precision and the right timing for doing so. The game has creeds, which act like the coventant in the Soul series, which offer a variety of goods and gear depending of the current creed. To be noted, there's the absence of map as well, despite some people disliking it, drives you to memorize places and be aware of your surroundins while looking for secret rooms.
The game also blends (very well, by the way) with metroidvania aspects, like upgrades that allow you to reach new places and backtracking for valuable items and gear. The bosses are memorable and fit the lore, which is explained through NPC dialogues; While the lore isn't very deep per se, it brings up a lot of questions regarding the said bosses and creeds.
The game also offers a jolly local Co-op mode along with a PVP that works in the same way, which improve the replayability and fun factor of the game.
The only complains I have with Salt and Sanctuary are:
- Lack of online Co-op/PvP.
- A little unbalance regarding certain weapons, like Whips and Poleaxes.
- No confirmation of a future DLC and/or sequel/prequel yet :^P
The single fact this one game was made by only two (awesome) people is a reason for you to check it out.
If you like metroidvanias, platformers or if you're a veteran in the Soul Series, this game is for you. It's hard, but fair and rewarding. You'll die a lot, don't doubt that, but the enjoyment of seeing that one creature vanishing from the face of earth by your weapons (and being able to craft its signature set/weapon) afterwards is a good feeling everybody needs to feel. :)

A fun and intense first person shooter set in the future of wasteland earth. So, it’s a little bit like Mad Max then? Well, it’s about 99% Mad Max-like. I mean you’re going to see insane weaponry, vehicular combat and bandit gangs, so it’s safe to say that this is a Mad Max themed shooter, but definitely not a movie clone.
For a game that is nearly 5 years old, it still impresses me on how good it looks. It’s not “perfect” by any means, but its good enough that you will think that this game is newer than it looks. Not to mention that you don’t need an overly powerful graphics card to run it; a GeForce 9800 GTX or an AMD equivalent is just enough to get playable framerates. This also goes for both the CPU and RAM. No need for a fancy £1000 rig to enjoy this game.
You are emerged into a wasteland earth full of bandits, gangs and mutants. You are seen as the ‘hero’ of the game and you learn more about the places and the people the more you play further into the story. It’s the generic story where you defeat all the mutants and gangs, whilst doing unrelated side-quests along the way and eventually “save” the world. It’s nothing new to the table in terms of storytelling and I wouldn’t personally call this one “story heavy”, the game is an experience and is for experience, not to be fully immersed in it. It certainly delivers that experience in a decent sense.
The sounds of gunfire, the roaring engines and the clarity of the voice acting is at its best. Every bit of soundtrack has been fined tuned to sound how they were supposed to be heard. I am proud of what id Software did here. What an impressive achievement.
It delivers very smooth and very polished gameplay that many is sure to enjoy for hours. The controls are responsive and the game difficulty is well balanced. The only downside is that you have to keep checking if you have enough ammo for a weapon as ammo in this game is very scarce, especially at the start of the game.
For the price of £12.99 and an additional £3.49 for a DLC, it is reasonably well priced and is definitely worth buying. Although, I suggest waiting until it goes on sale to get it.

Ok so you've looked at the game and think it looks fun, but you also notice the mixed reviews. You look down and see people saying it's pay to win and that it's not optimized well. These arguments do not hold weight. Here is the truth about the game, while it does have one major problem that's being worked on as we speak, I would like to show you how this is a good game that is worth your time.
First we'll start with what the game is. It is essentially a a mix of Medieval Team Fortress 2 and rugby, and yes that sounds weird. As mentioned earlier you do have to purchase each additional class, as of writing this they are $15 for all of them. Trine 3 has far more in comon with the first Trine than second one, in that it is shorter, less frustrating, and overall more enjoyable. You still play by alternating at will between three characters, a thief (bow, grappling hook), a wizard (conjuring boxes for easier platforming and activating buttons), and a knight (combat and smashing things). However, all skill trees and leveling from the first two games are gone. It actually works out well for the way the game works. You open side levels by collecting X amount of collectibles, and they can be played in any order, so having to wait to have a certain skill would make the game more linear. Lack of advancement also works with the story; your heroes are basically at the height of their power, in retirement, and their desire to be rid of their skills and go back to an ordinary life is actually the catalyst for the plot. So it works. Also, it's nice being able to complete an entire level, including collectibles, in one go without having to wait to upgrade to a certain skill to be able to get that one last collectible you couldn't reach.
The puzzles have a great difficulty curve. There are some that are obvious, some that are obvious but harder to execute, and some that have "a-ha!" moments. But overall, it's not brain-breaking. A few side missions are very combat- or platform-heavy, which is a nice extra bit of difficulty. The boss battle is insane compared to the normal levels, because if every other combat situation, you don't have to do any platforming while you fight. For the final boss, you have to dodge 1- or 2-hit kill shots while levitating or attacking the boss. I did it the first time without a TPK, but it DID take a while because I was constatantly reviving my characters.
Plus, the game's savepoint system is very fair. There are some levels where you play solely as one character, and when you die you go back to an arbitrary point. But on the main story levels, where you play as all three characters, when one character dies, you switch into another character. Your dead character pops up at a nearby spot (usually behind you but sometimes slightly ahead depending on where you died), and you can revive them by standing in proximity to them to "share your spirit". Basically, it's a 3-life system. But if you constantly revive you characters after they die, you really never need to worry. I think I only killed all three characters and had to restart the level ONCE, and that was due to overconfidence.
Unfortunately, the game is pretty short. I played about 9 hours, including all main story missions and side missions to 100%. This wouldn't be a problem except the story ends on a cliff-hanger. You introduce (reintroduce) the main characters, introduce the villain, are presented with the solution (find 3 MacGuffins), you find one, and then the characters say, "Two more to go! And another great adventure awaits" (or something like that) and THE GAME ENDS.
Trine 3 also differs from its predecessors in one major way: Trine 3 is a 3D, not a 2D platformer. (In reality, it's more like a 3D game made my devs who don't know how to design in 2D, so 75% of the game is a 2D side-scroller, 15% is mainly 2.5D in which you go backwards and forwards in the third dimension, but mainly to get around an obstacle, and 10% is actual 3D, with your character facing into the 3rd dimension for grappling airtime or pushing buttons on the back wall). It's like the 3D was done after the fact, and only with certain levels. You unfortunately don't get any control over the camera, and it doesn't follow you consistently, meaning there are times your character goes into the depths of your screen and just gets tiny due to perspective, or there's a hidden collectible you didn't know existed behind a wall because the entire level is 2D except the collectible which exists in a 3D plane. It's also hard to tell which plane things are in, requiring blind jumps and lots of falling. There are some flying baddies that you have to jump to hit, but since they're non-humanoid, you don't know how big relative to you they're suppose to be, leading to the questions "Are they big because they're closer to the screen or big because they're large creatures?)
tl;dr Great puzzles, but some 3D frustrations and a cliffhanger. Definitely still worth it. A good addition to the franchise, if unfinished.

An open letter to SI
Like many here, I have been a fan of this series for many years, there is a special place in my heart reserved for this game, and even though it has single handedly caused me to lose girlfriends and jobs, I forgive it and you, because when the game is good playing it is an incredibly rewarding and immersive experience.
So in a sense I view this game as a bit of an old friend, and as a friend I feel duty bound to point out when you take a wrong turn or begin to make choices that hurt not just yourself but us too, now is one of those times.
Twenty five years, this game has been around for more than a quarter of a century, it predates the internet, it's older than many of your customers and let's be frank, it has netted you over the decades many many millions of £'s, and of course now you are making money off the back of the database, thanks to various partnerships with businesses in the real world, so it's fair to say that the old cash flow situation has never been better.
So why is the game getting worse while simultaneously getting more expensive? If the database is effectively a standalone business with it's own revenue stream what exactly is it that we are paying for here? I mean we all know it costs next to nothing to clone packets of code, there's no manuals to be ordered from the printing press, no haulage firms freighting units from warehouses to retail outlets, if anything you could easily afford to charge less the last couple of years and still be making more.
Let's talk about Public relations, you don't like criticism do you? Let's be honest about it, you pretty much ban anyone who voices reasonable criticisms on your official website and indeed on Steam, even when no rules have been broken, if you can't answer the post with reasoned debate it's 'delete and ban', now over the years how many good customers do you think you've alienated? a few hundred? a few thousand? and that's just by being over sensitive and employing trigger happy moderators, SI that is very bad for business.
And then there's the chinese, the most populous nation on the planet, and one of the fastest growing economies to boot, where football is gaining ever increasing traction, look how you lied to them, look how you refuse to properly cater to them, alienating one fifth of the worlds population lol, I mean seriously, whose bright idea was that? It's not like you can't afford to hire a couple of translators ffs.
I don't know if it's arrogance, poor leadership, naked greed or just that you don't care anymore, but what goes up must come down, nothing lasts forever and once the competition smells blood in the water it's only a matter of time before a successor appears on the market, a rival who will absolutely value every single customer and shall strive to deliver real value for money, don't make the fatal mistake of thinking your position is permanent, I personally know many of your customers who pray daily for a competitor to step up and teach you a painful lesson.
I think you need to take a step back and have a serious rethink, about your relationship with your customers, about the business model, you can't keep charging AAA prices for a reskin and a database that has already been paid for, you might want to stop pretending to release sequels and actually start work on an actual proper sequel, while that's in development you could sell database updates as DLC, in fact you could sell all kinds of things as DLC, stadium packs for example, anything cosmetic that doesn't directly affect the players ability to manage a team.
Think about what kind of game you might have had with an approach like that, after 25 years and countless millions to invest, it's never too late to change direction and admit where you've gone wrong, it's time to listen to your friends before it is too late. I think years without any real competition, and customer willingness to shell out AAA cash every year for a patch has made you dangerously complacent, and if you don't snap out of it soon and get serious again you're time at the top will end.
The state of this game right now is frankly a disgrace, why aren't you embarrassed? where's your pride? you really need to get a grip and fix your♥♥♥♥♥♥ it's time to climb out of your bubble and start working to win back the trust and respect of your customers, and most importantly of all for Gods sake make FM great again.
How to salvage something from the wreckage
step 1
Apologize for years of charging AAA prices for a patch and a database update (that's already been financed by 3rd party business partnerships)
step 2
Roll back to FM 2017, update the database and offer a partial refund, at least 50%
step 3
Announce a new approach and business model, tell your customers the era of fake sequels is now over, explain that from now on you are going to charge customers a fair price for the database update while working on the first ever actual real sequel
step 4
Begin work on the sequel, start with the foundations and completely rebuild the entire game, new AI, new engine, new UI etc
step 5
Stop deleting uncomfortable truths and perma banning anyone who presents you with criticisms you can't argue with. Regain the trust of your customers and begin cultivating a more positive relationship built upon mutual respect. Employ a team of Chinese translators.

You play as a sailor, be you a knight or a mage or even a chef, and (without giving too much of the tutorial stage away) find yourself stranded on a random island in the middle of nowhere. A few steps up the beach and an old man tells you that you aren't the first to find yourself here and lets you pick one of three creeds. The only advice he gives you is to take a nearby sanctuary for your creed, but no other direction is really given. The game pushes you forward with two objectives: find the princess you were on the boat with, and survive.
As you get further and deeper into the labyrinthian island, survival becomes your primary concern as you find enemies who can (and will) hit you with all kinds of attacks that will leave you open to be murdered by other enemies.
As you traverse the island, you come across a few other people on the island who are there for different reasons. A knight who is on a quest to defeat an evil dragon, as is his want. A thief who is trying to find treasure. Some random swamp guy sitting in (you guessed it!) a swamp who sells things, mostly dealing poison damage. The NPCs have quite a bit of distance between them, so the journey feels a balance of both lonely and occupied, especially if you play co-op or bring in merchants, blacksmiths and alchemists to your sanctuaries.
As far as game look and feel go, the game looks great. There isn't a ton of color on screen at many times but when there is, it usually looks great. The swamp is a dark, mossy green color and the caverns underneath a dungeon area are very blue and purple with the glow of the crystals and mushroom-like objects. While outside, due to being an island full of creatures and overloaded with salt, the sky is a very dull overcast with salt raining down, almost like snow.
The gameplay is also very responsive. The controls are on point with little delay, the hitboxes on enemies are mostly on point; some bosses won't get hit if you attack them as they attack the area you dodged from.
The enemies are plentiful and hard hitting and the bosses feel awesome when you fight them and defeat them. For some Demon's Souls nostalgia, the tutorial boss will most likely kill you! Although it is possible to kill the tutorial boss, and doing so rewards you with two crafting materials, one of which there is only *one* of in the game. Most of the bosses have attacks that are mostly easy to dodge and, with a little effort, you will prevail. HOWEVER, there is a certain boss towards the last few areas of the game that is an absolute NIGHTMARE!
The game also has a really cool mechanic (in my opinion) where when you get hit by an enemy, you lose a small percentage of health that can't be healed with potions, much like Dragon's Dogma. Using spells or resting at a sanctuary of shrine will fix that, so it's good! And whenever you perform an action that takes stamina or focus (jumping, rolling, attacking, spells) the stamina will decrease as well. I feel that this makes field combat and platforming much for hectic, as that rush to recharge your depleted health/stamina bar feels all the more necessary.
The game does have its flaws, the worst one (in my opinion) is the lack of music. The game does have boss music (with a really cool final boss theme) and a calming theme that plays in sanctuaries, but out in the rest of the game there's only the occasional guitar playing. Even the boss music plays during every boss bar the final one. The silver lining here is that the final dungeon in the game has a theme to it that practically shouts "The end is here!"
The weapons, while cool looking, aren't plentiful. There's only a few greatswords in the game and barely any greathammers. Compared to the weapon selection in Dark Souls III or II or even Demon's Souls, there could (and should) be many more. On the bright side, weapons and armor don't have durability!
All in all, I believe that this game is a must have for those who love the Souls series. Minus the three dimensions, it has all the same things that Dark Souls has, including new game plus but minus random invasions from people with terrible internet connection. The lack of music does make it feel lonely at times, but it's still a great game.
Assuming you got this far into the review, thank you for your time! Enjoy your day :)
