This is one of those games that makes me wish Steam had a "meh" button. I had enough fun with it to finish the story, but overall it's hard to recommend it when there are so many better shooters out there. So I'm giving this one a thumbs-down, admittedly partially because I think that will make more people read it.
So RAGE is an open-world-ish game about driving between locations and shooting things. It takes place in a post-apocalyptic wasteland that's too reminiscent of Fallout. The game isn't a true open world but rather a free-roam hub world that connects a series of discrete levels. The levels themselves, for the most part, are very linear corridor shooters. Your character is frequently tasked with your standard "go to this place and get this thing from the bad guys" sorts of missions. Unfortunately, these don't happen dynamically within the world, so you don't get that Far Cry-style freedom of being able to approach a target in a multitude of different ways. Instead, you drive to a place, enter a door, and are thrust into an entirely linear corridor with virtually no options for varying your approach to the enemies.
Now, the fighting itself is pretty good, especially once you get a couple more guns, and the numerous extra weapons that you can get in addition to guns - such as RC car bombs and a boomerang-like weapon - do introduce some combat variety. Weapon animations and recoil are pleasing, and enemy AI is generally good, with enemies employing the same dodging and cover techniques that your character does. So overall, the fighting is tense and enjoyable, and is the main reason I was able to continue playing through to the end. That said, it's not revolutionary, nor is it a callback to the Id shooters of old - it's still a health-regen cover-based combat system, just one with a few more tricks up its sleeve than your average COD game.
If that were all the game involved, I could give it a thumbs up and recommend it as a decent "budget" shooter to pick up in the Steam sale for $5. However, Id's managed to ruin the game by throwing in a bunch of extra crap that's not shooting. For one thing you're expected to drive everywhere and sometimes race other drivers in order to advance the story. The car handling is crap (ever with a controller) and the car combat is abysmal. You actually don't even have to do the car combat - you can just drive past the enemy vehicles and easily make it to your destination.
There's also quite a bit of walking about in hub areas looking for people. While the hub towns are kind of interesting to look at, they don't have too much to do in them and both these hub-area strolls and the irritating race sections just serve to pad the length of the game and prevent you from getting to the stuff you actually want - the shooting!
Overall, the open-worldy, side-quest elements of the game just aren't very well-realized. The game drops just enough "open world stuff" to start to feel like a big expansive adventure, but unfortunately Id didn't seem to care enough to either make those side-quest elements good, or to actually put enough of them in the game to make the world seem vibrant and interactive. Instead of finding a world teeming with possibilities, you're instead presented with a world peppered with occasional annoyances. It's almost like Id was developing a corridor shooter and then decided at the eleventh hour to slap an overworld onto it and say "hey, look, it's an open world game!"
That lack of care for making a good open world game also extends to the game's issues with performance. It's abundantly clear that the Id Tech 5 engine can't handle the game's expansive open settings. It suffers from horrible pop-in and frame pacing issues any time you're out in the overworld areas. I have a decent rig - i5-3470, GTX 970, and 16 gigs of RAM - and even on the lowest settings I wasn't able to get a smooth 60 fps in the overworld area. The corridor shooter sections run fine, but you'd expect that.
Also, the texture quality is awful - like worse than vanilla Doom from 1993. That, combined with the terrible judder and frame-pacing problems, means the game is frequently unpleasant to look at.
Last, there's no sense to the story at all. Why are all the factions in the Wasteland represented by different world nationalities? Why have cockney Londoners and Russians both formed gangs in the US in the wake of the apocalypse? The game never bothers to explain this. Overall, there's very little explanation of why the wasteland turned into a random collection of free towns and bandit camps, why the big baddies are so bent on domination, and why your character should even care. Once again, this is a consequence of the open world not being fully thought-out.
So overall, it's a decent shooter ruined by Id's insistence on mashing "open world" elements into a style of game that doesn't match and with an engine that can't support it. Buy on sale if you're a huge FPS fan like me and you've exhausted every other option, otherwise, look elsewhere.

Obvious comparisons with the Hotline Miami cannot be avoided and it’s influence is widely spread through the game. Still, 12 is Better Than 6 somehow manages to better its paragon is some aspects.
This top-down, kill everyone and everything shooter has somehow unexpectedly landed on-top of my desk the other day and I’m still having trouble letting it go, despite finishing the campaign several times.
Addictive and distinguished, 12 is Better Then 6 (or as I like to call it ‘Hotline Texas’) provokes that perfect mix of having fun while constantly trying to better yourself throughout its surprisingly short campaign but hugely rewarding campaign. With no health bar you will die from one well placed bullet most of the time. So get ready to die a lot. That makes room for planning two, three and sometime even four or more steps ahead in order to finish a single level.
Finishing any level feels like a reward but at the same time levels are designed with such care and precision that it shouldn’t take more than a couple of retries to compleat any of them. And it never ever feels unfair. There are over 100 levels in total spanned throughout four acts, each about a couple of minutes long if you know your way around it.
Combat revolves around quick reflexes and tight aim, complemented with unique ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mechanics. Basically it works like a real gun does, you have to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (the upper trigger) your bullet inside the barrel to take the shot, repeating the action every time you take a shot. I found that mechanic to be a breath of fresh air in the shooter genre in general and hope to see that gameplay mechanic being implemented in more games.
Graphically hand drawn in exclusively black & white tone, with only the blood being red, I see why some players might find this game to be repulsive, or even jump to a wrong conclusion of lacking the in-game depth. I myself enjoyed the simplistic overhead presentation as it allowed me to sharpen my senses to the fullest and just get on with what the game wanted me to do.

At first I loved this game, and even gave it a positive review... but I found a few game breaking (online breaking) updates ruined that. Now, going back to it, the game is incredibly monotonous and slow paced. I feel like this game needed more love with developer updates, but maybe they just gave up?
Original review below.
Like Scott Pilgrim, this game has a pretty steep learning curve. It starts out pretty tough as you have no special skills, weapons or mods. But perservere; what may seem like a frustrating beginning (if you do find it tough) pays off in a huge way as you forge your own knives, build bizzare guns and blast your way through loads off brilliantly designed levels.

This game is the cutting edge of "meh". Played 5 minutes of it with a friend on console, decided to get for PC. Controls are awful for PC and quite frankly it's only good in couch coop, and even then it is indeed limited.
I have a lot of gripes with this game, so I'll try to stay constructive where possible, but generally this game is guilty of every "passable" class sin in the book.
-Enemies reskinned painfully often.
-Static-y AI, bonkers damage. Limited lives that makes you need to go back to camp, load, select your mission, talk to your pilot, and reload the level. Dear god. This is frustrating beyond belief.
-Great weapon customization system, but you can totally build weapons WAY too specialized and since you get only 1 gun, special weapons have no real use long term.
-Boss reskins. Because why the hell not apparently. This is by far one of the worst sins in the book IMO.
-Grindy as hell farming resources and the like. Some missions send you out hunting hostages or resources, and god damn is it boring to all hell. Forget a second playthrough outright. I put 47 hours into the game getting all the things the first go, but attempting a 2nd playthrough is murdering me to death.
-Both playable characters (there's only 2) are painfully uninteresting. First playthrough I played the chick because at least she wasn't "rambo clone guy", but even she wasn't a particularly interesting character.
-Bosses run away from you after a certain time, and their fights are based off learning attacks almost exclusively. This is a painful combination, but having to jog around the level, find the boss at any of 3 combat points, and re-engage him hoping he doesn't run away in front of your face (because that can happen, too) is absolutely there.
-Reused levels and levels generally lacking much in the way of true definition, with a few outlying exceptions.
-Virtually non-existant plot, dialogue, and soundtrack from what I can gather. But expect to get talked at about uninteresting crap for hours anyways.
Look. I liked this game enough to play it through my first go, but coming back, every sin in this game is magnified exponentially. This game is long, uninteresting, and littered with so many time wasting, sluggish core mechanics I legitimately wonder what the hell they devs were thinking.
Crap. I was trying to be constructive. See? It's that hard. Oh well. Detailed negative criticism beats enraged or understaffed negative criticism any day.
Save your money. Don't buy this game. It's fun for a few hours, but then all the charm wears off. I legitimately regret buying this game outright.

Mercenary Kings is a game that doesn't understand itself, leading to many missed opportunities.  Gun customization is fun, and it controls and plays very well, sadly level and enemy design are not up to snuff to make it all come together.
The source inspiration for a title like this seems obvious to most players, but I don't know if the developers really got into what made those games work.  The graphics are great, building guns is fun and shooting enemies is entertaining.  The biggest complaint you'll see for Mercenary Kings is that it is too easy.  And this is true.  The enemies are placed in ways that make them easy to dispatch, and the ones that shoot don't do it enough to be threatening.  It's rare to have even two projectiles on the screen at a time, let alone enemies.  Even with that handicap on their part, your character can take multiple hits AND increase their health later on.  Because of this, the most dangerous parts of the game are the very rare pitfalls that actually kill you.  The game ramps up a bit towards the end, but considering how comotose the first five ranks are its just a little too late.
Now, I put this as not recommended but that's only because there is no 'on the fence' option.  On one hand the game is entertaining enough and has an enjoyable art style, and on the other I can't lie and tell you this is a game you are going to remember.  I would consider this a casual side-scroller, and honestly that isn't a game I would recommend.  If you have no hands you may find this game challenging but this is something you play when an alternative would be to take a nap.

Wonderful game. Take Metal Slug's high fidelity sprite based graphics, add Monster Hunter type missions and a vast crafting system, top it off with a sensational soundtrack and you get Mercenary Kings.

I will preface this review with the disclaimer that I don't think I will be able to express the beauty and wonder of this game in words. I will do my best, and I will keep it short.
Immersive and subtly complex, OneShot perfectly executes a difficult storytelling technique to pull off: involving the player in the story as a character but in a way that makes them forget the world built by the creator is simply a game. It feels real, the characters feel real, the player feels a part of the world and comes to care about them as though they are real people. Unlike a lot of other immersive narratives and games, OneShot is more than an escape. It is a transformative experience, a story that is dear to my heart and feels like a real part of my lived experience.
OneShot is more than worth it. Niko is counting on you.
After all, you only have one shot.

OMG. This game absolutley blew my mind. I fell in love with the art and the characters so quickly, and the puzzles were challenging yet simple! Absolutley loved the player to game interaction, very excellent programming done.

DISCLAIMER: I have not done Solstice yet and will most likely update this review once I have
This review is as spoiler-free as possible
OneShot is an amazing game that is definitely worth the price of admission, especially as someone who has played the freeware version from 2014. The story improvements and extra content in this Premium version make OneShot and even better game and help flesh out the story even more. It made me care for the main character almost immediately and the worldbuilding is done very well with the limited amount of lore provided. It's one of the few games that actually makes me feel for the characters of the world. This may be a controversial opinion but I believe OneShot tells it's story and makes me care for it's characters much more than Undertale did. Your decisions have major consequences for the world and all the characters within it, and you will have to deal with the consequences.
The puzzles are obvious enough that you shouldn't need to look up a guide on how to do them but they do require a little bit of thought to complete.
There is no combat in this game, you just walk through it and interact with the world while experiencing the story. The art is phenomenal as well. I can heartily recommend OneShot to anyone looking to experience a well-written story.
EDIT:
So I've just finished Solstice.
Solstice is the reason to buy this game over the freeware version. I'm not going to talk about it because going in blind is the absolute best way to experience OneShot and the Solstice chapter especially. OneShot is probably one of my favorite story experiences ever. I heartily recommend anyone reading this review play through it.

I see the players who've spent hundreds of hours on this game and I can...I can really understand it. This isn't just one of the best tower defense games ever made, it's one of the best games ever made, period. There's a finely honed balance between clever level design, basic resource management, and tower type & placement. It all adds up to a truly nailbiting experience, with just enough brain-teasing frustration to make you feel accomplished once you beat a campaign.
It's a superb example of what game designers can accomplish by layering simple gameplay systems on top of each other, and fine-tuning through play balancing. Post-release support and free DLC updates only make the game that much more replayable.

I'm going to try very hard to avoid saying "this is like X meets Y" because those types of comparisons kind of annoy me.  With that in mind, here goes:
This game is side-scrolling run-and-gun at its very finest.  Tight controls meet challenging level design and enemies that aren't (always) simply mooks that charge at you full speed.  There's a very interesting crafting system that allows you to mix and match weapon components (receiver, magazine, etc.) to make a gun to suit your desired method of mayhem.  This same system also has in place "implants" which confer bonuses (and disadvantages too!)
My favorite part of the game, however, is that it takes item weight into account.  Weapon parts, implants, consumables you carry to battle,
has weight and weight affects your movement speed.  This creates an interesting strategic balance: do you bring the massive crush-everything loadout, sacrificing speed in the quest for power?  Do you streamline to what you think you need and nothing else, trusting in agility and a quick trigger finger to win through?  Or is your path to victory somewhere in the middle?  This game doesn't judge, instead setting the options before you and letting you decide how best to assault its varying missions.
And oh, the missions!  Not content with simple "run to the right and kill it if it moves" gameplay, the game will present you with sections of a whole area that will become familiar over time, but ask different things of you each visit.  Sometimes you'll be gathering items, other times it's search and destroy, still others your task is to seek out and rescue a captive (or more than one!)  The variety of tasks you take on keeps the game from feeling repetitive, instead rewarding thorough exploration and familiarization with each map with secret passages and hidden treasures, not to mention helping to get quick times if (when) you go for speed-runs.
TL;DR = This game is a lot of awesome.  If you like run-and-gun sidescrollers and you like customization, it's amazing.

Metal Slug meets Monster Hunter? Oh hell yeah!
If you're a Monster Hunter passionate, such as myself, you will definitely
this title. The feeling you get is very close, and a lot of mechanics are present in both games:
Weapons can be forged, and they come in various shapes and colors. Not only that, but weapon parts are divided in categories which alter the way they work.
The main area is a small village, where all the NPCs live. Many of them also resemble ones from Capcom's franchise: the general who gives you missions, the cook who... erm, cooks you food (which gives fixed AND chance-based bonuses), the gunsmith who forges all your gun parts from monster materials, and so many others.
Areas work similarly to how they do in Monster Hunter, being divided in zones and having enemies indigenous to them. However, in this game most enemies tend to respawn as soon as they leave your field of view.
Oh, and I didn't talk about boss fights yet! Bosses can be killed OR captured, and overall the pattern-learning process behind defeating them for the first time feels the same.
Then comes CoOp. You can play together with up to four people, and you all share the same lives. There's a built-in voice-command system, too.
I could go on, but I hope you get the point.
If, however, you're considering buying Mercenary Kings for the Metal Slug part, you'll be slightly disappointed: while it mantains all the glorious 2D shootin' goodness, it lacks a bit of the fast-paced and action-packed gameplay that makes Metal Slug what it's well known for. Also, there are no power-ups scattered around the map or dropped by your foes, for instance.
Overall? I don't even know where to begin: some great but not overly complex pixel-art, an amazing soundtrack, interesting characters, an addicting gameplay and the CoOp mode are all important points that give a strong first impression.
Maybe it's not really worth €20, but you should totally get it if it drops below €15.

This is a Paradox game. For those who haven't bought a Paradox game early on, let me explain the process.
You buy the game, and at first it seems incredibly confusing and complicated. You play a bunch of games and get your butt handed to you because Paradox sucks at tutorials, but it's still fun. You slowly get better, and for the first 20 hours or so it's a great experience. Then you hit the point where you've mastered the game, and suddenly the veil is lifted. The shallowness becomes apparent, and the failings of the AI make every game a steamroll. And yet, the game is still somewhat enjoyable, if only to screw around with dumb strategies like conquering the world as Bhutan/Ryukyu/etc.
Over the next few years, Paradox will release a tonne of patches and DLC that slowly increase the game's depth and fix the glaring issues. You buy them all, because at this point you have 200+ hours and need your next fix. Then, Steam has a summer sale, and the price of the game plus all DLC is half the price you paid for the base game. You cry softly into your wallet as you invade Poland for the 264th time.
Then Victoria III comes out, and the cycle begins anew.
TL;DR: If you're bored of EU4, you've probably already bought this and there's no help for you.
If you aren't already in the Paradox cycle and don't have an abundance of disposable income, wait a few years for the game to be finished. Go play EU4 instead.

I have to say that this game took me by surprise. I picked it up on sale for less than a dollar. I wasn't expecting much. The screenshots and videos looked alright and the description sounded cool. Yet, I had been fooled by games like that before. I had never heard of the game before but decided to spend the extra change in my Steam Wallet on it, figuring I really wasn't losing out on anything. Am I glad I did!
First off, let me tell you I haven't played anything quite like this before. I have played FPS's and Tower Defence's, but never together. I enjoy both, but was wary of how they would mix. Needless to say I didn't come into it with high expectations, but I should have.
The graphics are decent/good, I like them, and for less than a dollar, they are great for sure. I also really like the art style as well as alien, turret, weapon, map, and character designs. It all seems really cool, especially since your weapons and turrets do change color and look when you upgrade them.
Maps have varied layouts, some with multiple paths to the end, some of which you can block off, and some with only one straight shot, and you have to maze your way from beginning to end. Some maps may have only one spawn for aliens, while another may have two or three. Another aspect I like is that you just don't build on the side of the path, you build on it, which allows you to create mazes, funnels, and plan out paths for the enemies. It also allows you to block of paths you don't want to deal with on multiple-path maps.
You have the ability to carry three different weapons and four turret desings into a match. All of these are upgradeable, which will lead to increased damage, range, fire-rate, piercing, etc. Your weapons do not have ammo, but can overheat, and upgrading them increases damage, range, and the amount of shots before overheat. One type of turret you can build is a mix of a teleporter and elevator. Basically it will lower itself, allowing you to get ontop of the turrets you build, allowing you to shoot down onto the aliens. YOu can also hit tab to go into overview mode, which shows the map, allowing you to teleport to these specific turrets.
Gameplay can get fast and frantic, especially if you get overrun by numbers or your design fails. Other times it can be a breeze, while you sit there taking pot-shots at oncoming aliens, while your turrets do most of the work. Each map you can play on three different difficulties, and there is also surival mode, which can really test your skills.
There is co-op multiplayer, I haven't tried it myself yet, but I plan too and it seems very fun.
All-in-all it is a very good game, a great mix of FPS and TD. A pleasant surprise for the cheap price I got it for, although I do believe it is worth full-price. There are map-pack dlc available, and I am looking forward to picking those up as well. Would recommend! 8.75/10

Where to begin?
OK - it's laggy as hell and the UI has been fiddled around with so much it's actually unpleasant to play.
The root of the problem is that the core code of the game is 15 - 20 years old, and what they've been doing for the past decade or so is ripping code out, grafting code in, removing features, changing features and adding features, and now what they have on their hands is a bloated tangled overcomplicated outdated mess, so clogged up with pointless fluff that it's barely able to run anymore.
What most developers do is this, they develop a concept, take it as far as they can and release the game, then they eventually understand that it's time to start over and begin work on the sequel, so they take all the best elements and features, introduce a few more and then put all that into a brand new game, taking advantage of advances in technology they streamline and optimize everything, lay new foundations, design a new engine and new UI, program new AI, incorporate modern graphics rendering technology etc, basically they bring the concept up to date slap a #2 on it and call it a sequel.

i dont usualy play tower defence games but as i got the Steam code for this in my LootCrate coupled with it being owned by a friend i think has good taste in games i figuired i would give it a shot and it genuinely suprised me. the game is a 3d tower defence game set on a futuristic planet torn apart by various wars. you play as a millitary commander in charge of the planets last defences against the aliens and are accompanied by an Artificial intelligence who was a participant in the previous war. the game itself is relatively simple, you build towers to hold offf waves of enemies until the waves are depleted. interesting feature in that instead of tower health you have power cores which can be retrieved from the killed enemies who have stolen them means you no longer have to worry about the enemies reaching the tower but more focus is puit on preventing them from escaping if theymanage to reach the tower.
the graphical look of the game is both very good and very simple. the enviroments and towers are 3d and very nicely finished. its not the most outstanding look for a game that i have ever seen but for the scale of this game it has look that suits it and that again is very nicely done and reminiscent for me of the older breed of RTS games such as Command and Conquers early games. i guess the animations are the most important part of this kind of game in the way the towers will look when firing and the aliens when taking damage and being defeated. the towers each have independant animations for the type of attack they use and they are apart from a select few that are of a relatively similiar type distinctive. the animations for construction, recycling, upgrading and general tower movement is great, kept simple and yet stylish which i like from a game.the way the have been designed aswell are a great feature and quite diverse creating the need to use specific turrets at specific points in a map and making the player  deploy with a more tactical mind creating for me a great experience in each mission.
the gameplay itself is very basic at first but gradually becomes more difficult as you gain access to new towers and abillities. at first you start with the standard staple of any tower defence game the humble cannon. as you pass throught the levels you gain access to a wide range of shiny new toys to wage war against the aliens with such as missile launchers for flying enemies, temporal distortion towers for slowing enemies and various other nifty little toys. as you pass through the misions and gain access to new towers the game has a great sense of rewarding when you unlock something new or complete a level. the sense of progression is great which i rarely find in a small game these days. i beat the first few missions and was hooked. the wide range of weapons also makesthe game a more tactical one. having to use turrets wisely as not to eat up your resources and be left both with no resources and without the turrets you need to defeat that specific enemy. this creates for me the one of the only two issues i could have with this game. the difficulty fluctuation in this game at points can be a bit drastic going from a simple mission to a complex mission straight away. this isnt a constant in this game so its not a major issue but for me it was a tad annoying at times. the second issue for me is the time it takes for a turrent to construct or upgrade. admitadly it only takes a few seconds but when you have an alien horde bearing down in force on your powercores its a lifetime (this may not bother everyone but for me it was a pain)
the story for this game despite not being ast the forefront is good in this game. it primarily focuses on two aspects, firstly your battle against the alien armies trying to ravage your world and secondly it goes into the story of the AI companion, his story from the previous war and how he tries to aid you in fighting the current one. the companions voice acting and story for me makethis game so much better than the standard TD game. you begin to feel for the companion and his story and it draws you in making you want to learn more which is a good feature for agame to keep you drawn in.
in short this is a very good little game, great design, great gameplay with a good sense of progression and most importantly its a massive amount of fun. i recommend this game in hope that you'll enjoy it as much as i did :D

Have you ever played a Tower Defense? Of course you have.
Have you ever played a Tower Defense with 3D models? Who hasn't!
Have you ever played a 3D Tower Defense with Aliens, 15 different game modes, and Community Made levels? No?
You have now.
Defense Grid: The Awakening is a very tense game, that takes Bloons, Throws it in a blender, adds some 3D and Aliens in, and gets drank like a protein shake.
It has specific Aliens, which react to different towers; Including Aliens with forcefields that require taking bullet damage before flaming towers can finish them off, and boss battles. (but what TD doesn't?)
Keeping up the good graphics, considering it's a six year old game is always good, and while it's not the most important thing, is still one thing that gets my attention in a Tower Defense, making it Non-overhead view.
While it has nice little touches, like towers getting in the way of each other and Aliens going through your towers to grab something, and take it back, there is one thing that I wish they'd had more of.
Towers.
Of course, they have a ton of maps, I mean, variety is what you want in a Tower Defense. But only having 8 or so different towers makes the gameplay repetetive and boring.
While they have community made maps, it'd be nice to also have custom towers, because growing up playing on the internet in 2006 or so, I loved how they had a good amount of towers/monkeys to keep the gameplay fresh and add new strategy.
Another thing that is quite bothering is how EASY the main story is. In a regular Tower Defense, you'd have the enemy come from one direction, and head to another. In this game, You have them come from one direction, go to a spot where they have to pick up these "cores", then go to the path they came in BEFORE to get a second mow down while carrying the cores. (of course not all levels are like this) Except when they die, the core gets returned and goes on a reversed path slowly to the point of which it was taken. I like how they evened it out with enemies being able to carry 2 to 3 cores, but i've completed half the story as of this review and not struggled once. The most cores i've lost are 3 out of 15 or so.
But if you want to have some quick and strategic fun, while the game looking pretty, look no further than Defense Grid: The Awakening.

Story: Now a massive asteroid hits earth in the year of 2029. There is several areas that have pockets of survivors that are forced to begin a new civilization. The world is populated by human survivors of the impact, who have come together to form settlements around oases and other practical or habitable locations, including racetracks. These fragile homes are diligently defended by the inhabitants against bandits and mutants, which are divided into various gangs and organizations of their own. Now you the ark survivor comes into the world in the year 2135. Now this game gave me the feel of Fallout which I liked very much. Now people may say fallout rip off. Which I admit ok. But really its not exactly the same. It might start nearly the same but its just a different game. Any way. You fight your way through three area's to help bring the world back from the brink of its near destruction from the Asteroid. I liked this. A nice fit for survival.
Game Play: The game primarily consists of FPS and driving area's, with the you using vehicle's to explore the world and travel between missions. Combat is in first person view. You are armed with a variety of firearms from pistols to a nice rocket launcher and my favorite weapon wing sticks (They are like boomerangs). You get different ammo for each weapon. Which you can change to your style. There is two types of enemies Shooting and melee, no need to explain what they do since its easy to figure out.
Now there is several vehicle events for you to participate in. Races and checkpoint rallies. Racing events may or may not have opponents, and some of them are armed races while others are not. You have the ability to augment you cars with various items and upgrades you can gain by completing events. Rage also some (RPG) elements, inventory system, looting system and Also able to build a wide assortment of items using collected recipes. There are also side missions and a number of other minor exploratory elements to the game.
Now this game is not fully open world like many out there. Yes you are restricted. But there is still a lot you can do. So do not let the closed world put you off. The game is fun and an interesting story to it to.
Controls: Easy and simple for anyone to use. Not much else to say on that. Controls can be customized to how you like it of course via keyboard and mouse.
The Graphics: The Graphics are really great. The characters and weapons had me drolling. Never seen such good graphics on my system like that and I am not usually some one for graphics.
Music: It was good for the game. But for this game I turned it off so I could pay more attention to the game, sometimes I find music distracting in games.
Bugs and Glitches: Right this was a big issue. Poor pc compatibility with this port. Rendering issues on the graphics and glitches in the sound along with (CTD's) But with user tweaks and fixes the game got better there was still issues but not as many for me it was just CTD's caused by my xfire. Technical issues with the PC version has led to articles explaining to users how to "fix" Rage's problems. AMD had released drivers that attempt to fix some the issues. Then on October 10, 2011 patches for the Windows version were released which added various graphical options to the game and fixed a number of driver-related graphical issues.
Reply Value: Sadly I do not find any reply value in this game at all. Its a one time play in my books.
Overall: Now the story is good in my books. Game play is good to but there is room for improvements. Controls are easy as I have said. Graphics are amazing. Music is good. Graphics really great. There is bugs and glitches in the game and most are fixed via user help and drivers and a patch. Even for a poorly ported game. This was quiet fun and exciting for me. The ending was nice to shows for a possible squeal. But I am not going to tell you the ending. So my rating for this game will be 7 paws for this good game.

"Rage" is pretty mediocre. Not *bad*, just mediocre. It plays like an extended tech demo (which is probably is seeing how the marketing is hyping the game engine) that is, it takes the "kitchen sink" approach to game design, lacking focus. Everything you could want to do with a  game engine is represented and is polished to a glorious shine and it is shiny, just mediocre. The first person combat is entertaining enough. The driving sections are OK-ish and not actually broken in any way so they get a pass, I guess. There are RPG elements, but they don't *really* matter. There is crafting, which also doesn’t really matter. There is an evil authority, there are vicious mutants and there are good and noble rebels - which in game are called "The Authority", "The Mutants" and "The Rebels". You see? Mediocre.
What wasn't strictly mediocre was the enemy AI which would (depending on enemy type) rather effectively take and use cover. This made the combat sections with those enemies stand out from the rest of the game, but not too far out, because this game doesn't really get to far past mediocre.
I would also like to point out that for the PC you will most likely have to create a config file to fix several graphic and performance issues. Once this is done, the game will be beautiful and run very well, but a player should be able to run a game out of the box without having to do this, so instead of "Rage" getting and outstanding for polish, it again achieves mediocre.
For a gun-shooty game the gunplay in Rage just isn't very good, You also seem to spend a lot more time waiting for shop vendors to say their introductory lines than shooting stuff.
Recomended.

Positives:
1. Wonderful pixel art in all its pixelated glory. Seriously I'm not even kidding. The artwork is absolutely beautiful and completely functional. You can tell every different enemy or friendly apart instantly.
2. Tons of customization! You can customize your gun, knives, inventory, etc. to a great degree, allowing lots of potential.
3. Perfect learning curve. The game gives you a little taste of customization when you start out that gradually gets deeper and more indepth so the player doesn't feel overwhelmed at first.
4. Not a short game. There are lots of stages that give you variety.
5. The story is tight and focused. You're a soldier in an army trying to beat some terrorist because he's a jerk. There are a lot of amusing NPCs who are your back-up team. It's stylized a little like Metal Gear Solid (there are 'codec'-like conversations), but it's not crazy-complicated. You can fully ignore it if you want.
Negatives:
1. It's a resource-gathering game. The core game mechanic is killing an enemy then picking up whatever junk is left behind, then doing this a thousand more times. Can't ignore it or you'll never get the better guns. Ho-hum.
Nitpicks:
1. For each mission, you have a primary objective, a secondary objective, then a secret objective that the game doesn't tell you about. When you complete the primary objective, the mission ends and forcefully brings you back to the base, even if you want to spend time on the other objectives. It'd be nice if you could, say, complete the primary objective and then choose when you want to end the mission (or just wait for the timer).
Overall a very solid game. Recommended.

A solid 2D action game.  Some may describe it as a run and gun, but it has a much more deliberate pace.  While the learning curve may initially be a bit steep, the game provides a moderate challenge all the way through.  Rush or play carelessly and you will be punished.  The game expects you to learn the patterns of your enemies.  Positioning and purposeful movement are key.  The controls are crisp, but a controller would be highly recommended in this case.  I played using a Wii U Pro controller.
It is broken up into short missions which can usually be completed in 5-10 minutes each.  These missions are on a timer, but for the most part these timers are very generous.  However, if you are the kind of player who cannot stand having time limits you may want to avoid this game.  The missions come in a number of varieties.  Collect materials, kill a boss, clear out the enemies, or reach a destination.

This is a Paradox game. For those who haven't bought a Paradox game early on, let me explain the process.
You buy the game, and at first it seems incredibly confusing and complicated. You play a bunch of games and get your butt handed to you because Paradox sucks at tutorials, but it's still fun. You slowly get better, and for the first 20 hours or so it's a great experience. Then you hit the point where you've mastered the game, and suddenly the veil is lifted. The shallowness becomes apparent, and the failings of the AI make every game a steamroll. And yet, the game is still somewhat enjoyable, if only to screw around with dumb strategies like conquering the world as Bhutan/Ryukyu/etc.
Over the next few years, Paradox will release a tonne of patches and DLC that slowly increase the game's depth and fix the glaring issues. You buy them all, because at this point you have 200+ hours and need your next fix. Then, Steam has a summer sale, and the price of the game plus all DLC is half the price you paid for the base game. You cry softly into your wallet as you invade Poland for the 264th time.
Then Victoria III comes out, and the cycle begins anew.
TL;DR: If you're bored of EU4, you've probably already bought this and there's no help for you.
If you aren't already in the Paradox cycle and don't have an abundance of disposable income, wait a few years for the game to be finished. Go play EU4 instead.

I remember playing this years ago on Wild Tangent, long before I switched to Steam, and it's still just as fun as it was then, maybe even more now that I know what to expect.
Defense Grid is among the best you'll find in the Tower Defense genre, and rightfully so. This game has a tantalizing blend of simplicity, planning, general enjoyment and even graphics. One of the largest pluses to Defense Grid is that it allows you to progressively shape the path your alien foe take. You can also set up "kill zones," places where you concentrate your best towers and where most of the killing happens, hence the name.
Another huge twist in Defense Grid is that your enemies have to go to a central hub to take a power core, essentially hitpoints. If you kill an alien who is holding a core, the core will progressively float back to the hub unless another alien grabs it. This makes strategy much deeper than "don't let them get to the end."
Your AI friend who is booted up in the prologue is your constant companion, giving you tips and commenting on how you're doing or what's going on (this has saved my♥♥♥♥♥many times when I was focused on improving outer towers and he told me that aliens had their grabby little hands on a core, and they wouldn't left the map with it if my AI friend hadn't told me in time).
Another great, possibly unintentional twist is that your AI friend has a British accent. This somehow makes his warnings more spoken and his cheers more cheerful, plus it sounds so classy when he says "bloody hell."
Some maps also have multiple levels to them, where aliens have to go up in a spiral to get to your cores. This opens up a huge amount of possibilities for towers that help cover multiple levels.
Overall, I'd have to say Defense Grid is one of the best if not the best game you'll find in the Tower Defense genre. Your Tower Defense collection can't be complete without this game. Definately get this if you're into Tower Defense.

There is a point a game may cross when toying with the fourth wall, as seems to be the trend these days. I like to think of it as the "oh-so-we're-doing-this-now" point. It is at this point when what were once playful subversions or clever gags seep slowly and inevitably from the periphery of a game's narrative to center stage and become a defining feature of the experience. It is, in effect, the borderline between a wink and a nod, and the developers unzipping your pants. In many cases, it can be dissappointing or jarring for a player to stumble over this boundary in the course of a game's progression, as their tentatively-held immersion is irreparably shattered by the game's suddenly altered context. Claims of pretense, navel-gazing, and 'indie-♥♥♥♥ery' are usually soon to follow.
One shot reaches this point about ten minutes after booting the game. But then it... just kinda keeps going. For the next ten hours.
Never have I played a game so gleefully irreverent of it's own limitations. Irreverent isn't even the right word... "distainful" is more accurate. It does not laugh at the fourth wall- it laughs at the fact that you thought there was a fourth wall to begin with. While tentatively stepping into the abyss of postmodernist-meta-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t can sometimes be a game's undoing, One Shot dives in with such naive enthusiasm that I couldn't help but laugh aloud on several occasions at it's sheer audacity. It often feeds you as the player such blatant untruths that you feel it's treating you like an idiot.. until, somehow, it ends up winning over your suspension of disbelief anyway. This, at least, was my experience playing One Shot.
Saying all that, I haven't even mentioned the excellent atmosphere, expressive spritework, or writing that can be dryly hilarious and heart-melting by turns (also, I have to say, the single most likeable player-character I've
). Come for the gimmick, stay for the story. Come
for the gimmick
the story. One shot's far from a thrilling game, and maybe not exceptionally cerebral when compared to certain similar cases (alas, the Book Guy may never escape the Author's shadow...), but it brings ideas to the table that not even some of the most experimental of indie games have tried before, and executes on them far more successfully than I anticipated. All in all, One Shot is a game that will charm the absolute ♥♥♥♥ out of you if you're willing to play along. I'd say any fan of narrative-based games should at least give it...
...one shot.

From the day Evolve came out I was excited to try it and play. Unfortunately due to reviews while it was pay to play I only played the original beta. What other game pits players against a hulking all powerful monster? The only other one is Monster Hunter and the monsters are all controlled by A.I. Despite a couple of things, this is purely based on how skilled you are as a monster and as a team. If you have a skilled team and a bad monster, the team will win. If you have a bad team and a skilled monster then the monster will destroy the team. The best matches obviously then are the ones with good teams and a clever/skilled monster. I've had a couple of close games where we've lost or where we've won.
Again, like Monster Hunter, there isn' really any story at all. This is a 'kill or be killed' game. 4 hunters try and kill the monster for sport, food and research (from what I've gathered) and the monster does what it needs to to survive. Eat, evolve and kill all of the hunters or destroy the power relay.
Evolve's mechanics work really nicely as any class or monster. Each character of each class and monster has his/her own strengths, weaknesses and abilities. Unfortunately, some of the monsters can really be overpowered with their skills despite the downside to taking more damage and/or having less health and shields and they need to be fixed. According to other players though, it sounds like when the weekly rotation allows you to freely play as said monsters it will be unplayable (because of the broken monsters) or unlikely that you will win as the hunters. The Kraken is very tough but it is still possible to take him down with a good team. DO NOT even bother trying to kill the Wraith. The Wraith is virtually impossible to defeat because of its speed and overpowered abilities. While hunting for the monster you need to watch out for man eating plants and hostile animals. Killing certain animals as either the hunters or the monster can grant you useful temporary perks. But you can only use one at a time.
The graphics are beautiful and the sound is right on point. You really feel like a hunter trying to listen for monster activity and feel like a monster running around and stomping like Godzilla. Monster smelling is subtle and not overdone. Every gun sounds like how they should and even when you aren't directly communicating your character will shout things out for the others to hear what you're doing from time to time.
Evolve always had potential and despite some clear unbalances at times this will always be one of my favorites due to how unique the game is. I really hope Turtle Rock Studios steps up and makes the adjustments the game clearly needs. But for being in free to play beta? Really impressive so far. I recommend giving it a try even if you think you won't like it. What can you lose? It's free now.

I'm a bit new to the whole Dark Souls type games, and only got around to them after finishing Bloodborne in its vanilla stages, and I fell in love with that game. After doing so, I just had to pick up all of the Souls games, and seek out any other games that might give me that same rush I experienced downing a tough and grueling boss, where you had to become quite intimate with its phases, abilities, and move sets all while learning your own. Where as in other games, most bosses are simply just a regular enemy with a lot more HP.
In a Dark Souls or Bloodborne experience, the normal enemies are tough, and there are mobs and other types who might do just as well as they would a sub boss, or stand in. That is to say, the games aren't unfair...they are, you just have to learn the mechanics, and will be punished from the get go. Except here, it teaches you...drives you.
This is why I was happy to try this title out, and while it doesn't feel as "tough" as its 3D progenitors, as I'm admittedly only about five hours in at the time of writing this, I still find it as a good fill in for those games when I want to change things up, but still want to retain that magical feeling of accomplishment, and falling in love with every boss and becoming more personal with them than I would with other bosses in other games.
This hearkens back to my childhood love and challenge I found in the NES title of Castlevania, which a lot of games like these and God of War owe a great debt to, and even echo quite a bit in some ways. It really makes me feel nostalgic at the same time, because I really loved seeing my favorite horror icons turned into these challenging boss fights, before I even knew what a "boss" was in my little mind. The original Castlevania, like these newer, modern games make every boss unique, and in need of adjusted strategies or approach. Where as many games these days add bosses simply to increase the amount of hours you are required to play, and while this is great in concept, most become clones of a previous boss, or a simple change up. While these games aren't free from falling in that trap of repeating, you can tell, love and care was given in these games, which make up for it. You can pick up on the lore and history from their drops, their attire, and even move sets and mechanics can hint at something a little deeper if you look a little closer.
If you've played Bloodborne, or Dark Souls, or Demon's Souls, and you happen to love them and need a fix, definitely do yourself a favor and pick this one up!
The only negativity I've found is a few slight frame rate issues, which more than likely occurred due to a program I had not closed out of in need of updating, as well as the more "cutesy" and "chibi" style of the friendly characters and npcs that seem to contradict or at least give a stark contrast to the overall dark atmosphere, because make no mistake, while it looks like it could fall in the category of something a little more child friendly, there is plenty human gore imbued.
Which honestly, isn't really a problem for me. I wouldn't really call this a review so much as an impression, but maybe you're someone who happened to read through this, and in need of convincing to pick this game up. Well, if you like what you've read, and seen, and or have played games like this before, stop reading and pick this one up!
Do it. Now!

This game is a Dark Souls clone, but it's also a metroidvania game, which means that you can go back to areas you already visited, and get some items that you couldn't get before, but can now with some new unlocked abilities, etc. Game has a big open world to explore, smooth and fun gameplay, and fun abilities. As for boss fights, only few of them were good in my opinion, rest were meh and most of them were easy. And this was really disappointing to me. But I guess, you can't do boss fights much better in 2D, though they could have at least improved bosses design, because only few of them look nice, while last boss looks epic. 3 of 4 last boss fights were pretty good though. Other big disappointment to me was a design of the whole world. World is boring, gloomy, dark, and in my opinion could be done much better. All areas are kinda similar. All in all, this is an amazing metroidvania game, but if I analyze it as a Dark Souls clone too, it's not that amazing, but it's still pretty good.
And why exactly is this game a Dark Souls clone? Well you have stamina bar and stats like in Dark Souls. You have salt instead of souls, boss ears instead of boss souls, sanctuaries and shrines instead of bonfires. Creeds instead of covenants etc. Also you can parry(but you can't backstab), etc.
Amazing metroidvania game, pretty good Dark Souls clone. Boss fights and areas could be done better, but few of boss fights were pretty good though. Has smooth and fun gameplay and big open world to explore. If you want an amazing metroidvania game, get this, if you want a good Dark Souls clone, get this too. All in all, a pretty good game.

Okay, this was a tough one to rate. I gave it a "yes", but hear me out first: It's good if you're expecting DOOM, with a tiny bit of open world that was injected in. If you're actually looking for a game based on it being open world, then this is not the game for you.
This is DOOM. With the added freedom of a tiny bit of exploration (though there's not much to discover... at all) and some racing aspects, which was.... fine, let's say.
Let's just go through the cons first.
* Graphics, although nice, were poorly executed (ie. pop-ins)
* The "open world" isn't much of an open world. At all.
* The characters had SO MUCH potential, but they all ended up kind of dull. Like some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ 90's caricature, but without much personality.
* Story wasn't very interesting, and didn't have much explained.
* Without spoiling anything for you, the ending was... well.... it wasn't much of an ending. I was saving up all my best weapons, and then suddenly... the game's over. It did not feel like an ending. No boss fight. The final quest felt like just any other side quest.
With that aside, I want to say that, with the exception of that last point, as well as the point about texture pop-ins, those flaws are okay and can be overlooked..
you treat the game like DOOM. I played it on nightmare difficulty, and I have to say it was just as fun as DOOM itself. It really was. if you're looking for something like Fallout, turn away now. If you're looking for something like DOOM, however, I highly recommend it.

There are so many amazing things about this game, it is entirely underrated. Unfortunately a lack of marketing combined with the overall lack of content are what ultimately made this game less successfull than its 2011 classmates such as Skyrim. With that said, to this day this is easily one of my favorite games that I have played. What the game lacks in content is makes up for a million times in character, beauty and overall fluid gameplay.
In comparison, RAGE vs. Bioshock (any of them) Rage wins in actual gameplay and mechanics while Bioshock would win with the strong storyline. They are  both incredible games, but put the stoy-type that Bioshock has into this game and honestly you have the perfect FPS game.
I'll start with Cons:
-The game is short, there is no way around it.
-There is more more that they could have done with the 'racing' aspect of this game. It really is more of a mini game within the game but it offered versatility in a fairly constricting game.
-This is a FPS with linear story progression, there is very minimal sandbox-type capabilities
The Pros:
-Gameplay is just delightful
-Weapons are varied and the bow with environment interavtivity and ammunition types is just increible.
-The various ways to approach every single fight whether it is through exploding remote cars, guns blazing, etc... The game boasts strong versatility in gameplay.
-TONS of mini-games within the game that are all pretty fun.
-The story is very entertaining
-The game is full of vibrant characters and monsters
-The art style is great
-The graphics are just beautiful considering a 2011 release date.
-The engine was truely a pioneer, boasting ZERO, I repeat, NO replicated areas or terrain types. (To explain, in most games, areas are replicated, reconfigured and reskinned. For example, in Fallout you may notice that a lot of areas are quite similar. This does not happen in RAGE as the engine was developed to be able to specifically alter each area, each rock, each spray painted wall.)

Game with a lot of potential. If you're a filthy casual who has never played the series before and isn't very good at this kind of game, then by all means go ahead, you'll definitely enjoy it. If you aren't (or are) a casual and would like to play Multiplayer, then you should definitely buy the game. The multiplayer in HoI 4 is the best in any Paradox grand strategy game, by far.
For us WW2 "experts" and wargame enthusiasts, I cannot reccomend the game (without mods) at this stage. Why? Because of the terrible AI. It is sad when one single issues "breaks" a game, but that's how it is. The previous games in the series were even worse at release.
I am quite confident in that Paradox will fix most issues with the game, but it will take time. One must understand that developing a proper AI (especially when it comes to actual combat) is immensely difficult in a game like Hearts of Iron.
If you raelly want to try it out, though, at least do yourself the favour and install some mods. There's plenty of AI enhancing mods out there, and plenty of other mods for flavour, as well as total overhaul mods (although you'll want to wait with those until they're in a more finished state). If you're playing as a minor nation, I would advise you to install a national focus tree mod.
In short: BIG AI issues, mods can fix SOME of them, but the combat AI itself remains horrible. If you're not very good at this kind of games, though, you probably won't notice it too much.
I've decided to reccomend the game on Steam though, because with mods it becomes quite playable, and the multiplayer component is VERY fun.

The game's selection of achievements also present a lasting challenge to anyone that plays, as getting them all is no easy feat!
A fun, upbeat, and all around entertaining and visually impressive game, Mercenary Kings gets a 10/10 from me! The small details, incredible spritework and just plain old fun gameplay make this game a quality buy for any fans of the sidescrolling shoot'em-up genre!

Mercenary Kings is a pretty weird game in how it mixes the old and new in game design. Side-scrolling 2D shoot-em-up? Check. Gorgeous, elaborate pixel art? Check. Elaborate gun crafting systtem? Uh, check. Active reloads? Check. It's an odd combination, certainly, but it mostly manages to work. The actual issues with the game are more of the "mileage may vary" sort. If you actually care about unique mission structure, this isn't the game for you. Each mission follows one of maybe ten basic types, the differences between individual missions of a type being more based in mad libs requirements than anything more substantial. Swapping out one enemy set or materials checklist for another. For me personally, I don't mind.
That's because the joy of the game isn't in accomplishing the objectives, but kicking♥♥♥♥♥much♥♥♥♥♥as possible with a customized loadout that grows increasingly ridiculous as you unlock new parts. Completing the missions is only a means to an end. That being said, it is a repetitive game at the best of times. It just manages to be repetitive in a way I enjoy, Your tolerance may be substantially lower. Keep that in mind before you decide whether to make the leap.

This game is ♥♥♥♥ing dope. It takes the Paradox grand strategy model, takes out all the hard, boring♥♥♥♥♥♥ and leaves you with just one thing: WAR(and production and technology). It's war at a level of strategic detail you probably haven't seen. It has so. much. replayability. With each country you can essentially do 4 different things. Try to stay neutral and defend your own country, conquer as fascist and join the Axis, "expand the workers revolution" (conquer) as communist and join the Comintern, or defend freedom by joining the allies. There's also always the option of creating your own faction, but its rather difficult to convince the AI to join you, so I suspect this is most fun in multiplayer. The point is, this game is fast paced, replayable, and almost never turns out the same way. I've had a game where i formed the "Southern Socialist Front" as Brazil and absolutely kicked the Allies' collective asses. I know I don't have a lot of 'chieves, but that's because I typically play with a few flavor mods that aren't ironman compatible unfortunately. If you're looking to get into the grand strategy genre coming from more tactical strategy games, I would start here.

Let me start by saying that I do not recommend this game at its full price. I paid .99 USD for it so for that price you cant really go too wrong. I enjoyed the game at first, its uniqu(ish) blend of FPS and TD was amusing, but I soon started to see that the game was lacking in some areas. I played with a friend as well to see what how he felt about and found us agreeing in most areas. My biggest griped was polish. The game seems like it coulda used a decent amount it. I noticed animations gliching out a bunch of times, turrets having fits when enemies quickly moved in and out of range, the player often getting stuck and needing to teleport out (seems like a copout from a dev standpoint).
My friends biggest gripe was odd balancing. We often found that the first 4-6 waves of enemies we could stop before they barely made any progress out of the starting point, then the next wave would break right through to the end and we'd loose. Easy, easy, easy, easy, easy, insanely hard. Not a fun difficutly curve.
Also, while the fps portions of the game all worked nicely and looked good, the TD portions seemed ad hoc assembly of tower defense features that didnt fit together to well anf felt clunky. Like the game was designed as a FPS defense kinda thing, then someone added in the the tower stuff where ever it would fit. That being said if you love FPSs and are so so about TDs, then this might just be for you! But if you love TDs and could take or leave a FPS, then this isnt going to mesh well.
Its not a bad game, and Im sure there are lots of people who love it. But, it wanst my cup of tea. To me it felt like 2/10 TD and 8/10 FPS, where a smash hit in my eyes would have those numbers transposed. Over all i would give it a 6 out of 10. Not bad, but not good enough to keep me coming back for more.

OneShot-Where do i even start?Everything about this game is so damn good.
I'll start by summarizing the game before discussing it's strongest points and the usual cons.
OneShot in it's very core is a pixel-art,top-down,puzzle/adventure game.
The interesting thing about this game is,you yourself(yes you the player!).
Is a completely seperate entity from the character you control.
This game knows you are alive and interacts with you.
You guide a character named Niko on their quest to bring the sun back to it's already dying world.
A simple enough story and reminds me alot of JRPG games.
Now then,the strongest points of the game!
First and foremost are the character interactions,specifically,You and Niko's interactions.
Niko and the player communicate with each other,Niko sometimes take time to talk to the actual player.
You helping Niko with puzzles and whatnot.It does an INSANELY good job of making you care for
Niko and making you attached to them.
Second and something fans would also agree with,is how this game breaks the fourth wall.
Remember how i typed this game knows you exist?
Well that's how puzzles in OneShot work,you dig through files,check backgrounds and stuff.
It really is great as a puzzle game and something even people that aren't a fan of puzzles can enjoy.
Now then,on to the cons!
The major thing you will realize if you were to play the game is how you are at a disadvantage if you aren't tech savy.
Like i said,puzzles in OneShot mostly consist of digging through files,modifying them and whatnot.
You might have to look for guides and walkthroughs just to complete the game.
Which brings me to my second point.
This game is a personal experience,i would go against buying it if you've already watch someone else play it or have been spoiled,as the game isn't as nearly fun or interesting that way.
TL;DR All in all OneShot is a fantastic personal experience that's worth it for it's price.

is a top-down (bird's eye view) wild west-style shooter set in Mexico and Texas in the mid-late 1800's.  Many players make a comparison to
, but I haven't played it (yet) so I'm unable comment on that.  What I can do, however, is give you a rundown of the good, the bad and the ugly that I've experienced in this game.
++ Music
++ Artwork
+ Attention to Detail
+ Gameplay/Controls
- Storyline/Plot
- Potential Rage-Inducing Repetitive-ness
= Very fun and definitely worth a try, just don't expect it to have a very deep story!
: The first thing that comes to mind is, by far, the music.  Non-stop throughout the game I simply could not get over how great the soundtrack was.  It's even possible that I performed one of the best mariachi air guitar solos ever while watching my brother play for a bit, just sayin'.
Next up is the artwork and, as a bonus, the attention to detail.  Everything is hand-drawn with pen and paper and the effect is pretty amazing, in my opinion, especially when combined with the sharp contrast of all the bright red blood that is spilled in epic western shoot-em-up mayhem.  Plus, it's the little things, the tiny details added that catch your eye occasionally, that make it all the more special.  I can't tell you how surprised I was when I saw my character spit on the ground (patooie!) for the first time.  I mean, who would think to add that?  Awesome people, that's who.
As for the gameplay, while the controls can be a bit tricky initally, the difference in shooting mechanics between shooting a revolver versus a rifle versus a bow and arrow, etc, is actually quite cool and adds to the fun.  Not to mention how very smooth it plays and how fast it reacts makes for a great gaming experience.
:  Sadly, the story leaves something to be desired.  Sometimes I didn't even understand what was going on, and by the end I still had more questions than answers.  Maybe this is intentional -- upcoming sequel or prequel?? -- but I kind of doubt it.  It was okay, but I certainly wouldn't have minded more text and/or cutscenes (or even a longer game) if it pulled me deeper into the story and made me feel more invested in what was going on.
Finally, I should add that
contains a healthy dose of challenging gameplay where bullets are deadly and the enemy rarely misses.  Most of the time this is fantastic and makes the game very enjoyable, but on occasion it can be very frustrating to repeat a level over and over and over because you keep getting killed at every turn.  Some people thrive in moments like this, and others simply do not.  Personally, I don't find this as much of a "con", but I watched my brother curse and rage in a couple levels, so I thought I would add it here.
:
might be a bit on the short side and lack a little in the story department, but there's no doubt about it: the game is a whole basket of fun and mayhem!!  I'm quite impressed and definitely recommend it for its entertainment value, just don't expect it to be incredibly deep story-wise.

Hey amigo!

You're an escaped slave with no memory of your past, all you have is your sombrero and a revolver as you set down on a journey to find out who you are and what happened to you.
A top-down shooter with a peculiar art style, 12 is better than 6 is pretty short and has a simple gameplay but comes out as a pretty fun and engaging game.
-the hand drawn style works really well
-the soundtrack is quite nice
-controls and gunplay are quite responsive most of the time
-while there's only an handful of different weapons (revolver, shotgun, rifle, bow) they all have their pros and cons and feel useful in different situations
-offers a good challenge
-writing and story are somewhat bland overall
-enemies will sometimes be hard to spot when the action gets frantic, either lost in the background or amongst corpses
-reload mechanics can feel slightly unwieldy at times, same goes for aiming ( I feel a straight line rather than an aiming reticle'd have made things much easier)
-gameplay can get repetitive in the long run
-a few minor bugs
-pretty short at 3/4 hours to complete
12 is Better Than 6 is often compared to Hotline Miami and I can see why, you get missions where you kill scores of bad guys while trying to not get killed unless you want to restart the level from scratch: the gameplay isn't as refined as Hotline but it works well enough to provide a fair amount of fun. If a section gets too frustrating you can also drop the difficulty to low so that you won't be instakilled most of the time.
The art style is truly nice and original, the black and white world is only coloured by any blood you spill, and the soundtrack is quite good. The actual gunplay is interesting and has you having to ready each shot for most weapons with one mouse button before you can shoot with the other: I must say there were a few times where I felt the controls wern't as responsive as hoped and I died a few times due to that. The gameplay also never strays too far from stealth around/ kill everyone so don't expect much else, even more so if you consider that the characters and story are pretty meh.
Even if it's not perfect 12 is better than 6 is more than decent and has enough character going for it to be a worthy purchase if you enjoy the genre, even more so if you consider it can go as low as 3$ when on sale.

I finally bought EU IV. So that's the fourth Europa Universalis I have bought since 2002. I've never regretted any of the purchases - each one has resulted in many hours of entertainment, and each one has built on its predecessor's satisfying gameplay and added depth.
Having now played number four in the series for about a week, I can see I will be as glued to this one as I was to each of the older versions.
I guess my initial impressions are:
- "fabricate claim" seems too easy.
- trade is incomprehensible. I've tried reading various guides but my eyes just glaze over. Instead of the simple concept of provinces producing a trade good, the price of which varies according to technology, events, and supply and demand, and those goods being available in that province's centre of trade, there are now trade nodes as well as CoTs, and lines that join up the trade nodes, and your merchants can collect from trade or they can "steer", and what's more you collect trade from places where you haven't even got a merchant, plus your ships can be used to increase trade, although when you assign them the value it increases by seems to reflect your entire navy or something because selecting one ship or 10 seems to give the same advice about the effect on trade. Essentially, we need a checkbox to make all this detail go away, it's boring and pointless.
- the system of technological progress is radically different and involves juggling "currencies" other than gold - you collect Admin, Diplo, and Military "points" and those slowly accumulate to provide progress, although there are plenty of temptations to fritter those points away on other things, such as coring provinces, increasing stability, or changing province culture. I'm in two minds about whether this is an improvement over the EU3 system where all this was managed centrally through your basic finances.

All in all, unlike Crusader Kings (where bucketloads of obscure complexity added to CKII made me stop enjoying the game) I think EUIV will enjoy my attention for a fair while while I figure out how it works. I'm not convinced it's more fun than EUIII though.

From the day Evolve came out I was excited to try it and play. Unfortunately due to reviews while it was pay to play I only played the original beta. What other game pits players against a hulking all powerful monster? The only other one is Monster Hunter and the monsters are all controlled by A.I. Despite a couple of things, this is purely based on how skilled you are as a monster and as a team. If you have a skilled team and a bad monster, the team will win. If you have a bad team and a skilled monster then the monster will destroy the team. The best matches obviously then are the ones with good teams and a clever/skilled monster. I've had a couple of close games where we've lost or where we've won.
Again, like Monster Hunter, there isn' really any story at all. This is a 'kill or be killed' game. 4 hunters try and kill the monster for sport, food and research (from what I've gathered) and the monster does what it needs to to survive. Eat, evolve and kill all of the hunters or destroy the power relay.
Evolve's mechanics work really nicely as any class or monster. Each character of each class and monster has his/her own strengths, weaknesses and abilities. Unfortunately, some of the monsters can really be overpowered with their skills despite the downside to taking more damage and/or having less health and shields and they need to be fixed. According to other players though, it sounds like when the weekly rotation allows you to freely play as said monsters it will be unplayable (because of the broken monsters) or unlikely that you will win as the hunters. The Kraken is very tough but it is still possible to take him down with a good team. DO NOT even bother trying to kill the Wraith. The Wraith is virtually impossible to defeat because of its speed and overpowered abilities. While hunting for the monster you need to watch out for man eating plants and hostile animals. Killing certain animals as either the hunters or the monster can grant you useful temporary perks. But you can only use one at a time.
The graphics are beautiful and the sound is right on point. You really feel like a hunter trying to listen for monster activity and feel like a monster running around and stomping like Godzilla. Monster smelling is subtle and not overdone. Every gun sounds like how they should and even when you aren't directly communicating your character will shout things out for the others to hear what you're doing from time to time.
Evolve always had potential and despite some clear unbalances at times this will always be one of my favorites due to how unique the game is. I really hope Turtle Rock Studios steps up and makes the adjustments the game clearly needs. But for being in free to play beta? Really impressive so far. I recommend giving it a try even if you think you won't like it. What can you lose? It's free now.

TLDR: Don’t play Trine 3 with only a trackpad. It will frustrate the hell out of you. If you are stuck on a laptop, you’ll need a mouse.
I really enjoyed Trine 2 when I first played it a few years ago, and recently replayed all of Trine 2 to get all the achievements on a different Steam account. I am generally a fan of platformers, and as I enjoyed it’s predecessor so much, I figured I would pick up Trine 3 while it was on sale. I probably regret that.
The first thing I noticed was that there was a lot of lag, and no sound. I restarted with lower graphics, and while the lag subsided, the sound never appeared. I troubleshooted enough to know that it was a problem with the game’s sound, not my computer.
The second thing I noticed was Zoya’s inability to stick to any wooden surface, and while I did enjoy swinging with her, the limited potential made it so much less fun than with Trine 2 (swinging with Zoya was my very favorite part of Trine 2, and the reason I didn’t like Trine 1 much).
I did not realize that the game was 3d before buying it. I was surprised, but I’m not unhappy, the developers dealt well with the new dimension.
My biggest problem with the game came early on in the tutorial, when Pontius needs to smash an object. I realized I needed to press both mouse keys, which meant I needed to find a working mouse. I couldn’t. I was able to find one that allowed me to press the keys, but I still needed to use my trackpad for moving my cursor about, and it quickly became frustrating. I lasted only partly into Zoya’s section of the tutorial where I had to scroll as well before I gave up. I understand that a mouse is expected for these games, but I had been playing Trine 2 with no mouse and no problems, so this frustrated me more than it could have.
I will reconsider playing this game later, if I can find a good mouse or have access to a different computer. Hopefully then I’ll have sound and can actually functionally play this game.
However, I have read that Amadeus is nerfed, and I hope he isn’t, because if he can’t make towers of objects and bridges, what’s the point?
I also noticed the achievements were significantly more boring than in Trine 2- no Cirque de Zoya or Leaning Tower of Pontius style achievements that encouraged messing around or even getting friends to help.

- the 3D movement adds more "depth" to the puzzles, but also makes gameplay more tedious and complicated than the pure-2D movement in the previos games. I preffer 2D, but this 3D does work too and brings a bit of variety.
- in Co-op the second keyboard and mouse is no longer supported! I had to play the Trine using Steam Controller and as good as it was, using 2nd set of mouse & keyboard for Co-op was my favourite feature in previous Trine and Shadowgrouds games.
- The game's story feels unfinished. Developers had major financial difficulties that forced them to shorten the game, so the story got a hit, but it is not really an issue as the game is long enough. + there are some extra mod-missions to play.
So Trine 3 is a very good co-op game for 2 people, just not as great as the Trine 2 :) I hope Frozenbyte makes even more co-op games in the future for us to enjoy!
