RAGE is a first person shooter set in a post-apocalyptic world. These two things are some of my favorite things in the world, which means RAGE caters directly to someone like me, so why don't I like it? It simply doesn't feel tripple A. That's not to say indie games are bad (which this one isn't), because of course they aren't inherently bad, but RAGE leaves an impression of not having the budget to back up what the developers set out to make. They set out to make a sizeable world with living, breathing NPCs who require your help dealing with all sorts of different problems. The product they ended up with in the end is a mediocre first person shooter that oozes of what I like to call "MMO comprimises", which is really odd for a primarily singleplayer game. These comprimises include boring fetch quests, a protagonist without identity, very loose vehicle controls, poor sound design. Because of all these things the tone of the game suffers as well. Sometimes the game tries to be super dark and serious and at other times it seems much lighter and more playful and this disparity is damaging to the overall feel of the game.
The story of the game is as dull and barebones as it gets. You're the world's last hope more or less and so you have to fight the multiple evil factions, some more technologically advanced than the others. Your character has no personality and the story doesn't feel personal at all. You end up just being a stooge who the NPCs just boss around. Even with great voice actors like John Goodman, you will feel absolutely no attachment to any of the characters in the world, you won't even hate the ones that seem sort of antagonistic like Redstone or Starky. You will just hate id Software for making such flat characters.
The visuals of the game are for the most part also below average. I know I am writing this review 5 years after its release, but comparing RAGE to Borderlands, which has a similar art style as well as being 2 years older, RAGE doesn't stack up. There are ugly lowres textures everywhere, and half the time you turn you just 45 degrees you'll notice textures loading in front of you, even on objects that are 50+ metres away. The animations are okay-ish, but do feel stiff and rigid.
I was going to write that the shooting in the game felt good, but as I was typing it out I realized that I had more negative stuff to say about it that positive. So, the gunplay of the game feels lackluster. The guns for the most part feel weightless and shooting them doesn't leave much of an impact for two reasons; the poor sound design mentioned earlier and because most of the enemies in this game are bullet sponges, even on normal difficulty, each bullet just seems to have little effect on the enemies. For 95% of the enemies you're going to be better off throwing a Wingstick at them, a boomerange-esque consumable item you can throw at the enemy to, in most cases, chop their head right off and oneshot them. Even if it doesn't hit their head, they'll drop dead in most cases on normal difficulty anyway. So if you want to breeze through the game without feeling frustrated by the bullet spongy enemies, just stock up on these. Admittedly this makes for some boring gameplay, but so is filling an enemy with a magazine and a half from my assault rifle before it goes down, so all you can do is choose between the devil and the deep blue sea.
Driving cars in this game doesn't feel good either. The vehicles handle poorly and aside from a few mandatory races you have to win, the driving merely serves as a way to get from point a to point b and ultimately the game would have been better without it, but I guess the developers didn't want to cut that feature because of how heavily inspired by Mad Max the world is.
There's also some light crafting in the game. You can craft stuff like bandages to instantly heal yourself, even though you do not have a healthbar, but rather regenerative health Call of Duty style. You can also craft stuff like previously mentioned wingsticks, remote controlled cars with explosives, door grinders to gain access to sealed off rooms for rare loot. Yes, there's loot in this game. You won't have to manage your inventory as there is no limit to how much you can carry, but the environments you go through will be littered with glowing items that you have to mindlessly pickup en masse.
All in all the game has
of issues and doesn't really offer anything unique. This doesn't mean that it's a Godawful game, it just isn't "good". I don't recommend you playing this game if you were to choose this game over another. If you have absolutely nothing to play and really feel like playing an post-apocalyptic first person shooter, you
give this a go, but just know what you're about to play by no means is amazing.

Gue cinta FPS, gue cinta Tower Defense. Maka gue bercinta dengan mereka, lahirlah FPSTower Defense.
Gue menulis review ini setelah 2 jam bermain. Walau pun begitu, udah cukup buat gue untuk memberikan nilai kepada game ini 8,5 dari 10.
Kesan pertama: grafiknya diatas ekspektasi gue. Jujur, gue agak segan untuk memainkan game yang dibawah 2012 kebawah. Kenapa? karena biasanya sih grafiknya itu standart 'kotak-kotak' banget. Teksturnya kasar, resolusinya kecil, dan tidak 'wah'. Tapi ternyata Sanctum menawarkan gue grafik yang memukau. Banget. Waktu gue main di map pertama, gue bingung. Ini teh tower defense? atau FPS terus kita musti nembak nembakin monster? Biasanya pula kan tower defense itu FOV nya dari atas, ini kenapa malah ada dibawah? Hmmm... Sanctum bener bener membawa PENGALAMAN BARU buat gue sebagai gamer yang udah rajin main game sejak SD.
Grafik: WOW. Seperti yang gue bilang tadi, Sanctum memiliki grafik yang memukau. Gue merasa ketinggalan jaman banget baru nemu game seindah ini. Gak cuman cukup detail, tapi efek dari peluru, laser, listrik, kabut, dan berbagai atmosfernya bener bener menyatu. Gue heran, apakah ini beneran dirilis tahun 2011? Game tahun 2014 aja grafiknya belum tentu seindah ini lho. Jadi bagi yang merasa mempunyai fetish dengan grafik, tenang aja... hasrat lo dijamin terpuaskan.
Gameplay: CLASSIC ADDICTING PUZZLED TOWER DEFENSE. Ada banyak elemen menarik didalam game ini. Maksud dari classic disetiap game tower defense, selalu ada yang namanya upgrade. Dengan biaya tertentu, lo bisa mengupgrade tower lo menjadi lebih kuat, cepat, dan keren. Tapi gak cuman itu doang, elemen lainnya adalah PUZZLED. Yup, biasanya kan kalau tower defense itu lo hanya sebatas memilih tower untuk ditempatkan. Beberapa game malah membatasi penempatan tower. Begitu juga dengan map nya, kebanyakan game tower defense itu mapnya sudah diatur jalannya. Ditambah lagi, FOV nya juga SELALU DIATAS. Beruntungnya, Sanctum BERBEDA. Lo BEBAS menaruh tower dimana saja, lo BEBAS membentuk jalur untuk musuh, dan ini adalah game FPS. Yup, enggak cuman tower lo doang yang bisa nembakin musuh, tapi lo juga bisa. Ada berbagai macam senjata didalam game ini dan hebatnya, senjata lo juga bisa DIUPGRADE. Jadi ini bener bener pilihan lo, apakah lo ingin MENJEBAK MUSUH dengan tower lo atau HEAD TO HEAD bersama senjata lo. Belum sampai disitu, Sanctum juga menawarkan fitur multiplayer. Tapi karena gue belum mencoba, jadi gue gak bisa kasih informasi.
Storyline: SAMA SEKALI GAK ADA. Yup, begitu lo selesai tutorial, lo langsung main mempertahankan base lo. Tidak ada kata pengantar sama sekali. Padahal yah storyline bisa menjadi pemain memiliki pengalaman emosional yang lebih dalam dengan game ini. Simple aja, misalnya siapa itu Sanctum? Bagaimana senjata ini atau tower itu dibuat? Darimana aliennya muncul? Kenapa aliennya menyerang kita? Tapi apakah tidak ada storyline maka menjadi game yang mengecewakan? Nope. Game ini cukup menarik WALAU tanpa storyline.
Gue berani kasih skor 8,5 dari 10.
Kenapa? Karena Sanctum benar benar menawarkan pengalaman baru yaitu FPS Tower Defense. Sayangnya tidak ada storyline atau steamworkshop. Game ini pantas dibeli dengan harga $10. So andaikan kalau game ini mendadak diskon sampai 90%, LO BENER BENER MUSTI MEMBELI.

I’m a huge fan of both business sims and music, and you’ll be hard pressed to find many games that crossover into the music industry. There’s some out there, and while many of them are good, they sacrifice the large scale industry side of things to show a more personal, smaller scale side of the music industry, usually focusing solely on one band or only allowing a couple dozen artists to be simulated at a time. I say all of this because the Music Wars series goes against this trend, choosing to simulating the entire music industry, and Music Wars Empire is the newest, largest, and most polished game in the series to date.
Several big new features have been added to this latest iteration, including expanded regions (now supporting 129 subregions worldwide), digital streaming for releases, new charts, release types, buying out competing record labels and managing multiple labels, the ability for your artists to go Solo, as well as the ability for your artists to form their own Side Projects in new genres, remix songs, and online compete online via online leaderboards. In addition to these features, the game has been optimized to load faster than previous entries in the series, even when using large mods that would bring previous iterations down to a crawl.
In addition to these new features are returning features from earlier entries, several of which have been entirely re-tooled specifically for Music Wars Empire. Collaborations have been made easier than ever, while relationships and artist social networks affect who they will and won’t work with based on their opinions and experiences with those individuals (including record CEO’s, cough cough).
The combination of old and new allow the player to leave their own unique mark on the game's world. Whether you start off with a small indie label, or begin big with an already established international label, you truly feel like you’re running an empire as you start to expand and control several labels and recording studios.
Though if rapid expansion and heading a large WMG type company isn’t your preferred playstyle, don’t worry. Because Music Wars Empire is a sandbox sim, you get to play at your own style and pace. So indie purists, stay small and independant if you choose, or just expand as you feel comfortable.
Music Wars Empire is an ambitious and successful attempt to simulate the music industry. If you’re not a fan of text based games - like Football Manager, Hollywood Mogul, or Showtime - then this game clearly isn’t for you. But if you are a fan of the genre, or are interested in a record label/music industry sim, you can do no better than Music Wars Empire.

As a big fan of Music Wars Rebirth and text-based sims in general, I've been pretty excited for this game for a while now. After an hour or so of playing I have to say I'm pleased with the game so far. It's early yet and my opinion can change, but I like the changes I see from MWR -- that said, I largely skipped MWR2 because of bugs involved with modding near the beginning of its lifespan, so I don't really know which features are completely new here.
There are a few gripes I have with the game, though. The lack of fullscreen is pretty detrimental to the overall experience, which is a huge shame. I find it to be an odd design choice in 2016. Also, the outdated DRM is rather curious as well, but I can forgive this because the game designer has eliminated the machine activation limitation due to the negative response to this choice. Unfortunately the DRM seems to cause Steam to count the game as "running" even after you exit, which is a moderate annoyance. The pictures for all of the artists in the game, seen in screen shots, do not show up in my game at all.
I also think there are some balancing issues that definitely need a second look. For example, I put a decent amount of money into an unknown artist's first single. It bombed, which isn't too surprising, but I then released a rather successful music video for the song which is seeing about a million views a week while the single itself is selling about 4 copies a week with no signs of growth. The exposure from a popular music video would definitely have a much larger impact on a single's success but that doesn't seem apparent.
This is just my early feeling toward the game and that can easily change with updates. In the future, I'd like to see some progress made toward correcting these issues as well as ensuring that mods work as painlessly as possible. I like simming really long games and to have MWR2 crash constantly after adding a few acts to the game was rather disheartening (my reason for sticking to MWR1). Overall I feel pretty positive toward the experience so far and I'm optimistic toward the future of the game.

I have played every souls game for at least 100 hours each and I must say this game lives up to the quality I've come to expect. All the core mechanics are here: Range, melee, magic builds and hybrids, stamina management, equipment/weight management, fashion, and my beloved parrying to name a few so I felt right at home. I love the tweaks they made to this system as well, you get 2 weapon sets to adjust, and when one is equipped, the other doesn't effect your weight. Also parrying animations are legit and can distance other opponents. There are different combos you can perform from standard X, X, X ground combo to X,Y,(X or Y repeated) air combos. Using magic is really satisfying as well in my experience whether you need to zone or distance yourself.
Initially I didn't feel very drawn in to the world until I discovered that this game has something no other souls game has. Something I hold very dear to my heart and is becoming harder to find in any games these days. That thing is local co op. I had already played an hour before my older brother picked up the sticks and joined me, so I made a new mage/dex build while he went holy knight. We have been hooked ever since, I love how dynamic our methods in fighting can become as we increase our abilities to crush our foes. There is just nothing like playing along side a sibling or good friend in a game that requires both of you to always be on your toes. It is harder with two people and that is just the way we want it.
Now I haven't been exposed to Metroid or Castlevania so I can't use those as reference, but I love the way maps are designed for platforming, moving up and down, it all feels really smooth. Exploration is great as your field of view won't show you everything and you never know what you will find next. If my brother would die late in a stage's progression, I would have to make a choice to either return to a sanctuary and revive him or keep moving forward hoping I find a new one. Sometimes I found one, sometimes I came across a boss who wanted nothing more than to rip me to shreds. Oh and bosses have more than 1 phase like Dark Souls 3/Bloodborne.
All in all I highly recommend this game co op or not, it makes you work for success, and feel like a total badass while you do it. We are still learning a lot and have a long way to go, and I can definitely see the replay value this game has to offer. I give Salt and Sanctuary 3 thumbs up, 5 gold stars, and a burrito from your favorite mexican restaurant.

On the surface Mercenary Kings is the regrettable result of a one night stand between Metal Slug and Scott Pilgrim (because at least having conceptual intercourse with a video game franchise is easier than dealing with Ramona's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t), but MK really does rise to the occasion to try and set itself apart from its lineage with a great deal of ambition and love from its creators. If there is a fault to be had with MK is that it may be too ambitious.
Naturally, the first thing you notice about MK is the look of it, and anyone worth their government-provided meat-substitute recognizes the style as, as I said before, Metal Slug (in terms of tone and atmosphere) and Scott Pilgrim (in terms of art style and visual humor). For many, this acts as a barrier to keep them from wanting to try the game and instead ridicule it for being "too much like a Metal Slug rip off!" when in fact that couldn't be further from the truth, but more on that later. The art style is incredibly charming and fun, despite taking place on a militarized island populated with murderous COBRA rejects. Sadly, and this is where part of the over ambition comes into play, the environments repeat themselves a lot, a whole lot. This is not so much a fault of the level designs, but more due to the fact that you will play different (i.e. different objectives every now and then) missions in the same level over and over until you manage to advance in rank. If the level art was a tad more detailed and beautiful this would be forgivable but after so many hours it gets bland.
Sound is nothing really to complain about or praise, but it gets the job done. Simple, appropriate, though like the art it can get repetitive as you listen to the same level music over and over and over again.
Naturally the most important bit of information you want to know is "how does it play?" While some screenshots and/or videos may have led you to believe it plays like Metal Slug, it really doesn't all that much. MS had you going through a linear, left-to-right, level with occasional height changes. MK's maps are far more complex, the map probably even confusing some at first with the interwoven connecting paths, and should be looked at more like a Castlevania map - large and sprawling, with hidden alcoves, optional boss rooms, etc. You'll be jumping around a lot, ascending to reach a goal or carefully descending to avoid hazards. I would say it feels a lot like Spelunky in its controls, but how easily you move is dependant on what you have equipped.
The real meat and potatoes of this game are the guns. You collect materials from fallen enemies and found crates and use these resources, and money garned from completing missions, to craft components for your gun. Here is where the game really shines, as it doesn't restrict which part can go with what component, and if you want to try and make a terribad gun, you're just as able to as you are to make an amazing gun. The elements of any gun really work toward tailoring to your preferred method of runnin' and gunnin'. You could take a huge gun with tons of stopping power and a low clip, or you can take a smaller, faster gun so you can dodge enemy attacks more easily. Elemental upgrades for bullets allow you to gain an advantage or disadvantage against a given enemy, and many parts take advantage of the art style by looking silly, fun, or just plain ♥♥♥♥ing awesome.
Really, it's the gun crafting and shooting that keep this game from feeling too tedious (at first). However, as time drags on, you find yourself grinding levels for materials and money, fighting the same boss over and over, collecting X of that and Y of this, killing some of these and more of those. Honestly, if your main gripe with MMOs are the fetch/mob kill quests, this game may not be for you.
The co-operative play really helps keep this game feeling fun, as your friends can split up and explore are area to finish the mission faster or you can operate as a time with one being the fast shooter for smaller enemies and attracting the attention of big ones while the other player with the bigger, slower, guns take the kill shot. If you have some friends who are interested in this game and you think they would enjoy the experience with you, this is not a bad grab.
There are other crafting elements in this game, allowing you to customize your tent interior, or create body mods to gain a variety of pros and cons (like increased drop rate, faster speed, etc.), and meals before a mission to give you a nice HP stat boost.
Overall, this game is fun, make no mistake, but it feels tired at about 50% (it's a very long game, surprisingly), and that's why its ambition is its downfall. The creators tried to do too much and ended up spreading their efforts too thin, giving us plenty of features but no major depth to any of them (gun crafting excluded). Had they taken some more development time to craft some more levels, think up better mission objectives, or polish up the scenery it would have been a perfect game.
Still, I can still recommend it to anyone who enjoys action/platformers with a Metal Slug/Metroidvania/Spelunky/Scott Pilgrim heritage, though maybe wait for it to go on sale for around $10, at most.

I will preface this review with three questions, and if the answer is "Yes" to any of these questions then I suggest you give Mortal Online a long hard look; if you say "Yes" to all of these questions then stop reading this start downloading Mortal Online!
--------------------
Questions:
1.  Are you tired and/or burnt out on all the MMORPGs out, or coming out, on the market?
2.  Do you want to play a game where EVERYTHING you do is an accomplishment and reinvigorates that sense of discovery you had when you played your first MMORPG?
3.  Does the idea of an open loot system (you lose everything you are carrying when you die) fill you with a sense of excitement and adventure?
--------------------
Overview
Mortal Online is a Fantasy Sandbox MMORPG that takes familiar elements from games like Ultima Online and Runescape, and takes them to a whole new level.  The entire game is played in first-person, and there is no functionality to change the view to third-person.  All combat and actions within the game are based off of targeting with your reticle, so if you want to hit a boar in the head then you need to aim for it's head.  Character progression is based on skill points rather than levels, and you only have so many skill points to use.  You aren't safe anywhere, not even in cities, so always be on your guard, but don't turn into a jerk, just be wary.
--------------------
Skills
Skills are broken down into a ton of different categories that are based on Parent and Child relationships, so a player would need to learn Armor Crafting (to a certain skill level) before he/she can learn Soft Armor Crafting.  Many skills you can begin learning just by attempting to do them, such as chopping down a tree or mining for ore, but other skills will need to be learned by reading skill books.  Skill books can be obtained from Libraries (for a price) or from the Auction House, players can begin reading these (some can take 8 hours or more) and the reading timer will continue to countdown when the player logs off.
I mentioned that you have a finite number of skill points to use, and in the beginning, you will burn through over half of these pretty quickly.  Don't panic!  You can lock skills that you don't want to increase anymore and you can even decrease skills you aren't going to use to get the skill points back to use on something else.  This can be confusing at first, but this really allows the player total freedom in choosing what their character does without letting characters become masters of everything at once.
--------------------
Combat
Combat is based on using your aiming reticle and blocking or dodging the attacks of your enemies.  I haven't done much of this yet, besides slaughtering herds of innocent pigs, but I think it is very engaging, sort of a melding between Skyrim and Mount & Blade combat, but better.
--------------------
Magic
No comment at all on this, but it is very in depth, with required components for spells.  Healing magic, for instance, can require water.
--------------------
Crafting
The crafting in this game is intense.  I repeat: the crafting in this game is INTENSE.  There are spreadsheets and emulators online that help players calculate the required components to create other components to finally (maybe) create the item they want to create.  There is more than one way to make a particular piece of armor, and some components will make the end item heavier or cooler etc.  I think this is an amazing part of the game, but it is not for the faint of heart.
--------------------
PvP
Mortal Online works on a flagging system.  Here is the breakdown:
Fledgling: Yellow
Innocent: Blue
Criminal: Grey
Murderer: Red
Hidden Criminal: Grey with Blue Stripe
Basically, if you do something negative to someone then you will be flagged Grey, unless that person was already Grey.  The flagging system is one of the most important parts of MO to understand, so check out this Beginner's Guide for more information :
.
--------------------
Conclusion
Mortal Online is a really in-depth game, but it is most certainly not for the casual player, and I don't mean the time-casual player, but the player that is more instant gratification.  If you want your cake and eat it too then this game is not for you, but if you want to bake your cake, eat some of your cake, then sneak around to hide your cake in the bank until you can share it with your guild mates then this game is for you!
You can try the game for free, and all F2P Accounts can use skills up to skill level 60.  What that means is that you can raise your skills above skill level 60, but you can only use the skill at skill level 60.  I highly recommend subscribing to the game if you are 8 hours in and enjoying it.  The subscription costs less than other MMORPGs, and it is well worth it to support such an awesome game.
--------------------
Grimstein's Personal Tips
1.  Buy the Reading Skill Book (yes, that's an actual skill book) and begin reading that right away.  That will allow you to read other skill books more efficiently.
2.  Find a Guild on the official MO forums.
3.  Get out of the starting city.
4.  Turn up your graphics and other options as high as you can.
5.  Only keep what you immediately need on you.  Bank your money until you need to buy something, and keep your skill books in the bank until you want to start reading them.
6.  If you are going on a long journey, such as to join up with your new guild, bring along some food and bring everything you can with you.  Banks are localized, and if you store something in Tindrem, you will have to go back to Tindrem to get it.
--------------------
I hope my review helped you make an informed decision.  There is so much more to Mortal Online than I touched upon in this review, but I hope it gives you a taste of what's in store if you play.  Good luck, and I hope to see you in Nave!
Evris Grimstein

I am not a fan of topdown shooters, maybe its because I suck at them but 12 is Better Than 6 was one of the most enjoyable indie games I've played for a long while. It is tense, creative and offers a good challenge which you can approach in many different ways.
Pros:
- Incredible soundtrack. It is excellent, fits the game perfectly and gets you going all the time.
- Manual bolting and reloads add so much depth to gunplay thus makes the game rise above the other topdown shooters.
- Story. It does not have so much depth and certainly not a piece of high literature but it shows that developers have analyzed the tropes of western genre thoroughly and executed the story with a good sense of humor.
- All the weapons feel unique and your weapon of choice impacts your gameplay greatly, which makes more than one playthrough a viable option. Especially bow and shovel work quite unexpectedly well which is a nice change from the usual guns (revolver, rifle, shotgun)
- Upgrades are well thought of and they all serve a good purpose, unlike filler upgrades in many other shooters.
- I am not an expert on topdown shooters but stealth being a viable option most of the time is pretty good.
- When talking about stealth of this game, I have to mention the knife. The way they designed the knife is amazing. If the enemy is unaware of you, you will kill him with one knife hit if you are close enough to the head and two hits if you are a bit far. If the enemy noticed you, you have to get behind his back and it will take four hits to kill while front hits won't do any damage. Simple details like this greatly increases production value of the game
- You have to manage your ammo and know when to reload.
Cons:
- A few minor bugs which usually causes you to get stuck in a place, but it is nothing to worry about.
- Tutorial part is not very good, while it teaches you most of the basics, I did not understand how to reload and ammo count for a while.
- A few random chatboxes were not translated into English and were in Russian but I have encountered this for twice, so it's ignorable.
- Game has enough content for its price, but a co-op mode and workshop support for user made levels (which should be easy enough I'd guess as the dev made levels seem to have include a small amount of assets) could have increased the longevity of the game.
I think 12 is Better Than 6 is a must play for everyone in its current state, therefore I shall give a final score of 8/10.

Well. I finally played through the game after owning it for 4 years.
It's okay for a FPS. The whole landscape and atmosphere of the game is very nice and laid out fairly well. However, there's so much of the map that's not used and the rewards for exploring aren't really worth it.
Weapons, they entertaining enough to give you a variety of what to use against different targets. I really liked the Pop Rocket ammo for the shotgun. One shot most targets that aren't armored. The ones that do have armor it can take upwards of 6-8 rounds. This is when I'd just switch to my rocket launcher or sniper rifle.
The racing aspect of the game feels forced up on you - making you do a couple of races to at least acquire newer vehicles. I don't think it was well built into the story to make it feel like natural progress through the game.
The side quest jobs never really presented any kind of real adventure. You usually just go about doing the same type of things - drive to a location, get out on foot and shoot mutants or other bad guys. You complete the quest and turn it in to get a little cash for the most part. They're not necessary to do, especially if you pick up everything along the way as you move through the game, you should always have plenty of money to spend on weapons/ammo/ingredients for crafting.
The crafting part of the game is nice, it does add a little flavor to things. I really enjoyed crafting the advanced sentry bots. Spider bots basically, they shoot and jump and slice/stab at bad guys. They'll follow you around until you dismiss them (basically loot them), they die or you end up moving some place they just can't follow.
Overall it was an alright game. I wouldn't recommend this game as a must play, but it's decent enough to give most folks that enjoy a FPS some fun times.

is an extremely underrated game, and is definitely worth your consideration. It's another game where you find yourself exploring a post-apocalyptic wasteland performing missions for money and trying to survive— then wind up saving the world. In that sense, it feels a bit like a
game, but with a serious undertone and with realistic-style graphics. When you start to play it, though, you will find it definitely has the FPS experience of an
game.
It isn't an open-world game really in the true sense of the meaning. But it isn't exactly forcing you from one level to the next, either. I personally found the world immersive and the story engaging. The narrative is well written, even if it relies heavily on established clichés. And I thought the graphics were quite nice; very, very nice actually— there was several times I found myself taking a moment to look around at the scenery and grab screenshots. The gorgeous visuals and interesting narrative establish an undeniably captivating presentation.
As far as gameplay is concerned: the mechanics and controls were solid, and the combat is exciting.  There is a decent amount of gun and enemy variety, but there definitely could be more. It’s enough to keep you interested, but it is certainly somewhat limited. The desire to explore more beautiful landscapes and to finish the interesting story will keep you intrigued, though, if you find yourself growing bored with the combat in the later stages of the campaign. It is certainly a decently sized game. And there are sidequests and minigames that are pretty fun if you are into achievements and extras.
Besides the campaign, there is a coop multiplayer mode where you can clear dungeons with a friend. There are a good number of missions to beat and they tie into the main campaign as little background stories of NPCs and locations. It is quite fun, actually, and adds a very welcome bonus layer of content.
Also, there is a racing multiplayer mode (for which I had trouble finding games, to be honest). I was able to find a few games with a low amount of people— but it wasn't living up to its full potential. It matters little in the long run, as the rest of the game is well worth it.
And so: if you are looking for a story-driven, atmospheric, and action-packed FPS game with a high standard of quality, you would be wise to give
some consideration.

This is a really cool game with an interesting theme and fun combat however there are two main problems I have with it, so i'm just going to jump straight to them to get them out of the way;
1. Not enough players. I know this isnt the devs fault but its really sad the lack of playerbase you can pretty only much play multiplayer on certain days when there is a lot of people on or unless you find enough of your own friends to play with. Want to play during an oddball hour or day? Tough luck because no one will be on. To fix this problem, buy some copies for your friends! Seriously its a good game just not enough people play it.
2. Optimization isn't too great. It isnt the worst but at the same time its far from the best either. My specs are a good amount over minimum and it ran horrible at medium settings im talking not even a solid 15 fps. I had to turn my resolution down super low to get a somewhat decent framerate suitable in fast pace combat. With that being said some more optimization to the game would be nice. For example shadows and anti aliasing you can only turn to low. In my opinion there should be an option to turn it off entirely so those of us with lower specs can turn off something that we arent going to use without having to sacrifice stuff we will use.
Now that I have that out of the way I want to go over the positives
1. Good maps although the only problem I have with them is they aren't too complex or anything but at the same time I would rather have a simpiler map than one thats complex and confusing
2. Classes are nice and each one is unique from the next. A lot of class based games classes can feel almost copy and pasted while I feel like the classes in here are pretty well balanced and diverse
3. Lastly the combat is really cool. You have a basic attack, heavy attack and a block. That isn't including your abilites of the class you are playing. Its a cool system along with a shield break system so unlike other games with shields where you have people coward behind it the whole time *cough cough Chivalry cough* it adds a basic defense for a couple off attacks but nothing more to make it too OP. A basic attack and a heavy attack mean you alternate between them based on the situation you're in. I like it better than what most games have of just having one generic attack because it means you have to select the type of attack depeding on the factors of the situation which makes combat feel a little more varied. And most importantly of all the class abilities are fun to use and can help turn the tides of battle. And all of the classes abilities work really well together which encourages teamwork.
Overall its a really good game although as a heads up it may seem to some a bit lacking in content in terms of the classes and maps but I think there is enough to keep a person entertained for a while and also at the same time it is early access so im not too bothered by the limited amount of classes and maps as im sure there are more to come. Now in terms of the price I would say 10$ is pretty good but if you get it on sale like I did I would say its an absolute steal. I genuinely think this game has an awesome future. If you were to take the graphics and class system of TF2 along with the ability system of DOTA 2 where each class has unique attacks you would get this game. But really buy it for some friends to fill up the player base and I can promise you, you'll have a lot of fun.

From the day Evolve came out I was excited to try it and play. Unfortunately due to reviews while it was pay to play I only played the original beta. What other game pits players against a hulking all powerful monster? The only other one is Monster Hunter and the monsters are all controlled by A.I. Despite a couple of things, this is purely based on how skilled you are as a monster and as a team. If you have a skilled team and a bad monster, the team will win. If you have a bad team and a skilled monster then the monster will destroy the team. The best matches obviously then are the ones with good teams and a clever/skilled monster. I've had a couple of close games where we've lost or where we've won.
Again, like Monster Hunter, there isn' really any story at all. This is a 'kill or be killed' game. 4 hunters try and kill the monster for sport, food and research (from what I've gathered) and the monster does what it needs to to survive. Eat, evolve and kill all of the hunters or destroy the power relay.
Evolve's mechanics work really nicely as any class or monster. Each character of each class and monster has his/her own strengths, weaknesses and abilities. Unfortunately, some of the monsters can really be overpowered with their skills despite the downside to taking more damage and/or having less health and shields and they need to be fixed. According to other players though, it sounds like when the weekly rotation allows you to freely play as said monsters it will be unplayable (because of the broken monsters) or unlikely that you will win as the hunters. The Kraken is very tough but it is still possible to take him down with a good team. DO NOT even bother trying to kill the Wraith. The Wraith is virtually impossible to defeat because of its speed and overpowered abilities. While hunting for the monster you need to watch out for man eating plants and hostile animals. Killing certain animals as either the hunters or the monster can grant you useful temporary perks. But you can only use one at a time.
The graphics are beautiful and the sound is right on point. You really feel like a hunter trying to listen for monster activity and feel like a monster running around and stomping like Godzilla. Monster smelling is subtle and not overdone. Every gun sounds like how they should and even when you aren't directly communicating your character will shout things out for the others to hear what you're doing from time to time.
Evolve always had potential and despite some clear unbalances at times this will always be one of my favorites due to how unique the game is. I really hope Turtle Rock Studios steps up and makes the adjustments the game clearly needs. But for being in free to play beta? Really impressive so far. I recommend giving it a try even if you think you won't like it. What can you lose? It's free now.

I am checking yes because of the thought that went into the game and the potential it holds.  As of now, it is fun for a few hours as you figure out the mechanics (there is no tutorial), but after that it is tedious and impossible.  It is in dire need of tuning, which I will address below, but as stated above, I believe there is potential here for a fun management sim, especially if modding is allowed which it appears to be. However, right now the game is just not there.
There are a few points that are easily correctable that I believe would make the game orders of magnitude better.
First, the constant goals popping up with unrealistic timeframes need to be fixed. Maybe there is an option to turn them off that I missed. When you start the game as a new independent label, and then have 12 weeks to produce a #1 album in the USA… you’re not going to make it.  This in turn causes your reputation to go down, which makes it even harder to sign acts, and that leads me to my second point.
Second, there needs to be some tuning on the act signing / talent searching.  I understand that you should not be able to sign Justin Beiber (he sells a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of records) when you just start your label, but if you spend 9 weeks and $2,000,000+ on a talent search; there should be a chance for you to uncover a star.  I ran several talent searches and the results were formulaic.  Very few artists excelled in more than 2 areas. If they were good singers and had sex appeal, they weren’t mainstream.  If they were mainstream and had sex appeal, they couldn’t sing, etc…
Finally, and this is by no means the end of my list of corrections I would like to see but it is the end of this list, there really needs to be some corrections made to the double booking.  If you hire a manager and then turn around and book a tour for an act being managed, the manager can then book a tour on top of yours.  At one point I had an artist playing in Toronto and Los Angeles on the same day. Obviously this is logistically feasible, but it is not something that would be allowed to happen in real life.
Minor points, better feedback on what your artists and doing/accomplishing (ticket and record sales) on the home screen would be nice; hints or advice or even questions from your staff would be nice.  I have many more things I could list, but I am doubtful the developer will read this, so I will stop now.

Mortal Online is one of the most misunderstood and underappreciated gems in the world of video gaming.
I say this because there are those who have played this game for quite a number of years now and have come to love it, and I am one of them. If you want depth, freedom and complexity in a truly hardcore and unforgiving world, there isn’t another title out there like it that I know of.
My hours played here on Steam may be few, but that's because I've only recently switched to playing the game through Steam instead of the old launcher. I first played this game way back in 2010 then left for the most part, until September 2013 when I returned for good and have been playing it ever since as my preferred MMORPG over all others.
At first glance, this game may not seem like much, but once you’ve earned a decent amount of gold, crafted a set of gear for yourself, made a few friends and seen the world outside Tindrem city, you begin to appreciate just how vast and intricate this game really is. Then you realise that you’ve only just scratched the surface; there is the player-driven economy, guilds and individual players going about their business, and much more.
You can be any character you want, and pursue whatever activity you wish. If you’ve ever played The Elder Scrolls or Ultima Online, you’ll know exactly what I’m talking about. There are no traditional quest hubs that have you moving from one region to the next as you level up. There are, however, plenty of players who may have something that needs done or need help with, and if you’re interested then you can lend your services and make your mark in the world in a meaningful way. That is just one of the myriad of ways you can keep yourself busy and occupied, all it takes is a little imagination and creative thinking. Even after playing this game for over three years, every time I login there is always something for me to do.
I could keep writing a long review but it would probably be best if I said that this game is not for the faint-hearted or those who don’t know how a sandbox game is meant to be played. If you’ve never seen this game in all its glory, you owe it to yourself to give it a try. Create a free account and play the unlimited free trial for as long as you want, then upgrade to premium if you like what you see.

Defense Grid has everything that you might not expect from a tower defense game: original gameplay, a polished interface, great artwork and visuals, and even some nice voice acting. It also has the things that you probably would expect, like an assortment of different towers that may be upgraded, different types of enemies to defend against, and a variety of levels in which to try out particular strategies.
In Defense Grid, you must defend your planet from an old, forgotten enemy. You take control of a dormant defense grid to fend off these alien invaders. Unlike many other tower defense games, the goal is not simply to stop the enemies from reaching the end of their path. Rather, you must prevent the aliens from stealing your power cores, which reside in a special housing. Thus each alien will walk from a starting point to the power core housing, and then to the exit. In many levels you have the option of shaping the aliens' paths by placing towers in their way.
The cores provide an interesting addition to the gameplay. If an alien carrying a stolen core is killed, the core will slowly float back to its housing unless it gets intercepted by another alien. Keeping your cores in their housing allows you to collect additional "interest" on your resources, which can be used to buy and upgrade more towers. A particular core can trade hands many times, so even with a long and deadly path of towers, a large enough swarm of aliens will manage to get a core through if you aren't careful. You only need to keep one core protected to win a particular level, but saving all of the cores is necessary to get a silver or gold medal and a high score.
The game features 10 different types of towers, 15 types of enemies, and 20 levels. There are also a number of DLC packs which offer additional levels. Each level also has a number of challenge modes which can be unlocked. These challenges often mix up the gameplay, such as by restricting which types of towers you may buy, or by altering the aliens' direction, and so on.
But the most striking feature of the game is its presentation. Tower defense veterans may be used to playing Flash games with crude graphics in their web browsers, but Defense Grid's production values are comparable to most other high quality commercial games. The graphics, sound, interface, and level design were all executed very well, and there is enough content to last quite a few hours. The plot is fairly minimal, but it features a main character who has a surprising level of personality.
You really shouldn't miss this one. Defense Grid offers the best of tower defense, whether you're new to the genre or an already avid fan. I highly recommend it.

As tower defense goes, this game generally follows the standard layout/structure (bullets/fire/slow/mortar/missiles). They throw in some interesting ideas of what towers can do (sniper/tesla/command). Unfortunately there are entire levels where you never want nor need most of them - a real waste of options and menu space.
Sadly, the gameplay grinds along at what can only be described as "inexorable". Pacing was not a high point of this game's design, evidently. Waves of enemies came and went, but all I really wanted the entire game was a speed toggle instead of having to hold down a key to accelerate gamespeed. I really only looked forward to getting it over with, by the time each level was finished.
Level design was interesting but quickly became too big and too bulky. Getting to the end of ten minutes of planning out and building a massive gauntlet, just to find that a single unit can still make it through, was met with dread instead of a curiosity or anticipation. There is little room for error in most of the levels - if you want a good score, that is. Placing a tower that blocked unit pathing was allowed and suddenly they could just walk through your towers with no ill effect. Lastly, fine-tuning the towers (with upgrades) was never needed or necessary - new towers are just better and there is always room for more towers.
The final flaw was that each level was far too isolated, lending to a disruptive lack of cohesion in the story. Lost a core (life/hitpoint)? It'll be back in the next level! Lots of resources at the end of one level? Too bad, they're gone! There was great opportunity to build a bank&store system with persistence in campaign, but they obviously missed those chances.
The game has some intriguing ideas and some fun DLC (GLADoS content is always good!), but they introduce an obnoxious relay/replace gameplay mechanic that only serves to frustrate and annoy. In summary, the game under-delivers on the core elements of tower defense and underwhelms with its thinly-veiled attempts at innovating on this genre. I cannot give this game a recommendation rating, but it's worth throwing a couple of bucks at it (Steam sales! Woo!) just for the story mode and a single playthrough.

I'm finally getting round to my review for Europa Universalis IV (EU4). Many may be suprised to see that I am not, in-fact, recommending this game. No doubt this review will receive criticism, I can completely understand why. This game is dearly beloved by the Paradox community and is, without a doubt, the most played and most popular game of the franchise. The brutal, unavoidable truth is that, despite the things I am going to say in this review, if you haven't purchased this game and are contemplating it, you will probably enjoy it. The game does a lot right, specifically the way that it juggles war and diplomacy, and I would make the argument that EU4 is the epitome of grand strategy gaming. However, this review is not a pandering of the mass opinion. Rather, I am going to attempt to explain how I see the game in the hope that anyone like myself doesn't waste their money on something they will come to dislike.
EU4 does little wrong as a standalone game. It does what it says on the tin and it does it well. The issue comes with the wider picture. If this is your first venture into grand strategy games of any kind, especially Paradox grand strategy games, then purchase EU4. It is sweet and simple. To more experienced strategy gamers, on the contrary, EU4 sees its first onion right here.
The game is too easy.
Not that its so easy that you could achieve world domination on your first playthrough, mind you. Rather, what I mean by describing it as too easy is that the game is too simple - there isn't enough to do - and all of the difficulties are uncontrollable random events. Other games - its strategy brethen in particular - don't have this issue. Whilst random events do occasionally come in to shake things up, the emphasis is on the strategy, the methods you employ to improve your scenario and the risk factors involved in making these decisions. Other strategy games tend to work like an echo chamber. Crusader Kings 2 (full review on my profile), another Paradox grand strategy game, is a perfect example of this. When a random event occurs that hinders you - or when you employ a risky strategy that fails - you could lose everything. Your kingdom could collapse, you could go into serious debt and you might even be killed, whittling your dynasty down to the imbecilic cousins you've spent years trying to hide. However, and this is where the magic is, the game isn't over. In CK2 you are perfectly capable - and I know because i've done it - of taking this depleted position and slowly and methodically scheming your way to the top, courtesy of intrigue, murder and sex. By placing so much emphasis on the personal motives and intrigue, CK2 does as good a job as The Godfather or House of Cards. CK2 encourages you to fail and rewards you when you do. Success in Crusader Kings 2 makes the game harder - with far more internal threats - whilst failure motivates you to regain everything you've lost. Europa Universalis simply can't do this. It's so black and white. When you fail, if you truly fail, it's game over and when you succeed you are unstoppable. This isn't challenging and it isn't fun. It's simply a poorly made difficulty slider. The fact that EU4 lacks the political intrigue and threats of other strategy games means that its entire focus is on the military. It's a game about blobbing and colouring the map. There's nothing wrong with this, but it makes it easy and simple. the fact that it is entirely reliant on dice roll - quite literally - with two armies clashing and the winner being decided by randomly generated numeric values, means that it isn't a strategy game. It's gambling.
Strategy, by definition, is the art of creatively overcoming certain circumstances. When you have a game that presents either one nation being vastly superior to another, or, when the two are on equal footing the victor being decided by the roll of a dice, there is no strategy involved. It is luck and chance, and this makes Europea Universalis IV simple and easy.
Playing as a major nation, such as France, Austria or England, makes it impossible to genuinely be strategically outmanouvred. You will almost always have the larger army, the stronger economy, the better technology. You are fighting a downhill battle and the only things that can really defeat you are things out of your control - random events or coalitions. It's like a train without brakes - it ploughs through almost everything and the only thing to challenge it is when something else comes along and forces it off the tracks. When did this become strategy?
Truly, this game is akin to a Total War campaign where you only auto-resolve battles.
The natural opposition to what i'm saying is that you should play a more difficult nation - an OPM or technologically inferior state - however, even then it's not strategic. You only have one way to go: up. It's a slow grind, don't get me wrong, and you will often fail. However, the fact that your success as an OPM is based on a combination of good luck and slowly eating the bread crumbs until you expand large enough to steam roll, isn't tactical or strategic. It's just boring.
A strategy game should get harder as you progress - akin to what happens in CK2 - not easier. It is for these reasons that I cannot, in my right mind, recommend Europa Universalis IV.

I wouldn't recommend this title on its own unless you have a group to play it with. Allow me to explain a little further.
First off, this game is unfinished. I understand the devs apparently ran out of money and had too large a scope for this game. As a result the game literally just ends right where the story should be picking up the pace. Additionally, and maybe this is just me and my group, we found teh story to be thoroughly disjointed, confusing, and uninteresting overall. Also the humor attempts mostly fall flat througout the game.
The addition of the 3rd dimension doesn't add to the game. it creates navigation problems as endless pits lay just offscreen as you attempt to explore to locate all the "trineangles" in a level. It confuses the distinction between your characters and the world they can interact with with really expanding the gameplay in any meaningful way.
The game is also loaded with bugs, none we game breaking in my case but enemies would freeze in place or glitch around the screen. Individuals loaded into levels before the level and spawned inside the floor unable to move. Players passed through walls regularly and objects in the world behaved in uncontrolled and unpredictable ways.
All of the characters have been changed for the worse from the previous installment. Pontius has lost his hammer and magnetic shield, Amadeus can only summon a single box at a time and it always spawns over his head, and Zoya has been weakened (in this case she was far too powerful in Trine 2 but they made her feel almost pointless now Trine 3) Additionally all the ability unlocks and upgrades have been removed, the character you are at the beginning is the character you will be at the end. Removing any sense of progression.
The gameplay feels much less fluid than in the previous installments, partially due to limiting what each character can do, and reducing the impact each action has by blurring the distinction between your interactions and the environment on a canvas of highly saturated colors. TL:DR Over all, great game, it's not perfect, but the Cadet version is worth its weight in gold. Very mod friendly. Runs fairly well, but towards the end it can slow down slightly.
If you are new to this series as I am, I would recommend it. The learning curve is REALLY addictive.

The base game is really fun and "balanaced", but it can get a bit stale after a while. Thankfully the workshop is full of things to change it up, or you can easily mod it yourself to fit your own needs.
It's worth the price in full. A lot of replay value.
There is some short commings however, mostly the AI.
AI is.. unreliable.. Your own generals have a tendency to "even out" the front line, so if your on the offence and your frontline is expanding, the AI will move units from one side of the front to the other side. So many troops are not utilized during the pushes.
Enemy AI tend to spam crap divisions, instead of focusing on keeping an even number of fair troops.
Difficulty isn't really all that effective either, it's mostly just buffs and a little more aggressive AI. Tactics, politics and diplomacy are rarely used efficiently.
The modding is also alittle restrictive, it's really tidy and easy to do, but you can't really do much to the AI except set priorities.
Nukes are a little underwhelming, alot of work with little pay off.
Over all, great game, it's not perfect, but the Cadet version is

Having been a fan of Paradox Interactive for a few years with Victoria and Hearts of Iron as my personal go to choices, it's nice to see a new HOI that isn't just endless and tedious micromanagement so you can focus on more than one thing. That being said, there are some drawbacks. The AI(like a lot of strategy games) suffers a lot especially late game. It doesn't know how to prioritize fronts and I have seen them just stack troops on their capital. It's still a great game and some of the problems have been fixed with recent patches. There's struggles with the game late game when the remaining nations have hundereds of divisions and factories and possibly thousands of planes. The naval system and air combat system are improved significantly from HOI3. The production system is both improved and in my opinion, in a way worse. You now see what factories and resources go where but at the same time you can't really do like the previous games and choose how much of your production goes to different things through the industrial capacity. In hoi3 you could choose what you wanted your production to go to like, upgrades and reinforcement, in 4, you can choose what division type you want to recieve upgrades first but you can't choose how much of the equipment gets stockpiled. All in all, HOI4 is a great hearts of iron game and I personally recommend it. The modding community has come out with great scenarios and improvements on their own and Paradox hasn't really completed the game (dlc /: .....). If you get the game and want something different for the game I would suggest the War to End All Wars mod or one of the modern day mods (there's several each with their own unique thing they bring. If you're a fan of HOI get it, if you're a Paradox fan get it, if you're looking to get into grand strategy games this one is easier to get into than the previous games without losing the the complexity.

Initially, the game concept appears to sound like a cross between skyrim and Mount & Blade, but it stops after you complete the tutorial area. At the very instant you finish the tutorial you are introduced to the wide open world that is known as Mortal Online.
Firstly it is worth mentioning that there is a small group of players that sit outside the gates of the tutorial city waiting for new, ill-equipped players to appear so they can gang up on you, overwhelm, and kill you within seconds. I did not discover this from experience as much as I had people scream at me not to exit the city because apparently a clan regularly camps the "noob city"
The community is helpful but at the same time rude and completely annoying. When I logged in the first thing I saw in the chatbox was about 6 people comparing the size of their character's junk, but we'll get onto that later. If you ever have the displeasure of hearing the barely functional speech option in the game, and manage to understand anything in the game aside from static, you will realize most of the players who are on this game are 12 years old or younger. Trust me, adults don't speak like the cast of Sesame street normally.
On to the real deal, game mechanics. It's a weird puzzle of interesting concepts that are executed in horrible ways. The game uses the unreal engine, which has given us rather excellent looking games such as Red Orchestra 2 and Killing Floor, among many others. Unfortunately, the graphics in this game are far more akin to one of the games I compare it to, Mount and Blade, but lack all the features that make Mount and Blade interesting. The game's combat mechanics are more similar to Chivalry and Mount and Blade, but unlike both of those games, come off as clunky and broken in many cases, with the so-called emphasis on enemy weak points being completely pointless because striking the head of the enemy always does the most damage anyway. But this is a MMORPG, surely there are better features in it than just the combat and graphics? The game has interesting movement animations, and is completely in first person, but not immersive enough to become interesting. Permadeath isn't actually permadeath, it's just generalized respawn timers and a "spirit realm" that offers absolutely nothing to do while you wait.
How do you die? well that's simple. Steal in front of a guard and he instantly hits you with a lightning bolt which will kill you no matter what you have. I tested this theory by grinding undead corpse heads until I had the best armor available, and he still kills you in 2 hits. He hits instantly, and there is no way of blocking magic explained in the tutorial.
RPG mechanics? You learn new skills by reading books, they give you a starter book to read after you finish the tutorial. It takes 6 days real time to read the book, and there is no way of speeding up the process. There are features that are locked including max skills for "paying" players.
I left the game before even trying to do real PvP because the PvE in the game was already so horrifyingly bad that it felt appropriate to quit.
Never play this game, leave it to be one of the dead MMORPG games that fade into obscurity like the cancer they are.

This game is like the kid who got straight 'A's in school, knew all the answers to every test, then went to university, smoked too much pot and dropped out in the second term. In other words, it's a disappointing under-achiever. It looks very pretty (even though it's getting on a bit), and it provides the illusion of some sort of open world, but that's all it is. An illusion. You're ultimately just shuffling from room to room and looking at what's going on. Of course, "it's a corridor shooter by ID! That's the point!" You might say, but it's even disappointing in that regard. You have too much health, there's too much ammo, the enemies are too stupid and there is basically no way to actually lose the game.
I think I fell over about 3 times in total. And I mean "fell over" - I never actually died because you get a 2nd and 3rd chance through a "defibrillator unit" which wipes out enemies and revives you if you can manage to mash the E button at the sound prompt. And when I did fall over, it was because I couldn't be bothered using cover when I should have been. On top of the fact that you self-revive for no penalty, you get an endless supply of bandages that you can stuff down your throat to instantly restore your health. I used about 5 of those in the entire game, because it was just so easy. Of course, I was playing on normal, and I *could* have upped the difficulty (and I did for a while), but disappointment on top of disappointment, the higher difficultly levels just give the enemies more HP. This doesn't actually make the game difficult, it just makes every fight take longer and become not just easy but actively boring.
I think the actual worst part, and what left me with a sour enough taste in my mouth to leave a review, was the storyline and the ending. The game is hurtling along, introducting all sorts of characters, many of whom are absolutely brilliantly realised and fantastically animated, and then it just stops. Suddenly you're on the end mission, you're handed a minigun and told to go activate a satillite uplink in the enemy base. You do so, get a 15 second cut scene and that's the end. There's no boss fight, no challenge (because you just mow everything down with afore mentioned minigun) and you don't even meet the big bad leader of the Authority (the badguys). Seriously, you hear his voice, once, and that's it. You never even see him. There's absolutely no sense of closure, no sense that you've finished up the story, nothing. It just stops dead and gives you the credits.
I suppose I could also mention the races and vehicle combat. The races are ok. They're fun for about 30 minutes, but again way, way too easy and end up just a chore. This is compounded by the fact that the loading times are atrocious, so you spend almost as long waiting for the race to load as you do racing. Great. The vehicle combat exists. It's... there. That's about all you can say about it.
If you want a corridor shooter, go play Wolfenstein: New World Order. It's slightly longer, has almost the same story line, but is way more entertaining, occassionally actually difficult and has Nazis to murder. What more could you want?
If you've run out of everything else to play, and want to waste 7-10 hours clicking on bad guys, there are worse ways to spend your time than RAGE, but that's not exactly a recommendation, is it?

A game for anyone who likes history and grand strategy. You are basically the ruler of any country in the world from 1444 to 1820, and can colonize, build your empire, fight wars with your neighbours or even try to conquer the world. Countries have different difficulties and challenges - go on a conquering spree with the Ottomans, build a colonial trading empire with Portugal or simply just survive as Serbia or Byzantium.
People say it's hard to get in to, and the details of the game will likely take long time to pick up, I've not gotten the subtleties of the PU game or a horde World Conquest yet. The core of the game is basically the same as in EU1, when it came out around 2000: Conquer provinces to grow your empire. Pick a major nation for the first couple of runs, like France, Ottomans or Ming, it's a lot more forgiving. Also it's not really a multiplayer game although it is possible to do so, so the main goals are achievements and those you set yourself.
The DLCs adds a ton of new mechanics and content, but it's also the only real downside to the game. Paradox got a tendency to put some half-baked mechanics in them along a few good ones and they're likely gonna keep pumping them out at regular intervals. Basically it feels a bit like they're squeezing their loyal fans for all the cash they can, but me, I'll likely still be buying.

Trine 3 is an unfinished game. I want to make that clear imidiately.
The game is short (around 5-10 hours) and holds numerous bugs and issues which have not been resolved (at the time of this review), and lacks many components which would feel essential to some trine fans. I will state (my personal) positive and negative points on the current release of Trine 3:
Let's start with the positive side:
+ Story is enjoyable
+ 3D Elements take some getting used to, but are much more enjoyable (In my opinion)
+ Soundtrack is wonderful
+ Graphics are Gorgeous
+ Gameplay and story progress is smooth
Negatives:
- Story is Incomplete
- 3D elements may not be enjoyed by everyone
- Bugs are occasional but apparent
- There are (currently) NO forms of skill trees, talents, etc
- Game can feel dull, difficult, or too easy at times
All in all, the game is incomplete, this early release was to financially aid the development team so that they could finish the project.
Buy this if you think you'll genuinely enjoy what you see in the trailers (you won't be doing much more than that) or if you want to help the trine series.
If you want to read up on their post release response, you can find it here;

Playing thru trine 1 and 2 there was countless times where I reached a spot and thought 'how in the heck am I going to get up there.' And had to micro engineer my own path. Which was great! Glorified Confetti. the 2 only things it does: completely wreck the infrastructure (so far so good), and reduces national unity (the less national unity, the easier it is for a contry to give up, throw enough bombs at them and you'll turn a minor ocupation into a full surrender). And that's it. when in fact, it should do much much more; like: completely ravage the population (No, nuclear bombs don't affect the population, you read that right) and completely annihilate troops, again, no!... troops, ships, planes, they are not affected by nukes.
3: Although its a simple game, its slow (no, i dont have a bad PC) because the game is horribly optmized. And from what i understand from reddit, this is a common issue with paradox's games.
4: The game "ends" in 1948, however you can continue indefinitely (i read on reddit that one of the devs went as far as 1997). Nice (or so i thought). The game completely lacks a "late game" mechanics. such as a "Cold War" kind of confrontation, where you could, for instance, as germany, instead of invading UK, build a ginormous army and simply stare at them, watch them do the same and let the upkeep of their army eat their economy away (like what happened to USSR), or not (like the great US of A). There is no economy, no money, that has been replaced with the ammount of factories you can use for infrastructure and warfare, and that's bad, because not only of what i mentioned earlier (about the upkeep) but also that economy is a key part of war (read Sun Tzu and you'll understand). Also the technology reasearch tree simply end at 1950s technology. I mean, what the actual ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥, why would you allow the game to continue indefinitely if the technologies end at 1950. Here are a few suggestions: Space Program Research Tree, ICBMs research tree (Cold War escalation).
My last issue with the game:
5: Resource mechanics, you should be able to stock resources (rubber, oil, iron, etc...) also, and thei part is super easy, contact oil companies and search for the locations of oil basins and put that on the game. and, as time and technology progresses (more specifically: geophysical science) so does your knowledge of where oil basins exist (there are a lot of basins we know about today but they didnt know about in 1936, or they knew about it but had no idea how to get it out).
That's all, i know it sounds like a lot but this IS a a great strategy game, Blitzkrieg works perfectly, so thats a plus, there a lot of good things with this game, i stand by my initial rate: 7/10, could be better.

Tentative reccomendation that I waited a while to write until I was sure what I wanted to say:
My very first Paradox game was HOI3, which I loved. It launched me into Ricky, Rome (briefly), CK (briefly), EU3, Vicky2, CK2, EU4, Stellaris, and a few other things along the way. Finally we've come full circle at HOI4.
I like it, the base game's a bit underwhelming as someone who played a lot of HOI3, but the core mechanics are pretty good and there's room to grow. I love the focus trees, which really serve to differentiate some of the major powers. I hope that, given time, we'll see plenty more of those for more interesting minors, but I understand that's already the plan.  I really DO NOT like the simplified army-unit structure, I wish there were more layers of command structure, if not quite full HOI3-esque OOBs then something where I can see more actual leaders, because in all honesty I think having traits from your most senior commander affect individual units doesn't make sense since the actual leaders of those units probably would affect their behaviour more. I feel most of my complaints about the game center on this simplification of concepts present in HOI3, which admittedly was necessary since HOI3 was a beast to learn and master but even things like the "triangle of leaning Axis/Allied/Comintern" that made a LOT of sense are gone.
All those complaints considered, WW2 strategy games like this are harder to make long-term interesting than CK2 or EU4 or Stellaris for a very important reason: Over centuries of gameplay, wars start and end, and nations go on to different concepts or challenges. But for a game solely focused on WW2, that can be hard because the war has to be very detailed while also being simple enough to understand, as once that war starts it's a brutal fight to the end. And despite my complaints, this constant slugging-match feeling is where the game shines. The new battle-plan style army management is a real gem, as are more extensive conscription/economic options. Allocation of factories to specific production lines, something abstracted with IC in HOI3, is fully fleshed out here and makes for a MUCH more detailed logistical game, which again was a major issue with HOI3. I absolutely love needing to shift factories from tanks to planes and having a major loss of efficiency, which slowly ramps back up, it's much more realistic and engaging thing and really makes you need to plan out your production better. I really like the new division designer, which again allows for really easy organizational changes to your units. The air and naval systems, while simplified, are VASTLY improved because it was a real pain to manage most of this in HOI3, I usually assigned them to a random AI-controlled HQ and let them take care of it.
All of the above, on the balance, makes this a game worth playing. I expect they'll add plenty of flavor, new mechanics, and more, and tweak some of the more annoying stuff. Currently, it seems to have less development support than CK2 or EU4, but I expect this to change as those games start to reach their final buildout (or at least I hope they are, both have had more expansions than I could easily count), and that resources are shifted. Some of the things I really think the game needs are an in-depth espionage system, a more detailed nuclear/secret-weapon system, a lot more flavor, smarter unit AI, a national-focus & stratetgic AI that doesn't make stupid choices (oh, Finland is part of the Allies in 1939, well I guess I still better declare war on it, said no Soviet Union ever) that negate your strategic or diplomatic brillancy. I'd also like to see an extended postgame or pregame, and better peace conferences (Yalta and others being negotiated BEFORE the war's end, and the ensuing horse trading). And finally, something introduced late in HOI3 that wasn't fully fleshed-out, a resistance system that ties down larger numbers of units in a garrison format, there are so many different ways that could go.
Tl;dr: Needs more work, but pretty good and will get better as it's a newborn and PDS will alter it dramatically over the next 2-3 years. 7/10 at present, I expect it to go up with time.

This game is pretty bomb. And its a pretty one if you have anything approaching a classic gaming rig. It remids one of Oblivion, Achaea, and certainly Darklands, if you are old enough to know what that is. Sure the tutorial is weak, etc, etc. In an open, skill-driven world, multiplayer world it can be argued that this is an asset. Finish the initial tutorial to get a skill pack to suit the part of the game you are most curious about or you'll lose that opportunity for good. Your skills are capped in free mode, but there is plenty of room to master the basics. I chose a crafter skill pack and after one trash set of armor and goofing around for a few hours I went back and crafted decent entry level armor on my first try. Reading books to learn skills is VERY time consuming, so choose what to read carefully. There is even a "reading" skill. Just being able to use certain materials requires basic "lore" knowledge, so that would be a good start for crafting. A specific combat book on "avoiding knockdowns" will improve multiple skills and take forever to read, so stick with tiny gains in basic stuff so you can learn enough on your own to decide where to focus your reading time. I imagine this is a good plan for all similar games. Let me know if you have a better one.
