+++ Panzer Corps meets Warhammer 40k
- not as complex as pcorps

If you remember the old Warhammer hex-game "Final Liberation" -- I consider this game it's spiritual successor. Much like many games of it's ilk (just looking at screenshots should give you flashbacks to other games in the same vein) for those who enjoy the WH40k universe I call this a solid title. The game mechanics are fun, intuitive, and dare I say balanced (as balanced as any battle against an unending tide of Orks can be I suppose!) -- there is good voice acting and some real strategy to this strategy game -- for example I have needed to make choices such as bottlenecking weak enemy units to cause jams at choke points, where just mowing down enemies simply paves the way for more powerful units to break through -- I've seen keen initiative and calculated risk win through over a slogging sweep and clear (which often plays into the hands of enemies that are merely just getting stronger the longer you take your time) -- the atmosphere is right, and the mechanics are fun -- and CHALLENGING. Can you afford to groom experienced core units, or must you cast them aside to make room for the cannon-fodder you'll need to meet the enemy throng? Will there be air support? Can you afford it? placement and choices for troops matter and remain meaningful from turn to turn -- and that is the ACID-TEST for a good turn based strategy game.
The cons? : I haven't played the whole initial campaign yet, but it seems like a lot of content is day-1 DLC, especially relating to space marines, which lets face it are the reason many people love WH40k so much in the first place. Maybe they'll make an appearance at the end of the basic content... maybe... but making us pay extra to enjoy some of the best things about the game from day 1 is typical of many of GW's franchises slimy bilking tactics (like space hulk having 80% of it's day 1 content pay to unlock, but that roast is for another post, or most notably how TOTAL WAR: WARHAMMER has CHAOS as a pre-order playble faction only -- that's as slimy and manipulative as it gets.
So in short -- a great game like so many GW inspired titles are, and like so many of those, they similiarly have some slimy microtransaction crap to make you regret loving them to some degree.
Bottom line, most games would be verbally evicerated for pulling that kind of crap -- but I'm having too much fun holding trenches with my Ogryn long enough for my Basilisk Artillery to break the Greenskin hordes as I pray to the machine spirits that my Leman Russ' will endure long enough to hold the line down. For the Emperor!

After spending hours of frustration in this game I finally beat the thing. Not at all a perfect game its rather lonely. The only way that I know of to play with other people is to have them in the room with you. Which is an impossibility. I couldn't find a guest option, if it even exists which I found no evidence off. Not being able to play with friends online hurts the game quite a bit.
The content is a mixed bag later on. Difficulty seems to be there mostly in leaps of faith. The community doesn't help much either as they'll tell you to jump just to troll you. Which early on I became sceptical of any help they might provite. Bosses range from painfully easy or extremely difficult. Do note that I played through the game as a squishy caster so it may very from play style to play style.
Magic was far too shallow for my tastes which honestly hurts a lot of games in my opinion. Salt and Sanctuary does away with having 4 virtually identical forms of magic just with different damage or a different color. Which was nice but didn't make up for how shallow it was.
Finding magic was an absolute nightmare. I had to look it up online to find a secret passage just to get my second spell. Since I started with a fireball. It shouldn't have been tucked away like that in the beginning. Having access to your first spells and a mage early on was key to my overall success and having novice spells tucked away on a secret place really harms this for me. Mind you, I don't mind questing for spells. I quite in joy it. But If I haven't even got my barrings in the game or know what I'm doing this is a rather poor decision.
The end of the game was built up to fairly well with the little bit of diolog scattered through the game. Although its not much of a surprise, if at all, I wont spoil it. The community of the game does that for you as soon as you step onto the beach. Although the note in a bottle are more Cryptic clues from the community, it did lead me to the final conclusion I would have come to on my own long before facing the last boss. Even with that gripe, I found the story to be just enough to keep me interested in the world we where in. Which is a plus.
Punishment for death seems a bit steap. Sure, losing all your salt to a boss and some gold seems okay, but I died 99% of the time to falling damage alone. The game is DARK! Not "OMG, Like that's gross and stuff. You know, like Scary", well it is, but dark as in "Where the heck am I going. I can't see a darn thing!". Which becomes frustrating because it artifically pads out the game far longer than It really needs to be. You might thing that falling to my death is my own fault. A few times it absolutely was... But not the majority of the time. Most the time it was just remembering when and where to leap. I ended up just ignoring large chunks of lost salt because It absolutely wasn't worth the effort to find the bat that'd spawn then spend the next 5 minutes trying to kill the darn thing because its everything you hate about bats in most 3D games only with a monsterous amount of health.
Salt is used for everything. Just about. Armor, weapons, leveling. Which si fine. Having something else outside of normal experience seems fine to me. I can't really complain about that, its a bit different but not in a bad way.
The skill tree is an absolute mess with a tone of redundancy. It looks sloppy and it feels sloppy. Even after I got used to it I found it to be more of a chore to work with than actually fun. The passive bonuses you get from it replace what would be called Attributes or stats in other games which pads out the leveling even further. I feel like there must have been a cleaner way to create it. Although its not as bad as other games which tie spells into their trees it still wasn't a very pleasent experience. At least it didn't fall into the same trap of trivializing old spells. But the game does that for you anyway. Which I guess its not fair of me to judge that on since most RPGs seem to trivialize your early spells.
Athetically, there really isn't much I can say about the game. It fits for the theme. Some of the bosses looked really interesting and a few of the enimes where legitamently terrifying. Though the ones that where usually threatening didn't look that intimidating and the ones that looked trully nightmare enducing where push overs. I didn't care for the over all design of the game, baring a few boss and enemy designs I found particularly interesting.
The game was Bundled into the Metroidvania summer sale package. And I can't honstly say this is a good Metroidvania game. The returning to old Locations to unlock new things or find new items is all there, but progression is pretty locked on that and few sectret items you find actually change up how you go about exploring the world. I found myself just looking up how to get to the next boss because I got so tired of stumbling my way around in the dark I just wanted to get the game over with. Which isn't a good thing. Compared to other Metroidvania games exploring the world you are in shouldn't be a chore until you want to unlock 100% of everythign. And even then most that time looking for random upgrades, bits and bobbles should be fun and exciting. Salt and Sanctuary didn't capture that for me. I found myself despising the areas I was in more than looking forward to that next discovery.
I think for me, the major recomendation factor lies entirely with Multi Player and its magic system. Since It doesn't allow for online co-op and the magic system is still too shallow for me. There isn't honstly enough here for me to recommend based on my tastes alone.
If you like the Dark Souls type games and a cryptic story with a dark setting. You'll Probably love this game. If You're looking for a Metroidvania game or a Deeper skill system in your RPGs this game really isn't for you. And Since I'm in the latter camp, I can't recommend this game.

One is certain - this game will make you pretty damn salty.
And you'll absolutely love it.

tldr; first, then further reading below:
Pros:
- Beautiful game. From the graphics to the color choices to the excellent level aesthetics, RAGE has an immersive world to explore.
- Plenty of tense, enjoyable moments blasting everything from raging mutants to the coordinated assaults of the authority
- Enemy animations are a joy to watch. Enemies jump, duck, roll, climb from the ceiling and react to hits from your weapons in a way no other game does
- Mixes up the standard shooter genre with driving sections, a light crafting system and different ammo types for most guns offering various ways to use weaponry in interesting ways
Cons:
- The ending is cut short with a fairly anticlimactic assault sequence
- Driving mechanics and AI are not as well fleshed out as could be, almost an afterthought for the way some of it works
- Multiplayer feels tacked on with the co-op missions being rehashed levels of the campaign and racing that feels dry and boring
- Fairly easy game, even on the ultra nightmare difficulty added by the DLC
Rating: 4/5
RAGE... It's a game that a lot of people like to hate on. Looking at it from a perspective purely focused on game design and implementation, yes RAGE is lacking. There's one thing that most people don't take into account when enjoying games however and that is the perspective from games as art. From that standpoint, ID nails it with RAGE. It's a simply beautiful game that stands the test of time even now and because of that:
I LOVE RAGE
By far some of the most fun I've had with the game has been bullet spraying, sniping, shotgunning, wingsticking or otherwise pulverizing enemies and seeing their death and reaction animations. Having enemies duck and dodge at the last second, swing across the ceiling and stumble and roll as they're shot in the shoulder is extremely satisfying to watch. It makes the game much more immersive than most shooters where enemies stand there and then die like robots repeating the same motions over and over.
The graphics help with this and to this day RAGE has some of the best looking graphics there is. The textures may not hold up to modern ones but the overall aesthetic and graphical fidelity certainly does. RAGE looks gorgeous, check out some of the screenshots I or others have taken and see for yourself the colorful environments that are pleasantly in line with the setting of the game. Ruined cruise ships sitting on top of cities made from industrial steel sheets, a town converted from an old subway station, a maniacal TV host with a carnival themed arena of death, RAGE continues to amaze with each chapter of the game fitting a well crafted post apocalyptic theme.
Also of note is the attempt by ID to try new things with the standard shooter genre. Weapons have alternate ammunition types which alter the way they're used, some to a greater degree than others. There's also a light crafting system in the game that lets you construct items from health bandages to stationary turrets and even robotic spider turrets. While the game doesn't ever require you to need these items as even on the hardest difficulty the game can be completed without any of them, it's a nice addition that does allow for some different approaches to combat if desired.
---
RAGE does have it's negative sides however and it's unfortunate that this is all some people see in the game. It's been heavily criticized for it's ending sequence and yes, it does leave something to be desired. The last half of the game in general does seem rushed and not as creative as the first half although again the aesthetic and attention to detail is still there. Even right to the end the game each sequence is fantastic to behold with the level, enemy and weapon design being the saving grace for me.
With the mechanics ID added to mix up the genre they came close to creating something magical but ended up stumbling a bit in the implementation. The driving mechanics first of all could have been done better. While it's fun to turbo boost yourself around the wasteland firing machine guns and rockets at other cars in a Twisted Metal fashion, the vehicle controls and enemy AI do feel lackluster compared the rest of the game mechanics. An afterthought kind of feeling can't help but be conveyed especially after your tenth or so race with the enemy cars driving ever so cautiously behind you as not to be too hard on you but not too easy on you either and then immediately dumping their ammo supply upon pickup in a very predictable way.
While appreciated, the crafting and ammo system is also somewhat lackluster in it's implementation because while everything in the game is indeed fun to use on it's own, the game is not balanced well enough nor ever requires you to use any of what's given to complete the game. In fact if you play on normal difficulty you can very easily use nothing but the shotgun and the occasional showing of a rifle for the entire game. The disconnect between the ideas in the game and the implementation in conjunction with the enemy AI shows although. Again however, the fun in using the available mechanics is there should you choose to enjoy the game in it's fullest.
One more thing to note and is as much of an afterthought as the mode itself is the multiplayer element. While nice to have, multiplayer does indeed feel tacked on offering two modes that are entirely forgettable. First there is a co-op mission mode but the missions are just rehashed levels from the campaign. You and your partner compete for points by killing enemies the fastest and most efficient. The other mode is up to four player races and destruction derbys that are more fun than the co-op mode but the race mechanics are dry enough that it doesn't redeem it as something that will last you more than a few plays.
---
Overall I certainly enjoyed my time with RAGE, enough to buy the DLC and complete the achievements. It's going up as one of my favorite shooters despite it's flaws and it's a game I wholeheartedly recommend everyone try.

While I do recommend this game, it does come with some caveats.
I'll start by saying that the first game was better than this one. I enjoyed the first one a lot better than this version.
Even the Siberian Strike DLC played okay, except for a forced combat section.
In 18 hours, I played the main game and the DLC. That is kind of disappointing considering the game. I honestly did think that this second game would improve from the first and WANTED it to be more than anything.
The play seemed clunky in places and at one scripted point, the binoculars were meant to  be in front of me and I was standing up, unable to bring them back up ( I was able to break out of the scripted sequence).
For the record, I played on medium throughout and just went with the flow of the game. When they hurried, I did. When they relaxed, I did. I did do a lot of stealth knife kills.
On the plus side, when I hit my marks, they felt satisfying and even nicking them in the side of the neck shows an evil, borderline psychotic love of the animation as they struggle and wriggle at the sudden loss of blood then life.
Under thermals, the bodies react as expected as they lose life and heat in the DLC. The caves and indoor areas were pitch ♥♥♥♥ing black and rightly so. CryEngine 3 is really good even on sub-gaming rigs (like mine). While the settings weren't ultra hyper real 4k 3d zomg real lifeorz, it was easy to get immersed with the ambient sounds. Physics were almost perfect with some final corpse positions kinda dubious. But then again, my scope wasn't 12x so, couldn't see that far.
I satisfying it a 1572m mark with it, however and the bullet time captured the moment beautifully.
It does sound like I'm bashing the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of it and you could equally argue that I am but I don't feel bitter about it. More wanting, than anything. While adding content for the sake of adding content is in the Gamer's Cardinal Sin book (volume 3), I felt like I wanted to be more snipery (if that makes sense).
TL;DR: A good, solid sniper game with lots of action and beautiful scenery. This would be a solid buy, but replay IMO isn't high - so bear that in mind before you pull the trigger.
Oh and two more things: Load last checkpoint is your friend most times and millimetres matter. Good hunting ;)

This game is so much of a trainwreck that it's hard to believe it's not early access. The various unlockable abilities and the entire leveling system in general has been stripped away, leaving each character with two actions. Just successfully finishing a level without it being broken by the physics engine is a blessing in itself, especially when co-op becomes a factor. The sheer amount of physics puzzles in the game that just don't work makes me wonder if the game was ever tested at all, and it isn't helped by the unnecessary addition of a third dimension of movement that mostly just creates more problems. But more than that, the game is blatantly unfinished, and they don't even attempt to hide it. The last cutscene is of the characters grabbing one shard of the Trine, exclaiming "Two more to go!", and then that's it, time for credits in a game that would be like 3 hours long if you didn't have to restart so many levels or play so many smaller padding levels to unlock the levels of the extremely short campaign. Buying this game at all is a mistake; buying it for $21.99 is budgetary suicide.

Dishonored is a freaking amazing game.
If you're reading this review, you probably already know what the game is about. The story is pretty good in this game, but it's better known for the gameplay (which is some of the best gameplay I've ever seen). You can play high chaos (kill everyone) or low chaos (don't kill anyone/kill very few people). The powers are also amazing and fun to use, and incredibly useful to use.
I would reccommend playing high chaos then replaying the game with low chaos, because 1. you get to see how things change when you do low chaos and 2. it makes low chaos way easier, since you already know how all the buildings are designed, so it's easier to stealth.
It took me about 7 hours to complete the game on high chaos, and 6 hours to do low chaos, though it was way harder. I'm not a stealth person, but I had a lot of fun with the Dishonored stealth, and when you go "Ah ha! That makes it way easier to not be detected!" when you find some hidden passage or extra room with a second flight of stairs with no guards or something.
Not killing anyone isn't hard, it's just that you usually have to sneak past all the guards since there's too many. The sneaking part is hard, since the guards will see you pretty easily and then call for backup. After that, you have to reload your save and try again. During low chaos, I still killed all the main target except one, and didn't kill any guards except for one accidental kill which I didn't fix because I was already in a fight with a target. I still got low chaos, so you can kill some people.
There are three endings, the bad one, the good one, and the really bad one, For the bad one, you finish with high chaos, for the good one, low chaos and for the really bad one, high chaos and really screw up the last mission.
So that's some of my experience with the game, and how good it is. With Dishonored 2 coming, jumping into this game now would be a great time to do it, and play before that game releases. Hope this helped some of you!
EDIT: Definitly buy the Definitive Edition of this game. The DLC's are so good, and continue the story of Dishonored in an amazing way! Buy them!

So as always, I'm really late to the (metaphorical) party. The advantage is that, unlike a party, a videogame can be enjoyed whenever you so damn please. So the real question becomes: Did I enjoy Dishonored? F#CK YES! Although the game isn't exactly a sandbox playground (which differs from what I'm normally accustomed to thanks to the Assassin's Creed series), it offers a great amount of systems, mechanics and abilities for you to play with. You clearly know what you're meant to do – kill your target(s). But how you do it and whether you do it at all; that's all up to you. Will you become Corvo, the wise, loyal and merciful royal protector, or will you become Corvo, the brutal, vengeful and unforgiving assassin? The choice is yours.
TO SUM UP: I strongly recommend this game. It gives you a sense of freedom that only few games are capable of achieving. This is how games should be made. Hats off to you, Arkane Studios.

I was on the fence with this game for a long time. The main thing holding me back was the price. Holy pricey for a game with low production value batman! I read many reviews here and other places, browsed the Slitherine forums for ahwile, and decided to bite and fork over 50 hard earned dollars. Of course 4 days later it goes on sale 50% off! Needless to say, "steam" is coming out of my ears right now...but I digress.
The game is fantastic. Not quite as deep as "Panzer Corps", but deep enough to make you think about what you're doing. Do I pick up another support unit for my core force or another armor division? Do I deploy in one giant wedge formation or split my force into two battlegroups? Do I upgrade my artillery units to Deathstrike missiles for maximum effect against armor or do I keep my Earthshakers for better versatility? Do I use a turn to rest and refit my elite units or do I press on? Every mission had me asking myself these questions...the first time I played them of course.
The game has ZERO replay value; once you know how the scenarios will unfold almost all these questions will be answered for you. For this reason alone it's very hard for me to recommend the game at full price. If you're a big fan of 40k and wargames I can say this is a winner, but it's way, way, WAY overpriced. Wait for a sale, or get more value for your dollar and pick up another wargame.
I will close by saying that after 100+ hours of play I can say that most (but certainly not all) of the negative reviews I have read are from people who thought this was 40k tabletop on PC and are disappointed to find out that it's not, or are from people who are not wargamers and somehow ended up buying this. It's a solid wargame with no replay value and a way too hefty pricetag. If $50 is chump-change to you, then I recommend this to any wargamer.
One thing i forgot to mention...the "manual" is garbage. How can you not explain, or for that matter even mention "Zones of Control". This is an absolutely critical mechanic to understand if you want to succceed and enjoy a game like this on all but the easiest difficulty. If you're not well versed in wargames and are thinking of picking this up I strongly suggest you look up ZOC on forums or whatever. You will get alot more out of the game, trust me.

I never played Panzer Corps or Panzer General which people keep comparing it to, but the game is virtually identical to Elven Legacy which I did play.
It's virtually identical with the following differences:  it doesn't seem to have the time pressure (in games turns, not realtime) to beat the missions that Elven Legacy had (great, the time pressure in Elven Legacy was oppressive, made it feel like a puzzle game); Armageddon's mechanics seem more complex which makes it difficult to predict the outcome of actions; Armageddon's mechanics are also more random which makes it impossible to predict the outcome of actions; units take longer to die which gets irritating, you have to pummel and pummel and pummel the enemy before they're gone; several factors make it harder to keep your units alive which sucks hard; Armageddon has a bewildering variety of units which you might think is a good thing but isn't, it's confusing, and you never know if you're using the *right* units; and, most dispiriting, it doesn't have anything like the rewards that Elven Legacy did.
In Armageddon your units go up levels just like they did in Elven Legacy, but you only get the stat increase.  You don't get to choose a special ability for them which makes it much less interesting and doesn't allow you to customize your units the way you could in Elven Legacy.  Armageddon also doesn't have magic items which were another level of customization for your units and meant that you could take actions other than just attack, attack, attack.
Armageddon isn't a bad game, but it's confusing with a very steep learning curve and doesn't make you want to keep playing.  If I could go back in time and tell myself not to buy it, I would.

You know already: 2d Dark Souls clone. Metroidvania. Looks great. Developed by 2 people. What's more to know?
S&S has a great game hidden beneath a very rough outer shell. The first playthrough is harsh. The difficulty and the very real possibility of falling to your death impede Metroidvania exploration. The lack of a map doesn't help either. Several ingame mechanics are never explained like the creed system or the crafting system. If you know Dark Souls conventions you can guess some of it, but not all.
If you do manage to finish the game though, every subsequent playthrough will be a blast and the real core of the game will shine - finding out how to play with different classes. At that stage you can compensate for shortcomings you didn't know your character had on the first playthrough. But getting there is unpleasant.
The combat system has a lot of flaws. Two-handed weapons are way too strong. Heavy armor is basically useless. Magic flip-flops between completely broken and underwhelming one-trick pony and the elemental imbalance system is suppressed from the get-go. High level enemies drop crap noone needs and vital crafting materials are limited to one per playthrough.
But all of these problems are a testatment that I played long enough to be actually aware of them. There is a brilliant game right here. After I finished I immediately started a new game+ and a new character with a different build. And I still want to play more. I'd advice everyone not comfortable with the harsh first playthrough to make liberal use of the wiki. As long as you don't spoil yourself on the crafting or on boss tactics it provides the missing information in game.
Overall a diamond in the rough.

If you know me then you know that I absolutely love games such as Castlevania, Metroid, Ori and the Blind Forest and so on. In other words: Metroidvanias. Those games just have their rather unique charm. You’re not
by a linear story-line nor are you unable to visit certain location whenever you want. Those games take place on a huge overworld that you can explore to your heart’s desire.
Also you’d know that I absolutely love the Soulsborne games. Demon’s Souls was one of the best and finest gaming experiences I’ve had not only on the Playstation 3 but during my entire gaming career and I’m around since the NES age (for better or for worse … oh well).
You’re thrown into a world without any guidance or help and everything’s able to kill you and ruin your day. Not to mention the whole souls system. Without souls, which drop on death (and vanish for good if you die again), you’re unable to do anything in the Souls game since you need those in order to level up, buy and upgrade items and so on.
So some games feature a skill tree but this game features a tree of skill. Same thing just with a better name. Basically you'll find items like black pearls which let you, after you've spend quite a bit of salt in order to level up, learn a skill. There are skills such as increase strength, dexterity or will. You also find that you can increase your main heal item by one or learn to wear better armor. Weapons and armors do have classes ranging from one to five and you have to learn the right skill in order to be able to equip a class five weapon or armor.
Grey pearls you find randomly through the game and those act as erasers meaning you can choose to forget one skill. Haven't used it myself yet but I figure it comes in quite handy if you happen to learned a skill by accident.
So a love child between Metroidvania and Souls would be the absolute blessing and here’s where Salt and Sanctuary comes in: It IS that love child.
If you’re wondering what Salt and Sanctuary is about well … the name says it all. More on that later.
But beware … the salt is real.
It’s the bomb. It’s the best thing that happened to gaming, in my eyes, in a long time. Also it’s about Salt and … Sanctuaries. I’ll explain in a jiffy.
Salt and Sanctuary is rather unique in the way it approaches the usual Metroidvania. You’re not running from point A to B in order to find certain items or upgrades. Instead you do those things just as you do in the Souls games. That means that you’ve to kill and slay enemies in order to get salt which you then use to level up your character or to upgrade your gear for example.
However if you do die you lose all your salt, just like in the Soulsborne games. However there’s one difference; If an enemy has killed you then you have to go back and slay your killer in order to regain your salt. If you died because you thought it might be a good idea to listen to one of those bottles and jump off that cliff you’ll encounter a specific enemy on the location of your death and if you kill it then the salt is yours again.
I mentioned Bottles right? So remember those messages in the Soulsborne games on the ground? I mean the
or
. Exactly. Those Bottles are messages written by either players. Most of the time it’s useful information like
and so on but then there’s also stuff like the aforementioned jump of that cliff. So it’s up to you whether or not you decide to listen to those.
Right after you’ve arrived on the beach you’re greeted by a dude with some questions and depending on your answers you’ll join a certain Creed. Covenants anyone?
It doesn’t matter which Creed you belong to you’ll always be able to rest at another Creed’s Sanctuary. Unless you’ve managed to turn them hostile.
The job of the Sanctuaries are basically to give you a brief moment to catch your breath and to stock up on levels and items. Also you flasks err I mean your main healing items recharge whenever you visit a Sanctuary. Each Creed has it’s own version but they all work the same.
During your quest you’ll find certain stones. Merchant, Leader and so on. Once you reach a Sanctuary you can make an offering by selecting from those stones. Depending on your choice you’ll summon certain NPCs like a merchant or a blacksmith. You can also offer a leader stone in order to summon a Leader of your Creed. You can trade in specific items in order to raise your devotion. Raising your devotion will give you extra items each time you respawn or rest at a Sanctuary of your Creed.
Then there’s also Sin. If you decide to leave your Creed in order to join another you gain sin.
You can be absolved of your sin by paying a certain charming woman a visit. With a big ol’ pack of salt of course.
With certain items you’re even able to convert Sanctuaries of another Creed to your own. There’s an easy and a hard way but it’s best to find that out for yourself. Just more fun that way don’t you think?
The combat works basically just like the Soulsborne games. Thrust, slash, hit, block and parry.
Every action requires stamina so you should feel right at home.
There are a variety of weapons ranging from daggers to pitchforks to greatswords and so on.
Also there’s magic but it works a bit different.
Also just like in the Soulsborne games you're able to transmute weapons or armos with the ashes of bosses for example.
Basically using Spells consumes Focus and will lower your max Stamina. In other words the more spells you cast before resting in a Sanctuary the more stamina you’ll lose and you end up being unable to cast spells at all.
Enemies have and follow a certain attack pattern which you’ll have to get used to in order to see another day. Bosses in particular. They all have a few mean tricks up their sleeves to make you hate your life and them. Remember the salt is not only sacred but real in this game.
What I noticed during Boss battles is that depending on their current HP they mix their attacks a bit up so you can’t just follow into a rhythm like: slash, roll, slash, roll slash.
I mean you can and feel free to do that but you might get rekt fairly easily that way. Trust me I know what I’m talking about.
Just like the Soulsborne games you’ve no idea how or why. By that I mean story wise and so on. However during your encounters with numerous NPCs you’ll learn a bit more about the world and the game each time you talk to’em.
So if you’re like me and you enjoy a good story listen to what they have to say.
I could be really specific about the mechanics of the game and so on but I feel this is enough.
The beauty of the Soulsborne and Metroidvania games is that you don’t have a real clue how to get to anywhere or what’s really going on.
All in all Salt and Sanctuary has managed to become my favorite game at the moment and overall since it mixes up to genres which I absolutely love.
Not to mention that the Music in this game is just so fitting and exceptionally good.
I bought it full price without regret and to be quite honest I believe that the Devs have earned their money so don’t be salty about the price and support’em.
Also I have to mention real quick that the only two devs behind this gem of a game are husband and wife.
Pretty neat eh?

Ok. Do you like Dark Souls or similar games? Do you like metroidvanias? Do you like side-scrolling action-rpgs? If yes to any of these, do yourself a favor and buy this game.

You will spend your time gathering salt (like souls) to level up, upgrade equipment, or transmute equipment into more powerful versions. While doing this you will defeat bosses, gain items to allow you to further explore the game world, and meet NPCs that may have requests for you.  The only downside is I wish there was a map like in many other metroidvanias but I guess in keeping with the dark souls tribute, there is none.
Overall an addicting game and I highly recommend it.

First the good:  Rage looks great.   The graphics, animations, character designs, etc, are all fantastic.  It also plays great.  The gameplay isn't anytihng really new, with the standard fps weapon selection and enemy types.   However, good enemy AI combined with their unique tendency to bob and weave and climb around levels, combined with very solid game mechanics, keeps things fun enough.   Vehicular combat is also enjoyable; rally racing itself seems like it could be a fun PVP standalone, and I'd love to have a local multiplayer version.
Now for the bad:  Nothing in Rage feels like it matters.  While the world and the characters in it look and sound great, none of them do anything or have any particular characteristics to make you care about them one way or the other.  They are merely window dressing.  The storyline itself is a bare bones mash up of Half Life 2 and Fallout, with bland generic factions like the Resistance and the Authority.  There is no main antagonist.   Missions are repetitive, with side quests basically just sending you back to zones you've already cleared in story missions.   It's also far too easy to actually be engaging, and you'll never really experience any of the tension that the games great looking enemies could have inspired.    Also, the game was also clearly designed and optimized for console, and some of the UI elements are just awful on PC (for example, only being able to assign 4 useable items to quickslot keys, rather than just allowing the player to assign them to whatever keys they like).  The game doesn't intelligently determine when you're using a keyboard/mouse or a controller, so controller propmts will stay on the screen even when using a keyboard until you disable the controller in settings (something I don't like doing, because generally I  use a controller for the driving portions of the game, and a keyboard/mouse for shooting).  There are also notiiceable performance issues, with framerates occasionaly plummetting for no good reason, and textures bouncing back and forth between high and low quality versions (this is on a gtx 960, which should be more than adequate to run this game at full settings).
I'm kind of on the fence about whether to recommend this game or not; really I'd give it about a 60-70 at most, and there are certainly better games out there to play.    Since Steams system requires giving it either a yay or nay, I'll recommend it with a couple of strong caveats: If you're looking for an engaging story, avoid it.  If you want a game that's perfectly optimized for PC, avoid it.   If you are strictly looking for a pretty looking, decent FPS, by all means give it a shot.

Coming into this game from Sniper Ghost Warrior 1, I wasn't expecting much. I gave that a negative review even though I tried very hard to like it, but comparing this game to its predecessor blew my mind.
Let's start listing some things. I'll be combining Pros with Cons since some things offset each other.
+The graphics are BEAUTIFUL. This game running on Cryengine puts its predecessor on the Chrome engine in the dust.
+The story in this is slow to start going, but once you get into it you just want to keep going. It's very immersive and intriguing and I wish it was longer.
-The point of 'longer' is true. I beat this game's campaign in 4 hours. Hardly enough time to enjoy everything the game had to offer.
+But what else did it have to offer? Well the general gameplay mechanics are much better. The mission flow is much smoother. There are much less gameplay bugs to be found in this game. It makes it predecessor look half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥in comparison.
-However, the game does suffer from a severe lack of optimizations. For one, the V-Sync does not work. For two, the game suffered so many graphical glitches on DX9 that it was rendered unplayable. DX-11 ran correctly, but not as smoothly. With my beast of a rig I was only able to mantain an average of 50 fps (Meanwhile I can run games like Arma 3 with well over 120 fps). Lastly, I experienced one CTD while playing the second mission of the first act. Not sure if its a common thing or a one-off, but I feel obliged to mention it.
- The multiplayer is eh. It's just two teams staring at each other across the map, taking shots at each other, while one guy on each team is running around rambo as if this is call of duty, and at least one person is smack-talking every other person in the match. It doesn't do much to extend the life of the game. A co-op mode would have really helped this game.
Overall this game blows its predecessor out of the water. I'll give this an 8/10 for what it is. If it was properly optimized, if the story was a bit longer, or if the multiplayer was really worth playing, it may have earned a higher score. This is still twice the rating I gave to its predecessor, and so I would definitely recommend picking this title up whenever you get the chance.

This is a great game to playby yourself or with friends.
First, it's important to note that the game is free to play at
However, the steam edition offers several more features like ship customization, private servers, beta features, and most importantly in my opinion, no ads. Plus, getting the steam edition gives you a key to use on the web version to access most of thoes features.
The fact that this game also has a web version means it is super easy to get your friends to play; Just give them the join link and they can play with you, even if they don't have the steam edition.
Beyond the ease of playing with others, the actual gameplay is excellent. There are currently four gamemodes: Survival, team, deathmatch, and invasion. My personal favourite is team mode. Invasion and deathmatch are much quicker, and can be played without setting aside time. And invasion is a wonderful gamemode to play with your friends, as teamwork is vital.
All in all, this is a wonderful game. Buy the steam version, and invite your friends to play the web version with you!

Starblast, once and now still a browser game, is a mix of Diep.io and Asteroids with something extra tossed in.
More specifically, it's an MMO-lite game which can have (most likely) up to 200 players in a single game, though currently this isn't too likely unless everyone decides to play on one server and match.
You shoot asteroids, collect gems, and kill enemy players and you use those gems ot upgrade your ship. You can either hoard gems to get ship tier upgrades, or spend them asap on smaller upgrades that'll make your ship better in the moment.
When you die, you have 3 lives to waste, but if you have 0 lives upon death, you revert back to the last ship you used one tier back. You can collect gems, enough to get a tier upgrade, to instead get a life if you're under 3.
There's no windowed mode and the options are fairly basic and limited. Hopefully this is changed as development of the game progresses via patches (again, hopefully).
There's 4 modes.
Survival is your quintessential Starblast experience. Free For All, with a maximum time limit that if reached, no immortal enemies spawn in to 1-shot you to oblivion, but gravity wells emerge, repelling players within them which will slowly creep farther and farth as the match continues to not finish. In this phase, nobody has any lives, and nobody can join the game.
Team Deathmatch is essentially Survival with no time limit, teams (3 of them) and bases that can be upgraded by cashing in gems. Certain ship tiers require work to be put into the Stations, reaching higher levels, and eventually filling the gem stores completely. Currently has alot of problems in my opinion, this gamemode is highly susceptible to snowballing that honestly would be mitigated with a higher playerbase. Spawn Camping is also an unfortunate reality and there's really nothing inferior-equipped ships can do to combat spawn camping at all.
Invasion is pretty much Asteroids, mixed with Space Invaders, only you can ofcourse move about. Shoot asteroids which fragment in this mode, and destroy tons of enemy aliens. Best with others, but this is rarely played, atleast at the time of writing. It may be more popular during peak hours.
Pro Deathmatch, is basically this.
You and anyone else both choose one of two ships to play for hte round, and you just kill one another in an asteroid field. Infinite lifes, no downgrades, no mining for gems, all players start with 200 gems, and (probably) a maxed-out ship. Ends when all enemies leave the game, or someone gets to 10 kills (maybe).
The soundtrack is nice, the visuals are very good in my opinion, the server browser or "Galaxy Map" is also really cool. Nice array of customization options, though I'd like to see some sliders to allow us to make our ships more vibrant, or more dark in a specific color.
Altogether a nice game for 10 CDN. I can see myself playing this alot more often. Lost myself in the game for the 5 hours I first played this game for.
Some suggestions:
- Windowed mode.
- Volume Sliders.
- Resolution options.
- Better color customization.
- More Ships.
- Spawn Protection in TD makes the player ethereal, and gives a huge speed boost.
- Station Defenses to maybe mitigate early-game spawn camping.

I've been playing the web version for about 3 months, and when I heard that it was going to be on Steam, I was thrilled.
After buying the game and playing it, I still really enjoy it, but keep in mind that this version is not perfect and there are a lot of improvements that can still be made. This doesn't worry me because in the 3 months I played the web version, this game recieved constant updates, changing and improving the game drastically every time.
Since I already love the gameplay itself from the web version, here is a quick run down on what makes the steam version different, for better or worse:
-Amazing Galaxy Map UI: This is probably my favorite feature on the steam version, allowing you to visually see all games currently running on various servers and various game modes, with filtering enabled. Previously the only way within the game to play a specific server was to get a link from somewhere else, and all other games joined were random (Which still remains a feature if so desired)
-In game ship tree: Now this is a big one for beginners who are unfamiliar with all of the ships in the game. Now you are able to see all possible future ship upgrades based on your current ship while playing, making the decision of what to upgrade to much easier.
-Built in ECP features: In the web version there were certain features you could only get with a donation of over $10, called the Elite Commander Pass. Now that the game costs money on steam, it is only fitting that we have access to all these features(ship and map customizations, prodeathmatch rankings, etc). Also these features are nicely built into the UI of the game differently that the web version. The only downside is that, as far as I know, purchasing the steam game does NOT give you an ECP transferrable to the web version, which would be nice.
-Invasion Mode: I'll only breifly go over this as new steam feature since it will be released soon to the web version. Overall, this gamemode is unpolished and, though fun, hard to play in it's current state. It's a cool idea, but right now there are so few people with this version that it can be extremely hard since it is a group coop mode. Also some of the ai ships are a bit laggy, and the gem drop is much slower than it is for killing regular ships. Also it is a bit unclear how to clear a wave, do astroids need to be destroyed? Some of these things may be fixed by the time it makes a full release, so don't take these critiques too heavily. As a said, the developers are very good at making good quick fixes and updates to the game.
-Steam Achievements: This is a pretty small thing, but having steam achievements really improves the overall experiences, felling rewarded for killing more people and giving you goals to reach. However the progress for these achievements seems a little broken right now.
OVERALL CONSENSUS:
If you are looking for a full complete game, this one is close but not quite there. It's a lot of fun and I really like having more control and the UI, but the gameplay is identical to the free web version(barring invasion). If you were ever considering getting ECP, this game is a perfect alternative for you. If you've naver playing Starblast, try out the web version first. If you like it, then support the devs and buy it on steam. I would personally suggest waiting for a couple more updates, but there is noting gamebreakingly bad about the current version, it's just a little unpolished.
I LOVE Starblast and it has quickly become one of my favorite games, so I hope you love it just as much.

Sadly, entirely disappointed with HOI 4, what a mess.
I have thousands of hours in HOI 1-3, with the bulk of that in HOI 3. I play entirely solo since my schedule and blocks of time are irregular.
Solo play in HOI 4 is a joke. The AI is entirely non-competitive.
I have played through as two different majors, and have started short games with the others for a comparison.
AI does not appear to have any unit upgrade plan, or worse maybe it does the research but never builds the units.
AI ground units run in endless circles around the map, tying up convoy units in the process. Allied country units will show up and move through any of the player fronts as single units. Mostly they stop and sit somewhere for short while then move again. Sometimes they attack, badly, paying no attention to what you may be doing. They cannot hold any ground.
Playing as the US, joined the allies, and they very quickly filled up all my airbases in the United States. I had UK Naval bombers sitting Kansas? Allied air unit deployment was everywhere on the map except where the ground units are actually fighting, so as far as I can tell they are useless under AI control. Never once were my ground units bombed or fighters challenged.
Ground support shows animations of planes, but again no indication of the effect or even if there is one. Fighters are very much the same it appears they kill enemy planes but you have no idea how many or even if they are. This also means you have no way understand how many or where they should be deployed. For planes it appears your biggest enemy is attrition which seems to destroy a lot.
You can build, deploy and assign bombing missions to strategic bombers, but there is no indication that they do anything. Without feedback how can you every understand the effect based on numbers, so 10 or 1000, all the same.
Naval bombers do attack ships from time to time and appear somewhat effective.
AI navies only sometimes make anything close to a real fleet. Fighting against Japan, I frequently faced isolated battleships, BC or 2-3 cruisers together. None of these had any screens so they easily fall to a well-built fleet or a submarine squadron. AI aircraft carriers after a while will be empty but still cruising around.
The army and orders concept seemed like a good idea. The only time it has even a remote chance of working correctly is when it has one objective, from one army. You are forced to use this for any naval beach landing or para-drop operation. Once you have done one of these, you have quickly remove all units from the army and create a new army to get rid of any orders otherwise the AI starts doing something stupid. It does do a good job of rotating units in and out of the front line, although the low organization units sometimes wonder off a long ways and sit way too long.
The AI can make a beach landing, then it plugs in a bunch of units and randomly attacks, it may attack left for a while, then change its focus to the right. An amazing game. If you're a huge fan of history, particularly World War II you will absolutely love this game. Now for me, this game was worth the price. I bought it on sale for about 5% off. This game has a fairly weak tutorial, it will teach you most of the basics but in a game like this you'll need to know much more than just the basics to succeed. In any case, it will take you a while to figure out how to effectively play. My tips: 1. Assign units to Generals and set front lines and then offensive fronts. 2. The reason your naval invasion won't take effect is because you need to assign your naval units to scout ahead in the ocean areas in which your invasion is heading to, and because you have assigned too much units to the naval invasion. Start out with 2 units for each naval invasion until you finish researching more naval tactics which will allow you to set an invasion. Oh, and lastly you have to hit the arrow at the top of your general's head if you want your invasion to start. These are just a few of the things you won't be aware of when playing. One last thing, the mods. The mods are amazing. Be sure to get the millenium dawn and cold front mods. I am also in huge anticipation of the Great War mod. This is a very addicting game, time will fly by. Overall, it is an incredible World War II simulator. If you are a huge fan of World War II, History, Grand strategies, difficult games, and very complex strategies, this is the game for you.

The all-time best tower defense game. Full stop. Seriously, for TD fans it gets no better than this. The graphics, balance, design, implementation, everything is just great. It is pure tower defense, nothing else, no mucking about with heroes, no leveling up, just levels for you to build a network of towers to kill the baddies.
I’ve played a lot of TD games, and this one still has no equal. If you haven’t tried it, you really owe it to yourself to pick it up.

Gameplay - This is a tower defense game which means you build towers on a map which have their own unique different ways of attacking waves of enemies.  These type of games are all about strategy and experimentation.  You have ten different towers available in each level and have to find the best way to kill all the enemies before they can escape the map.  Unlike the early tower defense games in Warcraft III, Defense Grid has a set number of places where you can build so it becomes important to learn how best to use the space you have and what towers should go where.  You can also shape the paths that enemies take (you always want them to take the longer and more difficult path) which is a cool innovation for the genre.  The designers were smart to put a fast forward button in Defense Grid.  It helps more experienced players get through most maps in 10-15 minutes.  The only downside is much like the Run button in Final Fantasy 7, you have to hold down the F key for long period of times which does get tiring.  It is almost as if a slow down button would have been better than the fast forward.
The most important thing is that this game is fun and even addictive at times.  There are over hundred-fifty different modes in the base game alone.  A new player to Tower Defense may find that this game can be challenging without a good strategy so I highly recommend checking out Youtube for any levels that give you trouble as there are lots of good strategies already out there.
Story - Like a lot of action-oriented games, Defense Grid tries to have a story when there really isn't room for an interesting one.  It is more like there is an "announcer" for the game who makes comments about certain things and encourages you to beat the game essentially.  The story does not get in the way or waste any of your time which is probably for the best.
Presentation (Graphics and Sound) - The graphics in Defense Grid are not very impressive but that isn't the reason you play a game like this either.  The textures are not very detailed and look aged, but this has a nearly top-down and zoomed out camera so it is hard to make the graphics look that great anyway.  The effects of the towers do look good and the game never lags no matter how much action is going on.  This is a plus because old tower defense games could not handle huge waves of enemies.  The sound is good with nice explosion sounds and the announcer is charming and never gets annoying.  What little music is in the game is very good.  If you play through everything in Defense Grid, the music will eventually get repetitive and you'll probably want to listen to something else instead but that is true of any game you play for a long time.
Overall Score - Defense Grid is a great game if you enjoy Tower Defense.  It is probably daunting to a beginner, but if you know you like these kind of games, this is easily the best 2D one on Steam at the time of this revew.  This game is now cheap and if you catch it on sale, it is an incredible value.  There are three DLC packs and all three of them are pretty good and add new level designs to the game.  One is tied into Portal so if you like Glados,  you will definitely like that.  While it took me just over 100 hours, this game is pretty easy to get all the achievements.  A few achievements are a grind, but every achievement is pretty easy to get and there are plenty of videos on Youtube to help you figure out how to get them.  I never expected to play this game so much, but the fact that it is fun kept me playing for over 100 hours.

Mercenary Kings = Metal Slug + Monster Hunter (with just a dash of metroidvania). Unfortunately as good as this combination sounds, Mercenary Kings doesn't live upto any of those games, instead it seems to awkwardly straddle the divide between them.
If your expecting a fast paced sidescrolling run and gun game like Metal Slug or Megaman X, you will be disappointed. Movement is in no way terrible, but in comparison to games that excel in the genre the characters will seem sluggish (I know that running speed is affected by equipment weight) and the controls will feel loose and a bit unresponsive (especially jumping). Also being unable to shoot diagonally seems like a big oversight for a game like this. Don't be expected to be oneshotted by enemies but at the same time be prepared to spend more taking enemy grunts down. Once again though this doesn't make Mercenary Kings a bad experience, you just need to manage your expectations.
Anyone familar with Monster Hunter will be right at home with the way that Mercenary Kings handles missions and crafting. Missions are selected from an npc in the hub basecamp, mostly fetch/kill quests which take place over a handful of levels (encouraging you to explore new areas of each map) with a few boss battles sprinkled through each tier. A new tier becomes available after completing specific missions which usually involve the introduction of a new boss, which can be captured or killed depending on the mission and/or your preference. Enemies(and Bosses) will drop items needed to craft new gun parts and knives. Just like Monster Hunter to get your favourite equipment you will find yourself grinding. All though this formula worked great with Monster Hunter, unfortunately Mercenary Kings doesn't pull it off half as well. Although maps in Monster Hunter were reused in every mission, you didn't have to wade through 15 min of the same pattern of enemies to get to your objective, you could generally just run there. Weapons in Monster Hunter varied greatly, feeling very different to use and with very different stats, in Mercenary Kings it really just boils down to dps. I also feel like there are some real balancing issues with the different gun types. Who wants to grind for gun parts when the guns just feel like reskins of your current weapon. For grinding to be viable gameplay in a game like this bosses really have to be something special, with random attack patterns and unpredictable AI, every fight needs to feel different. This is also something that Monster Hunter gets away with but Mercenary Kings seems to struggle with.
I don't know if this review will help anyone and I really have just scratched the surface on what to expect but overall although there a lot of questionable design choices in Mercenary Kings, I HAVE enjoyed my time playing it, especially with my friends. It may not compete with other games from similar genres, but what it does do is provide a enjoyable unique hybrid experience, and for that it was worth my money.

This game is, to put it very simply, Metal Slug meets Monster Hunter. Looking like Dark Souls ≠ being Dark Souls.
Sadly, I must confess that the game falls short of what it tries to be; a fair and manageable 2D Dark Souls. I use the word "manageable" because what turns this review into the negatives all has to with poor gameplay:
The good:
- Decent Dark Souls-like atmosphere
- Nice music
The bad:
- Lack of decent i-frames
- Sloppy input registration
- Shoddy timing
- Badly designed hitboxes
- Enemies with no tells for unavoidable one-hit-kills
- Non-fluid animations
- No wake-up action (can't roll/block as soon as you get up)
- And the list goes on, but I'm gonna stop here for brevity
All of this makes the game frustrating due to fighting the controls and bad coding more than anything resembling a fair fight. Trying to string together hits turns the combat into - dare I say it - a salty experience. Button presses not registering makes it difficult to queue hits or rolls. React 0.02 milliseconds too fast for the extremely narrow window, and your character doesn't perform the action at all. Imagine Tekken, Street Fighter, or Dark Souls forcing you to wait until the hand from the first move retracted all the way back before you could activate another action? Good luck stringing together combos.
While trying to make a 2D-souls is a commendable effort, the QA was skipped in full and it shows. I'll return if the developers revamps the controls. For now, I can't bring myself to pick it up again, as the worst controls this side of NES Rygar-jumping makes it intolerable on a KarTRASHian level.

Salt and Sanctuary is a really fun and difficult game that mixes  Dark Souls with Castlevania. As fun as it is, the game "borrows" way too much from its Dark Souls inspiration IMO. There's a difference between paying homage to a beloved game and ripping off almost the exact same UI, fonts, sound effects, even the weapon scaling and the way they list defenses (ex. a whole list of things like vs Strike 28.2, vs Slash 14.7, vs Fire and etc- done EXACTLY the same way Dark Souls did it). They have a message system near identical to the Souls' orange soapstones (messages in bottles), there's item lore that's done in the exact same way the Souls' games do it, and they even have candles and a level up system so close to the Souls' bonfires you'll have to recheck to see what game you're really playing.
I jest of course!
While most parts of the notoriously tough Dark Souls could be overcome by a competent player, some skill, and a lot of trial and error there are parts of S&S that I find to be borderline bad design. There are for example some axe tossing enemies whose axes can magically increase in range and arc to almost never miss you, teleporting skeletons that will make you pull your hair out, false floors during boss fights that probably shouldn't be in there, super strong wraiths in early areas of the game that swarm you and lob exploding grenades at you, etc etc. In these cases yes skill is still necessary but many times it feels like the difficulty is cheap.
Enough of the bad though! The way this game handles its skill tree is very cool and thankfully DIFFERENT than Dark Souls for once. You can use black pearls (1 is awarded upon each leveling up at the candles) to branch out into many different areas of expertise or stack points into a single area like Increased Strength. Go far along another path to gain the abilities of another class that started off near that circle (you'll see what I mean, it's tough to explain). I started off as a paladin but quickly discovered that I wanted to be able to cast an enchant weapon miracle, which was a class 2 cleric spell. So the next 10 or whatever levels I put points all along the way towards that Cleric class 2 goal. I find the skill tree / hub thing to be very awesome the way they did it.
Also unique to this game as far as I'm aware are the small stone characters you'll find scattered about the world. You can then offer them to a sanctuary and have them turn into real people who'll live in the building and help you out later. These guys can range from miracle-selling clerics to blacksmiths who'll upgrade your weapons and armor to Leader characters who will exchange enemy parts for rewards (example batwings or ears). To keep any one sanctuary from becoming too OP there's a limit on how many of these guys can reside at any given sanctuary. Another great idea!
There are many many weapons which you'll use to kill things ranging from swords to pitchforks to crossbows and halberds. Many of these weapons are very fun to mess around with, even if you don't have the stats currently to deal gobs of damage to your enemies. The halberd for example seems to be able to hit an enemy twice with one of its attacks. The bow and arrow is almost a necessity against the aforementioned axe-throwing S.O.Bs however the aiming mechanics of bows in general leaves much to be desired and I ended up wasting a ton of arrows just trying to HIT anything. Luckily foes killed by your bow will almost always have arrows on them to reclaim for later. The paladin starts off with a morning star and it's pretty friggin' awesome too. The only thing that would've made this game even better is for the devs to scale back the giant damage that every greatsword seems to do. They have the range, they have the damage.. They outclass almost everything else that I've gotten so far. I'd like to see a bunch of random end game players who AREN'T all using greatswords, wouldn't you?
Graphically, I love this game. Yes I know bloom effect has been done to death but I think it adds to the eerieness this game is trying to pull off. The art is hand drawn and every glove and helmet you equip shows on your character. Your character also seems to be constantly on crack, as their eyes dart around in a most creepy way in eternal paranoia! Music is very good though that high-pitched shrill shrieking sfx at the menu screen is pretty grating. As for sound effects they are exactly like those found in Dark Souls so if you liked how that sounded you'll like this too.
tldr;
Game is awesome
Game rips off too much from Dark Souls, which I feel helped get this title a lot more sales than it would have otherwise
If they didn't copy so much of Dark Souls it'd stand out better than it does (and it already does)
The original ideas they do have are great, we need to see more of them
Enemies are often cheap which sorta' sucks
I'm just being honest with my criticisms
Recommended!

It seems that success was never in Rage's destiny. id Software (known for their genre-defining shooters, Wolfenstein 3D and Doom) released their 2011 open-world shooter in a post-Fallout 3 gaming landscape, choosing to leave their world fairly empty and uneventful aside from car combat encounters. It's testament to id Software's brilliance at making a polished combat system that the many flaws Rage has don't massively detract from the fun you'll have playing through it.
It's glaringly apparent throughout Rage that much work has gone into the combat. Guns feel great to fire, with multiple modes of fire and different kinds of ammo to suit the varied situations and enemies you'll be encountering. There's a decent selection of them too, with the Combat Shotgun being a particular favourite, as you blast shells into mutants and bandits alike. There's also an Engineering (aka crafting) element, where you combine components to build certain tools. It's quite fun to build Sentry Turrets and deploy them, as well as RC Car Bombs that you can drive into a group of enemies and detonate. You'll quickly find yourself creating bandages to heal up more quickly, and making a ton of Pop Rockets for your shotgun for that extra explosive bang. Simply put, id knows how to do guns and do them right.
As mentioned before, there's a fair bit of car combat in the game. We've since had games like Mad Max that do this quite a bit better, but here it's not too bad. You get a selection of cars throughout the game, and you can arm those with machine guns and rockets. Most of your encounters will be as you drive from one objective to another, and you can earn money from destroying bandit vehicles and returning to Wellspring or Subway Town for rewards. There's a decent amount of things to do in the game, with races and mini-games, plus the two main towns with their Job Boards that offer side quests.
The biggest issues with Rage all concern its story and quests. You're mostly looking at a run of fetch quests throughout the game, and everything feels a bit samey. There's a general feeling of "meh" throughout the experience, as you venture into locations (sometimes more than once if you have to go back for a side quest) and dispatch of enemies, then either pick something up to bring back to town or plant something there. This is mostly a game that concerns itself with the fun feeling of shooting things, so in that respect it succeeds, but you'll not be playing this for any interesting or in-depth questlines. It's all going to wash over you, as the story limps to its conclusion. It's clear a sequel was planned, given the rushed, open-ended final cutscene.
Overall, I do recommend Rage. I enjoyed my time with it, because the things that id gets right are the things that tend to matter in their games. You're getting a polished combat system, with plenty of nice guns and tons of enemies to shoot them at. You're even getting a small open-world to enjoy, even though there's not all that much to do in it aside from drive around, shoot other cars and occasionally pop in for a quick match of Bash TV. There's a bit more to do in the towns and those are the activities that will take up much of your time. The quests are the major flaw here, being generally uninteresting and uninspired. Rage is still id's most underrated game, and while its flaws will be apparent to you as you play through it, there's some good, solid stuff here that makes for an enjoyable experience.

Not bad I guess....dunno why this game has mixed reviews overal, I thought it was pretty enjoyable...will have to give them a read to see why the're negging this game....
So the story contrinues off where you left with Trine 2...well, not a direct sequal but sometime later, like a few or several years later kind of "sometime later" time...
The store page sums up the story well, but in case it's removed for whatever reason, here's a copy for your convenience:
They removed the skill tree that was present in its prequel, not that's a bad thing but it looks like they've gone back to its roots with Trine 1 and having no skill tree at all. But yeah, other than that, gameplay is similar to the prequels, except instead of a 2D plane platformer side scrolling action adventure puzzling game, it's a 3D one! So now you have depth into the areas you can explore, but I think this also removes the ability to play with only a keyboard or only a mouse - but I suppose they could add it in if they wanted to, just that it probably would be more awkward to play in....it'd be like playing
and that's a pure keyboard only game in a 3D plane world and I found it awkward using keys to define the viewing direction....
Anyways, as usual, you solve puzzles to get to the next area, fight bad guys, explore, admire the nice scenic environment and collect collectables if you want to 100% complete it.
Oh yeah, I just noticed they went away with the difficulty so I guess the game is to be played how it's meant to be, not too easy or too hard, but how the developers intend the game difficulty to be...that can be a good or bad thing depending on peoples' taste, for myself - I don't really mind....
I'm not sure if it's still running the same engine as the prequel or if it's a newer improved engine, but nevertheless, those scenic backdrops do look really nice and vivid! Naturally I play with all the eye candy enabled, including anti-aliasing maxed out, which the launcher warned that would result in a huge drop in performance, but in my case it wasn't *that* bad as it stated, as fps ranges from 50 to 70 @ 1080p144. As with it's prequels, this game also runs well and is optimized for SLi as I have two 770s that are actually working pretty hard to keep my frames above 60 on the "Very Highest" graphical setting with AA maxed out, you can check out the rest of my specs at the bottom to see what I was running when I was playing this game. But if I wanted to run with a minimum of 144 fps so that it would sync with my monitor's refresh rate, I think I would need a much more powerfuller GPU, as SLi 770s doesn't cut it(so that means you'll want something stronger than even an Asus 780 Ti Matrix card - which is supposedly equivalent to my SLi eVGA 770s 4GB classified(which is also pre-overclocked) thanks to its pre-overclocked out of the box).....either that or drop AA....especially SSAA.... .
Game appears to be in 7.0 channels, I have a feeling it's 7.0 wide....because the center channel is not used correctly for speech and voice and they were coming from the front two channels.... So far, at least up to chapter 7, including all side chapters up to that point - so having at least 1025 trinaangles, I have not seen the LFE channel spark any life at all....and yes, I believe there *could* have been some points in the game where the LFE *could* have been lively, but I guess the developers didn't think anyone would play their game on a surround sound setup.....and assumes all gamers have 2.0 and thus no LFE channel.....idk....that's what I'm thinking...
The score and sounds affects are well done...no hiccups or issues there!
Now here comes some comments I wanna point out....

I've thoroughly enjoyed the other two Tine games, but sadly I can't recommend this one.
It is a desperately unfinished, unpolished game.  Whilst the art and music are as beautiful and enchanting as ever, the gameplay isn't up to the usual standards set by the previous entries in the series.
* There is no character progression - all three have a stock set of limited skills that remain unchanged throughout the game.
* The XBox controller support is extremely buggy, with the wizard's levitation ability significantly impaired; I had to switch to keyboard + mouse on several occasions just to move items (including the final boss battle, which made it harder than it should have been)
* The game is generally buggy, requiring exiting and restarting levels on a few occasions
* The game ends halfway through the story, with no resolution.  The developers are now working on "Nine Parchments", set in the same universe as Trine but not continuing the story.  This is inexcusable.
* The difficulty of the puzzles seems to have been dialled back - the only time I encountered problems was when the game design was obtuse/unclear, rather than the puzzle being particularly challenging.
The addition of 3D doesn't particularly add anything to the gameplay (other than controller frustrations) and the series didn't need to go down this route.  Given the number of sacrifices and compromises that have been made with the rest of the product, this doesn't seem to have been a worthwhile trade-off.

A vibrant world, the most endearing main character you'll ever meet, decent exploration elements, and intriguing gameplay mechanics made it a joy to play. The ending, which though I praise for being a powerful climax, didn't give me closure. OneShot felt like it was leading up to something much bigger, and the ending didn't satisfy that criteria.
As much as I hate to say it, before yesterday's patch, OneShot didn't feel complete, despite my love for it.
The art compliments the story well, using its pixel graphics to acheive a surprisingly pretty and unique aesthetic. There are a few cutscenes which use more detailed illustrations that are jaw-droppingly beautiful, though that's for you to decide. During communication between characters, portraits depict their emotions. I really enjoy the aesthetic, but it's not for everyone. Besides, the art isn't meant to be the star of the show.
OneShot's soundtrack is absolutely brilliant. The music pefectly creates the moods the creators of the game were going for. At times solemn and mellow, and others, convincingly dangerous and heart-quickening. Rarely does it capture a happier mood, but when it does, it's chipper and a delight to listen to.
Iif you aren't a fan of games that are less combat and gameplay oreinted and are mostly mediums of narrative, be warned that there is absolutely no combat. If you're familiar with any rpgmaker horror games, it's in the same vein. To continue the story, you gather and utilize items and problem solve. Occasionally, though some may think it gimmicky, it forces you to tinker with the gamefiles to progress, which, needless to say, is pretty  ****ing cool. People think OneShot to be similar to Undertale, but definitely not in terms of gameplay. Controls are extremely basic. Z and X on the keyboard to confirm/interact and cancel respectively. Arrow keys to move only in the four basic directions. A on the keyboard brings up a menu for quicktravel, settings, and a refresher on controls. S on the keyboard brings up the items menu, wherein combination and equipment of items take place.
I find OneShot's narrative remarkable. If you want an idea of what you're getting, I can say little without spoiling it. The main character is extremely endearing and adorable. Even if you find the side characters lacking, Niko is continously entertaining. Some side characters aren't fully fleshed out. The gist of it is, Niko finds him/herself in a different, dying world, finding that she/he's been designated as its messiah. Without a sun, the world's residents rely on phospor for energy and light, but they find supplies are running low. Niko must transport the new sun, an oversized light bulb, to a tower in the distance, where she/he can supposedly save the world. In addition, the odd...anomalies threaten the safety of the world's residents, and Niko knows that you, the player, is guiding him/her. A third party, a character who contacts you often through a computer, also helps you and Niko progress through the story. The summary may sound boring, but the game does so much to make itself more dimensional.
Would I recommend this? Hells yeah. It's for a specific demographic; don't pick this up if you get bored of exploration type games or play games only for their gameplay. The narrative is what matters the most. It actually doesn't share much with Undertale, but if you like it for its story, you'll probably love this.
Here's a tip. There's a reason why the game is so short. It's so you can "replay" it. Have fun.

Emotional attachment to a character in a tower defense game?  Especially one that you never get to see on screen, and all development is done purely via the narrative?  Oh, and let's also make that character an AI.  Sound unlikely?  I never would have thought it would be done either - for that matter, I never expected a developer to even bother trying.  But in "Defense Grid: The Awakening", the narrative AI who guides you through the game really DOES develop a character that can bring an emotional attachment towards "him" even without any onscreen presence - especially towards the later levels of the story.  And it's a pretty cool tower defense game in its own right, too.  Strongly recommend checking it out for anyone who likes TD games, OR who wants to see an example of how to develop a seemingly impersonal character through narrative alone.  Well done to Hidden Path Entertainment with this one.
