Mortal Online is possibly the greatest mmo of all time due to many reasons:
• Directional based combat - swing left , right and middle to attack from all angles , do the same for blocking to create a simple yet intense combat system - in first person perspective for immersion.
• Full loot open world pvp game with 2 continents and loads of real players , monsters, and peaceful / aggressive animals alike spread across 3 different biomes .
• unique character creation class with 6+ races that takes age and lineage into account complete with attribute and skill trees to fill out (there are no item or character levels , just a pool of 1100 skill points and a huge list of skills to choose from - you make a character that's UNIQUE TO YOU !).
•Three types of magic schools (more on the way) ; ecumenical - of this as elemental magic, fireballs , lightning strikes , healing and anti-healing magic in this branch . Spiritism - become a ghost and trap other spirits (ai and human) using them as reagents for your spells , and shoot laser beams from your frickin' hand ! Necromancy - the most new and most interesting by far , raise the undead and have them fight for you , summon a ritual abomination that can be customized depending on the dead carcass you use to create it and it can be leveled up to evolve it's attacks, summon a ghostly Shade to be a back up mage for you as well ... on top of all these creatures you can perform over 12 unique necromancer spells invlolving blood and dark magics!! Become a wizard harry !
- New patch added custom house building, over 4 different styles of architecture to choose from and the textures of your house will change depending on  the materials you use to build your house!
• Explore ruins , caves hidden underneath waterfalls , massive rope bridges above hundreds of feet of jungle , Asian-inspired cities built into the side of a mountain, and large capitol cities (one nestled into the grassy steppes , another in the wide-open insect infested desert) . Over  30 different cities , towns, hamlets and ancient wonders to visit spread across 2 different continents
•A height/weight system that can be altered after character creation , which affect damage bonus , health pool and more .
• Ai guards protect innocent "blue" towns and the blue players within , but don't let that fool you , guards can be killed , they are not everywhere all the time and you CAN BE hurt , thieved from, and murdered anywhere in the world of Nave ! Be careful !
• Unique armor and weapon system that allows you to customize your character ANY WAY you want with mix and match armor (hair and tatoos are limited)
• Dungeons filled with special bosses that drop legendary loot and chests filled with random and static loot , some of it very valuable making treasure hunting a real career !
•A large taming system allows you to tame, train and use over 4 dozen unique monsters at your disposal if you choose to be a tamer (to fight for you or to sell) . These animals /  creatures grow in size as you train / take care of them , they also adapt new attacks and some even evolve into stronger beasts !
•Mount system WITH breeding : ride horses , donkeys , mules, camels, lizard horses (lyks) , and Molva beasts (bull rhinos), with a one of a kind breeding system built into the game you will be trying to find the perfect looking mount for you and your friends to explore the dangerous world with !
•skill based combat system ensures that you will have an intense , first person experience in EVERY battle , wether it be fighting an AI skeleton or a player controlled Murderer .
•create a modular house anywhere and customize the look of it using different materials , also create furniture and furnish your house !
• largely complex crafting system - craft weapons , bows , shields , armor (12 + different styles of armor and over 50 types of materials/metals to use for all crafting !)
• Meteorite drop system - watch a cosmic star fall from the skies as it actually tears through the atmosphere of Nave and crash lands randomly , leaving a defening sound which can be heard for miles .. after the meteor cools down you can mine it for precious (very valuable !) metals that normally must be refined by an experienced player controlled metal refiner
• relic / relic weapon drop - Similar to the meteors , these relics are statues that can be placed at guild reliquaries to provide passive bonuses such as leveling pets much faster , also sometimes a temporary (sometimes not temporary) "relic weapon" drops , imbued with godly powers , it makes anyone who wields it powerful beyond imagination .
• player versus world : lots of creatures to farm for all sorts of materials , which can be simply sold, or traddd to crafters to make armor , weapons , shields and bows (soon to be houses , right now houses are created but won't change HP, color or texture with different materials)
• Raiding system : BE A VIKING ! With the newly added Ramps you too can raid like a Viking ! Free placement ramps can be built for a way into enemy palisades - be ware this is in its infancy stages
• Sieging system : build Battering rams , Manganons , fire arrows , and even trebuchets to destroy enemy fortifications , walls , palisades , really anything that you want to destroy that your neighbor has made ( NOTE : sieging is NOT EASY OR QUICK).
• one of a kind thievery system allows you to pickpocket from others and pick chests ! Be that professional thief / con artist you always wanted to be ! Complete with fall damage , the games physics make it a thieves playground , doing special jumps to get into rooftops and high ground the thief finds hidden treasure chests (some right under the average citizens nose !) and sometimes perfect opportunities to assassinate .
• open world and open ended battles mean you can be fighting one person outside of the capitol city of Tindrem one minute - and then be attacked by two lance wielding horse riders the next - the choice is yours ... and theirs .
• free to play with an optional (but preferred) subscription - unlimited free trial means you can play the game up to 60% power of all players who subscribe each month , this does not mean pay to win obviously, as you cannot buy anything that gives you an advantage , but it does mean as a free trial user you aren't expected to be able to be a master at anything .
This game has SO MUCH TO IT and all of this on 8 years , and one massive server , but yet the world still hasn't caught onto the greatness that is Mortal ONline , most likely due to its rough start (the game was very unbalanced and broken up until about a year ago when the devs furiously started bug fixing and balancing) but now the game is greatly improved and the devs are releasing patch after patch to revitalize it .
Play Mortal Online free today ! It's only getting better , and it needs more newbies like you , reader !

This is a truly fun game. I really like the tower defense genre, but I am more drawn to games that look and play like this one. With a more real-world look and sci-fi atmosphere and story. Rather than the more fantasy oriented games with magical abilities, and cartoonish look. I like Fletcher, with his British accent. He is the AI that helps you on every stage. He operates the defense system and processes the the remains of destroyed aliens into resources for you to build and upgrade the towers. You never see him but his voice always encourages you and he provides an interesting plot for the game. You can see I have a ridiculous number of hours in this game - but that is because I became rather obsessed with playing a perfect game on as many stages as I could. For that you need to play through the stage without allowing any power cores to be stolen by the aliens. To accomplish that I would quit a game once the aliens got through my towers with a couple of cores, and then revise my strategy and start over. The amazing thing was on some of the perfect games that I played, there were still 50 or 60 thousand games on the leader board with higher scores than mine! Getting all of the DLC for this game greatly adds to the playing time by adding new stages and plots including one that had the voice of GLADOS from Portal! And there is replayability by playing the same stages with different circumstances and goals. Like playing the standard storyline stage with the alien entry and exit points reversed. Some of these are very difficult, like the Super Grinder mode which has 99 waves of aliens, instead of 20 -30 waves. THis game has very few weak points, and I'm looking forward to Defense Grid 2!

Defense Grid: The Awakening is the definitive tower-defence experience on PC. Although indie-developed, it has a certain polish to it you don't often see with this kind of development, and the mechanics are very tight. Easy to learn but hard to master, Defense Grid kept me coming back time after time to better my strategies and challenge my friends' high scores. Challenge modes, along with the high-scores give the game a degree of length, variety and replayability.
Jim Ward, voicing Fletcher with a distinct British accent is also a great little addition to give the game a little story depth that, while not necessary in a game like this, is a welcome distraction and provides a little bit of fun.

I must say, I wasn't expecting such an original, refreshing and really captivating experience when I started the game for the first time. For what I had seen, it looked like an interesting adventure game with an interesting story.
What I played, or, more likely, what I experienced was so much more. I liked...basically, everything about it. The unique style, the story, the characters...the more you progress in the story, the more you really feel...involved in it. This game, even though having a simple appearance is, for me, a true hidden pearl. Being someone who really likes good stories, I was enthralled by it from beginning to end. I smiled, I laughed, I frowned, I worried, I pondered...my heart strings were pulled here and there too. (...Well, here and there, do not get me wrong. It was here and there, but the strings made a quintuple loop and a leap of faith into an ocean of feels before coming back and high-kicking the heart into pieces)
So, for me, the story was on point. On a more "gaming" aspect, some of the puzzles were simple. Some other puzzles my brain wished it could've got out my ear to explode somewhere safe. I was baffled by some of the things the game was able to do by times. Puzzles, items that you can combine...it's an adventure game. Sometimes simple, sometimes...not so much!
The humor made me smile and laugh, I really cannot find a joke or a comic relief that wasn't well done there (Although I must say some of them were...let's just weird, and one was even a bit disturbing in a...bad-good way????).
So...yeah. This game is really something I won't forget. It was an incredible adventure, original, with clever ideas and a well put story that is, for me, really interesting, keeping it's most important mysteries hidden until the end.
It's really something that should have more attention in my opinion, and is better experienced when you know nothing about it, like said in the beginning. It's really something you must play for yourself.
A story you must take a part in. A little adventure where you'll have a part in.
........And like, seriously, you cannot resist the Main Character's level of cute and loveliness.
Everyone who worked on it : it's something incredible, thank you so much!

The problem with 40k: Armageddon is that it overcomplicates its subject matter and fails to explain it for newcomers. The tutorial is bare-bones, nothing but lip service is paid to the attributes and statistics for the huge amount of variants of units. That means, unless you're knowledgeable in 40k weapons, you'll struggle to figure out what weapon is an anti-tank variant and which is an anti-infantry variant.
So poorly explained are the attributes and mechanics that, if you go check the official forums some of the most common posts are trying to decipher, explain and figure out the attributes. Has it improved since launch? Yes, UI improvements which should have been in the game at launch have finally come out, but it is too little, too late.
Unless you're an ardent tactical turn based fan or Warhammer 40k fan, this isn't something I can recommend.

A fun game to be sure, this title is a prime offering for individuals that want to dip their toes into TBS fare.  While not worth the outrageous offering price of 40 dollars, the game is worth purchasing if you can find the game on a hefty Steam sale.  Unfortunately, the game lacks the deep, rich tactical combat that it purports to have and, instead, exists as an annotated view of the the tactical/wargamer genre.  Warhammer 40K fans will be delighted at the amount of units but most individuals would probably be better served purchasing the game on the iPad.  The game runs just as well, controls just as fluidly, costs less and its difficulty level better matches a portable/mobility environment.
In fact, had the game not shipped on iOS almost a full year after I purchased it on Steam, I'd never have bought it for PC.  Weapons are said to affect different units in different ways but this is wholly untrue most of the time.  What's truly disappointing is paying 40 dollars for this game, which lacks any appreciable cut scenes, fleshed out story, unit animations, complex combat system or pervasive mulitplayer/modding community and yet experiencing Slitherine's absolute gall at asking for 20 dollars a scant year later for what amounts to a small expansion.  Seriously? You just charged us the price of a triple A game, despite obviously providing a much simpler experience and you can't give us some goodies and support before you hit us up again for money?
If you can get it on sale, and like TBSes or WH40K, this game is a solid 7.
Otherwise, 6/10.

now that the game's finally out i can make another 1-sentence summary of it instead of actually reviewing it (but nah I feel like this game deserves some unbiased nitpicking instead of me ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on it and leaving)
it's a game that really wanted to be contra mixed with monster hunter. It feels like the developers played and loved MH, but in the end didn't truly know why the features in MH made it what it is.
When the kickstarter first went up one of the big things I laughed at was the fact that they wrote "add in a little monster hunter and you got our game" or something like that when describing the features. Now that the game's out, it's not immediately apparent, but it's true. Most criticizable aspects of the game stem from the fact that it wants to emulate Monster Hunter.
The missions are stale, primarily because they use the exact same 3 modes that MH has: kill X small enemies, gather X items on the field, or kill X boss monster. Rarely, the game will also have "talk to this NPC" quests also but that's negligible since they're just preludes to one of the other types of missions. They're meant to introduce the level by having you navigate it for specific area.
Additionally, upgrades and bonuses are gained through the same general "luck of the drop" system Monster Hunter is both rewarded and criticized for. This system is in place in Monster Hunter because the monster duels are not only fun but also dangerous enough to make players want to play it safe and stick to familiar tactics at first. Repeating the boss a couple times for certain drops, or changing weapon or strategy to try to get a drop that doesn't match your playstyle, are ways of making Monster Hunter more enjoyable. You get to see how the monsters are designed to act differently in different situations, plus with the tight combat already in place, it's a thrill either way.
That's not in Mercenary Kings. in MK, you dodge the same 3-5 attacks over and over, shoot the weak point (usually the back) of a boss, and eventually it goes down or is left open to capture. These nuances are found in MH as well, but aren't put there for the same reason. The lack of health bars in Monster Hunter is to encourage awareness in the player. They want you to look for signs of weakness, signs of battle damage in the creature you're hunting. a health bar would ruin the point of that. In Merc Kings, the enemy constantly flashes bright red when they're injured enough to be captured, so with zero subtlety, it just says you're 2/3rds done already.
Monster drops in MH were to indicate playstyle in a way. You could only get the tail of a monster if you were attacking its back. You could only get the horns if you actually were able to smash the horns off with a kill, or if you could capture it with the horns perfectly intact still (meaning no face hits). MK is just pure percentile chance rewarding you for the kill.
I don't HATE the game, because I still enjoy the simplistic gameplay and item grinding to some extent, but I think it's fine to like a game while also knowing it's full of developer mistakes.
For $10 I think it's a perfectly dandy 2D platformer monster hunter knockoff with full online co-op.

This is not a complete dissaproval of the game, but it certainly has some huge flaws which should be considered before buying.
Rage is a game of famus studio id Software, which still got much fame credits from Wolfenstein, Doom and Quake (till part 3) but after that failed to develop along with rest.
Rage is gameplay wise an old school shooter set in post apocalyptic earth, after a huge asteroid hit earth. The silent protagonist emerges from bunker called "ark" quite some time later. Due to the fact that he got some nanites into his body he is quite an Ubermensch as he starts to kill entire bandit bases not 5 minutes after the beginning, as he immideately gets thrown into the action. This is already quite most of the very thin story.
Gameplay is as already mentioned rather oldschool-shooter like without any coversystem, third person or such things. Also there is a very limited stealth system with weapons like a crossbow, but then again there is no real use in stealth.  A point where Rage does have some moderately modern impact is this pesky autoheal feature, so that after hiding for about 10 seconds you are fully healed a make craftable items like bandages or health booster rather pointless.
Craftable? Yes, you read right. You can loot and buy spare parts and reciepes to construct better ammo, consumables and gadgets like exploding RC cars, sentry turrets and sentry bots. Sounds nice but less useful than you might think.
For the weapons arsenal: its really standard. Fists, pistol, assault rifle, shotgun, crossbow, sniper rifle, machine gun, rocket launcher and a pulse gun. furthermore (I think via DLC) you get an SMG like nail gun. These guns get also different ammo, like armor piercing, EMP slugs and so on, but nothing to get too exciting over.
For the world: Rage is promoted as an open world shooter. You get a buggy (which you can exchange for a better one) to drive thorugh some sandy, rocky canyons. There is barely anything to explore. You just drive from you homebase/town to the mission and back. No reason to explore the world. All that happends is that you get randomly attacked by suddenly spawning raider buggys. Quite boring.
The levels: You think a call of duty had straight forward levels? Well, Rage lets a CoD look like an open worlds RPG like Fallout. You absolutely have zero chance to go the wrong way, as there is no way. Almost everything looks the same. I mean, ok, i get it, it's post apocalyptic but does EVERYTHING to be just in grey and sandy-yellow? Only few levels differ from this style and manage to create some atmosphere. Also the levels design is very cheap. You gun your way through an area, pick up the final item/press the final button and suddenly there is a formerly closed door or a zipline which brings you back the start where you can leave the level. The WORST THING is that each level gets reused in cheap ways, so that you have to revisit a level with a different objective, but relive the level almost the same just reversed. I understand that you reuse game assets, but the way it was done here just looks cheap. The absolute joke is the end of the game. You get what looks like another boring mission, drive from A to B, enter level C. You gun down hordes of stupid enemies, press some buttons and suddenly after 30 secs of video without any speech or the like the game is over.
The enemies: Some reviews praised the enemy AI. I could not imagine why. Meele types just rush you, maybe dodging once or twice. Ranged enemies stay mostly in cover and throw grenades from time to time. If you get to close they go in to bash you. But there is nothing you haven't seen in 1998's Half Life. Another point is the missing diversity. You shoot you way thorugh dungeons with dozends of the same mutants. Literally the SAME. All in all there are maybe each half a dozend skins for raiders and mutants. But you almost always encounter just one or two and the same time as they are different tribes.
Graphics & sound: Sound is nice. I enjoyed it in 5.1 sourround. Graphics: Rage gets promoted as "Powered by id's revolutionary id Tech 5 technology" with "jaw dropping graphics". This is just a bad joke or marketing lie. NPC skins in the town areas may be quite decent and some shader effects from explosions or energy weapons may look nice, but in generell the graphics were and are mediocre. Especially the world textures look horrible, but smallish indoor levels as well.
Playtime: I took my time, did all the boring, repeating side missions, did all the boring racings to tune my cars up to max eg, and saw the ending after little more than 20 hours. The most interesting missions and the (by far) most fun boss fight were included in the Scorcherers DLC, so consider buying this if you decide to buy Rage.
Summary: Would I recommend Rage? Well, at least not for 25€ (incl. DLC). You could consider it if there is some like 75% sale and you are looking for a straight forward ego shooter and don't care about story.

Deus-Honored: Steampunk Revolution
While obviously it's not a guarantee, there's a pretty good chance you'll like this game if you enjoyed Deus Ex: Human Revolution (DXHR). The games have a -lot- in common, and that's a good thing. Graphically, the games are very different, though each has its own easily identifiable, unique look. For Dishonored, it's the art style in a steampunk setting, and for DXHR, it's the gold-and-black coloring throughout the game and its cyberpunk setting. Obviously, the music of each game is extremely different as well, but neither game has bothersome music. To be fair, though, despite having beaten both games three times so far, I cannot recall a single song from either game when I'm not playing them.
So how are these games alike? The gameplay. In each, you are exploring maps with multiple paths to an objective. The more direct paths are typically more filled with enemies and security devices, while the indirect paths have less opposition/security and often rewards. Both games can be played stealthy, taking your time and surgically rendering baddie after baddie unconscious (or killing if you'd like), hiding their bodies from their friends, and both can also be played with the "direct" approach, engaging the enemy in combat, which can be very deadly for the player. Heck, on normal difficulty, 3 gunshots will kill the player in Dishonored, so you're certainly rewarded for being sneaky.
I've tried the combat in both games, though, and despite my general preference for modern/futuristic settings and equipment, Dishonored has the better combat in my opinion, as it doesn't feel like any other game, but feels fully competent on its own with its quick sword-swings and flintlock pistol-firing, mixed with summoning rat swarms, contesting sword-locks, etc. DXHR's combat feels like most shooters without any standout features to make it memorable. Even your main targets can either be taken on in combat or using clever ways to kill them or make them commit suicide, or even save their lives but ruin them or make them disappear. DXHR just had poorly executed forced boss battles in the main game, though the Director's Cut (worth it!) added ways for a hacker to kill bosses, such as turrets and robots.
Oh, back to summoning rat swarms, another similarity between these two titles is the reward of new passive and active powers/augments. Throughout the games, you can seek out items to give you what amounts to skill points you can invest and spend in various abilities, making you jump higher (actually that's in both games) and other differing things. Blink is a teleportation "spell," and boy is it fun. See an enemy below you while you're perched above like Batman? Poof, you teleport right behind him, choke him out, then teleport away to hide the body before his buddies see you. Blink is just euphoric to use, and as long as you wait like 3 or 4 seconds before using another power, all the mana you spend to cast it regens. So. Good. I would have to say I enjoyed Dishonored's powers much more than Deus Ex's, as well as the gear you get, and the micromanagement of the Diablo-style DXHR inventory distracts from playing the game, while Dishonored just lets you carry every weapon you can get in the game until you max out your potions/ammo, etc. for each type of gun/weapon/item.
The stories are drastically different, and I can't really say which I like better, because they're both quite good in their own right; both the writing and the presentation. Dishonored's plot is more focused and easy to keep up with, though it does have some little twists/surprising facts and events. DXHR, on the other hand, has a main storyline that is more convoluted and philosophical than Dishonored, but they are both great for the games that they're in. DXHR only has one ending, but Dishonored has two: one you get if you don't kill any (or very many) humanoids, and one you get if you kill a lot of folks.
Dishonored does -not- have city hubs like DXHR does, though. It is divided into a prologue and 9 missions, with a small map where you can talk to people and make purchases on in between missions. In DXHR, on the other hand, there are two cities you can walk all over, featuring hidden items, side quests, and much more. Since Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines is my favorite game, it should be no surprise that I prefer the city hubs over Dishonored's mission areas, but to be completely fair, Dishonored has some of the finest mission hubs I've seen. Although I'm a heretic who completed but didn't really like the original Deus Ex, the mission maps in Dishonored are kinda like that...like how Liberty Island had people on the outskirts of the mission area who you could buy from, who could give you info on completing the mission, etc. I really liked that aspect of that game, and I think it's done like that in Dishonored, whereas it wasn't really that way in DXHR.
Although DXHR has DLC and I thought it was decent, Dishonored has a lot more DLC. One is a "challenge maps" sort of thing. It takes everything from combat to power use outside of combat and tests you to your limits. If that's your thing, then there ya go. I'm more of a story/progress fan, so the other two DLCs, The Knife of Dunwall and The Brigmore Witches, appealed more to me, as it is a two-part (3 missions each, so a total of 6 missions) story DLC. Each has a lazy map...what I mean by that those two DLCs have one map each that has been repopulated with enemies (a different faction on one) and new security devices and loot, but it's almost the same map as the original game. You start at the end of the level instead of the beginning, and run through the same map with very, very minor changes. If you get them for cheap, they're certainly worth playing, though, as there is a fair amount of new content in them.
This sounds like a competition, but both of these are games that I love, and I would highly recommend both of them if stealth games with multiple approaches, gradual ability upgrades, and nonlethal options appeal to you. They're two of my favorite games.

From the start I was well, skeptical if I was going to like this game or even play it much. After sitting down for about 30 minutes to give it a chance I found out a lot. The combat was so immersive and challenging, I just plain loved it, something that I'd rarely experienced before, but nothing quite like this. Then their was the story. To put it bluntly the story was so captivating and elegant. I mean I genuinely cared about what I did and how it might affect the story and the characters around me, including poor Emily. Then one of my favorite aspect of the game was the abilities, my god I've never enjoyed special power so much in a game ever! Blink itself would have been enough, but no so many things to choose from and all of them had been so perfectly balanced and made that it was hard not to just enjoy it so much. Like the other Trine games, this is a puzzle platformer featuring a wizard, thief, and knight.  Unlike the previous games, Trine 3 features a fully 3D environment and does away with character progression / customization.  Characters generally feel like stripped down versions of their former selves, but the thief has a new ability to tie objects together with rope, leading to some very interesting possibilities.  The 3D movement looks very nice, and can lead to some interesting combat (especially the final boss fight), but takes some getting used to and often feels unnecessary.  I feel like another 2D game would have been better, especially since the story ends abruptly with the villain still at large and the heroes having accomplished very little... as though development took longer than expected, and the full game couldn't be completed due to time/budget constraints.  All told, I don't like Trine 3 as much as I liked previous Trine games, but I still like it... and hopefully I'll have the chance to finish it someday.

Honestly, a lot of Trine fans didn't play this because 'it's short', 'it's different', 'it's short', 'it's different' or somesuch babyish whingery. If you liked Trine, if you're a fan, just shut up and give this a go, you'll actually have more fun playing the game than you would stitting around wondering how it might suck. Not everything has to be exactly the same all the time. And, you will like it.
My only gripe is that I didn't really need to go hunting for the collectables this time. They were mostly placed in my path. Many of the abilities from the previous games have been removed. Some may be due to the transition to full 3D, but not all can be justified with that. The story also ends abruptly with a cliffhanger, just when it feels like it's about to go into "act 2."
Another point of note about the transition to 3D is that the camera is fixed at such a low angle that it's difficult to judge depth. In several situations, this makes platforming harder. However, the level designers seem to have been aware of that, and made sure that most of the jumping is still done sideways.
For starters, it still has the gorgeous environments that have remained throughout the series. It also has a couple of interesting new mechanics, such as Zoya being able to tie objects together, and Amadeus being able to slam his boxes down on top of enemies. Zoya's rope now also acts like a physical rope instead of clipping through objects. The level select also allows you to go back to any checkpoint instead of just the beginning of the level, to make it easier to find the collectibles you've missed. Additonally, what you do get of the story actually feels like a story this time, instead of just an excuse plot. It even gives some additional backstory to the events of the first game.
If it didn't feel so unfinished, I would say that it's better than Trine 1 but worse than Trine 2. However, since it does feel so unfinished, it left me feeling very disappointed.

Every Paradox game focuses on a part of history and an aspect of strategy gaming that makes that period special. Europa tackles one of the longest periods (CKII actually being the longest with DLC) and has you play a nation as the world enters the Rennaisance all the way until the death of Napoleon. No game gives you the amount of options or challenges that EU4 does and for years the game has improved with constant updates.
A lot of people say that the game is ruined without DLC but they don't know what it was like before. The game now even with no DLC is now deeper and feature complete than it was at launch thanks to the free patches that accompany ever DLC release. The DLC usually releases extras that add more depth to an already existing part of the game or additional flavor/flair to a segement of the world. Sometimes useful, some would argue balance breaking, features are locked behind DLC but this is rare and the arguments are blown out of proportion. If you worry that you could be missing core-upgrades then go for the founder pack as it includes the "Important Features" DLC that people will fuss about.
If you enjoy strategy games and are willing to put in a little time to learn how to play (YouTube Tutorials are highly recommended) then you will find nothing more engrossing in the genre unless you are willing to dedicate an entire table in your house to the game board and a rulebook/result reference the size of an old phonebook.

Salt and Sanctuary seems to be one of those games that I play for half an hour, close, and then immediately reopen. The game delivers a bloody good time with a dreary atmosphere and narrative to boot. The soundtrack is very Diablo-esque with some more Perfect Circle and Castlevania influences (that alone should be enough to convince you). Sure it still has a few quirks, like the main menu does not pause the game despite there being no online multiplayer (so only stop when you're sure you're safe), upgrading equipment feels a bit underwhelming (but still necessary) when there COULD be new loot right around the corner, and checkpoints are nonexistent, as instead of bonfires, you have very rare Sanctuaries where you level up, hire shops, and heal. So yes, you have to do a lot of backtracking, but you'll need to do all the level grinding you can to hold your own against the tougher enemies.
I should point out that this game is not for everyone. It's barely for me, but I can't put it down. A second player is almost a necessity. It's going to make you salty, but you're going to enjoy every minute of it.

I must say, I wasn't expecting such an original, refreshing and really captivating experience when I started the game for the first time. For what I had seen, it looked like an interesting adventure game with an interesting story.
What I played, or, more likely, what I experienced was so much more. I liked...basically, everything about it. The unique style, the story, the characters...the more you progress in the story, the more you really feel...involved in it. This game, even though having a simple appearance is, for me, a true hidden pearl. Being someone who really likes good stories, I was enthralled by it from beginning to end. I smiled, I laughed, I frowned, I worried, I pondered...my heart strings were pulled here and there too. (...Well, here and there, do not get me wrong. It was here and there, but the strings made a quintuple loop and a leap of faith into an ocean of feels before coming back and high-kicking the heart into pieces)
So, for me, the story was on point. On a more "gaming" aspect, some of the puzzles were simple. Some other puzzles my brain wished it could've got out my ear to explode somewhere safe. I was baffled by some of the things the game was able to do by times. Puzzles, items that you can combine...it's an adventure game. Sometimes simple, sometimes...not so much!
The humor made me smile and laugh, I really cannot find a joke or a comic relief that wasn't well done there (Although I must say some of them were...let's just weird, and one was even a bit disturbing in a...bad-good way????).
So...yeah. This game is really something I won't forget. It was an incredible adventure, original, with clever ideas and a well put story that is, for me, really interesting, keeping it's most important mysteries hidden until the end.
It's really something that should have more attention in my opinion, and is better experienced when you know nothing about it, like said in the beginning. It's really something you must play for yourself.
A story you must take a part in. A little adventure where you'll have a part in.
........And like, seriously, you cannot resist the Main Character's level of cute and loveliness.
Everyone who worked on it : it's something incredible, thank you so much!

I won't include any SPOILERS in this review, but I will include a few TIPS for new players (so you don't need to use a walk through).  If this sounds like you, read on!
OneShot is a game unlike any other I have ever played.  The basics of the game are you play as Niko exploring the world in isometric and side-profile fashion, looking for clues, and solving puzzles.  The UNIQUE aspect of this game is that is breaks down the fourth wall - the wall between the game and your life.  TIPS:  The first time the wall is broken you should be able to figure out the solution on your own.  HOWEVER.  Later in the game, there is a puzzle that requires you accessing the game's Steam folder, rather than the folder you previously accessed to solve the first out-of-game puzzle.  I never would have guessed this in a million years so I consulted a walkthrough.  You might have to as well (which doesn't detract from the game at all) but let me just say that the file you want is an EXECUTABLE (.exe) file in the game folder shaped like a clover leaf.
Whether you use a walkthrough like I did or muddle through on your own, OneShot is an experience you will never forget.  I recommend this game to EVERYONE, whether you like this style of game or not, whether you like the artwork and screenshots or not.  This game TRULY goes "above and beyond".

Lackluster and anticlimatic are about the right words that can be used to sum up this game.
The combat is decent. It's nothing awe inspiring, but it holds its own. The AI seems a little smarter than the norm, as it will allow squads of enemies to work as teams to advance, retreat, or attempt to outflank the player. It has its holes that can be exploited and sometimes does some dumb things, but for the most part provided for satisfying combat.
Car combat can be a little frustrating due to clunky controls. It also seems to serve no point other than a novelty or to disguise the game world to seem more open and exansive. It is mostly a boring affair that wouldn't have been missed if it was not in the game.
There is an illusion of an open world, but the game areas are actually quite linear. There are many side missions that seem pointless and unrewarding. It probably didn't help that rewards were mysterious and the game is not very forthcoming in communicating what they were. They also tell little about the world you are in. Very thin and bland and could easily be avoided, in favor of sticking with the main mission, without much loss to the experience whatsoever. The game world itself felt rather shallow and it was difficult to relate to or care about anyone or anything within it.
Lastly, and probably my biggest gripe, the game just seems to abruptly end in a very anticlimatic fashion. There really wasn't any real main antigonist in the game. You hear rumors and details of the promise of some kind of rival that the player may have to face, but none of it ever comes to fruition. There is never even a single encounter, dialogue, or anything with a supposed main antagonist. The ending of the game lacks any kind of boss encounter at all, even though it leads the player to believe that one should be expected. It's as if the developers ran out of time and resources to flesh out anything the game teases the player with and just abruptly ends. Very lackluster and disappointing, nearly feeling like a waste of time.
Only get it if you have a serious hankering for a single player FPS and you've played everything better already. Only get it on sale as well. Or better yet, save your time and play something better.

A fun romp through side-scrolling shooty action. The game plays very similarly to Metal Slug and games of that nature but with a bit more forgiveness. Gameplay's pretty standard and fun without too much innovation in terms of controls and whatnot but what keeps it interesting is the customizable weapons. You completely customize your loadout with 6 different weapon parts at any given time that have different stats that affect how your character plays. Will you take a handgun with only 2 parts and be super fast and agile but with limited firepower? Will you take a huge minigun with tons of ammo that pierces walls and completely destroys things before it gets on screen with the side-effects of moving slower than a slug in molasses? The entire game revolves around finding loot to craft new weapons and mods that change how you play your character. It works extremely well because of the focus that it has on variety and uniqueness to each weapon. It's not perfectly balanced yet but it's still in development so it's not an issue. An excellent game that really gets the visceral fun of just raining bullets down pat.

Trine 3 is a puzzel/adventure game which uses both 2D and 3D, while Trine 1 & 2 are only 2D, or actually 2.5D. The 3D could be a refreshing twist if it wasn't for the weird perspective it can give you at times, resulting in you missing jumps etc. Playing with the wizard wasn't suited for 3D either,  moving your boxes around was a pain. You'll quickly notice they implemented 3D but didn't really optimize the game enough for it to work as they intended.
First, let's talk about what will probably be the first thing you'll notice when playing Trine 3, or any of the Trine's for that matter. The scenery looks absolutely amazing and you'll come across beautiful locations every few minutes. I found myself taking loads of screenshots throughout every level. The environment keep changing aswell, one moment you're walking in a dungeon, and the next moment you're walking on a beach or through a beautiful breathtaking forest.
Trine 3 has a quite long introduction in which you get to know all of the 3 characters and their skills/mechanics. This takes a bit to long, but this also explains the story about how the 3 of them get together. You can switch between the 3 characters whenever you want and they all play different. While exploring the level you'll need to solve small puzzels. Most of them wont really be much of a challenge since they're quite simpel. There are 8 main missions and a few side missions which you can complete in about 6-10 hours. I personally found myself enjoying Trine (any of them) alot more together with a friend. Helping eachother through the levels by using your characters unique abilities, while messing around a bit was really fun.
The trine 3 soundtrack is amazing to listen too, and never gets boring. Unfortunately Trine 3 has alot of bugs. Way more than Trine 1 and 2 did. Alot of buggy animations and objects. But those bugs gave me and my friend things to laugh at and mess around with as well. Luckily the game itself runs really smooth. Besides this, an annoying problem I ran into is that the game forces you to collect gems in each level. you'll need a certain amount of gems to progress to the next chapter. And although this might be no problem for the achievement/collectable hunters, it's much less enjoyable if you're just having fun with a friend not focussing on collecting all the gems.
Unfortunately combat has been dumbed down aswell, it has never been the strong point of the series but is now even easier. Just switch to pontius(the knight) and spam your mousebutton until everyone is dead. The removal of upgrading your characters and their skills doesn't really help with this either.
Overall, I still recommend this game if you're looking for a fun co-op game with a friend. If you're planning on playing this by yourself, you might get bored after a while. Now is it the best Trine? No. Trine 1 and 2 are better if you ask me, but that doesn't mean the game is not enjoyable. It has amazing art, fun levels to explore and an interesting twist because of the 2D/3D mechanic.

What can I say about Defense Grid, other than it's the best tower defense game I've ever played, and I've played a lot.
The graphics are beautiful, and gameplay is addictive. As with most TD games, tower placement is key, and I feel that the towers are fairly evenly balanced (although I've seen on YouTube how the inferno towers are kinda OP in mass). Every map has a story mode along with a variety of map challanges (use only level 1 towers, tougher enemies, cores that do not float back to their housing, etc) making replayability very high. It also has the standard bronze/silver/gold medal to try to achieve from the maps and thier challanges. There's also a bunch of DLC that has been released for this game, extending the life of it even more.
Speaking of the story, it's pretty solid. You're fighting back an alien invasion while trying to power on the Defense Grid of the planet. You pretty much get the first encounter to defeat them and if you don't smack them completely, in the first go, they flee to another part of the map, immediately spawn (if someone is there or not) and start going through their pattern. By the time you get to the location where they spawned, you get a few prescious seconds to attack them before they flee again. Now, you could leave the game running where they last spawned and eventually they will come back to that location, but that is boreing. This is not just one boss- but one boss they use over an over again.
Also, the massive amount of levels are mostly repeats. I could have done with a more cogent/crafted set of story driven levels, one leading to the other, or an open world, or a big overworld map, but this constant revisiting of places I just wooped up on and finding them completely repopulated with bosses that flee and hostages and all that . . . jeez. A conquer and conquest strategy game doesn't get this in-depth and realistic. There are many aspects in this game that I find to be the most astonishing that prove it different than others.
-Graphics-
The graphics in HOI4 are amazing. The top down world view makes it feel like a board game like Risk or something, but the detail when you zoom into a country is awesome. Factories, mountains, cities, and so much more are all designed in beautiful graphics.
-Political Changes-
When you change your country's political party (ex: Democracy to Fascism) the country's name, and flag changes! No other strategy game changes the flag let alone shows it, whether it simply adds a soviet anchor to it, or it changes the flag completely. The names are also very creative too, for example, Romania can become the People's Republic of Romania.
-Country Choice-
Want to take on the world as Luxembourg? Want to bring kangaroo's to the world as Australia? You can play as any country that was around during world war 2 (not EVERY country, but over 90% of the countries at the time). It's possible to conquor the world as any country if you're smart and learn the tactics of your enemies.
-Research Tree-
The research tree is huge. With over 70 research options to research, from tank armor, to nuclear fission, to simple oil plants. All countries start at different stages in their research, whether they're still using WW1 technology, or they're using high tech up to date technology.
-Troop Combat-
It's INSANE how in depth and realistic troops are. You have to give them a front line, an offensive line, a garrison area, and so much more. It may sound confusing but it gets easy once you understand what the different options mean.
-Realism-
The historical accuracy of the game is amazing. There's a huge list of political leaders who can be elected per country, and they were all real people! Alf Landon elected instead of Franklin D. Roosevelt in America? It can happen! Also, countries will be historically accurate (if you turn it on) as long as you don't interfere with them. Real battles happen such as the anexing of Ethiopia as Italy.
-Conclusion-
When I first saw this game, I thought it was just a civilization clone. But that thought is long gone. This game deserves a Triple-A title. Though it is a little tough to get into, watching a couple tutorials online will help you start out and learn from there. The fun never ends, it's so addicting.

So what is Mercenary Kings?  One part Metal Slug, with an inventory and crafting system, with that familiar 4 player game play.  Either for a 'serious' play, or casual, it's honestly fun.  Great old school handling and the soundtrack is a nice mix of classic bit work and modern rock.
The inventory and crafting systems are pretty simple.  You need X amounts of Y materials to craft Z part for your gun.  Plus some cash.  And for those of you who like to customize and build and have MULTIPLE gun builds? They have you covered.  Everything from pistols, carbines, assault rifles, shotguns, machine guns, toilets, and trombone's (to name a few), with elemental ammo, armor piercing, buckshot.  Lots of options here for scoring some ludicrous gibs (yes!).  OH and knives too. But who needs a knife when you can build a freakin' minigun?
The game handles well, overall. You move your character, and they get there.  Feels like something taken right out of an arcade cabinet and put into your hand with such simplicity it's nuts.  Any fan of the Metal Slug franchise WILL feel right at home here.  You needn't worry.  For everyone else?  This game is quick on the uptake.  You shall find no sloppy handling here.
My one issue is that the default input is a keyboard. I would highly. HIGHLY recommend the use of a game pad.  Otherwise the keyboard controls are a bit spaced out and kindof irregular.  The gamepad makes everything RIGHT at home.
Overall, for a game that's in 'early access' it feels fairly rock solid and fairly 'done'.  Yet they keep adding to and tweaking the game.   And the price tag certainly makes this a worthwhile investment.

Captures the oldschool spirit of traditional run-and-gun games like Metal Slug while adding in a deep crafting and weapon customization system that keeps the gameplay fresh.  The gorgeous pixel art ties everything together.  Even playing it in early access I'd call this one of my favorite games in years; I really can't recommend it enough.

The definitive Grand Strategy game, in my opinion. The vast number of countries to chose from really adds to the replayability-- and all are playable (albeit lacking in flavor for many) with just the base game. I've been playing it off and on since it first came out in 2013, and there are still countries I'm looking forward to trying! The addition of unique national traditions, plus the ability to customize your country's "ideas" each game, can make each playthrough feel very different.
The focus of Europa Universalis IV (EUIV), as in most other Paradox games, is on strategy rather than tactics. You'll spend plenty of time at war with your neighbors, but the real focus is on administration: managing newly conquered lands, maintaining the balance of power, and exploring. You'll look at a
of maps and map-modes.
EUIV does have tons of DLC, which is a bit of a sore point for many players. It's certainly something to be aware of, but it shouldn't stop you from getting the game if you're otherwise interested. The game is still great without any DLC-- like I said, I've loved it since it first came out. Many of the DLCs can also be safely ignored-- anything labelled as a "content pack" is just unique unit models for specific regions, and music packs are self-explanatory. The "Expansions" are a lot more substantial, and generally add new mechanics for specific groups of countries or regions. I'd say that the only truly indispensable DLC is Common Sense, which adds the Development mechanic. Even with that, though, I'd recommend playing the base game first, and then thinking about DLCs if you like it. Wait for them to go on sale (which happens fairly regularly). With that said, if you like the game, you'll probably end up getting the major expansions at some point, and they add a lot of depth once you've mastered the basics of the game.
EUIV is not an intuitive game. You will
know what you're doing at first. Reading the wiki or the Paradox forums will help, and there are also plenty of Let's Plays up on Youtube. Just jump in, though, and be prepared to be eaten by France a few times before you even figure out what went wrong. Hell, I've been playing for 1600 hours and there are still plenty of mechanics which I don't fully understand. The feeling of satisfaction when Paris is finally yours will be all the sweeter!

Mortal Online has A LOT of potential, that being said, it's also hindered by some strange features, aspects, and requirements. Mortal Online is a sandbox, survival, mmo, that let's you do, just about, whatever you want. You can be a merchant, a hunter, a crafter, a warrior/knight, a carpenter (builder), a tamer (horses and such), the possibilities are nearly endless! The graphics look good, but this game requires the best of computers to play efficiently. Also, it is VERY realistic, but sadly, that can be a downfall sometimes. This game has no casual elements, and requires A LOT of time and investment.
Pro's:
Very Rewarding
VERY Realistic
Unique Setting for an MMO
So much to do!
Con's:
-Performance is not optimized and requires a top end machine to play on even the lowest settings.
-Very difficult (not normally a Con, but in this case, it takes SEVERAL hours, just to prepare to journey out, then, it takes SEVERAL hours to make it anywhere, and there is a very high possibility that you'll die on the way, losing all of the things you gathered before leaving..resetting your progress. Prepare to die... in 2D! Most people wouldn't really think a 2D Dark Souls-ish would work out, but Salt and Sanctuary does exactly the opposite. The combat system/controls is similar to the Souls series with 1 or 2handing weapons, parry & riposte, combat rolling and equipment load among others. The leveling system is different, where you need to spend points in a MASSIVE talent tree (if you would spend a life time on it then you could truly become a Jack-Of-All-Trades).
The levels themselves are quite short (but shouldn't be considered a bad thing), for example that when i defeated the first boss i managed to find the third (and later on the second) boss in as short as 10 minutes. It is worth checking out for anybody who is into Action RPG's. Stay salty my friends.

Salt and Sanctuary is a 2D hardcore action RPG which is obvious Dark Souls clone, but offers enough deep gameplay to stand tall on its own.
The game might not be original in the mechanics, but the original art style and sounds blow me away.
There are about 100 different monster types, including 23  bosses. As was the case in Dark Souls, figuring out when it's best to block or roll is very important. The game also offers a wide variety of weapons with unique move sets.
There's even stats for Strength, Dexterity and Magic that scale your weapon damage output on an E through S ranking system.
Salt and Sanctuary wants new players to feel lost and makes memorising its locations part of the challenge.
Each area is littered with secrets, hidden items and shortcuts that were previously separated by hours of playtime.
Overall, despite some minor bugs, Salt and Sanctuary is one of the early contenders for indie game of the year.

I got this on sale (I would recommend that if you're interested in it, you wait for the sale), and when I first started playing the first real mission, my thoughts and feelings were positive. I thought, "Oh! This is like if Fable were set in Gangs of New York - let's see where this goes..." I haven't played the DLCs, and to be honest, I won't, even though this is one of the few Steam purchases of mine to actually work on my machine in recent years - but that's another story.
The game itself is good, if frustrating, I'll simply list the pros and cons.
The Pros:
Evocative world
Interesting architecture
Interesting powers
Enemy AI reacts to missing buddies
The Cons:
Terrain clipping/bumping into things that it looks like you shouldn't
Controls so sensitive and finicky that even when remapped, you'll end up reloading saves because the controls got you hosed instead of the game actually being difficult
The Blink power not having a clear targeting reticule, especially when you're using it to move physically upwards
The Dark Vision power sounding like Corvo is saying "It Hunts Dice" every time it's activated
The game actively punishes you for killing enemies of the state
Shallow story line that's difficult to care about
Apparently, you're a doctor also; you can flawlessly put people to sleep every time in seconds without risking breaking their necks ever or suffering them smashing you in the balls, not to mention the potential for brain damage, eye damage and possible broken/dislocated bones
The game really doesn't take long to play at all
The game is linear with a veneer of choice overlaid onto it
To be honest, Tenchu Z is a better, longer and more challenging stealth game - it does practically everything that this game does but, you know, smoother. It's not that I didn't like Dishonored (must remember the American spelling), but to me it felt like a game that doesn't fill its potential. It could've been expansive and immersive like the Fable series meets Fallout New Vegas, or it could've been dark as hell like Gangs of New York - it could've been both those things. But it's like Diet Gangs of New York meets Fable the demo.
Don't get me wrong, it's a good game, but it could've been so much more.
Being able to create your own character would've been nice too...
...But overall, I recommend this game.

This game is the most broken turn-based "tactical" shooter I've seen.  Cover means nothing (you will be shot through it), line of sight means nothing (you will be shot when not in it), range means nothing (you will be shot from miles away while behind cover and out of line of sight), grenade arcs mean nothing (it will bounce off of objects on its way to the destination and then detonate to damage anything within about 6 inches)... you get the picture.  The tutorial gets you all set up for something... and then throws you into the first mission against about a dozen enemies where you have no choice but to engage them in a bottleneck.  Tactically, this sound viable right?  Consider the previous issues and you'll relaize it's an exercise in frustration.
It has nothing to do with learning the mechanics.  The mechanics are broken.  There is almost no chance for tactics.  What you end up doing is trying to trick the AI into bumrushing you where you can defend yourself.  Hopefully... but even then you have 3 men against a dozen.  You get overwhlmed.  If anyone dies at any time, it's over.
Listen, I'm stubborn.  I gave this game a shot several times.  I have major problems getting past the first mission.  Most people do.  It's that bad, and it never gets better.  Avoid this game.  Do not even buy it on sale for a dollar; it's not worth the aggrivation and the devs shouldn't be rewarded in any way for this garbage.
Love tactical games like this?  Try Breach & Clear... for a cheap title, at least that game works.

Short version: A big surprise. If you like tower defense at all and don't mind FPS, give it a shot. A great blend of strategy + action.
Long version: Sanctum is great for TD fans that either like or don't mind some FPS action in their games. The two aspects blend together very well; on lower difficulties, one can pretty easily focus on one over the other and do fine, while on higher difficulties both are needed pretty equally. Additionally, there are towers that help your shots and a gun that helps your towers, ensuring that the two aren't just separate parts of the same game but actually integrated together.
Even aside from FPS tactics, there's a fair amount more strategy than in most TD games, as the player must build a map for the enemies to travel on and building good maps can be necessary for survival. Building a map that makes enemies take longer to travel necessarily means less space for defensive towers, balancing the game with a choice of longer path or more firepower. And of course, correct positioning of towers for the most effective use of each one is as important as always in a TD game. Even the size of certain towers can be a strategic point for ensuring the player can move around flexibly.
One can bring 3 different guns and up to 6 different towers to maps, ensuring many different ways to play the game, although the total number of guns and towers may be a bit low to take full advantage of that.
If there's one problem I have with the game it's that some of the map designs come off as very lazy, but you'll largely forget about that when constructing a maze. I haven't played much multiplayer or survival mode myself, but in later waves of longer games, guns can also come to be seemingly ineffectual, as damage doesn't scale at all with the growing power of enemies. Sanctum does what it does near perfectly and there are very few changes I would consider making to improve it.

I have a great personal love for the warhammer game and the ideas behind the races, for quite a few years I played the warhammer 40k epic game and this game certainly bring sback a lot of the same things as WH40KEpic does and if you are a fan of warhammer 40k and turn based strategy I would highly recommend this game.
The good:
- A large variaty of units all different (to a greater or lesser degree).
- Each unit has a different role on the battlefield.
- There is a storyline and you get to pick a few responses allowing you to become more immersed.
- Each move of a unit have meaning.
- Pre-battle deployment is very important.
- selecting the right mix of unit is important and there is a need to get more than one kind.
The bad:
- The amount of men/vehicles in each unit is displayed by a number rather than each member visible on the screen.
- The AI seem to enjoy just mass assault and not much else, this sadly makes most of the battles not very varied.
- The AI have no clue how to effective use of it's unit and will often go for a low value soft target as oppose to letting the big guns slowly wear down the big heavily armored units. The downside is that heavy units usually gets really good and you can annihilate the enemy by throwing cannon fooder at the AI, however basic units will rarely survive for long.
- Each mission have a limit over how many units you can own/deploy, this means that the game quickly becomes about massed armored assaults whyere infantry have little real purpose except standing behind the armor and grabbing the objectives.
- Most of the battles is about grabbing X amount of objective spots, I found that a little dull. Especially since they are usually placed that it means you also have to annihilate the entire opposing force.
- Enemy command units while tough have a nasty habit of parking themsleves in the open on the front line to be fairly easily desposed off. With grand commanders like no wonder the AI have such poor tactics.
- Killing the enemy commander have no real effect on the battle.
- Enemy commanders fail to have significant impact on the battle. Yes I am really annoyed at the pointlessness of them.
- Each battle is LONG so if you want a full battle beware it will take probably between 1 hour and 1h 30m to play one battle.
- Some unit variants seem to have no purpose.
- It is not always clear what effect a tile will have on a unit.
- each weapon have a ton of statistic, but little to enable you to decide if it is a good or a bad unit when you are starting out.
- a minor point but I was really sadden that there was no option to customize your titans considering how many options other units has this seems like and oversight.
Overall the experience despite the flaws is overall good and very engaging, I have played several games like this over the years and this is in many ways one of the better ones and overall really well designed. The only real issue I have is that it doesn't feel (visually and mechanically) like a recent game, but rather as a game that could easily have been made 10+ years ago.
(and because I like the idea of scores!)
Art: 6 (it's good and fits but it isn't impressive)
Combat: 7 (lots of option everythign feels meaningful, however the AI and focus on heavy units brings the game down a bit)
Interface: 5 (clear and with a lot of options right at your fingers, as long as you already knows what everything means)
Story: 7 (it's a warhammer 40k story it's about war, fits well but could use a bit more... life).
Voice acting: 8 (surprisingly good)
Level design: 7 (excellent level design with interesting challenges to overcome, only downside it is a design that mostly make things difficult rather than enabling certain units to really shine).
Overall: 7 (or 6.7 if you want to be exact)

A surprisingly good turn based strategy Warhammer 40,000 game considering the game looks like it is using the old panzer tanks hexcell based engine. Multiple unit choices for the Imperial Guard Steel Legion, the Orcs and the three Space Marine Chapters (Blood Angels, Ultra Marines and Salamanders). Plenty of tank types and/or variants is where this game shines as there are many different weapon types and load outs depending on the tank type.
This game is set during the Armageddon campaign of 40k lore where Commissar Yarrick first takes on Ork Warlord Thrakka at Hades Hive. The game sticks mainly to the cannon lore, but there are one or two surprises along the way. You eventually get to use 'hero' units towards the end of the game. (Sorry but no spoilers - if you want to know, play the game!)
Graphics are a bit dated, but the game is using a dated engine, but this can be forgiven as the game play is pretty solid. You get a tutorial campaign, then the main campaign which is broken down into three acts. There are extra missions which you can play if you get tired of the main campaign and a recent free dlc has added an additional 5 extra missions that can be played.
MP is good depending on who you are playing, but i feel that MP needs to have some kind of time limit in the case of players who aren't making any moves over a period of time. IMHO i feel that a player should forfeit a match if they haven't made a single move within a 2 to 4 weeks time. An option to force forfeit in MP would be appreciated from the devs. :)
Overall i rate the game 7.1 / 10.

It has a lot of potential, and unlike some of the other 40k games out there, it shows that this developer has an understanding of the universe and as such I would recommend this if you're a 40k fan, if for nothing else, help support a developer who might actually contribute a lot to this franchise and possible genre in the future, I'd love if they sold enough to focus on a much more detailed and improved version because while this game isn't top notch, it reeks of potential and it truly shows the passion of the developer.

First things first, I bought this game solely for the multiplayer.
This game is a great improvement over the first, but my singleplayer experience was ruined by various bugs and glitches.
They started off small in the beginning of the game, small graphics glitches, floating objects, getting stuck on terrain, etc.
Near the end of the game I ran into something awful. The game literally crashed my computer during one of the cutscenes. My pc can max this game without breaking a sweat, and this wasn't a crash to desktop, the computer completely turned off. When I powered back up my save file was corrupt. This is why I haven't even finished the single player yet, even though it is so short.
Was I devasted? Not really, multiplayer was unaffected in any way. The multiplayer experience in Sniper Ghost Warrior 2 is an enjoyable one, if you enjoy sniping. Matches are around 20 minutes long and often never score higher than 15 or so kills. The sniping mechanics are really great in this game.
Pros
+Good mechanics
+AR/SMG sections of first game are gone
+Multiplayer is fun
+Environments are very nice looking
Cons
-Poor story
-Very buggy
-Lack of a multiplayer community, theres hardly ever more than one server
-Crashes for unknown reasons
-Character models look horrendous
As I bought this game for the multiplayer, I would reccomend the multiplayer portion to a friend. As far as the single player experience goes, try out any of the Sniper Elite titles.

The singleplayer contains bugs where your companion literally stops and and doesn't do anything, as well as sometimes refuses to do the takedown it promised. Enemy AI will spot you easily and the only thing to really avoid that is going prone. Yet somehow your companion doesn't need to do that. I didn't got that much into the story, but as far as I can tell it's not really interesting either.
The main reason why I bought this game however was the multiplayer, it looked interesting and I always wanted to try a full on sniper vs sniper team battles taken place in a game actually optimized for sniping and stealth.
Yet even the multiplayer is poorly executed. You only have 4 multiplayer maps (without DLC) who all contain glitches. You only have 2 gamemodes: Deathmatch and Team Deathmatch. The different sniper rifles don't feel much different from eachother. Sure diferent scope/look/sound but somehow a lot of 'm feel the same. Multiplayer has only 2 zoom toggles. (singleplayer has 3 btw). The multiplayer characters are just characters from the singleplayer but still look poorly, and only 1 of those has the sniper feel ghillie suit on.
Sometimes the server disconnects online and you'll be send back to the main menu or the game will completely crash.
The graphics are OK, and actually some grass and plants actually move when you touch them which is nice.
But the overall feel to the game is just meh.
If they ever decide to make a Sniper: Ghost warrior 3, I atleast expect:
- High end graphics
- Customisable characters and snipers
- More gamemodes
- Improved maps and more variety
- Stable servers
- An actual interesting story

We have all been waiting for the next indie love affair since the adoreable undertale by toby fox. Unfortunatly i cannot say this game is that next classic. Oneshot is set to put a child in a strange world meant to save its inhabitents, with 4th wall breaking mechanics that are unique and interesting. Where it fails to meet Undertale is its iconic characters, and the ability for the player to understand what to do to proceed, and the stunning and clever soundtrack Undertale offered. This game has you set to try to combine different items in your inventory untill you figure out what small thing you missed, and deciphering exactly what file on your computer is nessasary to proceed in the game, and thats where i have my issue. The game has presented a world on the brink of destruction that the developers obviously wanted the player to look at in awe, however since im treking back and forth constantly im more frustrated by its layout than interested and the characters are cast away by the time you progress to the next area. The pitter patter of Nikos own feet is something you should get used to now because they flood any sort of ambiance of the area you are in, making it seem like there is hardly any music at all. By the time its all said and done (which for some) is frustratingly short , you are faced with an ultimatum for Niko that feels like the few and far between meaningful interactions with him are supposed to be some sort of great buildup up to this point however fails to do so. This is sad considering that the game recognizes you and Niko as a team and not just Niko the character. I personaly beleive that if there was a mini map, more interactions with Niko and the characters around him that felt enjoyable, then this game would certainly feel like it was a new Undertale for us to enjoy
I give the game a 6/10 : Certainly interesting for the one playthough that you buy it for.

This game is a good way to waste time. You might enjoy playing it for awhile but there's not much to do. Most of the gameplay is horribly designed. A lot of the textures look like they just paid for stock images. The combat is very clunky and attack telegraphing is ridiculously bad. Bugs bugs bugs everywhere, including hair textures that still, after 6 years, haven't been fixed. Movement is so slow that it's more fun to run around when you're dead. I'm not joking, when you're dead it's so much easier to move around that being alive feels like wading through quicksand in comparison. Generally speaking, this game is a chore and it's even worse if you play solo. If you decide to play, I highly suggest you join a guild so you actually have a community to interact with outside of the temporary help chat. This game is very much a sandbox when it comes to the question of 'wtf do I do'. Guilds help a lot with giving you a clear goal and providing a motivation for pvping.
To be fair, the main draw is the pvp. I haven't voluntarily participated in that much yet...by which I mean I've just been randomly murdered a bunch. Oh, by the by, there is no real penalty for murder until you've reached the lvl of a serial killer which to me makes no sense whatsoever, but hey, I'm sure the murderers enjoy it. If you want to seriously get into pvp, I highly recommend a guild. In fact guilds are one of the game's few saving graces, though there are plenty of bugs and other problems going on in that respect too. Outside of pvp however, there's the crafting.
The crafting system is passable and has some interesting aspects to it with how materials affect the appearance and stats of crafted items. However, you have to dedicate a character to crafting for it to really be worth your time. You CAN make a hybrid sure, but, because this game DOES have traditional lvling in the sense that the more you do what you do the higher your stats go, up to a cap, you will be gimped compared to a min/maxing player.
Stats are very important. Do not let people tell you that it's skill based and your stats don\'t matter. Stat differences determine your health, stamina, and mana as well as your movement speed, attack speed, damage, combat move speed, move speed while using armor, swimming speed, mount speed, etc etc. See a trend? Your skill as a player is limited by what your character is actually capable of. AKA it doesn't matter how good the player is when your character moves like a slug in comparison and does a fraction of the damage.
Ultimately it's your equipment that's most important in determining how much damage you actually do, but you CAN win with skill using crappier gear if your stats are comparible. Blocking/parrying is important but your gear and stats also affect how well you can do those too, so they won't save you against a character with better gear and stats. Damage potential is not nearly as important as movement ability. If your movement speed was determined soley by gear instead of stats maybe combat could be properly balanced, as of right now though, whoever's stats are higher and has better gear is usually going to win over skill. In that respect, this game is very much an RPG. There's nothing wrong with games that put character skill over player skill. The problem is that this game is not presented that way so you go in expecting something very different from what you actually get.
All this talk of stats brings up one of this game's main issues.  MO is guilty of one of the problems F2P games are most criticized for. It is P2W. You could argue that the free to play option is actually just a trial, but that doesn't change that there is a 40% stat difference between a free and subbed player. This game is not listed as a demo on steam, it is listed as a free to play game. Unless that suddenly changes, to say it's just a 'trial' version is a fallacy. It's true that the game is free of the cash shop aspect, techinically. Instead, players receive special items and perks if they donate enough. Sounds a little sketchy right?
TL;DR
Basically, this a fun game to♥♥♥♥♥♥around in if you like exploring and hardcore rping pvp, but in the long run it's not worth your time. If you join up with a guild you could definitely spend hundreds of hours pvping, rping, and exploring, but it can feel more like a job than fun times with friends. I do not recommend this game for the average gamer. It is for hardcore pvp players only. I don't mean that as a compliment. I mean that only hardcore players will be wiling to put up with all the game's crushing flaws out of desperation to find a game that provides an immersive sandbox rp/pvp environment.

A fantastic game. I'm not usually one for stealth, but Dishonored made it fun enough that I want to go back and play it again and again. In fact, you can do just that; the game is designed so that any kind of playstyle you can dream up, stealth or action, is feasible. Want to assassinate enemies and disappear like a ghost? A fantastic stealth game with a richly detailed world to play in.  Whether you choose to fight your way through the enemies or sneak your way past them on a pacifist playthrough, you will have a ton of fun with Dishonored.
Getting a stealth game right is a difficult thing to do.  The enemies have to be intelligent enough to pose a challenge, but brain-dead enough not to notice the player's every move.  Dishonored's enemies are just the right mixture of smart and stupid.

This game is something truly beautiful.
On the surface, Dishonored brings an amazing mechanical stealth experience that gives the player so many ways to carry out the missions. Fun and unique abilities coupled with an adequate arsenal of weapons enables you to hack and slash your way through the game or remain in the shadows and hold back your blade (or anything in between).
Deeper, however, Dishonored has a crazily immersive atmosphere and perfectly layered background/lore. Exploring every room, every corner, and every crevice enables you to experience one of the richest story-driven games I have ever had the pleasure to play.
Dishonored is probably the best game I have ever played, and I implore you to play it too. Take the game slow, thoroughly explore the maps and absorb the atmosphere. I think you'll love every second.

+ Much more
