The main positives of Mortal are it's first person perspective, marginally flexable skill system(but inflexable attribute system), and full loot sandbox world. Those are the only positives.
When originally released in 2010 this game had potential, unfortunatley this potential has been squandered by poor development prioritization and an inability to bring the game's stability and playability up to a satisfactory state. 6 years on new players will notice that mortal online feels like any other game's alpha test, riddled with critical world breaking bugs that are created almost as fast as they are solved, leaving the game in a state of perpetual brokenness.
The developers will say, "its better than it was on release!" and while that is true in some aspects, now there is far more in-game to be broken and the same percentage of content is broken as was on release. Ultimatley the current state of the game speaks for itself, to illustrate: nearly a year on from the second continent, sarducca's, release, guilds on the other side of the world are assigned ownership of towns on the wrong continent, due to a simple oversight to add a new coordinate system for the new continent. Countless similar problems in the game's foundations sit well documented yet the developers press on with adding trivial scribing minigames that will likely be broken within a year and not be fixed for another two.
The excuse for this is always that their (contracted) artists cant fix bugs in their game, or that only some of their programmers can fix bugs, and yet here we are 6 years on and those artists sit bored diluting the game's original gritty swedish art style with ugly capes, cartoony spike armor, rams with spikes intersecting player models, lizard mounts, halloween helmets, and phallic player houses. It's long past time when they should have fixed their priotoriazation, for artists to be fired and programmers to be hired for the express purpose of fixing all the game's issues, yet this has not been done, 6 years on. Instead, excuses are proffered where applicable and otherwise only silence is heard.
You would think in a harsh full loot game measures would be taken to ensure when you lose everything, the game intended for you to die. Instead you will find yourself dying more often to client crashes, buggy ai, and hackers than other players(hackers who are often let back into the game by starvault only to be banned twice more). There is one area of the game that is polished enough to be enjoyed, and that is foot pvp, which is currently one of the only reasons large groups play the game. Even here, balance issues, node-wide crashes that leave dozens of people's clients crashed, and various other issues are rampant. The developers of this game rarely listen to community feedback, even when there was a dedicated balance testing team, they were largely ignored and it took teeth pulling for tiny numbers changes. The rare instances where Starvault makes changes suggested by the community, they shout it from the rooftops as if to try to paint a very different picture from the reality, "We listen sometimes!" Yeah, great.
Newbies will find that their first character will likely need to be deleted and remade unless they followed a guide, as of the tens of thousands of potential race, size, and age combinations, only about 6 are viable for combat, with a bit more room given to crafting characters whos attributes simply don't matter outside of int. Most crafting characters in MO are dull to play, taking up a whole character slot just for you to sit in town yellspamming your wares, assuming you don't take the sane route and simply keep that character logged off the majority of the time until you need him. 6 is an improvement from the 2 combat races that were viable on release, but when such a huge depth of customization is available, so few choices means the race system feels arbitrary and poorly balanced. Ultimatley the game's character system does not give the flexability to players that it claims to, in fact limiting it more and more as changes such as dex tiering are made, which causes dex to only matter at arbitrary milestones (110, 93, 119, 85 etc)
To top it off, Starvault maintains immense disrespect for the small playerbase by running their official forums poorly, advising moderators to ban anyone who is negative about the game. For example, "its not worth promoting the game in it's current state" will net you a ban. The game's forums are considered extremely toxic due to moderation that shuts down legitimate discussion while allowing trolling to thrive. Website ticket support answers only once every two emails you send, and in-game support is a mixture of unhelpfulness and complete incompetence. Expect to be lied to by game masters ingame, who despite their status don't understand basic gameplay mechanics and are a nightmare to deal with. Expect to be temporarily jailed by a game master if one of their buddies complains that you must have used cheats to kill their naked character. Expect policies as amazingly stupid as asking you to "contact a gm before you kill a boss mob" just to ensure the loot your entire group worked for appears at all.
Client performance is poor, settings menus are often nonfunctional, and keybinding is a nightmare unless you edit the .ini text files which also happens to carry the penalty of an in-game permenant ban, if you are caught. Why they think editing a text file on your computer should be bannable speaks to their incompetence, and also the lack of functioning anticheat, demonstrated (there is no information or guides on how to cheat, exploit, or hack in my link or linked from my link, just a demonstration of the hacking issues that plague the game) here:
It's possible that some point in the future that these issues will be fixed and i have heard that population has been staying at  stable since the massive dropoff, and i will update my review if that ever becomes the case. I do find myself coming back to this game repeatedly as i muse about what may have been fixed since i last played and all the wonderful mechanics in the sandbox that might work, but every time it becomes a case of "reroll a character, max him out, find out some obscure bug makes my intended playstyle unplayable, get annoyed and stop playing."

Otherwise, you would have nothing to look at really.
The gameplay is solid, but music is basically non-existant (a great shame, People's Generl for example had great music that made you want to go back to the game). Others sounds are simple, units have no animations (outside of shooting). There are several scenarios and campaings.

I like the atmosphere of this game. The storyline is very faithful to the "history" of the second war on Armageddon.
The game feels, from my point of view as a Panzer Corps owner, very different from Panzer Corps. Game mechanics vary verry much. I tried to play this like PC at first, and I got my beating. But once you are into the new mechanics, it feels different but good.
Since it's just three days after release, there are still some minor bugs and anoyances in the game. But the creators are known for their ongoing support und enhancements of the games they did. I have no doubt that mechanics, tooltips and even content will improve and grow vastly over time.
If you don't like Turn-Based-Strategy games, or if you think this is a 1:1 conversion of the 40K TableTop-rules to a digital game, then this is probably not for you.
If you like a good tactical challenge and the 40k universe is appealing to you, then give it a shot. The easy modding capability of this game will guarantee you many many hours of fun.

A punishing mess of poorly amalgamated DLC mechanics. The game years ago was fine but the constant pumping out of DLC has added far too many mechanics and made the game unenjoyable, leaving it more of a mess of tedious micro-management. Too many of the DLC do not work together leaving many disjointed systems that feel incomplete but contantly demand the players attention. It's not even a matter that these features would not work if they had more effort put into them - that's the worst part, instead they are rushed out before they feel properly implemented and stamped with a steep price tag.
The game feels so alien and tedious to play compared to the game that I originally bought that I struggle to play it coming back to it after one or two content releases. So many of the added features feel unnecessary and do not add extra depth to the game but simply add gamey mechanics that do not add any balance or historical accuracy to the game. The best example of this I think is England's parliament system which just means every so often you can gain a bonus by trading an inconvenient amount of other bonuses or resources away. Does this help England become the great power it was in history? No, AI England just sits there colonising what it can and losing most wars it enters with any other European power. Can the player do well as England? Yes of course, but I feel the point of playing a historical game is to play through decent historical accuracy (at least to a point) which seems to get worse with every new mechanic they add because the AI does not improve to handle everything.
It really upsets me that my opinion on this game has changed so much over the time I have played it but it's not the game I started playing and I wouldn't recommend that others buy what the game is now. It is way too expensive in its entirety and needlessly complex in many areas. I hope sometime they stop adding new content and instead focus on balancing and working with the many mechanics they already have to fix their glaring issues - until then I can't recommend buying EU4.

Yeah it's a good game, but it's also got flaws. One of the important things to remember, is something a lot of these negative reviews don't take in account for, if Paradox were to simply make Hearts of Iron III again with new graphics, all it's going to do is reduce the amount of players who are going to purchase the game. So in order to compromise between the hardcore players and the new players, they needed to dumb down certain systems, which is perfectly fine for anyone who wants to play a game and not obsess over it, regardless it is still game which needs hundreds of hours to fully master. With that said, it's very fun when playing with your friends, it's easy to get used to after the time put into it, and can be a ton of fun. If this game wasn't a sequel, many reviews would be positive which is important to note. Some of the major flaws however which are quite game-breaking are the following: - Germany is extremely underpowered. In real life Denmark surrendered within a few hours, in this game I've seen Germany stuck in Denmark for years. Germany also fails to invade Russia, I have yet to see any playthroughs or games where Germany actually makes remote progress into Russia. Same with some of the other Axis powers, including Japan who struggles to take China, and I've never seen actually go into the Pacific and become a real threat. Italy however is quite balanced, but perhaps even too strong, I've seen Italy become much more powerful than Germany several times which can be a problem. - Terrain plays very little part in Africa which needs to be fixed. I'm tired of stretching my front lines into the Sarah desert, because it's aparently in this game a really easy place move through. In most ww2 board games the entire Sarah Desert is blocked out becaues it is IMPOSSIBLE to move an army through there. I'd like to increase the amount of provinces on the coast of Africa, and remove accessibility in the Sarah almost entirely. - Russia's army... It's never really a struggle when Germany and Russia fight, it's just sort of Germany throwing a few jabs and Russia having Germany by a headlock, slowly suffocating them until they completely break. - The game is a little too fast paced, it's very rare that the year is going to get to late war 1940's without the entire war ending because of mass invasions, so simply reducing Allied agressiveness and replacing it with extensive planning would be great.. Also by the time you get to a late game 1942+, the game sort of starts to feel like it's breaking. If anyone has played Europa Universalis IV, you'll know if you start in 1444 and finish an entire game by the 1830's, it begins to become very clunky by then; this seems to happen here unfortunately with certain spammed units, and resources. - Speaking of mass invasions, the naval invasion planning for the AI is decent, but the naval invasion defending for the AI is awful. The AI seems to not defend it's shores properly and so is invaded every month by a bunch of suicide squads of a few divisions. The defending nation should properly set up on the shores, and the invading AI should instead of invading a bunch of mini times each month, invade one major time each couple of years (if neccesary). Regardless of these major problems it is still fun when playing multiplayer, so make sure you play with friends. If you're looking at it less from a ww2 historian standpoint, and more of just a regular game standpoint, it can be a great sandbox for molding your nation (even if it's not historically involved in ww2) into whatever you want it to be. Very nice game, with simple balancing issues. Overall I'd like to see Germany stronger, Japan stronger (at least in 1936), less cahos on the map with more solid fronts, completely reworked naval invasion mechanics, a reworked Africa, and some rework to the endgame.

It's a nice little game, don't get me wrong, I've played it through - but there's so much space for improvement that I'm left completely astounded as to why do people think it's such a great game.
I've always had problem with Dishonored, since the first time I've played it, with blink-blink type of sneaking. Not to mention that fighting isn't all that good neither. So there's really little left for me to do. Arkane has managed to make a game that, even at its hardest setting (and I've gone for hardest achievements immediately as well), isn't that much challenging. AI is simply stupid and doesn't represent a real challenge. Environment design is such that is easily enables anyone to sneak around and do whatever they want. Fighting is really bad; there isn't even a system in place so it's just mostly run around and mash left-click to make sure your enemies are down and dead. Maybe if Arkane decided to commit and make a sneaker, maybe then they would've made something better. But maybe is a big word...
As for other aspects of the game, I'd say that it looks perfectly fine. Story is also fine. And everything else you might come up is... well, just that - fine. And that's where the biggest problem lies: "FINE" is not cool. "FINE" is boring, predictable and easy to deal with.
And don't even get me started about DLC prices. It's a bloody insult when a game costs 5€ and discounted DLCs cost around 7€. I get it that some people might say that it's a "whole game worth of content" (which I seriously doubt) or some other crap like that, but it's still a bit too much for me.
Yes, I said it - 7€ for DLCs is too much.

Where to begin? This game was a blast to play through, from start to finish (mostly). Dark Souls' heavy influenence on game mechanics is apparent, but there is also some new and inventive ways that they introduce game mechanics. Platforming is fun, especially when you recieve brands. The death system is also cool, where an enemy absorbs your salt after you die. While it is difficult like Dark Souls, it is sometimes difficult to the point where its simpily unfair (one boss in particular). Regardless, its still a fantastic title for anyone whos looking for a brutal expirence that's also rewarding. The last thing I want to mention is the story. The introduction is super vauge at first, with the story being completely missable. I think the only reason I didnt miss the story is because I'm so used to Dark Soul's method of storytelling now. Anywho, what really intrigued me was the names of the locations and the visual storytelling that it borrows from Dark Souls.
(Spoilers ahead)
The names are all so intruiging, such as "The Crypt of Dead Gods", "The Pitchwood" and "The Still Palace" among many more. Ska's visual storytelling is hugely important and impressive as well. For example, The Crypt of Dead Gods is dark bleak and moldy. Gargantual enemies patrol around and its hard to see where the next platform is supposed to be. The water here is flowing upside down too. This is what I would expect to see from a area so ominously named. The Still Palace too is another great example. The scenery is almost blindingly white, and neat and orderly compared to the rest of the game. The transition from the Crypt to the Still Palace is beautiful, with blinding white stairs after beating the final boss of the Crypt that indicate a seperated existence. The palace seems so detatched from the rest of the world its astounding. Not to mention its only enemy is the boss, a great way to build tension in the final act. Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed my time with the game. With solid game mechanics, a interesting but vauge story, and great set peices, I'd reccomend this game.

Salt and sanctuary fills the empty gap that dark souls left in my heart. I can feel that a lot of love went into making this game, and I think any player can have many hours of fun with it. This is of course particulary true for Souls players. Also, I really enjoyed the addition of classic platformer elements in a souls-like game.

Salt & Sanctuary is a truly remarkable effort by the husband and wife team of Ska Studios. I looked forward to this game for two years since seeing VaatiVidya's alpha footage of it. Now that the game is out, it does not disappoint in the least. Everything that I hoped for is here, and any slight issues with the game just don't stack up when compared to the love and care put into everything else.
S&S is Dark Souls combined with Castlevania: Symphony of the Night. That's actually how I described the game to a friend. "Imagine if every enemy in Symphony of the Night was actually a challenge."
If you're thinking you can play this game like any of the "Metroidvania" games out there, remove that misconception from your mind. Every attack must be calculated. Every roll timed perfectly. Your surroundings must be studied and investigated as you progress. Secrets must be sniffed out. And bosses sometimes require a high degree of patience to learn their movesets.
This is a side scroller for patient people. Impatience is the bane of any Dark Souls player, and that aspect is 100% shared with Salt & Sanctuary. Clever planning, meticulous gear management, and a sharp eye will get you much farther in this game than a hack and slash attitude.
There is an impressive amount of content here considering only two people made it. Tons of weapons, armor, and accessories await you. There is also a respectable spell and miracle system. Some spells require a catalyst to be cast, like a staff or wand. But there is also the incantion variety that can be used from your item menu just like potions or throwables. However, there is an odd elemental imbalance system with spells that basically forces one of your four ring slots to be used up for a specific ring that negates it. Using a specific elemental spell too many times in a row without this ring causes an elemental imbalance that will cause you to take damage if you continue casting. It's an interesting system, but doesn't exactly feel neccessary when it can so easily be negated.
The large amount of content also applies to the numerous zones you'll be playing through. There are about 20 zones in the game, and each one has a style all its own. It is commendable that Ska Studios stayed true to the Dark Souls method of interconnecting certain zones like a worm in an apple, but it ultimately proves a little pointless since teleporting on a whim is so easy. Thankfully the devs recognized this and added items next to almost every backtracking gate that can be opened, offering incentive to seek them out.
A particularly interesting aspect of S&S to discuss is the bosses. While the majority of them are well designed, I noticed that some of them could be made utterly inconsequential depending on what playstyle or gear I was using. One boss would prove to be trivial on one character while another could be a serious challenge. While ideally it would be best if all bosses could be equally challenging, I believe this is a fair compromise given the limitations of making a boss that is creative both on a gameplay and artistic level. It also goes to ensure that there isn't a most powerful playstyle. No matter what you play, you will eventually hit a challenge wall. (And truly no matter what you play, you will hit a challenge wall when you reach a certain witch on a certain lake. A fight that I am still trying to decide if it's poorly designed or not.)
While I would love to say that S&S is a flawless experience, there are a few small issues. For example, in the original Dark Souls, you could accidentally break an NPC story line if you played a section out of order or didn't find that NPC in the next area that it was supposes to be in. The NPC would just vanish from your game and you would have to start a new game if you wanted to finish that story line. That is one of the less appetizing aspects of Dark Souls that somehow made its way into Salt & Sanctuary. Unfortunately, it's even easier to accidentally sequence break in this game and cause an NPC to vanish forever. During my third playthrough, I made sure to use a walkthrough so this didn't happen again. After using said walkthrough, I realized just how easy it would be to mess up and do things out of order.
Another issue that is a glaring issue for me is the music. What is here is good, but it was halfway through my second playthrough that I finally turned off the BGM because I couldn't stand listening to those same four guitar chords that play over and over again in sanctuaries. It literally got stuck in my head and I couldn't stand it. Other than that, the game is mostly quiet with the exception of boss fights and a tune that sometimes plays while exploring zones. Although I will concede. The tracks that play during the last 15 to 30 minutes the game are excellent. Perhaps not quite memorable since there's still not much of a melody to them, but they are powerful songs that truly grasp the gravity of the moment.
Another issue is the lack of a map. A map in a game like Dark Souls just wouldn't be possible, but this is a 2D plane. There are fan made maps out there that perfectly detail the game, but no map in the actual game. Perhaps the devs thought that a map would break immersion. To an extent I agree with that statement, but you know what else breaks immersion? Having to alt tab out to bring up a fan made map because I can't remember or figure out where to go next. Bottom line, have a map.
As I said earlier, these issues are nothing when compared to the sheer scope of accomplishment that Salt & Sanctuary achieves. A married couple set out to make a side scroller inspired by Dark Souls, and they succeeded. I have high hopes for either expansions to the current game, or even a sequel. Salt & Sanctuary is well worth the asking price of $17.99. I do not regret my purchase in the least.

9 Clues 2: The Ward is a hidden object game about murder in an asylum. Despite of it being a second serie, you can understand the game just fine without playing the first one.
The graphics are decent, although the animation is quite cranky. Some of the animations look like a cropped image of the body that's moved left and right (or up and down) just for the sake of the animation, while the face expression of the characters look like a 3D image on top of 2D body when they talk.
The music creates a spooky atmosphere to the story. The sfx also sounds great, especially for those that's meant for jumpscares. Note that the game doesn't really that scary though; the sfxs are just quite loud and spooky.
To be honest, the story is quite confusing to me at first. However, i understand the story more clearly after playing the game for the second time (although i skipped most of the cutscenes). Some of the story is quite predictable because of the hints of the notes that's laying around the areas, while the details are quite unpredictable. The story itself is quite straightforward with a lot of "mystic" elements in it.
The game is actually just an ordinary hidden object, point and click game where you're supposed to find items and solve the clues. The game itselfs offers in 3 difficulty mode. I played the easiest difficulty and i (obviously) don't have any problem in clearing the game.
The game, just like the story, is quite straightforward and you'll be given several objectives to give you general idea of what you're doing. You also don't need to move between areas too much; you'll only need to move between 3 areas at most to solve an objective.
The hidden object minigame is decent. Most of the items are hard to notice although you can also click on anything without getting any penalty on the easiest difficulty. If you don't like the hidden object minigame (although it's strange if you're buying this game in the first place), you can also switch the hidden object to mahjong. I honestly enjoyed the mahjong more than the hidden object itself, although it can get too repetitive sometimes. There is also an achievement where you have to play all hidden object and mahjongs, which means that you have to play the game twice to get the acheivements. I find the second playthrough to be boring because i already know what to expect.
There are also some other minigames that's available throughout the game. Some might be tricky while some might be too easy. There is also a skip button if you don't want to deal with it though. However, there is an achievement where you have to finish the game without using a skip button so you might want to reconsider it.
There will also be some hidden collectables in some areas which is carried over if you start a new game, although i doubt it'll matter that much since you'll just check a walkthrough for that one.
Pros:
- 16 hidden objects minigames (or mahjongs)
- Minigames
- Mahjong minigame as an alternative to hidden object
Cons:
- Second playthrough becomes too boring
This is an enjoyable hidden object games that you can try for fun.

Artifex Mundi-published games nearly always follow the same rote pattern of "literal demon causes havoc and must be defeated using a magic amulet or some nonsense," and I'm generally quite excited when I find one which seems to shake that off.  I should be excited by 9 Clues 2, therefore, whose sole concession to AM's supernatural obsession is clockwork dolls with spinning eyes which can trivially "hypnotise"/brainwash folks into doing just about anything.  Unfortunately, though, I found the setting and execution here to be much worse than the supernatural nonsense they replaced.
Namely, Tap It Games returned to that tired go-to location for "scariness" which is the mental asylum.  Mental illness in this game is treated with the same kind of care and respect as one might afford some rubbish left on the side of the street.  Artifex Mundi characters are always painted with fairly broad strokes, and generally feel "off" in a number of ways as it is, but their portrayal of the patients in the asylum here were, IMO, downright insulting.  I can certainly forgive the "insane villian" trope in a title like this, because what
would there be in this sort of game, but the portrayal of everyone else is straight out of a 4-year-old's conception of "crazy."  It's telling that by the end of the game, the main characters are slinging slurs like "psycho" and "crazy."
On a technical side, the game is competent as always.  The puzzles benefit, IMO, from having what for Artifex Mundi titles counts as a grounding in reality, and there weren't too many solutions which felt completely arbitrary.  I actually do really like the 9 Clues series's "detective mode" HOB sequences, even though I find their conclusions fairly arbitrary and hilarious most of the time.  The puzzles you encounter are the same rote set found in just about every other AF title, but that can't really count against it.
In the end, it's a competent AF-published title which is let down by its callous and insensitive setting, and offensive portrayal of mental illness.  I guess it's back to the demon-banishing for me!

Mortal Online is a type of MMORPG Sand Box that requires a lot of patience, dedication and hard work. While it is nearly a decade old, buggy and may make you think it is still in Alpha State... there is really nothing like it on the market at the moment. Some may say Darkfall is better... I've tried it... and it's just WoW with full loot in my opinion.
You can (and probably will) play for hours, building your characters, resources. Spend weeks...months... even years building up a clan that can stand the test of time, or crumble into dust at the first month! but you'll never forget the memories, never forget the adrenaline coursing through your blood as you fight your first battle or win your first tournament.
Gameplay:
The main aspect of this game is PvP, PvE and Crafting. Hunting, Mining, Fishing, Alchemy, Blacksmithing, Taming, Thieving (yes you can steal from Other Players!) Murdering, Raiding, Duelling, Dungeon Raiding, Sieging and Building. You can hire your self out as a mercenary, tame and breed mounts for a living, be a miner that everyone (and it is in VERY high demand) relies on. Or you can be that vicious bandit that robs people on the highway, ambushing caravans, clans or the simple peasant trying to make his way to a new town! The choice is entirely yours.
Terrain: The map is quite large... if you have played Skyrim, MO's world is probably bigger. There are massive mountains, deep jungles, scorching deserts, icey peaks, grassy plains and deep lakes, rivers and oceans (I swam around one of the continents once... took me about 5 hours).
PvP: This in my opinion is the main thing about Mortal Online. You create bonds of brotherhood or complete... utter.... hatred towards people. Respect, fear, loyalty... they actually mean something here. When you are a famous duellist or a warlord capable of decimating other clans or people in combat... you receive the respect you deserve. You build your legend... and it will be remembered, by the old and the new.
Clans & Companionship: This is also another very important aspect of the game... a person alone can only make it so far, but with a clan behind you, you can do great things. The bonds of loyalty you will make or break will determine your reputation by the community. Some clans may be casual, but betray them and you'll see a very different side of them. Bring them glory and power and you may rise to the top! or... be betrayed and left to die in a ditch!
When you die you have to walk to a priest to get your life back thenback to where you died to get your stuff back, Not to mention how slow you are.

Seemingly, this game is all about PVP, anyone can kill you, anywhere, besides guarded zones. (they can still kill you just they will call forth the wrath of the GAURDS!)

This game emphasizes stats and skills, but it also promotes personal player skill aswell, if you suck, no weapon in the game will help you agains that newb in rags that can parry your attacks.
Yes, its a challenge, Yes its painful, But why would you want to play if it was easy?

Full disclosure. I really enjoy sniper games. No better sense of gaming satisfaction for me than to pick one off from long range, and another and another. Unfortunately there really aren't a lot of options. You pretty much have the Sniper Elite series and the Sniper: Ghost Warrior games. While the Sniper Elite games take place in a WW2 setting, the Sniper: Ghost Warrior games take you to a modern setting. In the first one, you pretty much ran through the jungle looking to pick off targets as you pushed forward and completed your missions. In SGW2 you go from the jungles of the Phillipines, the war torn city of Sarajevo and fianlly the mountains of Tibet, all beautifully done using Cry Engine 3. Besides the graphics, the voice acting is surprisingly good and the sniper action is a whole lot of fun. I really felt myself using tactics and there were a few moments of genuine suspense of "will I or won't I get out of this mess".  There were a few issues, however. The main one being a bug which forces you to put you textures to "low" otherwise you'll run into a memory leak desktop crash. The first hour for me was a desktop crash fest until I finally checked the Steam forums. There are also a few bugs when you're supposed to be following an NPC and he doesn't want to go. Again, that's minor. The levels also FEEL big, but really are not. There are instances where you'll be firing at someone over a 1/2 KM away but once you get the hit you're back up close again. I thought the level design overall though, was very nice.  The game also does quite a bit of hand holding with the NPC as he'll pick your targets or you're having to follow him everywhere.  Overall I personally recommend Sniper Ghost Warrior 2. I am biased towards sniping games so I can understand this isn't for everyone.  It is a little "shooting gallery-ish" and there are some irritating moments but I enjoyed the hell out of it. 8.5/10 from me.
EDIT: Also completed the Siberain Strike DLC. An excellent "prequel" add on that gives you about 2-3 hours of extra gameplay. It doesn't bring anything new to the table but in my case that wasn't necessarily a bad thing. If you enjoy Sniper Ghost Warrior 2, you'll definitely enjoy Siberian Strike.

To list really quick (and just after 10 hours of gameplay) the + and - of this game i would say:
-Good campaign with interesting scenarios, and some cinematic moment, you will surprise yourself when you send three tanks to save this salamander scout just because you have it since the first mission and do not want it to die, alas surrounded by ork mobs this poor scout have known a dire fate.
-Solid wargame with good mechanics, deep but accessible.
-The w40k universe has really been respected, most units are used the way you would use them in the tabletop game, weapons loadout are almost the same (with some few tweek to fit in a wargame i guess)
-Huge replay value
-A decent Ai that will really test your skills on higher difficulties.
-It is a 2d game, wich i think is the best choice for wargame, you have a much better visibility on the battlefield and it is less tedious to move your units around.
As for the negative sides:
-Well the animation is not that good, but some people might like the minimalistic approach like this minimalistic approach.
-Some sounds effect could be improved, the music is quite good, and you have a different sounds for each weapons wich i find neat, but your units are quite, some things like different screams when the units die would have make the experience a bit more fun.
-It is a 2d game, you might not like it, if you can't stand 2d game, or are into superfancy video quality that might not be for you.
-I think the price is fair, you get much more content than a lots of AAA game, but it might be too expansive for some people. if you are a fan of dawn of war and was looking for something close to it you might be disappointed,
if you are a fan of the tabletop game, and the various adptation that has been made of it (rites of war and final liberation), or are into wargame and want a change of scenery you might consider it cheap.
I hope this opinion about this game helped you, it is really a good game as long as you know what you are getting into, i have been positively surprised i did not expect this game to be that good, and i really want to see it grow, it deserves it.

Epic scaled WH40K? Check
Baneblades, Stormhammers, Shadowswords? Check
TITANS?! Check
Very good so far.  Lots of vehicle variants, I can't believe they gave us Gorgons, and air units. A turn and army point cost system for Epic on PC has not been seen since Final Liberation.
With that said, I do wish people would point to Final Liberation rather than Panzers. That game had it all, live motion cutscenes, unlockable units after conquering a province, campaign map where you choose your next attack and see where the orks are going to attack next, assign garrison units to conquered provinces, units were animated (Titans actually walked) and each battle was scaled to the point cost of the units you choose (could be bad or good depending on your perspective), but we never did get the promised expansions for eldar and tyranid.
Pros
-Immense vehicle variants/unit choices
-Turn based and point limited
-Lengthy campaign
Inbetween
-Still can't make up my mind whether it would be better for cutscenes between battles or these dialogue boxes
Cons
-Unit animation (Titans don't walk, tank treads don't turn, etc.)
-Limited choices on strategic actions and no map to show progress other than wall of text between battles
-The story escalated quickly between the training missions. If the orks were already in the sky why not have your battalion go to alert? (I know the von Strab storyline for Armageddon, but this doesn't make sense to me.)
-Voice acting is so so.
-Minor graphical glitches (checkboard patterning during some conversation cutscenes and on some maps)

This is more of a first impression than a real review, but so far it's been a pleasent experience.
The elephant in the room: the graphics are bare-bones at best, and there is barely any animation at all. If this is a deal-breaker for you, don't bother with this game. That said, the sprites look very nice and explosions and other effects are are good too. The graphics are very clean and functional, you won't have to guess if a unit is in cover or has LoS blocked.
Sound effects are good, but music is disappointing. I switched to Dawn of War soundtrack after a few hours. There is some voice acting in the campaign and it's been fine so far.
Gameplay is similar (not identical) to old 40k titles like Rites of War or Final Liberation. This is a very loose adaptation of tabletop 40k rules. There are some balance issues that I hope will be adressed, but I haven't seen anything gamebreaking so far.
The game only has 3 factions, but the number of units they have is mind-boggling, including weird/obscure stuff like hive militia or space marines with grav guns. Very nice. Some options that I thought would be there are missing (for example sentinels can only have lascannons, no flamers, no multi-lasers etc).
AI seems alright so far, although it's sometimes a little too passive.
Can't really comment on the editor yet, it seems really simple to use.
Is it worth the price? If what I wrote sounds like the type of game you've been waiting for, then go for it. If you're on the fence, or don't have much experience with this kind of turn-based games you might want to wait for a bigger discount, this game is not for everyone.

EDIT 2: Constant crashes and black screens and trying to reload just to get back to where I was. Goodbye.
EDIT: Recommended if you like units walking through each other, no dying/fighting animations, imagining close combat, hex-based everything. Recommended if you like your strategy gaming in a very abstract, units-on-hexes, board-game style. If you're cool with "this graphic represents such and such", then this might be the game for you. The game is entirely 2D, and ENTIRELY mouse-click-driven. You will click on everything. Except that one menu that you can only use the ESC key to get out of. But you can't use ESC to leave any other menu, all the rest you have to click Ok to leave. Click an icon to bring up a menu - then move the cursor to the menu to click Ok. What year is this? 1992? I thought it was 2014, my mistake.
But maybe you're cool with that.
Honestly not terribly impressed (other than voice acting, setting, characters so far). I don't want to go off on a rant here, but... It's essentially a 40K skin on their previous products. You'll be doing a lot of clicking. Clicky, clicky, clicky. Click to end dialogue. Click here after reading lots of text (f... that). Click in this small little box for next unit. Click over there to end turn. Click click click. And click some more. No mouseover tooltips with shortcut keys on buttons. Graphics are what you would expect from a 40K skin on a Slitherine port, except the character portraits which are rather ...damn, nice. You're allowed a maximum of units, and buying more is a pain, you can't queue up units or buy more than one at a time usually. Then one dies and you can buy and deploy another, which magically appears in your deployment zone. If you're looking for immersive simulation-style gaming, THIS IS NOT IT.
Then again, that's just my opinion, I could be wrong. You may love it or hate it. I bought it because I'm a 40K nerd with a decent job and I'm old and don't spend much money, and maybe that means I'm a sucker who paid too much for something I should have researched more about. But it's 40K and I am just desperate for my fix. If you're short on cash wait for the sale, unless you're into this type of stuff.

Set over 500 years before the events of the original game in the series, Assassin's Creed 2 is a prequel to 2009's much-loved game of the year - Batman: Arkham Asylum.
Ezio Auditore da Firenze (it's Spanish for Wayne), one of Batman's long-lost ancestors, has his memories perved on by some random guy Batman Incorporated picked up off the streets as an excuse for training - and thus one of the greatest stories of revenge told in video game media begins.
Following the untimely deaths of his family in true Bruce-esque fashion, Ezio decides to  take on the mantle of the Batman, protector of Gotham: Italy Edition and its people. Despite his lack of training, Ezio immediately sprints out the batcave and begins to clean the streets (a broomstick is a viable weapon in this game, apparently). With the help of his good friend Leonardo DaVinci (French for Pennyworth), Ezio sets out with a positive arsenal of exotic weaponry; from an early Batarang, which due to technical limitations of the time, only has 1 hyper-sharp blade, and doesn't really come back after use, to the grapple, which instead of attaching to buildings from a long distance, functions as a way of holding close targets in place - with optional fatal injury.
What unfolds is a spellbinding and beautiful tale of family, redemption, revenge and mass murder.
Yeah, the whole "no killing" thing hasn't really been established yet - but  let's be honest here, I think slamming someone in the neck with a car door and leaving them, broken, miles from the nearest hospital also counts as murder.
Along with a majestic soundtrack, the game also improves immersion with a launcher inspired by renaissance-era technology. I found the 30 or so minutes I had to spend getting the piece of horse dung to work highly immersive, which, coupled with the painfully intrusive notification system, really made me feel the wonderment and awe of the renaissance.

To start, this review will contain spoilers! However, these will be clearly marked, so feel free to read and skip over these parts if you haven't played.
Overall, this game was pretty good. However, I wouldn't say it was amazing, mostly a lot of the puzzles felt like meaningless busywork. I'd still recommend it because I enjoyed it, especially towards the end, but I do have a few criticisms.
Pros:
-Great art.
-The world felt well-planned and intentional, and the characters were good (not Undertale-good in terms of personality, but still good).
-The music is wonderful.
-The ending sequence was both unexpected and interesting.
-The breaking of the fourth wall (both style and degree) in this game is something that you won't find in many (or any) other games.
Cons:
-As mentioned above, many if not most of the puzzles are just tedious busywork, searching a large world for a specific item which is easy to use once you have it, but you might have to scour every room for it.
-Because of the number of times one needs to cross each area, sometimes the music and art can become a bit tedious. (I'm looking at you, Barrens!)
-After reading the description again it seems this is intentional, but it is very easy to finish the game while having a lot of leftover items and unresolved parts of the story. Because of the style of puzzles, as soon as I had access to the tower I didn't have much motivation to keep looking around for more items and story elements.
-(SPOILER) The ending you get is determined entirely by a single choice you make at the end, making the rest of the game feel far less meaningful and definitely diminishing replay value. There is no entirely good ending, only one relatively good one, one slightly worse one, and one definitely bad one.
So in summary, I'd recommend it for sure, though I think it is far from being a perfect game and could be improved. I'll definitely be looking out for anything new from these developers, as it is their first release, so I have high hopes that their next game will be very good.
EDIT: Just a couple of hours after writing this review, I've done some thinking and looking, and I've realized that this game is far more deep than I ever realized. It is definitely worth playing through again, as there will be some differences each time around. In addition, it seems that (SPOILERish) many of the unresolved plot points will be resolved at the end of this week.
In all, I'd bump my rating up from about a 6/10 to an 8/10, to potentially increase in time.

RAGE is very shallow on the exteria, but if you give it the time, it does introduce a very wide variety of fairly intersting, (though most are not ground breaking) dynamics and makes them work quite well(which is what is so good), it is not the sort of game that strikes you as being elegant that much at all. But trust me it has has plenty of decent stuff to keep you busy and not keep you running around for hours doing nothing and getting bored.
Combat is good enough, shooting  and conquering is nice on Rage, in the usual ID way (Doom, Quake etc), but from the start the variation of weapons feels like it could be better(irronically in the ID way :P), as most are similar to any other game, though, I would suggest that all players endure this , until you get the full load of weapons and multiple ammo types which much more liberty with tactics and stratgy in combat; even with your seemingly standard load-out.
Whats more becuase there is a simple crafting system , it extends the weapons further and even accessories like sentry bots, whcih is pretty cool.
Its clear it trys to be Borderlands and emulates the environment, but the story is actually better than Borderlands and so is the game(or at least I prefer this).  In saying that I never really liked borderlands that much... I would play this over BL any day...
The story was good, and infact the usual 'you are a special kind of soldier type' in ID games is apparent on this game too, though the different kind of Post-Apocalypse scenario is quite intersting when you think about it.
The main forte of the gmae is an impressive engine via ID, which makes shooting, racing and exploring a really nice experience.  It looks nice, it feels nice in all aspects.
Because of this engine, the racing/driving  doesn't look shoddy(like Borderlands) and feels ok.  There was an issue at the start of the game with the handbreak that is not balanced with the first vehicles, but trust me when I say that it improves when you get your 3rd vehicle(you may have to upgrade it).  You can adapt to using the hand break in some capacity on the 2nd vehicle though...
Racing, though I am not really fussed about racing games, is not too bad, I enjoyed it.  There is plenty of variation in racing matches, from standard racing matches to the sequential  'Domination' matches(the first to get to a check point get points, the first to 40 points wins(Blowing others up gives you points too...) which does throw the strategy to race on its head(which I think is quite good).
The Music is fine, parts of it sounds un-natural to me, and some of the style of both the composer and the music suck, *To me*.  But in saying that, its not too bad and the music is good when you are playing through the game, and can actually be quite good in parts.
I will add the worst thing about this game was the difficulty.  This game is SSOOoo easy!  If you are bad at FPS: PLAY RAGE!  You have at least 2 lives and you heal constantly, so unless you keep passing out on the keyboard, you will be fine!  I played this on Hard and found it not much of a challenge at all and perhaps after some days that was nice, but I want a challenge from any game I play and Believe me , RAGE isn't challeging in the slightest!  I am keen to play through in nightmare mode , just to see if they actually have ANY challenging difficulty modes at all!

RAGE is a mix of FPS and Driving genres, set in post-apocalyptic desert setting and with some dose of RPG elements, this comes in form of inventory and hub world. Yep, still developed by id Software, who mostly were doing FPS games, and released in 2011, published by Bethesda by that time. It runs on id Tech 5, main point of which were mega-textures.
There were few versions of RAGE. If you pre-ordered then you would recieve Anarchy Edition. You can also buy it separately but no on Steam. Anarchy included few unique items to make players more powerful, including Double Shotgun. From what I understand some of Anarchy editions came with code for Sewers DLC. You could also buy this DLC separately on consoles. There are also some comics and "making of" videos, Collector Edition came with those. And then there was Campaign Edition for Mac OS X that included Anarchy Edition content plus Sewer DLC, but was singleplayer-only.
While Steam version is not Anarchy Edition, it comes with Sewers DLC for free. And that's good, because this DLC gives sewers levels that are filled with mutants which can challenge you only in the very beggining. Not something worth after beating game.
As far as I know the only good difference between consoles and PC is that consoles support split-screen for multiplayer.
The thing is that this game apparently was hyped as being really open-world RPG, but in the end people got hub of corridors between each traditional level, making people dissapointed. And because id is a brand and people expect revolution, even though id only did it with Doom1/Quake1 long time ago. And since people want everything post-apocalyptic game to be either Fallout or Borderlands, well, it got underrated.
Technically, it had a lot of problems at the launch. John Carmack came up with new feature called Mega-Textures. You may think of it as super-detailed textures, but what it means is that artists can can place something nice in one spot without it looping all over the wall. He must have been expected that hardware people would be the one who would rush to give proper support for that feature, but RAGE wasn't Quake 1 and no one cared. And so majority of players experienced huge issues with textures pop-in, where everything will take seconds to become clear when you look at it. Thankfully, game was patched around and hardware moved ever since, so it should be fine now.
At least it shows that programming fancyness of John Carmack is better at developing cutting edge VR tech than games, where "can most average players hardware run it" is more important.
It also has a multiplayer component. Which is being run by lobby system. And community of which is quite dead.
It has two modes. No, not Deathmatch and Capture The Flag.
The first mode is Road Rage, which is competetive and uses Racing genre of a game. Has a few sub-modes and is designed for 4 players. Didn't get to play it. Just check YouTube for gameplay.
Second mode is Wasteland Legends - cooperative FPS. It's designed for 2 players and seems to use unique short missions. Or you could play them in singleplayer, alone. Well, not all that unique, it uses assets from single-player, but it's not same layouts. Plotwise they tell stories of behind-the-scene events, something silly like "how Dan got Sniper Rifle". There are no inventories, few weapons, you occasionally come across supply which will max out your ammo, if you run out of defib then your friend will have to come and revive you. Not much value for singles, better drag a friend into it.
And yes, as many people will tell you, plot isn't good. For RPG. If forget that this is mainly linear FPS/Racing game. So it does job fine. Then again, seeing the hype it was dissapointed. But don't worry, setting combined with amazing graphics are still fun. Seeing all the new amazing NPC designs and hearing the way that each enemy clan communicates with each other, as well as finding out in what enviroment they live, is what was the driving force for me. Game also has great atmoshpere. It goes from surviving wasteland, to more of feeling of just well-stocked desert and then ends with more of techy and resistance feel.
The bad thing is ending. If you played enough id games then you will be smart not to expect epilogues. And then many games have some "you are awsome" ending, teaching players to appericate journey, not the ending. But then this time they forgot to put final boss or any climax battle in. You just got this cool gun that can shoot BFG rounds and you just derp through weak enemies. Still, not a huge flaw.
As for gameplay, it's a classic id shooter. Well, in modern linear level design, where you have one path and any other path is usually filled with knee-tall trash that you can't get over. But the shooting and action itself is great fun. Do people still consider having 9 weapons at same time as old-school?
Weapons can use different kidn of ammo types. Like shocking water with elector-bolts. Or beating the hell out of heavy armor guys by loading your pistol with Fat Mammas.
And you have a few items you can use, most notably explosive RC cars, placing turrets and using wingstick. Wingsticks is a boomerang that homes at enemy, is strong and can even return succesfully. It's Rage's title weapon, so to say. Shame that whether it breaks or returns seem to be based around randomness than skill.
Animations of enemies makes it feel like proper FPS too and not some RPG, with them getting wounded while running, falling onto ground and shooting at you from there. It's mostly hitscan-abuse type of game, but at least regenerating health keeps it sane. And defib, where you can still revive after death. Most common enemies are melee ones that rush you straight or ranged ones that hide behind cover. What is great is that later they take more hits than your average modern FPS cannon fodder and can maneuver around, while giving a look of intellegent enemies by communicating, making it dynamic. It also helps that each clan is a bit unique, like Shadow clan has bandits that are more acrobatic.
I once got sneakily killed from shotgun from behind, so it's cool.
Racing/Driving part takes a secondary place sadly. It delivers finely, in that you can drive between missions in a hub world or do a racing. Boosting, minigun and rocket-launching and all that. It has arcade physics and feel to it, aside from having to purchase ammo. But it doesn't have much aside from shooting rockets at enemy. And racing events don't have many tracks and don't seem to be too crazy, they just kinda get repetetive after a while. It still a good part with explosions and ramming, just not deep. If they had some physics rampage and destroyable objects, then at least it could be as "aw yeah" as Flatout games.
You also get some open-world stuff that are very few towns. Where you can grab some quests of racing. Or play some not interesting mini-games. Cards one is kinda cool. Or you can take a job quest, which is mostly redoing the beaten levels. Still cool lively locations, but don't put focus on them. Don't forget to purchase some ammo and ingridients. Game has too many ammo for few weapons to be survival, but very few for stuff like Sniper Rifle. Oh, and you can craft. This game also gives a bit of survival feel by making you scavenge, picking various trash in missions to sell it later.
Main issue with it is that it doesn't manage to mix FPS and Driving well. Those are kept separately. Hub and races for cars, missions and towns for on-foot. Which may be good, as FPS people have to beat only 2 mandatory races. But still, could make it more interesting this way.
Oh, and music provides background for action and varied but nothing to remember. And there were like, two bosses.
But overall, if you come here for your linear id Software FPS with a bit of racing and not some Fallout or Borderlands, then you will have fun there. Hub world with linear missions are still good games.

After finding this offer online for free and giving it a shot for a straight run of seven hours I can summarize that this MMORP is a compromise. The game elements are easily identifieble and like any other MMORPG this one is 'pay to win' with the free accounts serving as a permanant trial, being unable to progress into a situation where your character has any chance against: guilded players marauding the countryside, lone horsemen murdurers, pick pockets, 'low level' griefers, fatigue free hostile animals and many more, I find it difficult to find the positive in a 'full loot' environment where 4+ hours of grinding can be erased with a stroke of another player's hand (or a mouse click rather)
The combat system is clunky. The animations are delayed on both attacking and defending making the victor 'he who has a lower ping' combined with 'he who has managed to attain a powerful weapon'. Stamina is easily depleted and forces the player to stop and stand in place, or submit to a static animation (sleep or sit) and 'ranking' it up requires well thrice more investment in time spent training one specific skill. (or multiple skills) and similar goes for the majority of the other 'skills' that I've learned about. Certain portion of the 'skill tree' seem redundant- for example, the multiple different kinds of anatomy studies acquired when skinning different animals, or the variation of wood type lore which all feel like a weighted shackle on the road to adventure.

Ok, played it last night for a few hours.
The game, if you want to compare is pretty much a Panzer General with the Warhammer theme. Nothing wrong with that, I loved Panzer General, and I love Warhammer, so having them both in one package, not bad.
The campaign is pretty much similar also, it is a chain of scenarios with a occasional branch where you can choose one of two battle options.
The Units are pretty much treated also similar as in Panzer General/Corps. Before battle, if you have points you can upgrade to other models, if available, or you can purchase new ones. The units all heal complete from battle to battle.
The units do gain experience, but I have not seen yet if and what affect this has on the unit itself.
The manual is very basic, and could have been done better. It does not really explain what units support fire each other and such. But I suspect in no time there will be player made pages that give this information.
Overall the campaign is fun, but I suspect that once you played it through once or twice it will not have much replay ability. The game counts on its multiplayer battles to keep people interested.
I personal would have loved a map type campaign to give a more strategic feel and more replay capability. The problem with stringed scenario campaigns is always that they are quickly done and no reason to do them again.
Overall this game is recommended by me for anybody that likes the 40k theme and or the panzer general type of game play.

This is a second review after having had some time to play it and get to know it better.  First, let me get this out of the way: I truly do not feel like it is less complex than HOI3 in almost every way.  By that, I mean a large part of the complexity of HOI3 and all of the other related games by paradox is just understanding the UI in the first place.  HOI4 is much more fluid in terms of how you interact with it.
Frankly, I actually prefer the unit system in 4 as oppossed to 3 (plays more like a complex Axis&Allies and removes a lot of the tedium I felt in understanding units and hq system, etc...).  That being said, I completely understand the gripes of individuals who are saddened this was removed.  I think they tech system is very intuitive and well built.
The national focus system, although I enjoy the concept, gets burnt through way too quickly.  I am almost always finished with the entire focus tree by the time it hits early-mid 1941.  It's not that I necessarily think they should take longer, if there were at least more to the trees.
I saw somewhere people were upset that they couldn't just turn a country into whatever government system they wanted, or any faction they wanted, declare war, etc...  This I actually feel is more realistic.  You still have the ability to do these things but it takes a longer period of time and you must invest political capital.
One other person at least noted that the conquering system feels broken, and I completely agree.  I think one of two things should exist:  Either the war effort is further broken down into smaller theaters (level of effort in regions), or you should be able to just claim what you have conquered (perhaps increasing world tension).
If you are in the allies, you can claim as much territory you want without repercusions for a democratic country making such large claims.  I think it causes the world tension to increase, but because you are in a faction the AI ignores it and doesn't see you as an aggressor, so on multiple occassions I've conquered at least 1/2 the world as a democratic country... which feels weird.  It feels like you should be able to get kicked out of a faction for your actions.
I completely agree with the criticism of others with regard to battle plans and fronts. That's another thing, even with historical context on, in every single case Germany makes France its first priority, causing France to fall extremely quickly. To start, this review will contain spoilers! However, these will be clearly marked, so feel free to read and skip over these parts if you haven't played.
Overall, this game was pretty good. However, I wouldn't say it was amazing, mostly a lot of the puzzles felt like meaningless busywork. I'd still recommend it because I enjoyed it, especially towards the end, but I do have a few criticisms.
Pros:
-Great art.
-The world felt well-planned and intentional, and the characters were good (not Undertale-good in terms of personality, but still good).
-The music is wonderful.
-The ending sequence was both unexpected and interesting.
-The breaking of the fourth wall (both style and degree) in this game is something that you won't find in many (or any) other games.
Cons:
-As mentioned above, many if not most of the puzzles are just tedious busywork, searching a large world for a specific item which is easy to use once you have it, but you might have to scour every room for it.
-Because of the number of times one needs to cross each area, sometimes the music and art can become a bit tedious. (I'm looking at you, Barrens!)
-After reading the description again it seems this is intentional, but it is very easy to finish the game while having a lot of leftover items and unresolved parts of the story. Because of the style of puzzles, as soon as I had access to the tower I didn't have much motivation to keep looking around for more items and story elements.
-(SPOILER) The ending you get is determined entirely by a single choice you make at the end, making the rest of the game feel far less meaningful and definitely diminishing replay value. There is no entirely good ending, only one relatively good one, one slightly worse one, and one definitely bad one.
So in summary, I'd recommend it for sure, though I think it is far from being a perfect game and could be improved. I'll definitely be looking out for anything new from these developers, as it is their first release, so I have high hopes that their next game will be very good.
EDIT: Just a couple of hours after writing this review, I've done some thinking and looking, and I've realized that this game is far more deep than I ever realized. It is definitely worth playing through again, as there will be some differences each time around. In addition, it seems that (SPOILERish) many of the unresolved plot points will be resolved at the end of this week.
In all, I'd bump my rating up from about a 6/10 to an 8/10, to potentially increase in time.

I could wax lyrical about this game but I'll keep it down to simple pros and cons.
Pros:
. Beautiful environments, hideous enemies and bad♥♥♥♥♥weapons. It looks good!
. Enormous world with seamless transitions between areas. No loading screens!
. In-depth, tactical combat and genuine challenge. You feel skillful when you win.

. Other players online leave gravestones and corpses behind in interesting places. See how your friends are dying!
. Local co-op is smooth and fun and very rewarding.
Cons:
. The platforming can be very tricky and downright unfair. Enemies kill you plenty but falls kill you more.
. The story is oblique and sparsely referenced. You don't feel like you're part of any narrative aside from whatever you're telling yourself as you play. There IS a story there and a good one too, but you have to read the skill tree and item descriptions for it.
. Not all skill build paths are equally viable. Light armour for instance, has few good items, but you're tripping over plate mail. Magic almost trivializes the game with how strong it becomes.
. Hurtboxes and hitboxes are sometimes wonky. Prepare to get grabbed and slashed by attacks that you thought you had avoided.
. Certain enemies are arguably unfair. A particular boss is notorious for 1-shotting you and the fight is gruelling.
Overall recommendation:
Beautiful, challenging, sometimes frustrating but immersive in spite of itself, this game rocks. Buy it!

I want to make this review a meaningful one because I feel like the makers of Salt and Sanctuary have really devoted themselves to making this game, and it would be a great disservice to leave anything short of a heartfelt review.
I'll start off by making a Pros and Cons, because that's a very user-friendly way to approach such a massive adventure.
Pros: This game doesn't hand you a plaque for showing up, in my honest and humble opinion this is what Dark Souls 2 should have been. I know that says a LOT... but it's the complete truth. I've spent thousands of hours in the Dark Souls universe in all 3 games, but Salt and Sanctuary is the only ones that feels like a whole-hearted addition to the franchise (I know it's not the same company, but they are true fans of the "Prepare to be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; genre, and therefore it doesn't matter what their previous game-making history is.)
-Pro #2... Yeah, the first one was long, sorry. Weapons are unique! This was a special reason for me to love this game. The weapons in S+S all had their own unique playstyle, to the point that there was a survivability rating for the weapons I owned. I first got the highest DPS 2handed weapon I could, because it did a lot of damage. My wife and I roflstomped when I 2 shotted things that would take us a few minutes to take down. Soon after, though, I felt it wasn't a good alternative to my usual fast spear-type weapons. I had reduced swing speed, reduced recovery time, and unless I invested a lot of points into endurance or went naked I was also slower. I mean it's great I can topple a boss in a hit, but if I died the next hit, it's not worth it.
-Pro#3: Speed is consistent with your gear. This was seen in Dark Souls a bit, but S+S put a lot more emphasis on this, and to my pleasure, it was something that really added a whole different dynamic to an already advance combat system. I first played a hunter, and I didn't invest a lot of time chasing endurance and gear. In fact, I kept with my hunter garb because I loved it, and didn't switch it out for anything else. I did, however, choose to get heavier weapons, but it was a gradual process, and I didn't really notice... That is, until my wife's character joined my game. Her very light rogue-type character was swift, agile, graceful, angelic... and here I was, a very clunky, and seemingly obese huntard. Shuffling around barely able to swing his stick. I soon invested some points into endurance and was amazed by what an insane difference it was. The kind of difference you have in DS when going from over 70% weight to under 20% weight. It made the game much more enjoyable and my survivability went up dramatically.
Pro#4: The art style. It's nothing to laugh about. This game was well thought out. The areas and enemies are very diverse, and some are outright fricken creepy. Even some of the NPCs can give grown men something to cringe at. The weapons and armor are awesome, and some even had such good looks that I ended up sticking with them regardless of how much better rating other sets were.
Pro#5 The music is fricken great. I really loved the low impact graceful ballads that swept through the air, barely catching my notice, only to be followed by an awesome grunge guitar chorus when entering an awesome new area. It reminded me of Last of Us, in the best way possible.
Pro#6: Transmutations. If there was ever an option in a game that could blow me away more than transmutations, I'd love to see it. Transmutations are an updated, and amazing rendition of the boss souls weapon swap system in dark souls. The S+S team figured, why do players have to farm all fricken day long to upgrade a weapon only to have to xmute it, and then sit around farming again to upgrade it further? It's the most boring part of Dark Souls that wasn't well thought out. S+S has transmutations of almost every single weapon in the game, and some extremely special combinations that can only be achieved through xmutes. Like the Swordwhip. Some of the components required don't even have to drop off of bosses, but rather off of harder battles.
Pro#7: Brands. Remember how I said I'd love to see a system better than transmutations? S+S brought me Brands, and not in some "Oh, it's like a tattoo for cults" way, but in a very fricken game changing way. There are plenty of areas in the game you get to and wonder "How the hell would I ever get up there?" only to stumble upon a brand that lets you reverse gravity in special areas, or that lets you jump up walls like a fricking ninja, or light special platform while making others disappear. I haven't seen amazing combinations like this in games since I was a god damned toddler sucking on my dad's di-- I mean my mom's nipples, and it was literally the best addition to an already amazing game.
I think I covered the basics there of why the game is something to be treasured, and enjoyed. There was obviously so much time and effort put into this game that I hardly have anything to whine about. That having been said, I will be going into the cons of the game. There is only 1 con, and I think it's one that comes from the bottom of my heart. I loved this game, and HATED this one thing about it.
Con#1 and only #1: CRYPT OF THE GODS.... I know it's weird to just have one zone as a Con in a game, but seriously, this zone had so much wrong with it, I hardly know where to begin. I guess the first thing I noticed was that I had a lot of trouble finding a place to spend acquired salt. I mean seriously, the game should have just said "Oh, by the way, you're going to be needing any salt from here on out, unless you're a flawless clairvoyant that also happens to be an amazing player." This game does difficulty in all the right ways, and every area is set up to be both fluid and challenging. Crypt of the Gods loses its way, it is very disconnected, and ill developed. Usually, the obvious way in the game is one void of any secret platforms, or sanctuaries, or loot. But this area felt like there was no obvious way, in some of it's areas it simply felt like there was no way at all. There is a huge difference between challenging a player on how much they can pay attention and rewarding them for doing so, and punishing a player based on luck. A lot of the area is based on random platforms that you have to jump on in order to sink to the lower level where the boss is, except there is no way to actually tell where these platforms are, or where you're going. Unless you spend an obscene amount of time masturbating to Vaatividya's gameplay of this game(guilty and I liked it, no rag rets), it's just not something that was done well. Another thing about this area are the boss-like mobs. In the entire game, I have only ever run into a few mobs that felt really epic, but with good timing, and a great sense of flare usually all enemies can be overcome. The mobs in this area, however, felt as if they had the HP of a typical boss, they definitely hit as hard as the typical boss, and the opportunity you had to retaliate was one where an additional heatseeking attack would follow, and decimate you. The boss in the area was easier to kill than these mobs, which felt VERY weird. Further kind of letting me know that I had no business in stocking up salt. Lastly, once I defeated the boss, which took a few turns with my wife, pun intended, there was no easy way to spend the 60k salt it gave. In fact, I think I lost a good 200k salt in this area for that very reason. The mobs are so damned difficult, and the only sanctuary is WAY up top, and the next area is rather awesome, but a long ways away. It felt like the boss shouldn't have even given any salt considering how hard it was to reach the next area. I actually spent a good chunk of time trying to find a way back to the original sanctuary in the area, but as I mentioned before, this level doesn't have any easy way of navigating it, and the mobs only added to the difficulty and frustration.

Salt and Sanctuary is basically a loveletter to the Dark Souls franchise developed by a team comprised of two. Thought i'd point that out first of all because the final product is pretty damn impressive.
The game has some pretty good controls, they felt natural as soon as i started playing. (I say natural, not identical to Dark souls because it isn't.)
Also, you can play with a controller (which i recommend) and better yet, you can play local with a friend! So get that Stone Sellsword and call upon your homie to embark upon a very salty adventure.
Sidenote: Next to a Stone Sellsword, you need to have an already made character in another slot on your machine, your friend will pick one of your other characters to help out with.
The early areas in this game are relatively forgiving as compared to the later parts where you're expected to have learned how to handle yourself which is nice.  I would say there is a slight difficulty spike halfway through maybe but it's nothing you shouldn't be able to get past in a few cases of trial and error.
That's not a bad thing of course, we live in a time where most games continuously hold your hand throughout your playthrough so a game that expects you to... well, get good, is nice enough.
There's an enormous skill tree to tweak to your liking, a lot of armor you could wear and a good deal of weapons to choose from, always nice.
I personally cleared my first playthrough at just under 15 hours i think but i'll still be playing more of this game because there are NG+ options like in Dark souls and you can always experiment with different builds.
The enemies are plentiful and some a right♥♥♥♥♥♥♥to learn to fight but that's part of the experience really.
The bosses are different in many ways and where you may 'first-try' one boss, you can die six times on the next, only to defeat it the seventh but regardless it should feel nice and rewarding when you do.  I know i felt like that.
Personally, i couldn't wait for this to go on sale so i bought it as soon as i had the money for it.

Surprisingly good game. I am glad I didn't miss this game, it's a well executed game, and a welcome return to the classic hex turn based games. The fact that I love the Warhammer world certainly helps. I haven't played through the game yet, but I certainly will. But as good as I think this game is it does have some points that need improvement. Save games doesn't follow the storyline. By that I mean that if you save a game, you can't simply press continue and think the game will load up the latest save, and continue from there. No, it will instead reveal *all* chapters to you, and you choose where you want to play from. Nice gesture, but not so much on the first playthrough. All of a sudden you need to pick the chapter you were last time (and it's not certain you'd remember that) moreover it will start at the beginning of said chapter. Probably not what you want. Instead, you need to load the save and the save isn't named the text you gave it, no it's named after the place and time you saved it. Again, this isn't all that clear to a user. No, please fix so that a continue selection means just that, it will continue from whence you saved last. Also, please bring the naming into savegames, I typically (and I know others do too) save a temp file, that I want to use when I *don't* want to store a specific time and place. Seeing that name helps. Also, please don't let users see all the chapters on the first playthrough, it isn't helping the game at all. It breaks the story, it is like a kid winding the movie to the action scenes, skipping the booring (but oh so essential) 'talkie bits' :) But besides that, the game (at least to me) is good and very enjoyable.

Evolve is a pretty fantastic game, really. Takes a few cues from Turtle Rock's L4D and others from the source mod The Hidden. The transition to F2P is necessary to give this game a breath of new life. I've had a lot of fun with this game, but the lack of players stopped me playing. Sometimes the Monster felt overpowered (Kraken, looking at you) but other times it was a complete walk over by the Hunters. And other times, there was a brutal struggle between the two. I think the fully regenerating health for the hunters now is going to make it too easy for them, but benefits a team who don't know that healing is a thing - meaning most random teams. It kicks in a little too soon after being out of combat, and means monsters that rely on hit and run attacks don't really get anything out of them.
Time will tell whether Stage 2 creates a sustainable community for this game, but I'm hoping for the best for TRS, they deserve it.
