This is an amazing, groundbreaking game.  The developers obviously took a significant risk with the new fully 3D controls and I commend them for doing so: it must have taken an insane amount of work getting this right, but they pulled it off brilliantly.  Yes, it does take a while to get the hang of fully 3D navigation and in particular figuring out what depth you're at compared to where you want to land (or who you want to attack).  In this sense Trine 3 might actually be slightly ahead of its time: I suspect that this depth-perception difficulty will be significantly mitigated once 3D displays and/or VR headsets become more ubiquitous (probably not long now).  However, through highly-polished level design and controls, I found the game consistently extremely enjoyable and rarely frustrating (only in one or two places) despite the occasional depth-guessing challenges.
And yes, it is a bit shorter than the earlier ones, but the developers did such an incredible job on what's there that I find it hard to fault them for the slightly shorter game.  And as with the prior games, every part of every level is absolutely gorgeous; sometimes I just feel like running around and looking at the scenery.  The puzzles are clever and fun to solve, and the collectable "Trineangles" are often cleverly placed but generally with adequate clues.  The game provides plenty of replay value for anyone dedicated enough to try and hunt down and collect them all.

Checkpoints occur at various intervals throughout each mission and the player can simply hit "backspace" to return to the previous checkpoint (or hit backspace multiple times to go to a specific checkpoint).

It sounds great, looks great, and tells a cute and surreal story. If you've played and enjoyed other RPG Maker games like Ib, OFF, or Yume Nikki, you will love OneShot.
OneShot is best played unspoiled. Having said that, I will now spoil the heck out of it.
The gameplay is mainly about using puzzle items in the right order on the right object, with the occasional logic puzzle or outside-the-box puzzle mixed in. The puzzles are signposted well - often NPCs will give you hints when you get stuck, and a handful have multiple solutions. Items you can pick up will flash gently on the overworld, so you can identify them easily. Despite that, the world of Oneshot is quite large and it's sometimes possible to miss an item, or the entrance to an area. If you don't mind exploring, that's fine, there's lots of things to look at and interact with anyway. But you may need to consult a guide sometimes, to see if there's an item you've missed, or to solve a couple of the more farfetched puzzles.
The sound is lovely. The music, obviously - my favourite song is On Little Cat Feet, the song that plays in the third area. It's inspiring and catchy, but doesn't distract you while you're solving puzzles. Other highlights of the music are the authentic elevator music, and the strange mechanical noise that's plays when the antagonist talks. But it's not just music! Everything from the sound of your footsteps to the baa-ing of rams is a delight to hear. Well, except for the baa-ing of one particular ram. It must be unwell.
This game excels at mood. The world is plunged into eternal night after the death of the sun, and people rely on artificial light and bioluminescent creatures to see their way. Every area is illuminated by twinkling lights and multicoloured lamps, all rendered in loving and gorgeous pixel art. Yet the world is populated. People are living and thriving and often happy, in spite of the slow death of their world. Combined with the (often minor-key) music, this all creates a bittersweet mood that permeates the game and gives its world some real impact. And a strange world it is, too. It has robots, bird children, people with household objects for heads, and whatever Niko is. Settings from acid wastelands to exotic ruins to red-glowing skyscrapers. There's always something new to discover, and nearly every object has some flavour text to reward exploration.
Thematically, the game sets up, demolishes, rebuilds, and eventually throws away the notion of "saving the world". The protagonist Niko is constantly described as a "saviour", foretold in prophecy as the one who will bring back the sun. But many of the world's problems have nothing to do with the sun and will not be solved by returning it. Some NPCs argue that Niko's quest is futile because of that. But the perfect is the enemy of the good. Even though they are not perfect, Niko is a force for good in the world - repairing machines, clearing passageways, and listening to people in their time of need. Although the world is doomed, they do their part to make it better (but are they fixing it, or just easing its passing?). Of the possible endings, neither is acknowledged as the "good" ending. And neither lets you save everyone, but you can always save something.
To disagree with my fellow reviewers: I question the "choices matter" tag - the narrative is fairly straightforward, and there is one choice that really matters at the very end of the game. As the title suggests, you only get one shot and you won't be able to go back on it. Your choice will matter, but it's not the branching narrative you may expect. And the comparison to Undertale has been made. Both games have excellent music, a plot about a small child travelling across a foreign world to return home, and both break the fourth wall to play with the player-protagonist distinction. But Oneshot has no combat, no "good" or "evil" storylines, and is in many other ways a completely different game.
In closing: A hidden gem with a meta story. Come for the fourth-wall shenanigans, stay for the adorable scene of Niko eating pancakes.

Alright this is my 3rd attempt at writing a review, after calming down and thinking about my experience.
Is the game good? Yes, i suppose, mechanically. Is it fun? No. Not at all - therefore i cannot recommend it. Whilst the art style is very pretty, polished to perfection, and the game is mechanically sound, it is not enjoyable. Here's a few reasons why
[edit] just gonna preface this with the fact that, according to steam, I've played 241 hrs of dark souls 1, 431 hrs of ds2, 49 hrs of ds2: SotFS and 164 hrs of dark souls 3. (Thats 885 hrs of dark souls franchise). I've played a lot of dark souls games. I know how to learn patterns, find pathways, learn game mechanics myself etc etc. So I hope you can trust me when I make comparisons between this game and the souls franchise, and conclude that this game is not fun.
Many enemies stand on small platforms that require you to carefully jump, dodge and dash your way to them to kill them. However, many enemies have ranged attacks that stun or knock you back, leading you to fall to your inevitable death thanks to the 100s of insta-death distances. The general rule is, "if you can't see it before you fall on it, you'll die when you hit it". You see very little of what is above and below, meaning you will maybe survive 1 in 1000 falls, leading to very frustrating deaths. Furthermore, enemies with ranged attacks can be tricky to manouver around, and rolling in this game,
similarly to dark souls, provides invulnerablilty for a short time but has a range longer than the vast majority of platforms - meaning you roll through the arrow and straight off the platform and down to your doom. This leaves timed jumps which are incredibly difficult or just sitting around with your shield up. Very boring and poorly thought out
Before I get into anything else, let me rant about the injury system. When you take damage, your max health decreases. As far as i can tell, there is no cap on it - I once got to have my 'max' HP be less than about 40% of my health bar. Why? ♥♥♥♥ you, thats why. It can get particularly frustrating thanks to the fact that you can't level up HP. At least, not directly. It slowly increases with leveling, I believe, which means end-game characters are only slightly more tanky than your fresh-faced adventurer straight off the ship. As someone who likes to be a bit of a jack-of-all-trades, having the option to block, roll, tank a few hits, deal decent damage etc, this totally ruins my playstyle. You have to sepcialise very carefully into EITHER a glass cannon or brick wall that can't deal any damage, but even then your pitiful HP bar gets quickly reduced to being 1/2 despite your healing items, meaning only glass cannons are actually viable. The same system is also applied to stamina, but you can raise it through your stats so it isnt as much of a problem to me - losing 25% of 200 stamina is more managable that 25% of your base 100.
Actually killing enemies once you reach them is a bit... unrewarding. a long-range weapon like a big♥♥♥♥♥sword, spear, hammer, mace, etc. (which is what you want) easily outranges most enemies, meaning you can poke and run. I chose a spear and it made for an easy game. On the topic of weapons; you need 2. One for strike damage, one for slash damage. Most bosses are extremely vulnerable to one and very resistant to the other, making for a slight annoyance if you are like me in dark souls and like to swap out weapons every now and again, keeping a few weapons at +6 or +7 , with no weapons all the way up to +10. This game is pretty much the same as dark souls, except the highest is +7 according to the wiki, but i think +6 is as far as I got. Talking of bosses...
Boring. All bosses are boring. Very boring. Almost as boring as this review. Boring, boring, boring. Why? Because blocking is the magic answer to 90% of all bosses. I literally beat 3 bosses in a row, blind, without taking damage thanks to a 100% block shield. Wow, nice design. On the off chance that the boss can't be blocked, rolling and stabbing the butt is equally effective, if a little more tricky thanks to the involvement of timing. There is 1 boss, the tree of men, which is just a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ gimmick boss that I'm only mentioning because I hope you will look up a video of the fight to see how frustrating the boss is - insta-death pitfalls on either side, crumbling platforms and ill-telegraphed attacks / fire-spitting tubes and plenty of knockback
There are maybe 5 or 6 enemies types: flying, flying archers, walking dudes, walking archers, dogs and thats about it. I've described about 95% of the enemy varieties in that short list. There are few, if any, differences between each enemy within one of these types, and no tangible AI difference. All ground units mindlessly march towards you, swinging wildly, all flying units will charge at you in a figure of 8 pattern. Enemies rarely feel unique, and those that are unique are shamelessly copy-pasted into dozens of locations e.g. the flipping-samurai dudes with katanas that are kinda cool the first 7 or 8 times but get very boring the 30th or 40th time.
There are 2 currencies. Why? I haven't the foggiest. One is useful - salt, which allows you to level up. The other is useless - gold, which you buy things with. You lose all salt when you die but you can recover it bloodborne-style by killing what killed you. They don't tell you that the enemy is buffed by your salt though, which means a learned way of dealing with them might not work e.g. there are various enemies that 1-shot you (even in full armour) but take 2 hits to kill, except with your salt they might take 3 or 4, meaning you die again because you weren't expecting to suddenly get grabbed and 1-shot from an enemy that should be dead. You lose a portion of your gold forever when you die - the cost of "resurrection by a mysterious priest". Not a big deal, frankly, because there is little worth buying. Healing items are unlocked through the skill tree (for some unknown reason) and certain upgrade materials can only be bought from certain vendors under certain conditions - its much easier to farm them / find them.
What a ♥♥♥♥ing joke the system is. Put all your eggs in one basket is literally the only good way to do it. Spend your useless gold on a ♥♥♥♥-tonne of horns that let you travel to any sanctuary with a guide in it, and the guide will let you travel back to any other sanctuary. You then have 3 more slots for any NPCs of your choice - I would recommend blacksmith, alchemist and leader if you don't cast spells or a mage / cleric if you do use spells. Creeds slightly change what is available.
They are not explained at all, but unlike dark souls' covenants that maybe don't impact much, creeds can have huge consequences. You can join 1 of 3 at the start of the game, and there are 7 in total. Changing creeds gives you a sin, and unless you repent at a particular NPC (think cromwell the pardoner without the charm, easy-to-find location or other uses) then all NPCs from your previous creed attack you and you can't travel there. You can't rejoin that creed until you repent, and find a different sanctuary belonging to that creed. This can totally ♥♥♥♥ your game if you accidentaly change creed, die, and have all your sanctuaries turn hostile.
This, too, is stupid. The web design serves little function, really, and is needlessly complex in my opinion. It also forbids flexibility, forcing you to spec into 1, maybe 2 weapon classes if you want good damage output. There is also no way to increase health... Yup.
Oh and one last thing, I have only made it to the final boss, but haven't beaten it. It took me a little under 15 hrs to get there, so take what you will from that.

RAGE, a perhaps lesser known title that, like many of the games published by Bethesda, is often set off to the wayside while games such as the Fallout and Elder Scroll series take the spotlight. Mind you, just because it's forgetten, that doesn't mean it wasn't good.
While the developers behind the game, id Software, certainly don't bring much new to the table in terms of gameplay, it does have that classic FPS feel that always leaves you ready for more. With the addition of vehicle combat, it certainly is a nice change of pace.
Now, lets get into the nitty gritty of RAGE.
Overall, the combat is very simple. You're often fighting along corridors and linear paths, but on the occasion that you finally reach that big room, with the big mutant, you get to take out your big guns and go to town!
The crafting system is simple as well. Find items in the world, or purchase them from shop keepers, and craft them into useful supplies such as bandages, sentry turrents and sentry bots. Buy or find more advanced schematics to craft better items. The usual stuff.
The health system, however, was rather troublesome. It would have been better to use a health meter, rather than the over used reddening of the screen. Also, you can both increase your armor, and health. While increasing your armor is as simple as forking over the money to the vender, increasing your health requires you to go out and find certain herbs to craft a single use, permanent health increase item.
Basically, if you think this game is going to hold your hand, you're dead wrong.
"Now," you might be saying to yourself, "This review seems to be very positive. Almost biased, or something."
Well, that's true. This game has a lot going for it, but it is FAR from perfect.
As you continue to play the game, the combat seems to drone on, and on, and on, and on. In fact, there is one portion of the game where you can sit and farm authority vehicles indefinantly. I remember losing count at around fourty, but even after an additional hour of just blowing up cars, they didn't stop coming.
Boss battles are far and few inbetween. And the ending? No boss to be seen.
***WARNING***SPOILERS***
The ending itself is also very anti-climactic, and it seems to simply be a pat on the back. A sort of "You did it! You saved humanity."
The only issue is...I didn't.
I may have made the ARKs emerge, yes, but from what I've seen, most species of living... anything, has been wiped out. Furthermore, as you play through the game, you don't see a single farm. How everyone is still alive at this point baffles me. I mean, 106 years have passed, yet humanity as the game portrays it mostly survives off of scavanging.
At this rate, once those food cans begin to run out, we're all screwed.
Or are we? Surly, the Authority must have found a way to prevent that outcome?
Nah. They've only been around for about five to ten years before you, the protagonist, emerged. It's safe to say that General Donkey and his crew of mules have yet to even bring these logistics into play.
I mean, you don't even finish off the Authority. You just walk in, kick the hive, and walk out. Sure, with all the ark survivors now able to fight for themselves, it's possible to wrest control from the Authority, but why not take capital prime since we're already walking in there in the first place?
There are so many plot holes in the ending that you can almost feel the lack of a writer.
Or the set up for the sequel.
Which I'm honestly hoping there will be one, if only to finish the story.
So, would I reccomend this game?
Yes. While it certainly isn't perfect, it does have a special charm to it that you can't really find elsewhere. Provided, of course, you can run the game.
Oh wait, you thought this review was over? Hah!  Nope!

This game brings both worlds together.
But some basic features are missing, which make the gameplay kind of strenuous at times.

Most units are ranged (like the artillery in Panzer Corps) and you therefore dont have to move your units adjacent to the enemy`s units(unless you have a good melee unit or terrain doesnt allow it). i think its an interesting idea and i havent played enough to say if its a good one or not.
The graphics and effects look alot better than in Panzer Corps, eventhough im missing some cool movement animations for the walkers.

But at some points in the game it doesnt really seem finished.
I am missing the loss markers floating up in the air after a battle. If you dont memorize the unit stats of the battling units, its sometimes hard to tell the exact losses on both sides. i would love more feedback on the battles overall, like Panzer Corps did at least.
Comparing units in the shop-screen is also a bit of a drag, thanks to the lack of red and green numbers as indicators Panzer Corps had.
I really hope the devs will implement these features soon and i will really enjoy playing this!

3 years after the somewhat mediocre first episode, City Interactive completed its job on the sequel. Was it for the better or for the worse? Well, let's see it!
---Graphics: This certainly is an improvement! The game looks stunning with the CryEngine. I still think the first episode's graphics were decent but City definitely made a good choice by licensing the 3rd iteration of the CryEngine. Water effects and the jungles / lush forests look simply stunning.
---Campaign: Unfortunately, no changes here. The story is still very, very shallow; sections are quite repetitive and the campaign is overall very short. SMG / rifle sequences are now completely eliminated - this is now good as they were very irritating and made the game very difficult. Finally, emphasis is really on the titular sniper shooting and nothing else! There is now an urban (Sarajevo) and mountain (Tibet) area to make the story more interesting. This is all good but as mentioned the new campaign is also very short. Also, you can easily see how heavily the story mode is scripted: you can only go where the designers intended for you to do so.
---Multiplayer: Very few levels available for you to practice sniping on. Also, I am not a camper so lying on the ground for extremely long minutes to see something happen is not my cup of tea. It is overall very slow-paced; once you have found the best hiding - / vantage points on the levels available there is nothing else to see.
I still do not know where to put Ghost Warrior. The 2nd episode is better but still a very short, mediocre experience for gamers out there regardless of their affection towards sniping. Good sniping can be found in the Sniper Elite franchise which does offer much, much more.

I enjoyed this sniper game, and I think you'll like it if you generally enjoy this type of game.  It took me 8 hours or so to complete the single player mode on easy difficulty.  Since I'm not a great player, it took some time and retries to clear the missions,  Having checkpoints to avoid starting over each time I died was good, but sometimes I wished there were a few more checkpoints, because there were a few times where I had to replay the same tedious or annoying parts over and over because I kept dying before reaching the next checkpoint.
The story here is broken up into three acts, each made up of a few missions, and you're working as part of a team even in single player mode.  I think the story developed well, and even though game play can be a little slow at times (e.g., sneaking into areas means crouch-walking for a long-ish time), I think that helps get you immersed in the story.  I think your only weapons here are a sniper rifle, a pistol (I think), and a knife.  While the knife is useful for doing silent kills, I don't think I ever really used the pistol.  The game kind of seems designed to keep you using the sniper rifle, which makes sense.  At a few points you have to set up on a sniping point from which you cannot move at all, which makes things a little more difficult if you get spotted and shot at, since you can't slide over at all to try to keep the enemies from guessing exactly where you are.  There are multiple difficulty levels, though I haven't tried any but the easy one, and a multiplayer mode, which I also haven't tried.  But the multiple modes and difficulties should make this game accessible to all sorts of players.
A few notes on this game (SGW2) compared to Sniper Elite V2 (SE2), which I played before this:  easy mode in SGW2 doesn't mean line up the enemies directly in the center of the cross-hairs like it does in SE2; there is bullet drop and wind effects, but there's a kind of aim-assist mechanism where a small red dot appears showing you where the bullet will go -- you line that dot up with where you want to shoot.  As noted above, although the game play in SGW2 is a little slower, I think I got into the story more.  You don't have as many weapons/tools here as in SE2, but then again, you're in a team here and solo there.  Also, it seems easier to stick with the sniper rifle here; a number of times in SE2, enemies would get close enough that I had to switch to another gun, but that didn't happen very much in SGW2.  Both games are good, but operate a little differently (as expected).

I like this game.  It's fun, it's worth your time and your money.  Comparisons to Dark Souls is inescabable, but this game really has far more in common with classic Metroidvania's than it does the souls series and.  Imagine an inferior Symphony of Night with Dark Souls levelling system and enemies who can kill you in a few hits and you've got a decent idea of what you are in for.
Positives are the game is beautiful, the combat feels meaty and appropriately visceral.  When you smash the living crap out of a zombie you really feel it through the screen and the abundance of gore and sound design.   You kinda have to play it to really appreciate how bloody satisfying it is to crush your enemies and watch the body parts fly across the screen while the screen shudders with your power.   It's glorious.   The level design is also interesting, not quite the masterpieces that are classic metroidvanias but varied and packed full of varied environments and enemies that challenge you in different ways.
The problem comes from the fact that most of the game's "difficulty" comes from bad platforming (there's a reason there is no platforming in Dark Souls, playing this game will make you fully comprehend why they didn't even include proper jumping in the Souls series) and enemies/bosses whose attacks are wildly different than their sprites and animations.  You can definately appreciate the meticulous way Souls bosses are designed to be tough but fair while playing this game, where bosses can sometimes string together unavoidable death-combos, meaning that there is a significant element of luck to beating them.  It might take several tries to clear a boss, not because of skill, but just because if whatever RNG determines which attacks they do happens to hit a certain order there is practicly nothing you can do to survive.
Anyway, In DS when I die it always feels fair or earned, here you just roll your eyes the 10th time miss some jump and fall to your death.  In a game where dying can potentially cost you hours of progress in terms of Salt(souls), it feels like a pretty poor decision to put so many 'make this jump or die' segments.  The game is full of them, especially towards the end, and it's a problem.  For every death to an enemy I think I had 5 deaths to just bloody falling off some ledge that my character decided they weren't going to grab this time, or when my air-dash move just decided not to go off.  It's frusterating and makes you understand exactly why there is no platforming in Dark Souls.
The plot makes no sense whatsoever, and I never really felt like I was being guided along a journey.  The designers really adopted the minimalist story design of DS, but they didn't seem to realize that DS does a ton of world building and storytelling through the visuals, gameplay, and the overall layout of the game.  You always feel like you have a direction and a goal in Dark Souls.  Here I'm just kinda going from area to area killing bosses who I have no clue about or why they even exist or really what I'm doing aside from a vague 'save the princess' mission that I still don't fully understand.
TL:DR?   Flawwed but fun game.  Get it if you are a fan of either Dark Souls or Metroidvanias (but especially the latter) but be prepared to deal with some occasional poor design.

I got it after reading the reviews so I went into knowing it would be good but I was still caught of guard by just how amazing this is.
OneShot is a short topdown puzzle game that features a main character called Niko. Now... Niko, oh Niko. Its amazing just how attached you get to Niko. To the point in which you start talking back to them (Can't just be me) I say talk back to because this game breaks the fourth wall. It does it in a spectacular way. You and Niko have little interactions in which you feel as if you two form an actual bond and I can say that this game is made so much better because of that mechanic (Not to say the rest of the game isnt amazing)
The puzzles are not HARD, but they are challenging, in a way that they make you think, and use logic in certain situations. But this game does something unique, it uses your computer for puzzles. I wont give away what it exactly does, but it requires to you search around on your computer for answers to puzzles. I LOVE IT.

An Underrated Gem. Rage is one of the best shooters I played in recent years.
You play as a survivor in a post apocalyptic earth. There are mainly three types of NPC's in the wasteland.
Friendly NPC's in towns. They offer side quests, mini games, racing and shops to buy and sell inventory.
Bandits are hostile humans that formed groups. They attack in groups and use strategies like flanking etc.
Mutants attack you in groups. There are a few types of mutants. They usually attack you with melee attacks but instead of running to you in a straight line, the swing on pipes, jump over desks and roll to avoid your shots.
On paper Rage may sound like a RPG, but its just a great first person shooter. Side missions involves going to previous locations to get an item. The side mission levels are reused from the main campaign. You can craft weapons but the just requires the right blueprint and items. The wasteland is explored by vehicle. id did a surprisingly good job with the car combat. It's fun and arcadey. The exploration is limited however, since you will mostly be driving from point A to point B with your cars, fighting some bandits along the way.
The story is mostly throw away stuff and ends on a cliff hanger.  The bad story is nothing new for id software games. The unresolved cliff hanger suck.
Give Rage a try if you like shooting games or id software games.

Rage is an interesting game considering its pedigree. It was a game that was released too late. Allow me to explain.
Rage had many features that were standard in the industry by the time it was released, which made the game feel like it was either behind the times or just not developed with enough substance. I felt it impossible to not compare it to other games that were released in the same time frame and felt that it brought little unqiue gameplay mechanics to the table. The tropes of older games are also present such as bountiful backtracking, red shirt enemies and linear layouts disguised as open world.
Had this game came out a few years earlier I think I would have received it better, but the entire time I was playing the game, it reminded me of something better I had already played. So take my "Not recommended" with a gain of salt.

Evolve is a pretty fantastic game, really. Takes a few cues from Turtle Rock's L4D and others from the source mod The Hidden. The transition to F2P is necessary to give this game a breath of new life. I've had a lot of fun with this game, but the lack of players stopped me playing. Sometimes the Monster felt overpowered (Kraken, looking at you) but other times it was a complete walk over by the Hunters. And other times, there was a brutal struggle between the two. I think the fully regenerating health for the hunters now is going to make it too easy for them, but benefits a team who don't know that healing is a thing - meaning most random teams. It kicks in a little too soon after being out of combat, and means monsters that rely on hit and run attacks don't really get anything out of them.
Time will tell whether Stage 2 creates a sustainable community for this game, but I'm hoping for the best for TRS, they deserve it.

Solid sniping mechanics and great graphics brought down by bland protagonists and an extremely linear experience.  You play as several different characters and use a variety of rifles, but there was no difference between any of them (well, OK, the rifles each held a different number of bullets.  Which is at least more variety than the main characters had to tell them apart.)
With a few exceptions, every mission has you being led by an AI spotter who will tell you when/where to move and when/whom to shoot.  Fall behind and the spotter will yell at you to catch up, speed ahead and the game will stonewall you.  Either with a dead end where you can only proceed once your spotter catches up and tells you what door to open (yes, really), all enemies suddenly on high alert (even if you're in the same place your spotter would tell you to stand 3 seconds later), or a straight up "mission failed for no reason" screen.
Shooting targets out of order would have a similar effect.  All enemies would suddenly go on high alert (even when shooting lone targets out of sight of anyone else) or enemies would be straight up invulnerable until you went back and shot everyone in the order the game wanted you to.
The few sections where you are separated from your spotter really show how much this game could have shined as a stealth-sniping-action-shooter hybrid.  There's one part where your spotter gets captured and you set off alone to rescue him.  You run through several arenas where you can engage multiple enemies at your own pace.  It really really underscored how good the game could have been, if only they'd given the player some freedom.
Ultimately, there is too little player input required and the game is too linear to recommend to anyone outside of the "sniping mechanics in a rail shooter" niche.
Disclaimer:  My only play through was on Medium difficulty and I did not try the multiplayer.

So, Defense Grid. Is it worth your time and money?
The short version: yes it is.
The long version: keep reading.
To start of with the best part, Defense Grid is a TD that focusses on plotting your layout. There are no close to a hundred different tower types here nor are the levels a micro frenzy of having to click at spots at just the right time. Defense Grid is a game about strategy. It's about being so shrewd that your placement of only a handful of towers will obliterate wave after wave.Having only nine towers is a good thing as it focusses attention. You have these nine to master and no more. The learning curve is found in how to combine them.
Lasers set aliens on fire, meaning they deal damage even after they left range. But they are useless against shields, which means you need guns or cannons to bring those down. But what if there are speedy aliens in the wave? You need lasers again, or perhaps temporal towers. It's a game about combinations both in placement and upgrades. And speaking of upgrades, there are two upgrades for each tower, each merely increasing the stats of the tower. More damage, more range, faster firing speed. This again, simplifies the learning curve yet the doubling in price for every upgrade still makes it an important choice. You can upgrade two green towers to a yellow one for the price of upgrading one yellow to a red one. Which is better? Well... what's your layout like?
The aliens themselves offer variation as well, although it's not so much the power each alien type possesses. It is when these powers are combined within waves that real danger appears. You even might need to take the next wave into account. A wave of very fast aliens, having sped by your defences, stole cores. That's fine, you think. They are all low health, I get them when they re-enter my grinder on the way back. Unfortunately, the next wave arrived already and contains aliens that shield other aliens. And just when you plan your killing blow, the shield envelopes the thieves from the previous wave. Leaving you to hit backspace a couple of times to revert to a previous save. The smoothest quick load I ever encountered in a game.
Even the resource gain has a strategic consideration in the form of interest. This mechanic will steadily increase your resources based off a % of what's available. Less spending means more income, requiring you to look ahead. That's the reason why at the top of the screen the next wave is already approaching as a set of clearly identifiable icons.
The DLC offers new gamemodes and maps, Ranging from modes where building of the towers is changed, to modes where the behaviour of stolen cores is changed. Each brings only subtle change, but instantly changes the dynamic of any map.
The multiplayer aspect of the game is found only in the scores. Everyone on your friend list who owns the game will show up with their scores provided they played that map/gamemode combination, thus inspiring an ever increasing optimization race to eke out just a few more points than them.
Of course, afterwards you switch to the global highscores and you will cry silently in your hands as you didn't even realize numbers as big as those existed.
The downsides then.
The biggest problem is that once you get good at this game several of the gamemodes lose their lustre. Especially the Grinder modes become a bore, having to wait for a hundred waves doing nothing. Not even the ability to speed up the game can make this time go by fast enough.
Another problem is that the Tesla tower grows useless. This isn't because it is, but because its intended role as a fail-safe tower, isn't required for a good player. A good player doesn't need fail safes.
And finally, there are people who continuously manage to hack/cheat themselves into the top of the highscores somehow, leaving Hidden Path to squat them down again and again. As beating highscores is the endgame for Defense Grid, this is an annoying thing to face.
TLDR; There is a demo. Go try it.

The story is non existent. It’s just a straight forward army game (maybe the only aspect similar to the original ARMA series) against your random “terrorist”. It might be a good cellphone game, but it’s totally out of league for a PC game.

Salt and Sanctuary is a rather unique game. You play a Hero of your choice, who got stranded on an strange isle seeking to find his/hers lost princess. However, as always, things do not seem to be the way they are.
Story wise, this game is rather cryptic, this doesn't make the appeal of the game less interesting. It is very important to read item descriptions sometimes, though you can easily finish this game without being too much into this games lore so you don't need to be bothered about it all the time. This game is also for those who just enjoy quick action as it is for those who enjoy a very thoughtful and deep gameplay experience alike. This works thanks to the excellent layout of the World the game happens to be in, which is structured like a Maze of sorts.
And This labyrinth like Gameworld is, in my opinion, the best thing about this game. Walking around, finding the right place to progress further is a ton of fun. This is partially because on how connected the Gameworld is, paths previously blocked by an obstacle open up to the player later via unique Traits, which you get by many of the interesting NPCs that roam the world. These Traits let you change, for instance, the gravity of the player character which enables you to walk on ceilings, though only at certain places. Imagine fighting enemies from the ceilings with a bow or with a big melee weapon. "Coolness" is certainly written big in this game.
After you've choosen the Gender, decided on a class to play and changed the looks on the Character, you will be thrown into the game world. Tutorials are there, but its only explaining the controls and which they do, the rest is up to the player to find out.
This game does have very fast paced Hack and Slash gameplay if you use smaller/weaker weaponry, or the slower and more thoughtful one if you carry Heavy Warhammers. Logically, the bigger the weapon, the stronger the impact. This game makes no exception of this.
Fighting itself is rather simple, as you only have a Strong and a Weak attack. However, depening on what attack you choose, you can make combos. Beside that you can also quick-switch weapons with the press of a button. Imagine throwing your enemy into the air with greatsword and then using a bow to kill your foe while its in the air. You can do that in this game and it is tons of fun.
Besides attacking, you can also use a Shield to block attacks or use a dodgeroll to roll past the enemies. As this is a 2d Platformer this seems a bit unusual at first, but the games Dodgeroll is balanced enough that it didn't bother me to dodgeroll through enemies. It also looks more aesthetically pleasing as you might think.
However, this game isn't exactly forgiving as I make it seem to be. Some parts are quite tough to beat and it required from me to attempt certain parts a few times before I mastered them. If difficult games are too stressful you should still consider to purchase this game regardless, since the difficulty in general is just rightly choosen, there aren't many points in this game where the game flow stagnates and frustration kicks in, all in all the entire game was a breeze to play through.
However, if certain enemies are too strong for you, you can upgrade your Weapons and Armor at a Blacksmith, where you can use your Salt as a currency to upgrade them. Besides your Salt, which you will also use to level up, you will also use "regular" currency to buy regular items, such as Torches. You will need those to traverse the dark caverns of this game, which there are a ton of. You get both Salt and Gold by defeating enemies. The usual video game logic applies, the stronger the enemy, the bigger the reward. Often enough, you will find yourself being a bit overwhelmed by the enemy, as you are not a Tough Hero and will die if a Strong enemy unsuspectingly attacks you a few times. So you often need to go to a Sanctuary to recover.
Sanctuaries, the other namedrop, are your Safe Spots, where noone can do you harm and those are the places where you can fill up your healing potions and where you can level up and assign Skill Points to your character. Most Sanctuaries are hidden and must be found and claimed by the player first, which adds a bit of an exploration aspect in this game.
As I already wrote, Sanctuaries are used to Level Up your Hero. What makes it interesting though is that leveling up is done in a similar way to Final Fantasy X but on a Spiderweb-like board, where you can access certain skills only if you have leveled up the connected points leading before it. Otherwise you have to choose other skills to reach the stuff you want. There are also items which let you remove your already placed skill points so you can replace them on another place if you believe that you made a mistake. Be careful with this though, sometimes you realize that the mistake your made was actually the right thing to do.
There are 12 different Weapon Classes, such as normal Swords, Staffs, Bows, Spears and Lances, Scyths (yay!), Crossbows and even Guns. Theres more than just these of course. All and all I say theres about 500 - 700 unique Items and Equipment you can get in this game. Theres also a lot of Magic skills you can use, such as making the ground on fire or cast Lightning, if you rather fancy this. This type of skilling leads to some interesting "what would happen, if..." type of scenarios if you decided what to skills you want to pick on next.
Multiplayer is also included with the game, but only be played out on a Local setting, so make sure you have a Friend to play with!
Graphically this game is very excellent, even though it is no cutting edge 3D game. The characters all look lovely and the Monsters are detailed very metriculously. You can be sure that even regular Monsters look all very destinctive and unique. Theres a little less then 100 different Monstertypes in this game, including about 25 unique bosses. The lightning is by far the best about the Graphics as they nail the Atmosphere about this game splendidly. The games grim setting and colorful lightning just synergizes very well with one another, as it is already evidential by the screenshots on this games Store page.
While everything about this game is to the very least great, including the sound effects, I found that the Music is pretty lackluster. Even if its very Atmospheric and fitting throughout the game, after you heared a certain theme like 30 times things can get a little bit boring.
The game also has some slight graphical errors, such as weirdly placed walls, which shift depending on where you stand, creating a weird uncanny valley optical illusion of walls that seem to move unreasonably in places and tiny open holes where you can look right through the void, even though there should be a room right behind it. These issues are barely noticeable but regardless they are there if you pay attention.

Check SteamDB and you'll be surprised, they've already reserved 56 DLCs(including 15 already released) - FIFTY SIX DLCs. Current game state and DLC count just don't correlate in my mind.
I personally prefer Plausible WW2 where people don't build spacemarines templates, don't abuse game mechanics and don't do absolutely "stupid" things.
I've found that 1939 start; Majors only; Common sense community, where there's no need of book size house rules; Where Allies are allies including Soviet Union - Yes, in most game USSR players are ignoring Allies or are ignored by Allies; and Axis are Axis. And that's the place where I spent my ~500 hours in-game and probably will spend more.
Surely it depends on communities and people you play with, but most MP games are swarmed with cheesy tactics, exploits, meta and lack of common sense: "Spacemarines" Templates; Fort spam(Build 2nd Maginot anywhere in the world just in a year - easy); 1 Submarine glitches whole fleet(Probably fixed by 1.2 patch); Dilusional Minors; Half of world goes fascists cause Focus Tree bonus and etc. - It's most of MP games, if listed above is not fun for you, you still can find good community which match your taste.

Game is simplified to the level where it's absurdly becomes complex and not because there's lot of things to watch, to do or to babysit. No. Game lacks feedback to the player. You just don't understand what's going on. Game gives you so little information.
Air warfare is best example - all you know is that there is some air struggle and more planes you build more likely you'll win air "bonus". You don't know what enemy planes you encounter, you don't what's happening right now - seconds before you had air supperiority and area is green, then bam! Enemy teleported his whole air fleet to the region and are is red. That's it.
Bombing campaigns are blackboxes. You're bombing something, but don't have direct control on what you're bombing, all you know that N number of your Strategic bombers do some stuff, maybe they're bombing Reichstag, maybe Forts or maybe it's just village road somwhere 500 miles away from front line, you don't know and will not know, it's a mystery.
Another good example are battlereports, they're gone. Somwhere near El Alamain was a huge battle, where you managed to encirle and destroy three Italian divisions - no one cares. You were invaded by 30+ German army group cause your Royal Navy was bugged by german sub - no one cares. Hamburg was captured by British Paras - no one cares. Ok,
I started with hoi 3.  it had a nice autofunction that left the crap you don't want to mess with to the AI.  How is it improvement to remove this function?  I have to politic, build and fight every little thing through the entire war?  Waste of money, too complicated by far.

This is a second review after having had some time to play it and get to know it better.  First, let me get this out of the way: I truly do not feel like it is less complex than HOI3 in almost every way.  By that, I mean a large part of the complexity of HOI3 and all of the other related games by paradox is just understanding the UI in the first place.  HOI4 is much more fluid in terms of how you interact with it.
Frankly, I actually prefer the unit system in 4 as oppossed to 3 (plays more like a complex Axis&Allies and removes a lot of the tedium I felt in understanding units and hq system, etc...).  That being said, I completely understand the gripes of individuals who are saddened this was removed.  I think they tech system is very intuitive and well built.
The national focus system, although I enjoy the concept, gets burnt through way too quickly.  I am almost always finished with the entire focus tree by the time it hits early-mid 1941.  It's not that I necessarily think they should take longer, if there were at least more to the trees.
I saw somewhere people were upset that they couldn't just turn a country into whatever government system they wanted, or any faction they wanted, declare war, etc...  This I actually feel is more realistic.  You still have the ability to do these things but it takes a longer period of time and you must invest political capital.
One other person at least noted that the conquering system feels broken, and I completely agree.  I think one of two things should exist:  Either the war effort is further broken down into smaller theaters (level of effort in regions), or you should be able to just claim what you have conquered (perhaps increasing world tension).
If you are in the allies, you can claim as much territory you want without repercusions for a democratic country making such large claims.  I think it causes the world tension to increase, but because you are in a faction the AI ignores it and doesn't see you as an aggressor, so on multiple occassions I've conquered at least 1/2 the world as a democratic country... which feels weird.  It feels like you should be able to get kicked out of a faction for your actions.
I completely agree with the criticism of others with regard to battle plans and fronts.  I use them often, but end up editing the actions of individuals quite often to avoid the stupid unit swapping and pause of action I often see the AI do.  In one case, the entire world took a 1 year siesta in the war until I finally spurred it into action by attacking one location.  It's like the AI forgot that it was in a war and did nothing.
One of the things that REALLY bugs me which others have noted, playing as France in multiple games I have not once, despite being a part of the allies, had the luxury of allies actually helping me out.  Great Britain gets oddly transfixed (as does the US) on Africa and sents hundreds of divisions to Africa, where it lines borders and does not really move to take territory.  This leaves France to defend itself.  Until the last playthrough it resulted in Germany stomping France without even a chance, regardless of planning efforts.  The only reason I didn't have that happen last game is because for some reason Germany just decided to randomly attack the Soviets before anyone else, which gave me enough time.  That's another thing, even with historical context on, in every single case Germany makes France its first priority, causing France to fall extremely quickly.  With historical context on you'd expect them to focus on Poland and other places first.  I wouldn't expect it 100% of the time, but it seemed a bit too often.
Even with historical context on, I have never once.  Ever.  Not once.  Seen Japan take the fight to the US.  Never.  I feel like the AI naval game is extremely lacking.  It's like their priorities are just bad.  I'm wondering if Japan ignores the Pacific islands because they simply aren't considered valuable enough by the AI?
In all, I do find the game fun.  I wouldn't keep coming back to it if it weren't.  Still, the AI decisions and the diplomacy feel very awkward and unpleasant.  I wish there were an option as well to have a spy system or some better system of intelligence.  I feel like that's lacking very hard.
If Paradox remade some of the other games of this ilk from other eras I would buy them for sure.  I also wish there were something a bit more modern, or with more of an intelligence focus from Paradox, I think they could do very well in that.  In all, I cautiously recommend this game.  It's fun, but there are a lot of awkward moments which makes you question what the heck is going on.  If they plus AI combat and fix some diplomacy issues it'll be a very solid game.

I hate Dark Souls. All of them. I absolutely love this game.
How is that possible when Salt and Sanctuary is a virtual copy of it? It comes down to two pretty simply differences between the two.
First, it's 2d. The gameplay just works better in 2d. Yes, Dark Souls has better game feel for exploration (although not by much) because of the 3d expansive world. However, just like how spikes of death ♥♥♥♥ing suck in Ocarina of Time but are perfectly fine in a Link to the Past, Salt and Santuary lays out everything in front of you.
How many traps have killed you in Dark Souls only because there was no way to see them ahead of time and you simply had to know or react quickly enough even when going slowly? There are traps in Salt and Sanctuary, but it goes about them in the original Castlevania way. Just go slow. Nothing will come out of a blindspot. If something is attacking you, it's because you aggroed it, and you saw it.
Second, its learning curve actually lets you learn how to play. The zombies in level 1 (and level 0) take more than two hits to kill and only take 5-15% of your health per attack. Plus, you get a regen ring. This lets you actually experiment with combos. Remember the entry level zombies in Dark Souls? How they take only 1 hit to kill? Maybe even TWO! Yeah, not enough experimentation. Plus, if you do get hit, it's like a third of your health.
God help you versus your first big monster.
Once you get to level 2, Salt and Sanctuary starts with the ball rocking. Level 3 is even more so.
The main two limitations of the game are simply:
1) Gold is useless except for flooding your inventory with 99 of each consumable for new game+.
2) Bosses can be extremely easy compared to trash.
As a tip, if you want easy mode, pick paladin or knight. Make sure you have a shield with 100 block of the approriate kind of damage(s). Get as much stamina as possible. You are literally invincible with this setup. No, seriously. If you ever wanted to play Dark souls with 100% damage reduction, just play one of these two classes. Shields must be used more sparingly in the beginning, but by concentrating on upgrades, stamina, and endurance, you can cheese the final boss EASILY.
If you want a harder game experience, choose hunter or any other squishy that relies on dodging instead of blocking.

For some reason, I wasn't expecting to like this game because I hate RPG titles with so much passion. But when I saw the limited-but-active combat system, I felt like it was the Castlevania game we'll never get. In fact, it is crazy to think that this game does everything better than Lords of Shadow: Mirror of Fate. The apprentice has beaten the master.
Salt and Sanctuary is a 2D character-action game with RPG elements. With a focus on grinding and surviving, the game does have enough depth with the Tree of Skill since each class give you a chance to level up in a certain path. Using whip-based weapons, wands, poleaxes and, my favorite, the reapers.
Each weapon behave in a way that you may feel confortable or not and giving the choice to the player is sommething that I appreciate. You can have a Mage using Wands and Staves as expected or you can do something a little odd and go for Magic and Axes. A Knight has access to Swords but can use Reapers and acquires gear that will make that Knight look like a Lord of the Underworld, a Leader of the Damned.
The difficulty is real, I'm not too familiar with the Stamina system as I'm more used to pure character-action games like Bayonetta but Salt and Sanctuary has impressed with the presentation (beautiful art design) the actual freedom for the Tree of Skill, the overall design and the boss mechanics (and they are impressive to fight as awesome to look at) as well as the Brand system where they give you permanent upgrades to help you explore the world. The salt system can be frustrating at first but taking your time is a guaranteed pass for your survival. Patience is all you need.

So, OneShot. I'm going to give this a legit review.
I will refuse to spoil any of the story or anything of that sort. If anything, the only plot i'll say is the beginning and one little fourth wall break at the very beginning. I'll try to explain why this game is so great. I'm going to tell you what my first impressions were from the beginning of the game into about an hour in.
EDIT: I am adding onto the review as I now have beaten the game.
(Onto the review!)
This game is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing.
OneShot is a game about a kitten (named Niko) who wakes up in a house. I'm not exactly sure if it's a female or a male, if someone knows, please elaborate for me. Upon leaving the room she was in and entering the basement, HE comes across a lightbulb. This is the world's Sun. Your quest is to restore the dead sun and restore life to this dark world.
I will not spoil anymore of the plot because it's better you play the game yourself.
Now, onto the gameplay. As far as I can tell, there's no battles, despite being an RPG. It's more of a puzzle game with some light JRPG elements. You can talk to people and use items, and also combine items to create unique puzzle solutions. I have only seen a little of what this game has to offer, but from what i've seen...
This is my favorite RPG Maker game ever created.
Before I played OneShot, i've played a number of RPG Maker titles, such as Yume Nikki, .FLOW, Off by Mortis Ghost, Space Funeral, and Ib to name a few. Infact, before making my avatar Niko, It was Madotsuki from Yume Nikki.
The music in this game is very well done. I've heard of two of the musicians, although I know very little about them. Girakacheezer and Nightmargin (or atleast one of them? I've heard Nightmargin's name thrown around in the music world, may need to look this up.. Girakacheezer I've definitely heard, heard of him through the Cave Story Tribute Site) I love every single piece of music I've heard so far. I also really enjoy that all the menus use piano sounds when you select things on them.
EDIT: I now know where I heard of Nightmargin, she uploaded some LCDDEM tracks to youtube and I've heard her remix of Pulse from Cave Story.
Now, onto one last thing I've got to say about this game.
It's incredible how well made this adventure game is. I love the sprite work. I love the music. I like the story.
But why does this game impress me? ... I don't know! I always liked really meta games. This one may possibly be my favorite "meta" game. I love it when games break the fourth wall. OneShot does this aspect especially good. Infact...
Now, I've also heard that the game can change your desktop wallpaper. How can an RPG Maker game do that?! It blows my mind in every way! I never knew you could use RPG Maker in such a unique and mindbogglingly amazing way!
I love this game. I love it to the sun and back. This game is already impressive on how it actually made me care so quickly. From the first room of the game, I was really really impressed.
I'm editing this review as I've beaten this game. Oh... my god... that final choice destroyed me emotionally.
I've found only one real problem with the game, though. The later puzzles that involve trial and error were a little obnoxious. That was like... 2 in the entire game, though.
This is my favorite game i've played in 2017 so far.
This game gets a 10/10, and I'm not afraid to give it that score. This game is definitely worth your time. You will love this game. BUY IT. Give your friends a copy. Friend's already got a copy? Give it to your pets. Pet's already got a copy? Give it to the world. The world deserves a game this well made and enjoyable.
You will not regret it.

Another game I bought on release, stopped playing then picked it up later to finish. Where to begin?
- Release for this game had a BUNCH of problems. Most notable was the Megatexture system they tried. While they fixed most of it. Some of the problems still linger, such as texture pop in, blurry and mushed textures. Like any other games associated with Bethesda. The game looks great indoors and at close ranges, looking into the distance is nothing but blobs and blotches.
- The Gunplay is alright. There is some downs, some ups. But most of all, it stays average throughout the entire game. There is a good assortment of weapons and equipment you can use. But you'll just find yourself sticking to the same few weapons throughout the game, as using anything else is rather pointless.
Lets start off with the Wingsticks. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥these things are OP. There is no reason to use any other sort of equipment besides these. HE Grenades take to detonate, and won't always kill everyone. Turrets take forever to kill someone and can be destroyed with a few shots. Wingsticks however, once thrown will fly towards the enemy and one shot them, occasionally they'll fly back or you can pull them out of their skull. Which makes it easy to keep a surplus of them, later on in the game you can upgrade them so they'll fly around walls or cover, kill multiple people and then come back. You could compete the game no problem only using wingsticks.
Some of the equipment is useless, or very situational. You do a quest in the first zone to get some RC car bombs. During this quest, you can use them to great affect and to complete objectives. They have small tunnels where you can drive these RC bombs through, kill people in cover and all sorts of stuff. However, no where else in the game features these tunnels and all the NPC enemies will focus fire these car bombs down. So there is no reason to use them again.
Same thing can be said with all the ammo and weapon types in the game. Once you get a certain type, there is no reason to using anything else. Most of the pistol ammo is useless once you get Fatboys/FatMammas. The Crossbow is completely useless, as there is no stealth in the game so the Sniper Rifle works better for long ranged, all of the bolts are situational and much like the RC cars, useless outside of missions. Including the Mind Control bolts, which are supposed to be a "superweapon", but its just quicker and easier to dispatch people with another gun.
The Weapon Upgrades, Inventory, Crafting system and everything else feel forgotten about. There is little reason to craft anything, the inventory has no limits. The weapon upgrades can be checked, but they're so few and used for four weapons. In the all, they all feel useless and you'll likely very rarely use any of them.
- Racing and driving is seriously the best feature of this game. It handles better than anything else and feels great.
- The Story is a mixed bag, I really enjoy the first area to the game. Its much bigger and most of the content takes place here. The theme is nice, people trying to make it by. Bandit and mutant troubles all over the place with people occasionally mentioning "The Authority" like they're some big bad. However, as soon as the resistance comes into play, everything else is practically forgotten about and you're thrust in with them with little explanation.
By the time you're done listening to people mentioning that they're TOTALLY NOT IN THE RESISTACNE. You go do a quest in the Dead City. Which has a lot of hype built up around it, but in the end, it has little to do with the game. (Not to mention, it has a great atmosphere). You go in there, fight an extremely busy boss and then you're back out again. Then you're thrust into the resistance with no real reason to join them, other than "The Authority is bad mmkay."
You finally get to run into the Authority and they seem to be a real threat compared to bandits and mutants you've been fighting. But midway through the mission they become a trival experience, as you get everything you need to fight them. Including pulse shots that oneshot them. EMP Grenades, which disable armor and shields, and armor piercing rounds. Which leave little reason to use anything else when fighting them. Besides Wingsticks. After doing all this, you have to do a few more missions, the town you're in starts becoming occupied by Authority. Which provides a good feel and some seriousness to the story. Then you're offered to head to the second area with the Resistance to help take the fight to the Authority and help end them for once and for all.
The second area is completely devoid of any good feelings, atmosphere, etc. Its gray and bland. The most interesting thing in the entire area is a broken apart cargo ship. Which is only there for some neat factor. The rest of the story is suddenly thrust into your face and you're dropped in the middle of it. Then its promptly pushed to the side and you need to go do some errands for the towns Mob Boss Mayor and reputation so people don't rat you out to the Authority. However, the latter doesn't really affect anything. If you talk anyone in the town, they'll tell you that they already know who you are and that they're counting on you.
You run around, do about 2-3 errands for the Mob Boss so you can get his approval to work out of his city. Which once again, doesn't make any sense due to the entire having been there for ages, and him being anti-authority. (Not to mention, everyone says you need to do this before you can do any sidequest/shopping. But as soon as you talk to him you can do it all anyways without completing any of his quest). So you do them, and then suddenly it doesn't matter anyways, because the Mob Boss was taken away by the Authority. Which gives a feeling of "Why did I even bother?" Then you need to go back down and talk to the resistance to carry on.
You also have the option to do a few side quest, there is about 1-2 given by NPCs, and a few on the job board you can find. But is insanely lacking compared to the first zone. The second task given to you by the resistance, is to finally take the fight to the authority. You need to go disable some shields on the bridge and finally get to encounter some new Authority units, like their vehicles. However, you can one shot any of the authority vehicles with the pulse cannon on your own. So its another moot point.
Once you're at the bridge, you take the lift up kill a few guys (literally about 6-10 guys). Disable the shields and head back to talk to the resistance again. Which then they inform you that you're now at the end of the game and this is the final mission and you're gonna take down the authority. You get in your vehicle, head across the bridge and find a conveniently place side entrance. The final mission is a cake walk, they give you a OP gatling gun so you can blow apart what few enemies you come across. You go through a few hallways, take a elevator ride up. You're now at your objective.
It gets even worse, the final "fight" of the game is nothing more than a wave attack of about 6 fodder infantry, on three waves. So yeah, a total of 18 weak units. There is no boss fight with the General Cross, who everyone mentions throughout the game. You quickly dispatch these last few units, hit the console. Boom, game done. Cutscenes, credits. Overall, it feels like they ran out of production time. The second zone/part of the story is about 1/4th the content of the first area. The story is hamfisted and shoved in your face, which overall leaves a unsatisfying taste in your mouth. Which is a shame.

Amazingly good Tower Defense game. If you like straightforward TDs (no first person, no creating units to attack - just towers and baddies) you will love Defense Grid.
Great graphics - they're not CoD of course but this game does more than justice for TD with it's simple design that comes off looking very sleek and setting the mood very well.
Fantastic audio - each tower/gun has it's own distinquishable sound. The music is memorable and very well suited.
Moreso, the AI companion who keeps you company all game has depth and charisma. He's even got an announcer pack in DotA 2!
Tons of replayability - tons of very varied levels to play on, each with multiple different modes to change your challange, and (affordable, and imo very worthwhile) DLC content also add even more content.
Amazing gameplay - DG's gameplay is fast paced with a need for good reaction skills and planning, but it manages to also be marvellously straightforward. It's constantly skimming the line of enjoyable challanging and (occasionally) frustratingly difficult, but a well-designed "backtrack" feature in this game takes a big part of what tends to make TD games frustrating. You can always back up a few 10-second blocks of time backwards to re-think just where you place those towers - leaving your gaming time spent playing, killing, planning - instead of re-doing the first few easy waves of a level over and over while you try and handle the challanging part.
Whether you're just looking for a fun game to pass a half hour here, or a hardcore lover of Tower Defense, Defense Grid is a damn, damn good game that will get my stamp of approval any day.

This is by far and away the best tower defense game I've played. The game is very simple to play, pick a tower type, choose where you want to put it, watch it kill aliens. The aliens are trying to steal power cores, your job is to kill the aliens before they can make off with them. You start with limited money, but gain more by killing aliens. The challenge comes from making the best tactical use of that money. You need to pick the optimum type of tower for the available locations to place them in. Some of the maps are cleverly designed to let you place towers  and divert the path the aliens take to the cores. Choose wisely and your towers will kill lots of aliens, earn you more money for more towers, and the power cores will be saved. Choose badly and you will slowly be overrun and the cores lost.
All of the maps have massive replayability with different modes offering different objectives. Your scores are also ranked against everyone else who has played. Think you found the optimum way to play a map? Take a look at the highscores and think again! Scores are based on the number of cores you managed to save, the money you have left at the end of a map and the sale value of the towers that you have built. The less you have spent, the better your score will be. Getting the highest scores requires using the bare minimum of towers leaving you constantly on the edge of failure.  Experiment, improve your tactics, watch your name rise through the ranks. There are literally 100's of hours worth of gameplay to be had from the main game, and 100's more from the DLC, which is all excellent.

I've played just about every MMO out there and have several thousand hours invested in playing them (Over 2000+ hrs in Rift + ArcheAge on Steam alone) and this one is just painful..
A couple of my major gripes..
1) Graphics look like they are from the Everquest days. However, the inexusable part is the terrible modeling done by the designers. The textures/models  are so heavily reused.. they need some variety and stop painting the world with the same generic rock terrains.
A simple example was the frill grass poking up from the starting towns fountain.. just raise the base height to hide the frill. That's just lazy modeling by the developers. It looks terrible to have the grass poking out of the middle of a stone fountain.. (Which used the same stone texture without any shaders.. Very ugly to look at - Ingame is far uglier than the screenshots)
2) Combat was ok.. The fact that archery hits are calculated client side on the archer's machine is a bit annoying. It doesn't account for leading or latency.
I admit that I didn't give it much time to get into deeper aspects of combat, but I can't get past how ugly the game is..
3) Min/Max builds only - It seems the game has only a few viable builds, though it offers numerous skills. So, this leaves most people with a cookie cutter planner for maxing their toon.. It seems you end up with a minimum of three characters to experience the full gameplay  - One PvP, and two crafters.
This was off putting for me.. I have a full schedule, so leveling / managing three characters is not appealing. I prefer to have one character that I can spend building up.. I really don't want to waste time switching characters just to keep the cash flowing - that seems like just a time sink to avoid creating content.
If you enjoy hardcore pain.. (Such as drowning in a fountain, lol) You might like this one, but if you are like me and want to play a game that is less work and more entertainment, then stay away. The full loot and heavy PvP lured me in to give it a try.. but ultimately, it was just too ugly to give it much of a chance.

Plates is an atmospherically whimsical little puzzle game that anyone is capable of picking up. While not having any text of any kind throughout it effectively shows you how to play solely through its gameplay. The levels each have its own unique quirk to it and it's very simple to learn how each mechanic works, and with the soothing ambience in the background you'll feel quite good as you make your way to the end.
It's also disappointingly short, even for how little it costs to purchase. The game always throws in new ideas and gimmicks to keep the gameplay fresh, but once you start getting used to the new gimmick the levels have already switched to a new concept. Most puzzle games continuously build on an added gimmick and keep making it harder to find a solution, but because Plates is so sparse in content the levels skip to the next gimmick before the previous one had a chance to get challenging. That being said though, if you want a simple, casual puzzle game then this is definitely something for you. Even on a blind playthrough the game will likely take less than an hour to complete.
Overall Plates is a fun little game that's worth picking up during your downtime between more intense gaming sessions.

If you like Action-Adventure Games and Deus Ex then you WILL like this.
You play Corvo Attano the once bodyguard to the empress now disgraced and “Dishonoured” after having been framed for a crime he didn’t commit. Play it stealthy or go for it, it doesn't matter as long as you get the job done. However either approach will change the game world as you progress, for better or worst. The game world itself is set around an early industrial period when whale oil powers all. It is an interesting world ravaged by disease, but this doesn’t quail man’s duplicitous nature or his thirst for power. It shows that the road to hell IS paved with good intentions.
Corvo’s powers come from supernatural sources rather than tech augments but require finding the necessary amount of runes, artifacts carved from whale bone. Powers can then be selected from the menu and some are rather good, like calling up a swarm of rats to eat those that stand in your way. Also bone charms can be found to add effects like gaining health from drinking water and fast choke to knock out guards faster. There are forty charms but not all can be found in each play through so replays required to see them all.
All in all I would recommend this game to anyone who likes a first person stealthy or Kill kill kill experience. Fight the guards, assassins and the infected to get the job done. I have over a 100 hour play time on the pc and about the same on the Xbox but I like to go back and do it again. The game itself doesn’t change just your way of completing it, but it hits the spot for me.
Give it a go before Dishonoured 2 hit the shops.

I bought this game soley because of the comparisons to Dark Souls. The Souls series ruined most other games for me, and left me craving a similar experience. So, I went into Salt & Salnctuary with high (admittedly, maybe too high) expectations. I was sorely disappointed. It certainly nails the atmosphere of the Souls games while creating and maintaining its own identity, but something just makes the experience uncomfortable, annoying even. I can't quite put my finger on it, but playing the game just isn't enjoyable to me. Two flaws I can identify, however, are the combat and stamina system. The combat is just bad. It feels clunky and unresponsive. Fighting often results in the character randomly facing the opposite direction for some reason, completely ruining the flow of the fight. Like Dark Souls, everything in Salt & Sanctuary is stamina based. Swinging your weapon, rolling, and blocking an attack all drains your stamina bar; even raising your shield makes your stamina recover more slowly. The problem arises from the fact that everything takes so much stamina. You will run out of stamina at least a couple of times in a fight, leaving you completely defenseless. Boss fights make this problem even more clear. The idea is that a boss goes into an attack sequence, you block and roll to avoid damage, and then you use the boss' brief period of inaction to retaliate. However, after blocking and dodging, you rarely have enough to stamina to attack and then safely get out of range.
Both of these problems could be fixed (it's even possible that I'm simply not used to how this game works), but the aforementioned general lack of fun I experienced while playing the game means that I probably won't be returning to this title. If your a Souls fan, buy it on sale just to try it. I don't see it being worth the full price, though.

While it has some quirks I really like and have beaten this game, but most of the folks I recommend it to seem to hate it.  So I guess I will focus of the love-it-or-hate-it aspect:
-  As of this writing, this game has a complete lack of any item sort, manual or otherwise, and works with a hidden slot system (ex.  If you delete item 3 in your inventory and are left with 5 items the items will move together, but the next item you pick up will go to slot 3 and not slot 6).  For a game that boasts over 600 types of items for swapping and fashion good luck finding anything unless you sell/discard every peice of equipment you are not currently using.  There is no positive to this and I honestly find it a tad inexcusable.
*  The Island has a lot of interconnections between the areas and lacks any sort of hand holding to guide you through it other than minor npc interactions .  It really helps build the world around you as you explore, unless you have a bad memory and refuse to take notes as you go.  There are also many optional areas and you might even find yourself working backwards through the "intended" way to go.  There is a lack of information in general, which encourages the player to experiment with things.  This is a huge plus for me but if you like your games linear you will probably hate it unless you like to follow walkthroughs, which can take away from the feeling of exploration but to each their own.
*  You can build your character to match your preferences, but it has a more old school twist of having to spec into weapons and armor before you can use them.  The item you need to change points is pretty rare, and it is not a full respec, so you really have to commit to something.  Some weapon types have been given a lot more love than others in terms of availablility and movesets, but if you play blind you won't know until it's too late to really change anything.  There are also some lower class weapons and armor that really outshine some of the higher tier stuff.  I kind of like having to live with my choices (gives me replay value) and I can say that you can finish the game with any half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥melee setup (I cannot confirm magic...), but it's not everyone's cup of tea.
*  Gameplay-wise, the control scheme can take some getting used to, but you can remap every important action which is great!  Some of the movement and actions are a bit clunky though.  Dropped inputs can and will happen, especially when attempting to weave button presses such as trying to use an item after your heavy attack animation is finished (with plenty of stamina).  Sometimes you just can't seem to grab a wall or ledge that you would normally be able to and plummet to your death.  Enemy grab attacks have phantom range and there are no invincibility frames for being hit, so you can easily be stun locked to death.  There are some seemingly (I admit I could be wrong!) required jumps that you need to be lightweight in order to make safely, so low endurance heavy armor types will need to strip to progress.  Etc.  Etc.  Once I got used to the quirks I had quite a lot of fun with it, but it's still an indie game.  If you are looking for expert level polish you won't find it here.
