Review written the day just before the 20 March update
Keep in mind that the very first realese of OneShot, which was developed somewhere around 2014 on RPG maker 2003, has made huge progress since then.
Also, even though I compare this with Undertale, these two games are REALLY different and Undertale came AFTER OneShot, so when I speak of Undertale, take this just as a quality reference and not as a comparaison.
SPOILERS
This game is really beautiful
The ambiance is really original, at the beginning we fear something but thanks to the character we play it gets away quite quickly.
The music is singular but still incredibely good. It really gives the feel of a dying world, not too happy but not completely dark neither.
This game is pretty similar to Undertale in fact but they are still two really different games.
A kid coming to an unknown world, discovering it and its citizens to achieve his simple and final goal : save everyone.
But the thing is that OneShot has its own feel : while Undertale was really a lighthearted story with almost everyone loving eachother, here the world is more sad, not agressive, but still pretty depressing when we take a look a bit closer in some in-game lore.
The BIG touch of breaking the 4th wall is really a plus in this game. In Undertale, there is this feel but not as much as OneShot. Here, it is almsot the CORE of the game, going sometime really far by making you interact with some separate entity from the game. Even though the notion of reset is not as alarming as Undertale, it still plays some part even though it really doesn't bring much to the game yet.
As now for the negative aspects, well, one obvious thing is the characters.
Don't get me wrong, they are lovable but... really underdeveloped. I almost didn't feel for them exept Niko since we interact with him the most. This is more damageable later when we have to choose between "Save the world" and "Save Niko", I feel better to save Niko that we followed all along than some random people we barely interacted with.
The second negative thing is the plotholes. They are hopefully going to be filled with the new March update, but it is still pretty frustrating since there is also not much for speculation.
TL;DR : This game is a must play and might become a classic with enough visibility.
The game has a lot of pros with only minimal cons.
A lot of those things might change in the update, and I HIGHLY hope so. This game might not be remembered by many but it is still a gem in the indie gaming community.

RAGE:
+ Very nice graphics for a 2011 title.
+ Awesome FPS game with many weapons, including shotguns, sniper rifles, crossbows, pistols, pulse cannons, grenades, wingsticks and more. Really fun shooting.
+ Many craftable items like sentry turrets and sentry bots, which aid in combat. Other engineering upgrades offer dynamite crossbow bolts, electro bolts and additional enhancements.
~ Story is reasonable, it's not as bad as many claim. It could have been fleshed out a lot more, many details are left unexplained, mainly the 'whys' of the game, which tend to be pretty important. Overall it's not a great story, but it's OK.
~ Takes around 20-25 hours to finish on hard difficulty, doing as many activities as you can come across. Some gamers would say that's a good length for an FPS, but others would argue it's not much in the long run compared to other titles.
- Problems with pop in textures for users with Radeon AMD graphics cards. The textures fail to load fast enough resulting in an ugly background for a few seconds, until they've adjusted.
- Many of the side missions featured in RAGE simply require you to re-visit previously cleared locations in order to complete another objective. No new content, just re-hashed in a different way. Not really my idea of good side missions.
- Characters aren't particularly intriguing, dialogue is fairly limited. Again this ties into the plotline. You don't know much about the 'big picture' or who you're working for because it isn't explained. You just know you need to do this or that, because it's in your immediate interests to do so.
Overall Score 8/10
Despite a few issues with AMD Radeon GPUs, some pretty lazy side quests and a lack of attention to detail for characters, along with a mediocre story, RAGE still manages to shine.
It's an excellent shooter, extremely enjoyable and well worth it.

The incredibly bad voice-acting may scare away a few players, but if we look past that, then we find a decent hidden object game with the usual Artifex Mundi style puzzles and a solid, interesting murder mystery.
9 Clues 2: The Ward is more like a spiritual successor, rather than something that tries to continue Serpent Creek’s story. Heck, the game even tries its best to either completely avoid the events of its predecessor or just downplay it as some hallucination.
The plot it a much more straightforward crime story instead, where our detective and her partner try to investigate a series of murders at an asylum. As far as casual game detective stories go, this one is a solid job, with predictable killer and a few enjoyable minor twists here and there. Sadly, the cringe-worthy voice-acting can hurt the quality.
For game mechanics… well, apart from the return of the detective mode (which is sort of a reverse hidden object scene), there are only a handful of easy scenes and a few stock puzzles. I cannot say that the game really tries to shower the player with too much to do, pushing completion time around two hours at best, with no bonus chapter.

9 Clues 2: The Ward is a sequel of 9 Clues: The Secret of Serpent Creek featuring a new case independent from the first one.
Despite his little brother 9 Clues: The Secret of Serpent Creek was one of the less stunning (graphics) of Artifex Mundi, graphics are really awesome for this brand new sequel.
If you played the game before (first one) you’ll already know the two main characters: you (a young female detective) and her partner Owen Duffer. One day you receive a distress call from a psychiatric hospital: Mnemosyne Asylum on a secluded island. But upon your arrival, one of the hospital’s therapists falls out of the window to his death. Then begin a thrilling adventure and investigation about a serial killer on this secluded asylum. You’ll slowly discover everything about the past of Mnemosyne Asylum as well as all member of the asylum staff and some patients. The story remembers me a lot Batman : Arkham Asylum and the scarecrow and I loved that ! Adding to the story and graphics the voices are pretty good and make this game looks perfect. Now let’s talk about the gameplay.
As every Artifex Mundi game you can move freely in different area (of Mnemosyne Asylum) and need to solve some puzzles and find all objects in hidden objects scenes. The game has 3 difficulties and a guest feature: every one of the family can play an independent save and resume the game where they left it. When you first play the game you’ll have a notebook where you have all your objectives as well as all your notes. You’ll also have a map to not get lost and be able to fast travel with hit. Adding to that you’ll have a hint button that will help you in many ways but be warned that you may not use it at all during one of your playthrough to get an achievement. Hints can be used to know where you need to go, where is the next interaction or to show an object or clue in an HOS or IS or to skip a puzzle.
As some Artifex Mundi games you are able to play mahjong to skip a HO scene, I suggest you to play it on your second playthrough though. While playing the mahjong you need to remove all tiles in order to skip the HO scene, especially the golden theater masks tiles. To remove tiles you need to match 2 same tiles but you can only match tiles that are available: above the others or on the sides.
One of the very good thing of this game is that there are 2 (almost) unique features you won’t find in any other Artifex Mundi game:
•	You’ll have several Investigation scenes which come independently from the hidden object scenes. With a remastered concept of the first game. (like Crime Secrets)
•	You’ll need to find asylum model fragments scattered through the game.  (achievement)
To talk about the investigation scene: you see the current scene where there are many clues more or less obvious. You need to find every of them without the name or type of each clue. (If you play on an easier mode your cursor will glow when you are close to a clue) Then you need to place the evidence in the right order: that’s a linear puzzle where you need to order each tile to have the correct shape. After that you unlock a cut scene where you see how the events have happened.
During your journey to the asylum you’ll find many asylum model fragments which will show you the current model view in an extra menu. Adding to that there are also 2 others collectibles: the 9 clues and the morphing objects. The 9 clues are 9 hidden question tag/mark that will reveal a part of your investigation. Finally the morphing items will appears as you proceed through your investigation: delusion that appears half of the time.
(*) :
In addition to no skip or use any hint while playing every puzzles and Hidden objects scenes, there are more missable achievements. Some are obvious but can still be missed : finish the game without using hints at all or watch all cut scenes without skipping any of them.
Some are more challenging and ask you to solve 5 puzzles or 5 HO in under 5 minutes each. Another requires you to finish 3 mahjong in a row without shuffling the tiles. Then you have the collectibles : asylum model fragments, 9 clues, morphing items, information about the characters. For the first three collectibles I suggest you to follow a guide on steam.
Finally if you missed anything while finishing your first playthrough, you’ll still be able to get them on your second playthrough. Indeed you need to play the story a second time to get all the mahjong achievements. Also achievements are linked to your profile: you can track your achievement in-game so the good thing is you only need to succeed where you failed : meaning that if you failed to find 1 clue among the 9 : you just need to succeed the only one which is missing. But only if you replayed the story without making a new profile.

Done by these developers
A h.o.g (hidden object game) that continues on vaguely form the first. I say vaguely because the first one hardly ever took itself seriously and almost had a goofy scoobydoo type feel for it. This one on the other hand from get go launches a much more adult subject and story line and tries somewhat to mimic a 'shutter island' type of adventure.
The story begins with you getting asked by someone to investigate a secluded assylum. When you get there you get greeted with a 'nothing to see here go back' only to have someone immediately commit suicide in front of you. From that point on you begin to realise that there must be some really crazy people in there and there is. One of the most disturbing I came across was a guy whose whole life ambition must be to become a 'crazy cat lady'. The art room was full of paintings of 'mr mittens'. Disturbing i tell you.
There are a number of face palm moments in game like when a guy in a neighbouring cell just happens to have a stick of dynamite to give you, apparently they are easy to get in an assylum. But there are also many clever moments in the game too, like how you have to stop a dripping tap, and even the shot gun trap at the beginning.
I really liked the music in the game, though repititive, but it really did build the suspense at certain moments. The graphics had its moments, for instance there is one scene where a guy is placed in a wheel chair that disappears and magically reappears after you click on something and when owen is lying in bed you can make his head disappear lol. Don't ask me how, but you can. Hence in some area's it just seemed rushed to get the product finished by maybe a certain dead line. What further makes me feel this way is the fact that there are no rewards for the person after they have finished. No secret room, no prequel little adventure, no photo gallery, no behind the scenes gift. Nothing where the developer says 'THANKYOU' to the customer and fan base.
Instead for those that want 100% achievement rating they will be forced to play the whole thing again and play mahjong instead of hidden objects, and if you have missed certain clues along the way you may be forced to play a 3rd time. This is where the game, since it has very little replay value begins to get tedious. I really wish they would stop doing that.
A lot of people have stated that they found the twists and turns in the plot to be many and they were suprised to find out who the murderer was. REALLY? Seriously I guessed it pretty much straight away. It's not hard to work out that if they say a certain person is the murderer, you can bet your bottom dollar that they aren't. And how hard is it to work out that the murderer is the person NOT dying. Seriously as soon as you show up people start dying everywhere around you. So much so that I was really surprised that none of the characters pointed their finger at me and said, "YOU ARE THE MURDERER".
While i enjoyed the ending, I did not quite understand what they were trying to say. Were the developers trying to say that some murderers are just misunderstood people and really nice people inside? I've been with the series (and Paradox games) since a long time and I'm glad this one turned out to be great. Currently it's 3 months after launch and this game runs better, faster and more stable (I had not a single crash) than it's predecessor runs now. In my opinion, this is the best HOI.
People complain that it's too mainstreamed and easy, but I don't think so. The game is still very complex, but at times easier to use. Automated army management can be turned off, but is useful at times. As Italy, I put a general on auto, gave him targets in Africa, dumped some crap units on him and let him conquer bum♥♥♥♥-Africa while I micromanaged the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of my offensive against the Soviets.
The new factory system (IC is gone) is much more believable. Your man don't change but their equipment does as your technology improves. It's more realistic and palpable to see your men putting down their Great War Rifles and pick up some machine pistols. You are in a constant struggle to supply your front lines with up to snuff stuff, which really gives you a feeling of fighting the ressource war, which WW2 actually was.
Yes, there are downsides. The AI is sometimes crazy stupid, but it will most likely be improved over time as they did with the former HOI's. I also can see what people don't like about the new air combat, but it's fine for me.
This is a great game which will entertain me for a long time. I can't wait for improvements and DLC's. Paradox did a great job on this one. Definetly Recommended.

I usually only write reviews for the best games in my library, and Dishonored is no exception. At the time of writing this review, I've completed the game and all of its DLCs twice; high chaos and low chaos.
The game is designed with every possible playstyle in mind, shown especially through the level design. There's pipes on the sides of buildings, ledges, hidden secrets and plenty to explore. Want to sneak past all of the guards? Easy, just blink between ledges on buildings, over walls, and onto streetlights. Want to kill absolutely everything? No problem, just whip out your trusty pistol/crossbow/otherworldly-tool-of-destruction and blast away at the guards on the street, or maybe grab some whale oil tanks and start exploding things. The gameplay is smooth and phenomenal all throughout.
The game is pretty old, but the graphics (or art style, more like) still look pretty good. There's some nice bloom/light shaft effects, and the game doesn't try too hard to look realistic, just pleasant to look at. The closest thing I can compare it to is Borderlands, minus the harsh black lines on everything.
There's a hell of a lot of creativity and freedom when it comes to playing the missions. For example, let's say there's five guards in a room. You could throw a grenade in, stop time, and shoot the grenade midair with a crossbow bolt. On the other hand, you could simply blast everyone with a gust of wind, and finish off anyone who didn't die when they hit the wall.
This game can run on a potato.
The story isn't bad, but it's not great either. You're the royal guard of the Empress, she gets killed in front of you, other government-people rush in and frame you for it. There's that.
For new players, there is a bit of trial and error for certain things. This can be a pro or a con, depending on who you ask, but here's some help with that; you can't blink through a Wall of Light. Arc Pylons aren't so dangerous if you're above them or below them. That should save you a couple of deaths if you're new.
Not much else in the cons department.
9/10, only wish the game could've been a bit longer (there's 9 missions in the main game, give or take 5-6 hours if you know what you're doing).

Ah Dishonored, the game where you can do so much but half the time it will end up in someone dying... great. Now around the time of this review my icon is the outsider's mark so you can "easly" (can't spell) tell I'm a massive fan of this game. For those who want a quick and easy response to this game and if they should buy it or not... You should no doubt about that, best game in existance in my opinion. Want more info? Here's a more indepth look
Story:
So for story... how can you say it, umm... IT'S BLOODY EPIC. The games story changes so much due to your actions like (SMALL SPOILER) Emily's personality changing if you kill everyone or let everyone live. (ANOTHER SMALL SPOILER) I played a High Chaos run (kill anyone and everyone) and when I returned she asked me if I killed anyone and how many, freakin' dark ay?
Now the story is really good even though I had to play the game many times to understand, (Wasn't paying attention, too busy killing) but when you do understand it you will react in many different ways. Personally I nearly cried when I got to the end and... failed what I ment to do and still got the final cutscene. But the story pans out many different ways depending on your playstyle, only problem, it's a little short. 9/10 for story.
Gameplay:
You murder or choke everyone, what more to say? You can kill people in many different ways from springrazors to grenades to a pimped out pistol. But even for a game as great as this there are a few flews. One, non-lethel weapons. Sure in the main game you have a crossbow with sleep bolts but even when you play the DLC there are more non-lethel tools. Also Controls, left control for block... really? You fix that up to your likings and your sitting gold. Still doesn't mean there are lots, in the main game you choke, sleep bolt or evade to stay hidden. But that just makes being an all out brute a lot more fun.
And Powers. As you are chosen by the outsider to do... something, you are given a wide veriety of powers from speed too rats, yes rats. From the upgrading system to exicuting the powers are top notch. Higher power and level powers cost more 'Runes' to upgrade and you can easly tell they have been upgraded. Take blink a short teleport for example. At first that is really all it is, a short teleport. But when you get Blink II or 2 for 3 runes you can tell that it is much more effective, you teleport further which is so useful. Again, not many non-lethel powers. If your doing a ghost run (Never getting detected and not killing anyone) all you really have is Agility, Dark Vision, Blink, Possesion (I think) and Bend Time. That may seem like a lot or half of the avalible powers but it really isn't.
The A.I. is a bit of a push over, as long as your quite above them, they will never look up. They fight pretty well though, the guys with guns are a little stupid though since bullets deal so much damage (Understandibly) and they just stand there and aim for like a second then fire, you could just run up and swing at them to restart there firing time or you can just shoot them yourself then stab them while stunned.
Stealth... you can't say you aren't ment to be stealthy in this game but if you can, you should if you plan for low chaos. They did really well in this compartment. You hit C to enter stealth mode, your footsteps are muffled and make jumping practically silent, seems legit.
But all and all I can't just sit there and get mad over such small things because the things they do well in, they do really well. 10/11 for Gameplay

The main point of the game that I adore so much is the story. Its pacing, characters, how events revealed, and the twist and turn kept me going and it was somehow difficult to stop playing it. The gameplay also helped this wonderful game immensely. There are various options to choose in term of gameplay style. I finished the game in low chaos. But trying to go in a killing spree, albeit silent one, is something I enjoyed so  much. The mouse and keyboard control is superb compared to controller in this game imho. If I have any gripe about the gameplay is that low chaos play wasn't supported by as many gadgets as for the high chaos route.
Highly recommended. I hope Dishonored to brings more fun. I can't wait for it.

There is definitely some potential in this game - and it's not without some play value. (I spent 11 hours playing it, after all - enough to complete one of the two available story campaigns.)  That said, it feels a bit incomplete...  only one weapon of each type to unlock, only a very basic selection of non-weapon gear, no advancement aside from raising scores on a few basic skills which boil down to "walking", "shooting", etc.  If there was a bit more depth here, I'd definitely recommend, but as things stand, the poor AI and shaky gameplay make this a thumbs-down.  A few examples:
With 2 AP per character per turn, a lot of the tactical decisions involve guesswork.  A few examples of the sort of tactical frustration you'll encounter:
"I guess moving here will give me line of sight to that exposed enemy...  hm, nope, invisible wall blocks my shot.  Guess I'll wait til next turn"
"I guess I'll wait here in overwatch so the enemy will come to me, since none of my guys have good LOS...  hm, nope, they shuffled a half step and hit everyone - I guess that low wall wasn't really giving me cover in that direction"
It's a shame, because this game is very close to being a great high-value squad tactics game.  A few quick fixes to gameplay, and/or some added content (more campaign levels, advancement options, gear, etc) would make this a definite winner.

This game feels like the proper evolution of old-school point and click adventure games; Telltale have certainly done well for themselves with their cinematic, QTE-heavy story games, but OneShot properly adapts the laid-back, contemplative style of many old point and clicks into the modern era while fixing many of the issues present in the genre. The game consists of exploring interesting, atmospheric locales, talking to charming characters, and solving inventory puzzles, which is all pretty familiar, but where it really shines is in some of the late-game reveals which I won't spoil here, the depth and breadth of the worldbuilding crammed into such a small game, and the fact that the puzzles all make rational sense and are signposted well. It's got the writing and atmosphere to stand next to point and click giants like The Secret of Monkey Island and Day of the Tentacle, with a much smoother, more stylish, and cleverer presentation.

The story is that you follow Niko as a god and lead him as your Messiah to restore the sun to the decaying world. You have to make choices in this 4th wall-breaking puzzle game, and those choices will affect Niko as you help him along, but will it be enough to save this decaying world and Niko?
Pros:
- Enchanting story and environments!
- Each and every character you come across and talk to has their own personalities and mindsets about Niko and you saving the world.
- Each track for every area/enviroment fits it well and makes those areas come more alive.
- A grim backstory.
- A cat child named Niko!
- Choices that will affect how Niko sees you
- Replay! You can play this game over and over again and have different dialouge each time.
Cons:
- It felt like it was a bit too short. I feel like they could have expanded the game and it would haven't hurt it any.
- WHY WOULDN'T THE DEVELOPERS JUST PUT IN AN OPTION TO LET ME HUG NIKO?
Overall I would rate it 10/10. This is a game that is perfection and makes me actually regret the decisions I make for Niko. I went to a corner, curled up, and cried after the game was over. This game will ethically challenge you to what you think is right.

While it has some quirks I really like and have beaten this game, but most of the folks I recommend it to seem to hate it.  So I guess I will focus of the love-it-or-hate-it aspect:
-  As of this writing, this game has a complete lack of any item sort, manual or otherwise, and works with a hidden slot system (ex.  If you delete item 3 in your inventory and are left with 5 items the items will move together, but the next item you pick up will go to slot 3 and not slot 6).  For a game that boasts over 600 types of items for swapping and fashion good luck finding anything unless you sell/discard every peice of equipment you are not currently using.  There is no positive to this and I honestly find it a tad inexcusable.
*  The Island has a lot of interconnections between the areas and lacks any sort of hand holding to guide you through it other than minor npc interactions .  It really helps build the world around you as you explore, unless you have a bad memory and refuse to take notes as you go.  There are also many optional areas and you might even find yourself working backwards through the "intended" way to go.  There is a lack of information in general, which encourages the player to experiment with things.  This is a huge plus for me but if you like your games linear you will probably hate it unless you like to follow walkthroughs, which can take away from the feeling of exploration but to each their own.
*  You can build your character to match your preferences, but it has a more old school twist of having to spec into weapons and armor before you can use them.  The item you need to change points is pretty rare, and it is not a full respec, so you really have to commit to something.  Some weapon types have been given a lot more love than others in terms of availablility and movesets, but if you play blind you won't know until it's too late to really change anything.  There are also some lower class weapons and armor that really outshine some of the higher tier stuff.  I kind of like having to live with my choices (gives me replay value) and I can say that you can finish the game with any half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥melee setup (I cannot confirm magic...), but it's not everyone's cup of tea.
*  Gameplay-wise, the control scheme can take some getting used to, but you can remap every important action which is great!  Some of the movement and actions are a bit clunky though.  Dropped inputs can and will happen, especially when attempting to weave button presses such as trying to use an item after your heavy attack animation is finished (with plenty of stamina).  Sometimes you just can't seem to grab a wall or ledge that you would normally be able to and plummet to your death.  Enemy grab attacks have phantom range and there are no invincibility frames for being hit, so you can easily be stun locked to death.  There are some seemingly (I admit I could be wrong!) required jumps that you need to be lightweight in order to make safely, so low endurance heavy armor types will need to strip to progress.  Etc.  Etc.  Once I got used to the quirks I had quite a lot of fun with it, but it's still an indie game.  If you are looking for expert level polish you won't find it here.
I honestly think that if you think you can work through the quirks it is really worth a try!  Games with this level of exploration are fairly infrequent and I am enjoying it from start to finish.

Rage, developed by Id Software & Released on Oct 4, 2011. According to Metacritic
, it's rank 55th best critic review pc game & 9th most discussed pc game in 2011, respectively.  Does it hold any meaningful  value or worth purchasing in 2015? It depends.
The Controls are easy to grasp. Visually, it still looks good to date. Game mechanics is good, fun. Aside from the FPS, you'll have racing and some other mini games to play. The combat system is responsive@really satisfying feel. The AI are fairly smart. You'll get to experience it when you put up a fight against groups of mutants and the humans factions.
Rage is set in an post-apocalyptic time. It feels like a combination of mad max & borderland. I'll give you the bad news first. You'll be spending most of your time driving. The good news?  No nonsense farming for random glowing loot & you'll get to blow up lots of enemies/vehicles/mutants while exploring the land -or-trying to get from point A to point B.
Unlike borderlands, you'll only have a limited choice of weapons & customization to choose from. Some are pretty nasty & interesting (for instance the Nail Gun or the remote control car with bomb) BUT you'll need to replenish the ammo constantly throughout your travels. You either buy them or craft them from your salvages.
The road to richness is a long one, you'll get to play some mini games to to earn cash, a tv arena to earn more cash and a few racing arena where you'll have to invest your time to get the vehicles upgrade parts for your sweet ride.
The story is linear but definitely an interesting one. Not as funny/whacky than borderlands but is still refreshing to do them after X amount hours on the road (smashing/blowing up everything that moves).
There's Multiplayer option as well however I have yet to try it out myself.
My Summary:
It was refreshing and fun at first but after a XX amount of hours into the game, it gets pretty boring@repetitive but what kept me going was the story. The interesting fights/scenario you're put into. Late into the game however, there's a sudden spike of difficulty. That's a no-no for me. I wasn't pleased at all with ending. (There wasn't even an epic boss fight!) Despite the awesome guns/combat mechanic - there is no replay value for Rage. It was a sweet, one time experience for me. On the scale of 0 - 10, my personal rating for Rage is a 6/10.

So... I start up Steam. It doesn't show RAGE as an installed game. Interesting... I've been playing it for a past few days now, and why does it suddenly think it's not installed? So I click the Install button... Since the files are already there it won't take long until I'm able to start the game again. Now the plot thickens... Save game corrupt. Verrrry interesting... So I google it a little to no avail. I look inside the allegedly corrupt savefiles: most definitely they are corrupt. Although the file size seems legit, the files seem to contain only ASCII 32 characters. So yeah, no useful information there to be found. Fortunately it seems I don't have to start over, not all the savegames are corrupt, but at least 6 hours of playtime is down the toilet. Also I thought it is syncing the savegames with the Steam cloud but it doesn't appear to be doing so. It is syncing something but definitely not the savegames. Savegames are stored "safely" on local drive folder ?:\Users\?\Saved Games\id Software\Rage\base\savegame folder. Extremely frustrating experience.
But, all that aside I'm finding the game quite fun and playability is also good. I would recommend playing it. It takes many good aspects of other games and combines them. So there's nothing groundbreaking or original, it's all been there and done that. It's been fun and I've found nothing overly irritating. Durig the whole gameplay I didn't experience a single notable bug or glitch or a crash. Ok,that's not entirely true: only once I fell out of the map. Overall I am positively surprised, because all that negative feedback I read prior to playing the game had led me not to expect too much of it. But it seems that the bugs have been fixed and all the other issues addressed. Second part of the game (Eastern Wasteland) feels kind of short or rushed and the game ending is kind of anticlimatic. About downloadable content: Scorchers campain is just fine, but The Sewers - pointless... I played the game on Hard difficulty, it was challenging enough, didn't try any other difficulty levels. But it is a 7/10 game definitely, worth playing. Nice post apocalyptic game.

Rage is a fun game.  Although the game was reportedly rough out of the gate, Rage has since been patched to a stable state.  Rage plays as a close-up gun game with attention especially paid to NPC tactics.  The other part to the game is the use of fortified muscle cars (think Mad Max film) where you can parpticipate in races/point-battles and travel to and from missions.
Many elements play well into a great looking game.  Rage's id Tech 5 engine put to use a new technique called Mega Textures, and while this can make the game look stunning in certain settings, it can also break they immersion from time to time.  As I've seen others say, the skybox in Rage is very impressive and these "Mega Textures" can make the sweeping landscapes great eye-candy.  That said, Mega Textures can also look, well, goofy when view up-close.  The NPC models and actions are one of the great things Rage does but when you only have 1 Mega Texture covering an object the textures and look undefined and granular up close.  Especially next to Rage's very well sculpted NPCs.  You can see what Mega Textures can do to a large landscape and overall Rage looks very slick.

The game's not the best hidden object game I've ever played, but it's far from the worst. To break it down quickly:
~It's a little bit darker than your standard HOG, but that's not a terrible thing. It doesn't go overboard with, say, gore but it doesn't just hint at something bad happening in another room.
~The puzzles are somewhat simple to keep them from being time-consuming. Players who don't mind spending time on complex puzzles will be disappointed, They tend to be the same puzzles we've seen from Artifex Mundi -- this could be either good or bad depending on your personal view. I will warn that it seems like the hidden object aspect takes a backseat here, though.
~They pad the play time out with extra things you can find just walking around. I don't mind collecting extra pictures and things, but you never know when an area will become unaccessible due to plot. If you don't find the object before then, you just won't get it so heads up.
~The plot is bloated with so much extra crap that I think it actually falls through in the end. It's hard for a HOG to get players really invested in plot because the puzzles usually take center stage, but they try to expand it way too much. The big reveals are confusing and convoluted, the circumstances are strange and unlikely, they try to force-feed you character development that's not earned...there's just so many issues that could be resolved by shaving the plot down.
Despite the flaws, I did have some fun. I would heartily recommend not buying it unless it's on sale, as I don't feel it justifies the full price. However, if you like Artifex Mundi's games and usually have no issues with them, give it a shot either way.

Worth a play-through...if you can find it in the $4.99 bin. And if you've already read Ulysses. And assuming you've already watched paint dry, water boil and pigs fly.
Pros: nice weapon selection, really good graphics (aside from texture-loading), good sound (aside from the horrible drone of the trucks), great action (aside from the repetitive nature of questions) and... I got it for $4.99. Screenshots really do make for great desktop wallpaper.
Cons: landscape, although beautiful, is sparse and there's no real adventure... it is just point a to point b, back to point a, on to point c, back to point a, etc. The best areas - the old city - are far too short. Binding controls - still really, really annoying when I have to change an INI file simply to setup keyboard bindings. Just dumb. Sound - the truck drone is horrible and it cut in and out constantly. Texture loading is as bad as what you may have read. The story is weak and really short. (don't let the 18.5 hours of total play time attached to my profile fool you... I'm notoriously slow with game progression because I like to explore every nook and cranny and do every side-mission. A lot of the time I spent roaming the pseudo-sandbox world was just to find that I couldn't progress to a section of the map until I did some small, meaningless mission). Worst. Ending. Ever. There is SO much build-up and hype that when I got to what wound up being the ending, I actually thought that was the mid-point of the story - you know, where it all hits the fan. The final "boss" (there are none) is nothing more than picking off regular old baddies in pairs and triples for 5 minutes. Seriously. At first, I thought the AI was pretty good - dodging my fire, jumping off wals, climbing the ceiling, hiding, etc... but after an hour of game time, it was apparent that there really was no AI... the baddies follow what appear to be a very finite set of pre-determined rules for hopping around, jumping, etc., irrespective of what I did. Boo-hiss.

I got this in a bundle for $3, and it was totally worth that price. The singleplayer campaign is really unpolished, but there are some parts where it gives you a bit of freedom and these are often quite enjoyable. The game is also reasonably comitted to the sniper angle, and does it fairly well. You only ever get a sniper rifle and pistol, so you have to be stealthy. Occasionally, you actually have to think about the best way to accomplish that, and these sections are generally pretty good and evoke the patience and planning of a skilled sniper. At other times the game forces you into gunfights, and these suck. Enemies can kill you very easily, which is good for a stealth game but frustrating in an action game in which you have very little short-to-medium range firepower, since your pistol is crap and your rifle is always scoped and bolt-action. Still, a cautious and skillful player can avoid the great majority of these, so it's not a huge problem.
About the plot, not much can be said. Dull military bros shoot a bunch of dudes, and somebody's evil, and more dudes are shot. One level is set in Bosnia, which is pretty cool. I have no idea how historically accurate it is but it's nice to see some new settings being explored.
The game looks okay. It's got some nice CryEngine-y effects, but a lot of the assets are kinda fugly. Ultimately it gets the job done. Some of the level design is well-done, but checkpoint spacing is often poor, and manual saves are not allowed. Bugs crop up from time to time, everything from bullets passing harmlessly through enemies to your companion's AI simply not triggering, but it's not completely game-ruining.
Ultimately this is only for people who really like single-player shooters. It lacks the polish and bombast of stuff like Call of Duty, but it also lacks the flexibility and openness of games like Crysis or Far Cry 3. Still, for a budget developer it's a pretty solid release, and bodes well for a third game. I wouldn't recommend it at $20, as it's just not polished enough, but for $10 or less it's worth a shot.

I almost forgot how good Dishonored really is. The story itself is a tale of revenge and it does it well. Even though Corvo (the main character) does not talk, it is easy to understand why he desires revenge, and in that respect the story is very compelling. The voice acting for the other characters is good. It is not amazing, but it does the job. The gameplay however, is fantastic. If you played Bioshock, you'll be able to slip right into Dishonored. The game gives you A TON of freedom to play how you want. You can go through the enitre game and not kill anybody or you can kill everyone if you want. Depending on which path you chose, it will effect the story in a profound way. The powers you are able to use are pretty cool, but some are much better then others. Blink, Dark Vision, and Slow Time were the only ones I used, and even if you plan to kill everyone, the more agressive powers are not all that useful. The stealth mechanics are great and mesh very well with all the powers. Even though the game is almost 4 years old, the graphics and sound design have held up very well. The whole game looks like a water color painting. Overall, Dishonored is a fantastic game and a purchase you will not regret.
FINAL VERDICT: 9/10
BEST ASPECT: THE MULTIPLE GAMEPLAY OPTIONS
WORST ASPECT: THE VOICE ACTING...IF I HAD TO PICK SOMETHING

The 3D aspect of the game lends itself nicely to visuals and set pieces but makes moving magical boxes around incredibly frustrating. Trine 3 also ends about 1/3 of the way into the heroes' quest on a cliffhanger, and there's no sequel expected.

Let's be honest. When I played OneShot, I didn't expect much. I got interested because of it's very pretty arstyle, but I didn't know what awaits me here.
And, well...
I was very suprised. OneShot was the first game in many years that made me feel so immersed in the world and the story, and for the first time in a long time I felt really attached to the main character.
But what is the game about?
It takes place in a world where the Sun died, and people are living in darknes. They only have a little bit of light left, and even that is starting to die out. But  in this world there is a prophecy that says that a Messiah from another world guided by a God will travel to the Tower with a new Sun and will make the world like it once was. Then the Messiah will return home, and everyone will live happily ever after.
The Messiah is Niko, a small confused child. And the role of the God belongs to you, the player.
Which leads to one of the coolest things about this game - Niko knows about your presence and responds to your actions, asks for advice and even has little chit-chats with you. And let me tell you something - it's such a sweet, precious kid that it won't be long before you will start really caring about this little kid and you will want them to return home safely.
Sadly your journey is not a easy one. Without the Sun, the world is dying. While many people greet you with happiness and hope, others react differently. They don't believe that just bringing back the Sun will be enough to save the world, and they question the point of your journey, and so will you. Can the world REALLY be saved?
What also doesn't help is the fact that Niko doesn't realise that you are as lost and confused as they are. Luckily,
will help you on your way. But be careful - this world has many mysteries, and you will replay the game many times. You will want to know the truth, and more importantly - you will want to know if you can really save both.
But all of that will be answered in time.

9 Clues 2: The Ward is Artifex Mundi jumping the proverbial shark.
Though their library isn’t quite the flawless lineup their “premium” branding would have you believe, by and large Artifex Mundi’s hidden-object adventure games (referred to henceforth as HOGs) hit far more than they miss, especially given the fact that they seem to release half a dozen of them in any given month. They consistently manage to strike that perfect balance between above average production values, simple but enjoyable puzzle designs, and storylines just earnest enough to be entertaining. The first 9 Clues game, Secret of Serpent Creek (credited to Tap It Games, but so indistinguishable from Artifex Mundi’s own games that the distinction between them as developer or publisher seems a moot point), continues to rank as my favorite HOG to date, taking all the tenants of Artifex Mundi’s trademark design and wrapping them up into a lighthearted but endearing mystery thriller.
Though it shares the same series, The Ward is not only a dramatic departure from the previous 9 Clues but from Artifex Mundi’s HOGs in general. The Ward can best be summed up as Artifex Mundi going through a phase of overwhelming teen angst. Cue the inexplicable violence. Cue the barely intelligible plotlines designed for MAXIMUM DRAMA. Cue the misunderstood sociopath who was only murdering people because another sociopath told them to (it’s OK though, they’re actually good, I swear, so let’s just forget all that murder business).
If Secret of Serpent Creek was trying to be Scooby-doo, The Ward wants to be Shutter Island. It’s aggressively grim and (for a HOG) shockingly grotesque in both its story beats and how little it hesitates to delve headfirst into the most disturbing of subject matter. And this is where The Ward lost me. Even before its narrative turned into a convoluted mush of character reversals, deus ex machinas, and astoundingly convenient circumstances (again, even for HOG standards), The Ward alienated me with how little it cared. Where past Artifex Mundi games verged upon the repugnantly earnest, The Ward is a melting pot of “mature” themes and purposeless cruelty handled with even less care than you’d expect from this style of game. I’m not sure if The Ward came from a place unsatisfied with the casual branding of HOGs or if Artifex Mundi just ran out of ideas and started scrubbing through horror films for inspiration, but the second 9 Clues has managed to eject every ounce of the first game’s charm and replaced it with a nauseatingly poor attempt at tackling “adult” themes.
It’s all downhill from there, as the narrative flounders around attempting to find itself, puzzles become more obscure and tedious, and a veritable cornucopia of bad accents meander through lines as if the voice actors are simultaneously bored and learning to read for the first time. I even ran into some graphical bugs, which apart from being the most amusing part of the game cement how thrown together The Ward feels. I suppose it was bound to happen eventually that Artifex Mundi would release a colossal dud given the speed of their production process, but with how much I loved the first 9 Clues I’m sad that The Ward had to be the one to break the formula. The Ward exists then as a reminder of why we can’t have nice things. Only exploitative representations of mental illness and thoughtless depictions of suicide. Try not to cut yourself on all this edge.

The Ward continues in the vein of the first 9 Clues. It's a nice point'n'click/hidden object game, which does not have difficult puzzles, so, if you are an experienced player, you will likely not encounter any obstacles to stop you.
The story is nice too. Like pretty much all the Artifex Mundi games, it's a mystery with the elements of horror. I just wish the ending would not be so simple.
Still, 9 Clues 2: The Ward provides an entertaining experience for a couple of evenings.

9 Clues: The Ward, is a HOPA* game, developed by Tap It Games and published by Artifex Mundi.
This is the second installment of the series. The previous installment was 9 Clues: The Secret of Serpent Creek.
*HOPA - Hidden Object Puzzle Adventure.
I want to mentioned that the visuals for this game is nicely done with a painted feel to them. The visuals can be adjusted in the option menu.
I want to mentioned that the audio for this game is well done even if it's simplistic and somewhat repetitive. The audio can be adjusted in the option menu as well.
There are only three difficulty game modes to choose from: Casual, Advanced and Expert.
The game is divided up into acts. There are total eight of acts in the game.
Diary Notebook it has three sections. Game Objectives, Clues and Characters.
There is an option for locking the inventory in place. It's automatically lock in place at the start of the game.
The interactive map allows the player to fast travel between each location quickly. It also indicates there are tasks that needs to be done at certain locations.
Most of the game's hidden object scenes consists of traditional word lists with some or no interaction.
Mahjong mini game is optional for anyone who doesn't want to go looking for the items in the hidden object scenes.
Most of the game's puzzles are fairly easy to solve without having the need to skip any of them.
There are collectibles (sorta) in the game. Asylum Model Fragments, Hidden Clues and Phantom Objects.
There are thirty-nine different achievements. But each of these achievements has certain requirements before they can be unlocked.
There are total of six different trading cards. You only get the three of those cards from the game. There are several ways to get the rest of the trading card: Purchased from Steam's Market; Trade with friends; Booster Packs and it's Booster Pack Creator.
Final thoughts, I've found this game enjoyable to certain extend. The replay value for this game is low. I would recommend this game but not at the full price.

There are two towns that you vist and they function exactly the same. The RPG element feels rushed and out of place. The story seems intriguing at first, but then it seems to fade into the background as you keep doing repetitive tasks for the entire game: go get this from some place, shoot a bunch of enemies, and repeat. Sanctum is controlled first-person shooter-style in two phases. The first phase, the building phase, gives you all the time in the world to build your perfect tower maze with whatever resources you have available to you. The second phase, the extermination phase, sends a wave of creeps down your maze. You're even allowed to get in on the fun by blasting them to bits. Enemies will never attack, so, just like any other tower defense game, your only job is to kill them before they reach the end of the maze. If an enemy bumps into you, it will just stun you for a moment and then let you get back to blasting. It's a lot of fun for anyone who gets a kick out of seeing wave after wave of enemies die without resistance.
If you're a fan of tower defense games, Sanctum would be a good choice should you decide to add it to your Steam Library :-)

Europa Universalis 4 is one of the most successful grand strategy titles on the market, and it earns that reputation rightfully.
EU4 is a very complex strategy game, the shortest way to describe it would be "A country simulator". Although, like all strategy titles on the market; EU4's core mechanic is the combat system, but you also get a considerably well-made systems on all aspects of country administration, all shaped around the aforementioned combat system. Although the game is not difficult to play, it takes a long time to learn and an astonishingly longer time to master. In Europa, you choose a country in any time period between 1444 and 1821. You witness great empires crumble down, small nations being liberated only to dominate a whole continent, you feel the tensions between colonizer countries as they make their way to the Americas and the Indias. As you progress through time, you will notice that your country has evolved quite a lot - Perhaps not the way you would like it to. Perhaps, your greed took over you, making you conquer more than your neighbors would like, ending in a coalition war against you. Or maybe, your once-superior Asian military technology now has no chance against the rising European powers' armies. As you pay attention to every small detail in your lands from dealing with rebellious minorities to shaping your cities to provide a better trade income, your ruler will die and your dynasty might even end there. But worry not, unlike Crusader Kings 2, you do not play as a dynasty, you play as a country. And like all things, countries change. As the Karamanids, defeat the powerful Ottomans to re-establish the Sultanate of Rûm, or unite the Holy Roman Empire by slowly building up your authority. Hunt for valuable trade resources in foreign lands, or convert some heretics to get a more stable empire. All of this may -And will- happen, if you dare to play this addictive simulator. Should you get bored from this always up-to-date game, there is an incredibly large mod community to make sure you get the most out of your money.
While the price tag might scare some, you only need a few DLCs to experience the most - If not all - of the game. I would definitely recommend this game, and the Steam sales are the perfect times to start conquering!

Despite my dislike of modern military shooters and my added mental handicap when it comes to stealth gameplay - I really suck at stealth - I have a soft spot for any game that provides me with a good sniping experience. I mean the sniper is my favorite TF2 class and there's basically no realism about that, but I still enjoy it a lot.
So I obviously picked up the original "Sniper: Ghost Warrior", despite what I've heard. Thankfully I only paid €1 for it because it really wasn't all that good. It had to much faffing about in between the actual sniping and seemed to want to thrust in more close-combat sections way to often, so I never finished it. Because in addition to that, the enemy AI was terribly unforgiving and could spot me from ludicrous distances. Likewise, I picked up "Sniper Elite V2" when it was offered for free on Steam a couple of days ago. And similar to the first "Sniper: Ghost Warrior" it seemed way to concerned with having me get more into the action and as such, I lost interest really quickly. It didn't help that it looked terrible, even for the time, with shoddy textures, horrible animation quality, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ aesthetic, etc. The sniping was fun yes, but at the cost of having an empty world that failed to engage me, so I stopped playing a couple of hours in.
After that, I saw that Bundle Stars had "Sniper: Ghost Warrior 2" in a bundle over there, and even if it were the only game that piqued my interest in that particular bundle - which it wasn't - I could justify buying it for €3.66 instead of the full price of €20.
Let me begin with saying that this game isn't worth €20, for multiple reasons. For one, the single-player campaign is criminally short. It took me 5.2 hours according to Steam to get through the story, including my personal ham-handedness when it comes to stealth, so I assume better gamers will finish it even quicker than that. The story is really disjointed and makes the world feel really small. I mean it takes place in the Philippines, Sarajevo and Tibet and yet the main players are all the same 5 guys all the time, it's like this was conceived as a James Bond game instead of a realistic depiction of arms dealing. It's also one of those tired old military bravado revenge stories, because we always need something personal about it to justify going off protocol. And while the graphics aren't bad per se (and I'm by no means a graphics ♥♥♥♥♥), I've seen better, especially out of the CryEngine 3. Worth noting is that the graphics in the pre-rendered cut-scenes are substantially worse than the in-game graphics, which is quite a feat.
However, despite all those criticisms, I had fun playing it. Yes, it's horribly linear and bares little resemblance to what actual snipers have to do in real life, but here's the thing: I don't want my games to be recreations of life. I want my games to be escapism, and this provided me with what I sought for in a sniping game. It holds your hands a lot on the lower difficulties, but you can find a challenge here if you're looking for it. And for what it's worth, it really is committed to its theme of sniping and sneaking around. You can't absorb damage like in most other shooters and there isn't regenerating health. This is kind of an ambivalent point because for one it takes actual skill to get through the game, but on the other hand, it leads to a very tight level design that basically railroads you through if you need to use stealth. And with the aggressive linearity comes the heavy scripting of scenes that kill my immersion somewhat. I mean, there's an entire section where a cave system is collapsing around you and I never felt threatened, because a) I know it's a scripted sequence and b) my running speed is faster than the running speed of my AI partner.
Speaking of that AI partner, it really adds a lot to the game. Especially in comparison to "Sniper Elite V2" where you were just this lone wolf going around Berlin. Even if the dialogue is just terrible, it just makes the game more appealing to me and opens up some characterization. I mean it's not very realistic to have a spotter armed with a regular assault rifle being able to take out targets at the same distance and accuracy as me with my sniper rifle, but I'll gladly overlook that in favor of having a bit of dialogue in there, regardless of its quality.
The game doesn't seem to be too taxing, at least not on my machine. I cranked up all the settings to max and found that the game ran at 80-110 fps depending on locations, and this is with the CryEngine 3 so at least it's not badly optimized.
My final verdict on this one is that I can recommend it to fans of sniping gameplay, but only if you can find it at a heavy discount, because 20 bucks for 5 hours is way too much. I paid less than a dollar for it when I bought the bundle, and for that it's great value.

Hearts of Iron IV is a game that deserves a little extra attention. Let me explain.
After playing about a dozen campaigns as minor nations and major nations, usually Turkey (minor) and France (major) the finer details of exactly how strange this game is come to light. That is, it is very silly.
While your mileage may vary, the AI is in serious need of some kind of rework. For example, some of the major features of this game, the front-line and battle plan systems, lack any sort of internal logic. I can hear the dialouge in my head every time I right click to set the lines up;
ME: Set up a front line from Calais to Nice, please.
GENERAL: Didja hear that men?! Set up FIVE front lines and ONLY MAN THE LINE IN BELGIUM.
ME: No! Don't do that! Man the entire line.
GENERAL: MEN! Split the army into five parts and stick that tank division DIRECTLY ON THE BORDER. Because F*** that guy in particular. (tanks have low HP and defensive qualities)
ME:
GENERAL: And don't mind that one province minor (Luxembourg), you don't need to fortify that.
ME: *Is blitzkreig'd in a week through Luxembourg*
While this may seem like nit-picking, it really isn't. This is a feature used more frequently than any other in the game if you don't like micro-managing literally hundreds of divisions for hours.
And, sure, you COULD set up dozens of armies (my preferred method) and dozens of plans (that sweet combat bonus) and dozens of lines, orders and other things to fill your UI. You could, and WILL do this, or you will end up surrounded because you didnt fortify one province.
This would all be well and good. But this isn't even scratching the surface of the game. In fact, this is one small set of gripes on one part of the game. We haven't gotten into air combat where notifications are sparse and unhelpful, naval invasions that are either a joke or a slaughterhouse (but rarely succeed), and all of the tiresome, rediculous decisions the AI makes. For example, the Soviets changing their mind about an invasion of Germany (at war, mind you) and moving their entire army to starve in Africa instead. Or being forced to invade Japan navally because my allies won't let me use their air bases for paratroopers (I waited TWO YEARS). Or occupying territory for that very ally instead of for myself because his one unit was there first.
I could go on for...well, about a hundred and thirty hours. But I won't. Suffice to say, this game is silly.
Tl;Dr Wait a year for patches and DLC. And if the reviews are negitive, buy something else.

This review comes from someone who actually never played Dark Souls. Any of them. I might get into it after this, though.
That said, it's nearly impossible to not see the similarities just from what I've heard and seen of the Souls series prior. You get to create your hero, select class & looks, and then you're thrown in head first into a fight you cannot win and die horribly.
With that out of the way, the game begins for real. In a nutshell this is a 2D platforming action game where you navigate dank labyrinths while slashing/crushing/burningg/stabbing the enemies in your path. Along the way there are plenty of treasure and secret areas, spread out in a metroidvania-like pattern where some are accessible right away, and others locked behind an ability barrier.
The island which the game plays out on is seperated into differently themed areas, all of which have 1-2 bosses guarding the exits to the next. Each area usually have more than one exit, and several shortcuts to the others, unlocking the paths to earlier areas as you explore, so the way you progress through the game can vary. If you find a particular boss too hard, there's nothing stopping you from turning back and trying another one in a different area instead.
All the while you're exploring the island you'll accumulate Salt, the games "experience currency". Salt is used for levelling up (via the Tree of Skill, a system a bit similar to the sphere grid of Final Fantasy 10), as well as weapon and armor upgrades. Gold will be dropped by enemies as well, and is used for buying new items, as well as being deducted as a penalty for dying.
Speaking of dying, you'll be doing a lot of it. The platforming the later stages of the game can be a bit messy, and the bosses throughout the game are very deadly indeed. Dying means that all your salt will be lost and a percentage of your cash as well. However, the salt is absorbed by the enemy that killed you and by returning there you have a chance to reclaim it by killing him in turn. Should you die again before that, however, the salt is gone for good. Bosses have a containment threshold in their HP bars which you need to wear them down past for them to release the salt they've stolen, which means that even if you lose a huge chunk to a hard boss you don't have to actually kill him to get it back, hurting him to about 1/3:rd HP is enough, and you can quickly warp back to safety with the goods.
What will keep you playing this one is the allure of levelling up and growing more powerful, locating secret treasure, as well as finding new and more imposing bosses to conquer. The atmosphere of the game is a bit too oppressive sometimes, I feel, with the dark caves giving way to even more dark caves in the next area after that, even if some variety does exist (Dome of the Forgotten was great).
Like in the Dark Souls series you will find player-made messages strewn about the island in the form of bottled letters. Most are helpful, some atmospheric, and others just try to mess with you. You can write your own using a set of pre-written words to try and warm your fellow players of impending damge, clues to help them, or directions to secrets.
Or you can just trick them into jumping of a cliff.
Yeah, I fell for that. Pun not intended -.-
All in all, it's a fun game with visceral combat, RPG-elements and metroidvania-like exploration. You can use keyboard+mouse or a controller, whatever you prefer. Both are prefectly viable. I completed it with Kb+M without any control issues. The levels are well designed and the bosses hard, but all have weaknesses you can exploit (both elemental  and clearly telegraphed moves). With the exception of one of them, they're all imposing but fair (Curse you,  Disemboweled Husk! *raises fist*)
If you're into platformers and Action-RPGs, you definitely should check this one out.

I'm a big Souls nut, everybody knows that.
I've spent countless hours on the series as a whole, strarting with Demon's and ending with... Bloodbourne.
I couldn't play DS3, not only because my system couldn't play it anymore without dying on me, but it also was a step back after DS2, and just not as fun for me as it was before.
I needed a fix, and fast.
And i found it in Salt & Sanctuary.
Let me get it straight: i love Ska Studios, always loved.
I adore their recognizable art design - dark, gruesome, and somewhat cartoony.
And this game has it too, but it also has every good aspect that Souls had.
But it's not a ripoff, oh now.
This game has enough of it's own content to NOT be considerent a ripoff.
First of all, this game has covenants too, yes, but now they're called Creeds and they're one of the basis of gameplay.
You see, every Creed has it's own special things and specializes in different things.
Every covenant even has their own replenishable healing items which act differently, and i'm not even talking about abillity to get into your posession through covenant leader such things as Stamina recoverers, throwable items and buff items, which all replenish when visiting the Sanctuary (but only of your own creed, every other creed's sanctuary will have the items that you may got while working for them).
Or, what about combat?
It's much more awesome than in Souls.
Not only you can do secret COMBOS with almost any weapons, it also has two different ways of parrying (traditional and bloodborne method that actually now works with crossbows too) AND you can attack in air.
Leveling Up became much more complicated. Much. More.
With every level you now get a Pearl that you can use to get nods in you Skill tree. Each nod has something different, like raising your one stat by one point, up to 3 on one node, or leveling up your specialty in, for example, whips, which also raises your agility by some points. Yes, now you don't need stats to wield someithng, but you need to be more leveled in that category, which even includes armor. I don't really like that much, but it's interesting, at least it's different from souls.
Everything in the skill tree, even the ammount of healing items you can carry (you can also raise them at Creed's leader, though, but only for a creed).
Also, i could say that this game is really a metroidvania, it even has abillities which needed for progression, like wall jump. Which is cool, i like that.
But the most important part in this game for me was it's lore, world, plot, all that.
I won't say much but i'm really, really interested in this world. I want to know more. About the island, about the world, about salt, about everything.
This game is my favourite "Souls" game right now, and probalby will be forever.
I'm deeply in love with it, and i can not recommend it enough.
Good work, Ska Studios.
p.s. WHERE'S THE DISHWASHER? I WAS WAITING FOR IT FOR SEVERAL YEARS NOW SINCE THAT INCIDENT HAPPENED, WHERE IS IT?!

TL:DR
Holy crap. Rarely do I come across a game this amazing (especially now that Steam is one step up from Google Play), and I've played thousands of games in my 35 years. Its a 2d Metroidvania RPG. If you dont know what that means, go back to gamer school cuz I don't have time to explain it here. This game is awesome, period. Ive been playing for 4 hours at this time, and I feel like I've barely scratched the surface of what this game offers.
_________________________________________________________________
Its amazing, probably one of if not the best Metroidvanias I've ever played. Chars are very customizable, theres plenty of weapons, armor, and magic to choose from. And each item has an awesome description in the inventory. I'm a sucker for world-building like that.  You even get to choose a god, which affects certain things. You can change your god too, but your first god wont like that unless you get forgiven. The graphics beautifully are done in a really unique hand drawn style, not quite standard cell shaded and they are f'n perfect for the tone and setting. The game's tone is pretty dark. Lots of blood splatting out, undead and gross monsters shambling about, gore, dead bodies and so on.
Char development is done skill tree style (more like skill web), Its pretty fluid - you can make many different pure builds, hybrid builds, or jack of all trades build work. You can cosmetically customise your char when you start out too, which is awesome as most Metroidvanias have a set protagonist. Theres many different classes to pick from when you start, but that only sets your start - like I said the skill tree is really fluid. Want a thief that uses magic? Go for it. A Paladin that doesnt use heavy armor but relies on speed? Yep. Anything is possible. Of course, some builds are easier to play than others - theres plenty of guides out there to assist with builds if youre overwhelmed. But the game is balanced enough that as long as you understand the base mechanics, you should be able to make any build work
I was really surprised that its a PS4 port, because it actually works - no bugs, lags, glitches or anything so far that you typically find in ports. The controls are well done, and both K+M & controller are fully customizable (THANK YOU DEVS! I dont have to rant about people with physical disabilities and non mappable controllers in this review!). Theres a slight annoyance lining up your char to pick something up or go down a ladder on rare occasions, but its so very minor that it really isnt a big deal. Other the controls are pretty well done, although theres no way to interrupt an attack/roll/etc once you start, so youre committed and there appears to be a slight (intentional)  lag when using a healing potion which can really suck with a monster in your face. But you'll get the timing down pretty fast. You'll need it.
Dying is handled decently, as some areas and battles can be difficult. Theres "sanctuaries" (save points/rooms) and when you die, the enemy takes your salt (xp) and you lose some gold. Go get your salt back by killing the enemy, and youre good as new, minus a little gold.
If you say you like Metroidvanias, theres no way your library can be complete without this game.

This is a great entry point for someone wanting to try a "hard" game.
It's almost impossible to get into any discussion about this game without the phrase "2D Dark Souls" coming up, and with good reason.  The bottom line is that this is a very addicting, 'hard' game that feels like Dark Souls and Castlevania had a metroidvania love child.
Hopefully without gushing too much..
Pros:
-Rewarding gameplay that feels good once you get the hang of it
-Tight controls, this game is all about timing and strategy, not button mashing.  There are combos, to a point, and when you execute one perfectly and the monster explodes into a blood stain, it's some of the best 2D combat ever.
-The art direction in this game is perfect.  The island, the characters, the weapons.. everything comes together to deliver a beautifuly modern 2D experience that is cohesive, while still delivering varied locales on the island.
-The story, it's there, and it's a good one, but it's very much not in your face and you can breeze right by it if you choose..  Don't.  Talk to everyone, seek out new areas and people, exhaust all conversation trees, and talk to the scarecrow. Always.
-The sphere-grid skill tree and leveling system in this game is deep and when you combine that with New Game+ can produce some pretty interesting hybrid builds.
-You will get frustrated, and you will get mad, and you will want to keep playing this game regardless.
-Pumpkin Helm
Cons:
-Not really a con because it's more just part of the genre, but can scare away someone used to having a game hold their hand (If this is you I'm describing, push forward and keep trying even after seeing "Obliterated" splash across your screen dozens of times..it happens.. and maybe switch to a strength build using 2h when you can.  2H hammers in this game are a license to make monsters explode. You can also grind up salt from monsters and level up at a santuary a bunch if a boss is just too much for you)
-An in-game indication of soft cap breakpoints on skill-tree points/ more in depth weapon scaling info would be helpful, but thankfully there is an extremely good Salt and Sanctuary wiki with a lot of this information.  Same goes for boss weaknesses, although those are sometimes indicated on message bottles in-game.
-A map of discovered areas would be nice at some point in the game.

Arma Tactics is a very basic turn based strategy game where you command a small squad of men. Similiar to XCOM, Jagged Alliance 2, or stuff like that.
Its okay its the core design of a possibly good and deep game here but the only problem its not deep. If you play the first mission the rest are basically the same thing over and over. There are only 3 weapons, LMB, AR, and Sniper rifle, and affording the sniper is a pain in the butt because grenades and medkits. You can upgrade your squad members but you need to exit to the main menu then go back into the game. Its idiotic and on top of that the upgrades don't make a huge diffrence so its like why bother? And unless you explore the menu you would probably never know you could even upgrade them.
Its extremely basic and would be great as a pick up and play...mobile...game....on android....iOS
WELL WHAT DO YOU KNOW. Thats what it is. Unfortunately its a game thats main focus was a mobile market. So pick up and play was what they wanted. And since most people don't want a hardcore deep game while on the train or waiting room its fairly basic like solitaire or checkers. So if I had played this on a mobile setting I would have probably enjoyed it though I find it strange that it has no PSVita port or WiiU or even a home console version.
The AI is nothing special and will just throw men at you most the time so its relatively easy. The only challenge comes from when your men keep missing over and over or when AI just thrown at you en masse to the point it just makes you lose man after man because you simply can't handle the amount its throwing at you.
Its not bad but theres just not much content here. Thers nothing really to say about it I guess. They could have gone buckwild and added a metric done of content like in Arma 2 comparatively.
But what is bad I have noticed is that sometimes enemies can shoot you through walls or ceilings which is just plain bullcrap. Aswell at one point I was detected while trying to do a stealth mission and a squad mate got wounded when shot through a window. Except it was one of those type of windows game designers put in a map or area to fill up space and you cant see through because the glass is blocked with newspapers or some crap. In any other game you would expect that window to be basically just a painting on the wall in terms of gameplay. But instead the AI can see and shoot through it but you cant! Shooting through walls gets really annoying but this is just idiotic.  Sometimes grenades will hit something in the air you can't seen and not go where you want them to at all, and much more annoyingly your well trained and well armed American soldeirs will miss a shot directly in front of them while Jihadis mess them up in all kinds of Mujah ways. This randomness can really drain you from wanting to play the game along with casually enraging you.
So to sum this up, its just okay. Not worth much more than $5 if you want to play it on a stationary system but a worthy diversion if you want to blow 20 to 30 minutes waiting for something. But if you want something more deep than a very bare bones TBS there are better games for you such as Expeditions: Conquistador or either of the ones mentioned at the start. If you have a mobile device I would atleast consider buying this game along with GTA Vice City and Max Payne 1 (both on Android market).
Its really not that fun though unless you play it in short spurts to waste time.

People who are complaining about their progress being reset are ignoring that TRS completely changed the way character progression works now. Before it was you have a challenge for each of a characters abilities divided into three tiers. You progress to the next tiers by completing all three weapon challenges of the current tier. Each tier gave a specific bonus to the weapon, like extra damage or capacity. Player level progress unlocked different perks, of which you could equip one to your character at the start of the game to give a boost to some aspect of your hunter or monster.
Both of these systems have been changed. Now characters have their own individual levels, and leveling up a character unlocks/upgrades perks for free instead of spending ingame currency on them. These parks you will then have access to on every other hunter/monster. The only thing that they kept somewhat the same was character specific cosmetic items for your player icon. It's impossible to accurately tranfser character progression from the old format to the new one because it's impossible to tell how long it took to do the weapon challenges. To give an idea, I had characters who I didn't max out after playing them for 10+ hours, and others that I had to max after playing them for less than 5. It all depended on what the challenges were.
